The Root Manual of Noble Mañjuśrī. (Second Part.
Now begins the twenty-third detailed chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists in the extensive ritual manual of your own [teachings] a chapter titled 'The Exposition of the Enumeration of Sounds. Listen well and attend to it thoroughly."
I shall speak.

When this had been said, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and, bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times.

Having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and risen, he spoke thus: "It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would explain the Dharma discourse named 'The Instruction on the Calculation of Sound-Knowledge. Having heard it, all beings who have entered into the practice of mantras will possess the knowledge of the calculation of all sounds."
It will bring about the arising of benefit and the bringing of happiness for all sentient beings who have entered into the practice of all mantras,
as well as the knowledge that transcends the calculation of all sounds; therefore, may the Blessed One, desiring their welfare and seeking their benefit, speak it for the sake of all sentient beings.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you consider this matter—the perfection of the welfare of all sentient beings—to be worthy of being set forth to the Tathāgata. Therefore, listen, Mañjuśrī, and I shall explain it to you."
Then Mañjuśrī, having been granted permission by the Blessed One, rose from there and sat down upon his own seat to hear the Dharma, gazing intently at the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities with his fixed gaze, entered the samādhi called "the motionless state that transcends all calculation of sound.
As soon as the Blessed One had entered this samādhi,
Blue, yellow, white, crimson, crystal-colored, and other such hues emerged as great masses of light, networks of rays,
and circles of radiance; having emerged, they illuminated all world-systems and the dwellings of all sentient beings with a vast splendor on every side.

Having illuminated all the hells, the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and the world of Yama, as well as the abodes of the asuras, and having caused the cessation of great painful sensations, [they returned] once again to the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Their bodies vanished.
Having fully awakened all sentient beings, the Blessed One spoke thus: "Now, this knowledge that understands sounds is to be mastered as it is honored for its meaning and the Dharma;
and the Knower of the World spoke sweet words regarding even the calculation [of syllables]."
The word is to be understood from its base; the word is well-adorned by its suffix.
Through that [base], it becomes extensively expanded, ending in an affix and arising from verbal action.
The indicative mark (liṅga) is to be known through words; there is no indicative mark devoid of words.
Through the manifestation of both word and indicative mark, the purposes of dharma and artha are accomplished.
This is not a manifold; neither is the word joined to the cognition, nor the cognition joined to the word.
That entity which arises from the word and the cognition is the word that joins with the true meaning.
Conditionality should be understood as causality; a condition is the arising from a cause.
When there is that condition, which is the cause, it manifests through the application of activity.
Indeed, that which is called *dhāraṇā* (the root) is the basis, while the *pratyaya* (suffix) is the indicator;
through the conjunction of root and suffix, a word becomes the unifier of both meaning and purpose.
The word is not to be known through its meaning, nor is the meaning sought from the word;
rather, that word is designated as such by those who know the rules of grammar through its connection with the cognition of the meaning.
The elements were proclaimed in many ways, and the conditions depend upon them;
depending on those excellent supports, the sounds then resounded.
That knowledge of words by which mantras are spoken according to their true meaning—
one should not understand that [meaning] merely through the sounds of the words, without the underlying realizations of the mantras.
Just as [seeds] do not sprout without conditions and a support, so too mantras do not arise;
one should not seek everywhere for auspicious mantras that lack such conditions.
Know that to be neither a conjunction nor the accepted meaning of a word or sentence, which is empty of the cognition of objects and devoid of the [eighteen] elements.
255) No movement is indicated in the *liṅga*, for it is born from causes, conditions, and the elements (*dhātu*).
Likewise, accomplishment is joined with the horse; the *liṅga* is joined with the purpose of the Dharma.
A sentence is a word-unit culminating in an action directed toward a specific destination;
beyond this, one who would constantly utter speech in a word merely for the sake of its variegated beauty [is a fool].

The accomplishment of the goal does not arise from the mere sound; rather, it is applied to the signs themselves. The word "mūrdhaja" (born of the head) is declared, adorned with the meaning of the syllable *huṃ*.
Everything depends upon conditions and relies upon a basis;
yet, when the palate and lips produce speech, they are dependent on another—the manifestation of the basis.
The object of knowledge is approached through tranquility by means of unerring reasoning;
likewise, the intellect—vast and adorned with meaning—is established in reality.

The element (dhātu) effects the conjunction, marked by the meaning of the suffix; [the sounds] ending in 'da' are produced by the palate, those ending in 'ta' by the lips, and after that, the sound 'śa' is produced by the palate.

Through the power of the mantras, understand that the straight-tusked one [the elephant] moves everywhere throughout the worlds— emitting [light], active within the elements, and reaching as far as the very limits of the physical basis.
The suffixes born from verbal roots and primary affixes are always considered to have movement as their very essence;
both of these are traditionally held to be the basis for the production of words.
Having analyzed in many ways the mantras that rely upon the scriptures of true reality,
one sees that these sounds and mantras arise everywhere from the source of grammatical derivation.
The one honored [Goddess] discerns the objects of knowledge;
likewise, through the combination of one and two, there is the seventh meaning consisting of the number three.
It should be known that for human beings, the number eight is taught as being in addition to the innumerable.
They say that the support (*ādhāra*) is to be known in the worship of the meaning of mantra and tantra;
it is prescribed by rule in the seventh [chapter] regarding the attainment of mantras for those who recite them.
The seventh [topic] should be understood according to its sevenfold meaning;
one should apply the various explanations of sequence to the seven meanings of the seventh.
Sixty-six groups of mantras are proclaimed, as well as their constituent parts;
indeed, due to the relationship of the mantras, two types of indicative marks (liṅga) are applied.
256) Its transformation is said to be manifold, consisting of six types.
One should employ the sixth among women who possess the *liṅga* within the eight mantras.
The five types of mantras are those that strive for the fivefold purpose;
the meaning of the neuter gender mantra is said to be devoid of the purposes of *dharma* and *artha*.
Those mantras that have issued forth there, joined for the purpose of extraction,
are all remembered as life-takers;
they issue from the lips and teeth through conjunction with the sound of the head (the letter *m*).
Those here by whom the tongue is suppressed, who obstruct the vital breaths of sound,
and who are stilled through equal cognition— they are joined with the element of tranquility.
One should apply this method to those words ending in the suffix *as* which have entered [the system];
for those verbal roots whose purpose is nourishment (*puṣṭi*) are words beautifully adorned by the meaning of suffixes.
Those others who have been proclaimed by dividing them according to their respective places are known as being employed in rites for nourishment and in matters of withdrawal.
Nourished by words and syllables, that element blossoms clearly;
likewise, the mantras, which possess masculine gender, are endowed with great power and meaning.
The syllable adorned with the fourth [vowel] and the two [nasal] divisions is indeed declared at the beginning of the *pavarga* group; it is the most excellent and accomplishes all rites.
Born from the combination of the letter *ra* and the suffix *pra*, followed by the beautiful letter *u*;
the central mark is the *visarga*, and the letter *bha* is adorned with motion.
They know that speech is the most excellent means for accomplishing all actions and purposes,
when it is applied to a bodhisattva established on the certain and ultimate path.
They call this the unsurpassed sound, the path that is the way to great enlightenment;
by reciting which, a human being shall swiftly accomplish all mantras.
Therefore, the fifth meaning is declared to be marked by a single syllable;
those who know always recognize that which is born from the end [of the row] as belonging to the *pa*-group, ending with the letter *ma*.
Human beings call the second [source] "Sound," the foremost in the world;
yet it is not merely a combination of sounds, nor is it adorned by the end of creation.
257) She was born as the preeminent mantra, the most excellent, born from the source of sound;
she is characterized as the Buddha, the supreme teacher of the world, the *chatra* and *uṣṇīṣa*.
O Teacher of the World, the triad has been taught before the group of *ta*-letters;
for these mantras are everywhere foremost, accompanied by sound, and honored by the world.
That which ends in the vowel 'a', whose meaning is analyzed, which is awakened by the visarga,
which has a middle mark (*madhyaliṅga*), which ends with sound, and whose end is adorned with sound.
They know that sound to be the supreme mantra worshipped by the gods—
those who are employed in the fifth sense-object, which arises from calculation in the context of number.
For these, having the fifth [vowel] as their division, possess the meaning of the case-ending *sup* with the fifth;
these mantras are said to be infinite, spoken by the infinite Victors.
The mantras are the uṣṇīṣas, the hair upon the head of the Jina;
they should be known as infinite, the knowers of sound, and sounds that bring about the perfection of all aims. A mantra endowed with sixty-four [qualities] is joined with sound.
That sound is the most excellent of all, which is the fourfold pada in the pavarga;
the fourfold conjunctions of the letter *m* are employed at the end.
Those with sounds are indeed the primary mantras; they are known as "parasols" (chatra) because they accomplish one's purpose.
This is declared to be the fourth enumeration; these are the case-endings born from the source of sound.
The mantras intended for the purpose of giving, which have attained a dual gender as their basis,
are taught by the Lotus-Born One for the sake of nourishment and the attainment of wealth and purpose.
The fourth [chapter] describes the mantras employed in four ways:
the words consisting of four syllables, the head-consonants (mūrdhan), the sibilants (ūṣman), and the palatals (tālu).
It has been explained in the third chapter on the designation of sounds;
one should apply it for the purpose of expansion regarding the clear elements, and then apply it to the suffix and the gender.
The sound that exists at the beginning and at the end is the sound honored by the world;
it is the excellent mantra known as the primary, properly applied.
That sound is indeed called Puṣṭinī, arising from Abdaketu;
it ends with *tra*, is the union of the three, and its middle portion is highly praised.
258) That word is the foremost among those prevalent in the world, always preeminent in its meaning;
one should employ it at all times in accordance with the root and in its proper sense.
Then he chose Uṣas as his wife; learn of her who was endowed with sweet syllables and joined with the sound "ut" in the masculine.
That sound, the foremost in the world, is called the supreme mantra;
among the four [vowels], that syllable is to be avoided, as it is proclaimed to belong to the second [vowel].
This should be known as the supreme teaching spoken by the Buddha for the purpose of pacification;
it is the third, the labial *ūṣman*, devoid of any other objective condition.
Always joined with the signs of nourishment and conjoined with the end of the *bhū* element,
with the upward sign likewise rotated— that is the mantra spoken by the Buddha.
Regarding the third [category], the meaning of the two words *bhūti* and *saśabda* depends upon their grammatical case ending;
the first is to be understood as "prosperity" (*varṇataḥ*), while the latter arises from "peaceful" (*śāntika*) and "nourishing" (*pauṣṭika*) rites.
The second [case] is declared for the object (karman), and likewise the third for the instrument (karaṇa);
both of these case-endings are to be known, and this mantra-king is remembered as being accompanied by the word "sa" (he/that).
They say that the first [action] belongs to the agent who is independent in the two [activities];
likewise, the Lords of Mantra are beneficial in the mantra of the Conqueror, the Lotus, and the Vajra.
In the [section on] *hita*, all words ending in case-suffixes as well as those derived from verbal roots and ending in suffixes are to be understood.
The meaning should be understood through its characteristic signs; it arises from the sentence and from the words.
The mantras are said to be primarily those born from the Victors, the lords of the gods.
The mantras of the Jina and Padma families, as well as those of the Vajrin and the worldly ones,
grasp the transition in order to maintain the meaningful elements.

The mantras, indicated by the acute and grave accents, are to be understood as the means for accomplishing the intended purpose; they are contained within their characteristic marks, and having offered oblations in the middle, they are likewise raised up.
One should apply that sound which is without beginning or end, as well as those mantras;
they end with *nī*, end with *kala*, are joined with the letter *ra*, and are extensive.
That which is heard through the gender and phonetic qualities situated between the words of the subject matter [is to be applied].
259) One should quickly employ that *liṅga* (grammatical gender marker) endowed with the *svarita* accent within mantras;
it is applied to the preceding [elements], the subsequent bases (*anupada*), and the powers of temporal action (*kālakriyā*).
That meaning which arises from the middle of the two feet is renowned as "sound" (śabda);
therefore, that beautiful form described by its form is the meaning to be fully understood.
This mantra spoken by the Buddha is for the sake of the fruit and the supreme accomplishment;
it is proclaimed according to the time and according to its intrinsic nature as being devoid of intrinsic nature.
Their speech was tranquil, having worn away all impurities; it was adorned with the meaning of the Dharma, supremely beneficial, peaceful, meaningful, syllable-perfect, and auspicious.
That which is to be known by practitioners as the mantra spoken by the Buddha is praised;
this is the single-syllable Brahman, adorned with the meaning of the word "Oṃ."
He should be known as embodied, pure, praiseworthy, and bringing auspiciousness;
indeed, he is said to be the accomplisher of welfare, laudable, and endowed with blessings.
That mantra has been declared by the Lords of the World as preeminent;
it possesses various meanings and primary words, and likewise consists of supreme words beyond others.
That sound is the excellence of the substratum, arising through the sequence of action and time;
those mantras from the Solar Lineage are adorned with the meanings of radiant words.
The mantras, whether designated as gentle or fierce, blaze within the fire when properly applied;
they are always beautiful in form, possess a gentle mind, and are characterized by the names of the lunar mansions.
The mantras arisen in the moon are uttered through sounds produced from lunar syllables;
they are declared to be pure and stainless, consisting of single-syllable letters that are supreme.
Renowned as being beyond measure, of beautiful color, and possessed of great supernatural power,
these Uṣṇīṣa mantras are declared by the sons of the Jinas to be the most excellent.
The various applications of yoga remain like the satisfaction derived from yoga;
they are ever serene and pure, as taught by the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
The mantra of the two Pratyekabuddhas is praised for rites of pacification;
these mantras, ending with "svāhā," are honored by the meaning of the syllable "oṃ."
260) That mantra, which arises from the Pratyekabuddhas, is designated as "one" or "two" for all rites; it should always be employed for the sake of excellence alone.
It should be known that the end is conjoined with the beginning; the middle is between the beginning and the end.
The mantras possess many signs, and the syllables contain the meaning of many mantras.
Indeed, these elements are known in many ways as ending in the letter *ṣa*;
the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of those mantras lies in the first letter of the *ta*-group.
Those born from the lotus-mantra should first strike the end of the syllable *ra*;
O Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, save these suffering beings!
She is indeed the foremost Tārā, for her mantras are infinite;
in the *ture* mantra, between the sounds *tvaryāccha*, the labial class (*pavarga*) is remembered as Māmakī.
In the labial class (pavarga) is the goddess renowned as Kulamātā, the accomplisher of goals;
she is the goddess Ṣaṇḍaravāsinī, white-marked for the sake of well-known purposes.
Tārā was previously described; one should employ her for the sake of protection.
A warrior abounding in the letter *la* [should use] that which ends with the word *yodha*, arising from those three.
The sound produced from the limbs of the Victor is called the goddess Locanā;
one should apply this sound, which consists of the syllables of meaning, as the accomplishment in all mantras.
This [practice], renowned throughout the families of the Victors, Vajras,
and Lotuses, should be employed at the very beginning of all mantras for the sake of pacification.
Locanā is renowned on earth; therein, the foremost mantra is to be accomplished.
Since all this is to be known, one should apply it to the initial mantras.
For the sake of the success of mantras and for the purpose of self-protection,
that goddess Jinalocanā should be known as universally successful in every respect.
Mantras, possessing manifold forms,
always resound within the letters at the beginning, the middle, and among the sixty-four syllables.
One should employ mantras and tantras everywhere among all the classes;
and in all cases at the beginning, the *tavarga* (the dental class) belongs to those two classes.
261) One should employ all three types of those declared as peaceful.
From the letter *ta* among the letters of the *prakṛti*, all those ending in *la* are born from every womb.
Those are the *pauṣṭika* syllables, and others are *abhicāruka*;
furthermore, they should be known as threefold: *krūra*, *śāntika*, and *pauṣṭika*.
Thus those three types are indeed threefold, for they have been described as three times three;
those infinite ones, moreover, are again threefold through their association with yoga.
Know that the gentle syllable leads to peace; one should separate it from that [context].
For some syllables are bestowers of boons, while others are middling and serve as causes for nourishment.
One should know the supreme syllable ending in *ha* to be fierce, causing evil, and most excellent;
thus it is adorned with these applications and words as well.
Know that the syllables are indeed infinite, and the deities of the mantras are infinite;
in this way, by means of this yoga, one should apply the infinite mantras.
They know that king of mantras to be the male essence that accomplishes all aims;
that syllable which is joined with the letter *e* is the sound adorned by mantra.
They know that mantra to be neuter; one should employ it in intermediate rites. That syllable which is accompanied by the letter *i* exists as the mantra and is thus proclaimed.
That woman is well-known in the mantras for minor rites;
all of them are further divided into three types here, adorned with various words.
One should employ that [mantra], which is threefold and of three types, in all ritual actions.
That which is designated as masculine, the Person (puruṣa), is considered by all to be the ultimate goal.
One should know that as the *puruṣa-mantra* (masculine mantra) and employ it in all rites;
that mantra which is in the neuter gender, know that to be *napuṃsaka* (neuter).
One should perform [this] in all rites for the arising of all happiness and well-being.
Know that whatever mantra has a feminine designation is always a woman.
One should always employ even those who perform all types of work in the protection [of the mantra];
for mantras are the performers of infinite actions, possessing infinite purposes, and being the source of all sounds.
262) However, various [mantras] primarily consisting of sound, joined with the mantras of diverse tantras—
if one practices in that very way, the mantras will quickly be accomplished without effort.
The knowledge of sound has been explained as the means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras;
know that, O gods, it was taught out of a desire for the welfare of those who recite them.
Through the application of this expansion, it is said to extend up to a hundred [syllables].
Understand that twenty-five thousand multiplied by ten is one hundred thousand;
the number consisting of ten thousand is proclaimed as an *ayuta*.
Ten times ten thousand (ayuta) is likewise always [called] a prayuta; a hundred thousand is called a lakṣa;
a thousand lakṣas is a koṭi; the place after that is known as an arbuda.
Ten arbudas are to be known as nirbuda, and beyond that is samudra;
ten times another is to be known as sāgara, which is applied to ten times its own value.
One should know Akṣobhya in the next [tithi], and Niḥkṣobhya in the one after that;
the wise proclaim Sarvavivāha as the Devarāja.
Merchants say that when it exceeds ten digits, it is called a *khaḍga*;
the minister knows that as a *nikhaḍga*, and also a *khaḍgin* as a *nikhaḍga*.
Beyond that is indeed the Śaṅkha; its calculation is beyond even that.
That must be known by me as calculated, being the final stage of the Mahāmāyā.
Those mortals who know the incalculable [number] are other than those born of divine origin;
all of them are multiplied by five and joined with ten and a half.
Beyond that, what is possible and even what is impossible and difficult to conquer can indeed be achieved;
when one is honored and established in the proper place, the wise know this to be the "station of vision."
Then there is the superior and inferior [knowledge] born from infinite and endless wombs;
beyond that is the knowledge of the Buddhas, as well as that of the Śrāvakas and the Pratyekabuddhas (Khaḍgins).
The sons of the Buddha are great-souled ones, and even those gods who know reality;
for their destinies are infinite, yet their counting is in the highest station.
263) The station of those possessing infinite knowledge is not here for those who dwell upon the surface of the earth;
rather, that station has been described in calculation by the ministers who are experts in calculation.
For those engaged in the accomplishment of mantras,
the application [of the breath] at the time of recitation should be known as the standard for calculation, for the purpose of the mantra-recitation.
Or rather, for those who recite the meaning according to the prescribed rule, the measure of grasping the number is established;
one whose mantra is perfected may enter the Vindhya mountains, while one who has attained success brings benefit even in a cow-pen.
Likewise, one who has mastered the mantra should always go to the Himalayan mountain;
for that embodied being who has mastered the mantra, movement is as he desires.
If the minister were to go to the Himalaya for the sake of recitation,
he would not overcome the unbearable army nor the coolness of all dualities.
The attainment of the desired result is declared to be achieved with little effort and little exertion;
[one should seek it] on the slopes and ridges of the Vindhya mountains, which abound in many flowers and fruits.
He sent him to the Vindhya mountain for the purpose of properly reciting the mantra;
therefore, the Vindhya was always designated as the place for prior service on account of the recitation.
Therefore, one should know that success is attained in the mountain caves of the Vindhya range;
on the southern side of the Gaṅgā, one should apply all [practices] within the Vindhyas.
One should point out the Himavat mountain in the northern region;
from there, one should accomplish mantras as desired, according to the pure instructions.
The Siddha goes to the Himalayas; the Siddha [goes] to the slopes of the Vindhya mountains;
[he dwells] in mountain caves and along their banks, in dwellings and abodes within the caves.
Whether on the bank of the lord of rivers or constantly upon its shores,
one should accomplish the mantras everywhere, for they are beneficial and bring about satisfaction.

Thus concludes the twenty-first chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction of the names and the calculation of the knowledge of sounds, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avataṃsaka*.
264) Now follows the twenty-fourth detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, [spoke] regarding all the lunar mansions, planets, stars, and luminaries...
He addressed all those of great supernatural power who were most eminent, encompassing all world-systems and situated in every direction: "Listen, O noble ones!
You must explain your own words regarding the power and influence of all the planets and constellations."

May you accomplish all the purposes of mantra-activities! In this King of Ritual Manuals, within the teaching of Mañjughoṣa, may you apply yourselves with zeal toward attaining accomplishment here, as well as toward other King of Ritual Manuals in the future. May you do so!
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni,
for the sake of all sentient beings and for the sake of a single purpose, [taught] the entire conduct of the planets; and the purpose of the mantras was accomplished for all those who recite them.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā.
Indeed, these three types of lunar mansions are marked by the planet Mars;
they are declared to belong to the sign of Aries, and no success is achieved in them.
The highest, middling, and even the lowest success is seen to be attained;
however, one who is obstructed by malefic planets should not proceed on any path whatsoever.
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, and Ārdrā are said to be the lunar mansions; Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Aśleṣā are likewise proclaimed.
Both Maghā and Phalgunī, as well as Hasta and Citrā;
likewise Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla.
The two Āṣāḍhas are auspicious and highly praised, beneficial for those who recite mantras;
the constellations Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭhā are for cruel rites.
Both the constellations Śatabhiṣaj and Bhadrapadā are causes for success;
one born under Revatī becomes illustrious, skilled in battle, and wise.
The remaining principal lunar mansions do not arise in this lowest age;
however, Abhijit and Sucarita are proclaimed as meritorious for the attainment of success.
Tiṣya, Upapada, Kaniṣṭha,
Niṣṭha, Bhūta, Satya, Loka, and Āloka are likewise proclaimed.
265) Aniruddha bestows enjoyment and auspiciousness, while Ruddha indeed [bestows] restraint;
Yaśoda is the king who is the sovereign of splendor, and likewise the world itself.
The constellations are said to be manifold, numbering sixty-four thousand;
yet their power does not manifest in this time, this lowest of ages.
This has been taught solely for the sake of knowledge in the *Kalparāja* that brings about the arising of bliss;
for at that time, in the Kṛtayuga, beings indeed possessed the power of self-origination (*svayambhū*).
All were capable of traveling through the sky and were free from old age and death;
at this time, there were no constellations, no sun or moon, and no stars.
In the beginning of time, during that most excellent age, there were neither gods nor asuras in the world;
indeed, there was no designation, nor lineage, nor lunar day, nor birth-horoscope.
There is no fasting, nor indeed mantras, nor any auspicious or inauspicious ritual action;
these beings roam according to their own will, with neither food to be eaten nor one who eats.
For these beings are indeed pure, free from affliction, and equal in many ways;
it is only within this [consciousness] that the notion of the world as a vessel arises.
Then, drawn by their former karma, they go to the surface of the earth,
where there exists a divine assembly of celestial chariots together with gods and asuras.
From that, they arise in the middle [age];
indeed, in the middle age, having assumed human bodies, they fall [into the world].
For those greedy for food and drink, that radiance is destroyed;
there is indeed a harshness in the limbs and a manifestation of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Then the days and months were indeed obscured by the light of the planets;
from that time onwards, whatever knowledge there was of the luminaries arose.
Indeed, all that was done by me for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
formerly, there was the guise of a rishi, and then the guise of the wise Brahmā.
Having assumed the form of Maheśvara, or again the guise of Viṣṇu,
and having taken on the body of Garuḍa, he [acts] against the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Vāris.
266) "In this way, I declare that even a *paiśācī* body may be such [as one attains] birth after birth;
yet Bodhisattvas are skilled in those various births."
By the power of rebirth, for the sake of the purpose of the conduct of awakening,
I myself was that very Bodhisattva in that former age.
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, I was indeed foolish in the past;
for whatever skills, crafts, and activities exist in this world, [I knew none of them].
In the treatise, there are the principles of ethics and the Purāṇas, as well as the Vedas, grammar, prosody,
astronomy, mathematics, and the ritual manuals (Kalpa).
False knowledge, as well as true knowledge, and likewise false conduct—
all this has been sung by me in the world from of old for a long time according to all the scriptures.
And yet, I have not attained that knowledge by which this Sage is indeed so peaceful—
for the sake of awakening, for the sake of liberation, and likewise for the cause of release.
I am imprisoned in the prison of saṃsāra and not yet liberated from my karmas;
[yet I seek] Buddhahood, the stainless, peaceful Nirvāṇa, the immovable state.
That which I have long desired has been rightly obtained by me;
through my own past actions and according to the proper method, I have now personally attained that which is endowed with reason.
The primordial wisdom of Svayambhū, previously revealed by the Victors, has been attained;
I do not see any such state that can be obtained through an external path.
Deluded in the wilderness of saṃsāra, I did not attain the knowledge such as this which belongs to the Self-Existent One, even though the causes for awakening are difficult to find.
Now I have attained Nirvāṇa, being engaged in action and devoted to what is auspicious;
indeed, this compendium of scriptures is spoken by me solely for that purpose.
And no causes for accomplishment are found apart from karma;
this long thread of saṃsāra is bound and fettered by karma.
This is the greatness of its power: it ripens both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
these [other factors], such as the constellations, planets, and luminaries, merely indicate them.
267) No such sign is seen among other unrighteous men;
for this very reason, she is joined with the planets and is to be favored [or afflicted] by them in matters of good and evil.
The four world-protectors are proclaimed to have become water, earth, wind, and fire;
these great elements are the causes for the gathering of beings.
When impelled by the mantra for the sake of gathering sentient beings,
the accomplishment of the mantra arises through the regulation of their timing.
In those births, they must indeed be protected with effort from both auspicious and inauspicious [influences] by the foremost leaders of the world, such as Śakra and the other lords of the gods.
At that time, during the end of the age,
even those mantras conceived for the [preceding] yuga will be accomplished with effort, and they will succeed even in the lowest of ages.
For this very reason, Mañjughoṣa, the Greatly Wise One, was conceptualized by the Lords of Jinas as a young boy, appearing in the form of a child.
He wanders throughout this entire world, capable of bestowing grace upon sentient beings;
at that time, the accomplishment of Mañjughoṣa is seen.
At that time, there will be the science of astrology and the knowledge of the stars;
twenty-seven constellations and the auspicious moments (muhūrtas) will be proclaimed.
At that time, during that most degenerate age (yugādhama), there were indeed twelve zodiac signs;
those planets, having divided [their influence], took refuge in the zodiacal signs of the constellations.
All beings, having become manifold, resort to various [conditions]; established in the heap, they possess both births and past deeds.
But those born of delusion are perverted, giving rise to the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
for this very reason, those zodiac signs repeatedly proclaim the results of karma.
They imagine the auspicious and inauspicious as the basis for the success of sentient beings;
however, in the birth-astrology texts, the lunar mansion Rohiṇī is specifically designated for this purpose.
Glorious, endowed with patience, having many sons, and long-lived,
he is always a partaker of wealth and acts as a commander of the army.
268) This [person] will be of the sign of Taurus; he is crushed by Taurus.
One born under Mṛgaśiras is a knower of the world, righteous, and pleasant to behold.
Likewise, one born under the portion of Kṛttikā always sees the earth as king;
he is eternally the sovereign of the three oceans, provided his birth chart is clearly manifest.
If the planet Jupiter marks the natal ascendant, the king shall rule over a limited territory, a fortress, or a single district.
He shall enjoy the entire earth on all sides;
his sovereignty is ordained for fifteen years.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and a portion of Kṛttikā are prescribed;
this lunar mansion is indeed capable of bringing success in trade and the attainment of wealth.
If one is endowed with a favorable birth-chart, there will be an abundance of power and enjoyments;
his birth-chart [is determined] by the lunar mansion and the solar disc when it is red.
Just as when [the sun] has set, a transformation constantly arises within him;
he becomes cruel, impulsive, and a speaker of untruth.
Then, he is seen on the surface of the earth with thin skin and a reddish hue;
for him, the duration of a birth-moment is proclaimed to be equal to the twinkling of an eye.
And for that which is born in this interval, these are the detailed qualities;
yet the birth of these is proclaimed to last for only the duration of a finger-snap.
Therefore, fallen from their [proper] birth and devoid of the aspect of the planets,
various kinds of beings are born when the birth is mixed.
The accomplishment of rebirth is mixed, as is the excellence of enjoyments;
for this very reason, they are not born among those described as belonging to the [four] castes alone.
Thirty Jātaka stories have been told, which bring about auspicious and inauspicious results;
indeed, among these, the Krūra-jāti (the fierce class) is marked by the planet Aṅgāraka (Mars).
When observed by the planet Jupiter, one is born with a large belly, a glossy complexion, wide eyes, pleasant speech, and constant fortitude.
269) When the sun has risen to the height of a yoke, and the two deities Moon and Sun have thus appeared,
a birth occurring at that time is always considered to be perfectly auspicious throughout the day and night.
Other birth charts have been contrived with erroneous [planetary positions];
thus, the determination of the aspects of the planets and the auspicious or inauspicious results of false births are established as false.
The production of false fruits and the arising of right knowledge and virtue occur by depending upon the realms of existence and the wombs of birth, established within the field of rebirth.
The pure Mahāsattva [is situated] among the Bhārgavas marked by the planets;
Ārdrā and Punarvasu are said to be the portion of Āśleṣā.
This man who has been born is a great renouncer, yet he is deceitful, impetuous,
always attached to women, greedy, and a hater of wealth and misfortune.
One who approaches another's wife is born dark-complexioned or even black;
by color he becomes smoky (dhūmra), fierce, and indeed fond of sexual intercourse.
This Śanīśvarī is born depending upon the sign of Maithuna;
she moves there as Saturn, day and night, again and again.
This Jātaka, which arises from the manifestation of power at midday,
is declared to have the same measure as that which was born at that time.
The attainment of wealth and the manifestation of sovereignty upon the earth occur under the asterism Puṣya,
and likewise under Āśleṣā.
This Kaṭaka constellation is a heap joined with Jupiter, possessing great supernatural power;
it is yellow in color, the foremost, and is proclaimed as the Jātaka.
Likewise, one born at midnight is always declared to be a Jātaka;
however, if he is considered a true being (sattva), he must have been born at that precise time according to the measurement.
For this indeed accomplishes all goals through the causes prescribed by the ritual rules;
it brings about the attainment of sovereignty and wealth from childhood onwards.
Appearing with a yellowish or dark complexion and possessing a fullness of color,
he is born as one devoted to purity and right conduct, illustrious and learned.
Maghā, Phalgunī,
and a portion of Uttaraphalgunī constitute that field; it is ordained as the solar sign of Leo (Siṃha).
Born there, great heroes who are devoted to eating meat take refuge in mountain strongholds and indeed exercise royal sovereignty.
If the birth [ascendant] is complete, situated in a field, and fixed,
and if they rise just as the sun does, then the birth is proclaimed among these.
A man born under Uttaraphalgunī, Saṃśā, Hasta, or likewise Citrā among the lunar mansions shall be a brave thief.
If one who lacks self-restraint commits adultery with another's wife yet holds the office of commander-in-chief,
he will certainly become the cause of a kingdom, provided he is endowed with a favorable birth-chart.
Indeed, this would be the sign of Virgo (Kanyārāśi) where these stars are situated;
both of them would be their lord, or perhaps another one here at some point.
Among these, Tārakā is the most excellent; a fierce planet guards her, while Saumya, Punarbhava, and Bhadra are always her joyful lords.
Birth occurs when the midday [mark] is reached; among these, the birth-chart (jātaka) is observed in the portion of Citrā, Svātī, and more than half of Viśākhā.
The zodiac sign of Libra (Tulā) moves through the bodies of embodied beings as the Moon of supreme objects;
this is the field of Āruṇa, where Śani and Bhārgava have their abode.
Indeed, one born in these [lunar days] at the end of the night watches is called Jātaka;
mortals born in these times will always be addicted to excessive drinking.
Modest and possessed of a sense of shame, honored by those of great renown,
they obtain sovereignty in some cases, enjoyments in others, and in some cases, they attain what is certain.
In the *Jātaka* [astrology], it is observed that the mother is not fixed [in her lifespan] once she has passed childhood;
if she is endowed with a favorable *jātaka*, she will have many children and experience the arising of happiness.
One born under the lunar mansion Anurādhā is preeminent in accomplishing tasks;
being friendly by nature, he possesses many friends, and is always brave and courageous.
271) It is said that a person born under Jyeṣṭhā is indeed fierce in this world;
such a person is born cruel, enduring much suffering.
They say that Scorpio is a sign characterized by sharpness and constant recklessness;
it is taught that those born under these very signs always possess such a nature at birth.
Likewise, if a creature is born when the sun is at midday,
he certainly becomes a king who is fierce and victorious in battle.
At that very moment, he perceives himself in the form of a young child;
he who is called Aṅgāraka is the auspicious deity of the Earth.
For this very reason, he enjoys the earth, and his own son likewise protects it;
whereas for others, it is the opposite, and their birth is indeed auspicious or inauspicious accordingly.
One born under Anurādhā is long-lived, radiant, and high-minded;
indeed, such a person is born highly wise and affectionate toward friends.
This is the domain of Aṅgāraka, which is always mixed with other planets;
likewise, one born under the Mūla nakṣatra and Pūrvāṣāḍhā is also [subject to its influence].
In the northern portion of Āṣāḍhā, the zodiac sign of Sagittarius (Dhanuḥ) is proclaimed;
this is the field of Jupiter, and one born therein becomes a Jātaka.
Whether at midday when the sun is high, or indeed during the nights of the moon,
they say that for one born for the sake of sovereignty, this is his "birth" (jātaka).
One should destroy one's own family at its very root; it is said that effort [in this regard] is auspicious.
One born in the middle position will undoubtedly obtain enjoyments.
But when his youth has passed, like the orb of the sun,
the king becomes old, possessing great enjoyments and great wealth.
One who possesses power is renowned in low-lying regions, but not in other lands;
however, various other Jinas are seen to be the opposite of that.
Likewise, Uttarāṣāḍhā would be [the asterism], and Śravaṇa is proclaimed;
Dhaniṣṭhā is the most excellent asterism, and the zodiac sign here would be Capricorn (Makara).
272) This is the domain of Saturn; whether marked by him or by other planets, it is seen constantly present on the surface of the earth during birth ceremonies.
When the first part of the night has passed and the middle part has begun,
those born during these times are seen everywhere to possess great enjoyments.
Those who reside in low-born families become kings;
they are fierce, with a dark complexion, or they possess a swarthy hue.
Those with eyes red at the corners, who are gentle yet brave and always daring,
indeed exercise sovereignty in a region abounding in water.
For those who are long-lived are childless, enduring much suffering;
others, however, are their opposite—people who are poor and afflicted by disease.
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and likewise Pūrvabhādrapadā—
this portion constitutes the zodiac sign known as Aquarius (Kumbha).
This field is always inhabited by the chief of planets,
as well as by the mixed lunar mansions and by the wise Śukra himself.
Among these, birth occurs at night and is observed at dawn;
this is considered an excellent and constant nativity due to the purity of its activity in the world.
In the matter of cruel deeds, he is declared to be wise;
he shall enjoy a manifold abundance of pleasures upon the surface of the earth.
But others besides those are the opposite: people who are poor and afflicted by disease;
furthermore, the lunar mansion Bhadrapadā and Revatī are proclaimed [to be such].
In the portion of Pūrvabhādrapadā, established in the sign of Pisces,
she is constantly present in birth ceremonies and is seen everywhere.
During the middle watch of the night, or when the sun has risen during the day,
or when half a watch has passed after sunrise— at midday, when the sun has slightly ascended.
When only a small portion has emerged and one cubit remains, it is born at that single moment;
it is pure, exceedingly white, and perfectly endowed with whiteness itself.
273) The gods and those practicing celibacy know that as the field of Śukra;
it is presided over by planets that are yellowish-white in appearance.
That field is eternally conducive to the highest good, righteous, and supremely auspicious;
mortals born therein shall possess limbs that are entirely beautiful.
Desirous of sovereignty, possessed of great heroism, with firm affection for their kinsmen,
long-lived, and enjoying great wealth, they dwell in low-lying regions.
Taking refuge in the eastern direction, they will always attain prosperity;
for them, there is no doubt that growth will occur even in a forest region.
No fish were seen at all moving about the roots;
the floodwaters increased, and the abodes of the sages were submerged in the water.
Among them, the birth [sign] is proclaimed, and it is indeed proclaimed as a zodiacal sign (rāśi). For mortals born under those [signs] truly flourish exceedingly in low-lying regions.
The rulers of the earth, possessing great enjoyments, are always established in the east;
the most excellent planets, beginning with Jupiter and ending with Saturn, are observed there.
Those born under these [signs] undoubtedly exercise sovereignty over the East;
the zodiac signs have been described in many ways, and the lunar mansions in numerous ways.
The chief planets are indeed of three kinds, but not at present after a long time;
therefore, humans possess knowledge [only] of the fifteen lunar days (tithis).
Thirty days are proclaimed to be a month;
fifteen days and nights constitute a fortnight (pakṣa), and two fortnights are called a month.
Then, twelve months are proclaimed as one year;
this duration of time is indeed reckoned at the end of the age (yuga).
When the Kali Yuga has arrived, this number is proclaimed;
likewise, the lifespan of human beings is declared to be one hundred years.
Within their year, the seasons have been proclaimed;
they are described as being of three kinds—at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle.
274) In this world of humans, the lifespan may be intermediate, high, or low;
for them, portents in this human world have been proclaimed.
The lifespan of human beings is proclaimed to be one hundred years;
non-human beings in this world of living creatures run hither and thither.
Terrified and indeed struck with fear, they wander here and there whenever the battle between the leaders of the gods and asuras breaks out.
Then, in this world of men, they bring about the occurrence of diseases, as well as comets, tremors, meteors, and even thunderbolts and lightning.
The quarters of the sky are indeed smoky on all sides, and a comet is visible;
moreover, the orbs of the moon and the sun appear like headless trunks (kabandha) and spikes.
A hole is seen even in the sun and in the moon of great supernatural power;
indeed, in this way, various forms are seen again in many ways.
There will be famine, loss of longevity, and likewise the destruction of the kingdom;
there will be the death of the king and great fear for the ascetics.
And for all the worlds, there was a terrifying event in that region:
the earth shook under the asterisms of Maghā, Aśvinī, and Punarvasu.
Then the Middle Country will be oppressed by thieves and violent men;
the great kingdom will be plundered by those residing in the Deccan.
When a terrifying earthquake occurs during the asterisms of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, or Mṛgaśiras, fear arises among the people.
When kings die having resorted to the western direction,
then even those dwelling in the borderlands who live as barbarians or thieves [will perish].
Likewise, O lord of men, the ruler of the people was afflicted on the slopes and in the valleys of the Vindhya mountains;
at that time, they too were tormented, overwhelmed by disease.
O people, the arising of enemies for them results from mutual rivalry;
moreover, the Puṣya asterism, Āśleṣā, and Phalgunī are moist.
When these earth-asterisms (bhūmi-nakṣatras) have shifted, the lords of men [shall tremble].
Another, by obstructing the sunlight, causes all things to become disordered;
there arise slaughter, imprisonment, and afflictions, and famine arises for the people.
In Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Anurādhā, and Jyeṣṭhā—
if an earthquake occurs in these [asterisms], it will be extensive throughout this world-receptacle.
The Mlecchas and bandits dwelling in the Himalayas on all sides,
as well as those residing in the valleys of the Khaśas under the ruler of Nepal, [were subdued].
All the kings there will be mutually antagonistic;
they will all be inclined toward warfare, of this there is no doubt.
This earthquake occurred in the Mūla constellation; those two Āṣāḍhas, both Pūrva and Uttara, are seen among the constellations, and there is trembling upon the surface of the earth.
First, the regions and the people of Pauṇḍra and Odra, who possess the power of changing their form at will, [will suffer];
the king who is the lord of Vaṅgāla will die—of this there is no doubt.
The illustrious lord of the Gauḍas will be besieged by foreign kingdoms;
he will either suddenly fall ill or, in some cases, death will occur.
Likewise, the worlds extending to the edge of the ocean, situated along the banks of the Gaṅgā,
were all submerged in water and tormented by many diseases.
If [the moon] is in Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, or the two Bhadrapadas,
or if he is born in Pūrva-phalgunī, Uttara-phalgunī, or Revatī;
At midday, there was a great earthquake; the entire world-receptacle trembled, and the whole earth, along with its mountains and forests, shook.
All of them, scattered and arranged in various ways, are always seen in the sky—
the regions of the North and those situated in the West.
Throughout the southern region, in every direction,
excellent kings who possessed abundant prosperity were situated, obstructing one another.

During great calamities for sentient beings, during famine, and during the division of kingdoms; at dawn, during auspicious times, during peace, and during the trembling of the earth— for embodied beings [there is protection].
Then, at the time of the supreme [conjunction], a fierce trembling arises;
and even more intense than that is the destruction of the people of Magadha.
The Aṅga country was oppressed, as was King Māgadha;
then, at midday and in the afternoon, the sun grew dim.
If this earthquake were to occur throughout the entire surface of the earth,
all wandering mendicants would constantly be subject to the onset of disease.
They are constantly afflicted by diseases such as fever, illness, colic, and eruptions for seven royal reigns; after that, however, their welfare prevails.
If an earthquake occurs when the sun’s darkness has diminished,
the Brāhmaṇas who drink the Soma juice and are the most excellent among the four castes will perish.
The mantra-practitioner suffers and is even destroyed, as is the king— of this there is no doubt—
as well as the most virtuous domestic priest, the minister, or any servant of the king.
Or another who is a preeminent observer of vows and is skilled in the mantras and the meaning of the mantras—
whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or likewise a Śūdra.
Even one who is skillful, learned, and proficient in the principles, meanings, and ethics of the scriptures may be struck down,
perish, or be tormented by disease.
One who possesses mindfulness, knows the truth of the scriptures, and reflects upon the Itihāsas,
is swiftly struck down by disease, like a tree by a thunderbolt.
Then, when the sun has set,
or even later in the afternoon at the end of the age (yugānta), if a more violent earthquake occurs, it is most terrible.
Likewise, beings were intermingled, taking refuge in the animal realm;
yet humans, the leaders of the world, remained sovereigns during that earthquake.
Then, if an earthquake occurs during the first watch of the night,
a great rain accompanied by the falling of stones will be seen.
277) Then, at the very hour of decline, when the earth trembled,
having seen that omen, a great wind and rain occurred.
Then, at the end of the night watch, a terrible omen is seen;
one should know that there will be the arrival of a foreign army and a western king.
Then, when a second tremor arises,
there will be death, disease, foreign invasion, and severe abdominal illness.
It provokes diseases arising from bile and phlegm in living beings;
it agitates the spirits and causes them to move from one place to another.
Then, in the second watch of the night, an earthquake occurs;
from that one should know a great wind, which shatters trees and temples.
There were no doubt watchtowers and peaks upon the mountains,
as well as delightful monasteries, dwellings, and palaces adorned with arched gateways.
Furthermore, an earthquake that occurs at the time of midnight quickly causes the dwellings of living beings, as well as those in the animal realm, to fall.
Then the foremost and best of kings are slain, as is the sovereign of the eastern lands;
or his son perishes, or one should predict a famine.
Then, during the final watch in the middle of the waning phase, a tremor arises throughout the entire surface of the earth; this indicates peace and health.
Then, at the end, when an earthquake occurs at midnight,
the marshy regions and the central lands will be afflicted by disease due to the king.
Mutually antagonistic, they die through terrible sufferings when the third month arrives; for fools, this brings about the arising of happiness.
Flies, gadflies, moths, and all thieves perish;
a tremor at dawn brings long life, health, and abundance of food.
One should recognize a fire burning on all sides of the cities when an earthquake occurs at the rising of the sun.
278) Then, when the Middle Country and everywhere else are harassed by thieves,
the death of the king will be seen after seven days.
In whatever place and at whatever time a powerful earthquake is observed,
it is in that very place and at that time that the auspicious and inauspicious effects are seen.
One should predict a meteor, a thunderclap, and an earthquake occurring at the same time;
when a white meteor blazes, it destroys that which is crooked.
Likewise, a white color is always praised as bestowing auspiciousness;
a red color is most terrible and indicates a conflagration.
If [the smoke] is smoky-colored or black, it foretells the death of the king;
if it is yellow, tawny, or of a variegated color, [it portends other calamities].
Then one should indicate a mixed earthquake and a portent;
and a thunderclap is proclaimed in whichever direction it occurs, one should predict [the event] in that very direction.
If it is the middle [note], then it is proclaimed to belong specifically to the Middle Country;
being accompanied by its own tone and sweet, it portends security and health.
Extremely cruel and terrible in the world, yet bestowing auspiciousness, the sound of the drum is frightening and exceedingly terrifying; one should predict famine there.
These and other such planetary applications should always be performed;
one should then carry out rites for accomplishment during these auspicious lunar mansions.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Puṣyā, both Bhadrapadās,
Revatī, and Anurādhā are praised for the time of recitation.
In these [constellations], mantras indeed attain accomplishment and bestow their perfected purpose;
and the mandala itself should be drawn by these very stars.
These lunar days— namely the full moon on the fifteenth— are indeed auspicious for the lords of the weekdays and planets, which shine with yellow and white luster.
One should not go on a journey at all, but should rather draw the mandala;
specifically on the first, third, fifth, tenth, and seventh [lunar days].
279) On the thirteenth day likewise, let the lords of men arrange their expeditions;
for travel on this day is praised as bestowing auspiciousness upon all living beings.
One should not draw the mandala of all mantras for either the tantras or the mantras;
indeed, the mantras will not be effective in these cases, as they are declared to be causes of obstacles.
Success in the journey comes from the fire sacrifice when the lunar day is conjoined with the most excellent planets;
Jupiter, Venus, the Moon, and Mercury are the best for all undertakings.
These four excellent planets, when conjoined with the lunar days, always bring about success and auspicious journeys in this world upon the surface of the earth.
Free from malignant *ariṣṭa* signs, and devoid of the faults of cutting, breaking, or crookedness—
among these very [auspicious trees], one should determine the days.
One should employ exactly twelve muhūrtas at that time;
Śveta and Maitra would be thus, and they are proclaimed as having red eyes.
Raudra, Mahendra, Śuddha, and Abhijit which is most auspicious;
Bhramaṇa and Bhrāmaṇa are likewise proclaimed as bestowers of welfare.
Then there are Saumya, Varada, and the one celebrated as Śubhaprada;
Soma and Varada as well—these are the twelve kṣaṇas.
The characteristics of the thirty muhūrtas have been described in many ways;
thus, there may be rain during the tenth muhūrta, as well as during the fourteenth muhūrta at night.
The eighth and the twelfth [lunar days] are indeed to be avoided;
one should be diligent in the calculation starting from the night of the dark fortnight.
But the cause of obstacles for these is Vināyaka, who is here the fourth;
this is the proper method of counting, and this is proclaimed to be the [correct] time.
The opening and closing of the eyes, a finger-snap, and a swift movement—
this is the measure of time, though it shall be explained in detail again.
A hundred snaps of the fingers are proclaimed to be one *nāḍikā*;
four *nāḍikās* are called a *ghaṭī*, and four *ghaṭīs* are known as a *prahara*.
280) A day consists of four watches, and nights are likewise proclaimed by these [four].
Thus, when joined with eight of these, a full day and night (ahorātra) is established.
Ten *unmeṣa-nimeṣas* (openings and closings of the eyes) are reckoned as a mere *kṣaṇa*;
ten *tālas* in measure are likewise said to be a mere *kṣaṇa*.
Ten *kṣaṇas* are said to constitute a *muhūrta*, as determined by the sages;
four *muhūrtas* are reckoned as one *prahara* by those who know the mantras.
One should determine this measure of time for the three junctions (trisandhya);
likewise, one should apply it during the time of fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa), and the time of attaining accomplishment (siddhi).
Whether during sleep or while awake, at the time of bathing or drinking, or throughout the day;
indeed, "day" is the term used for both day and night.
Fifteen days are proclaimed to be one fortnight;
those experts skilled in calculation say that two fortnights constitute a month.
In the same way, the moon is swallowed by Rāhu again every six months;
therefore, after twelve such months, the term "year" (varṣa) is proclaimed.
Then, for twelve years, that is called the Great Rain;
the planets, lunar mansions, and the lords of the Dānavas are proclaimed to be adverse.
Then, in the twelfth year, they perform [the rites] here for both auspicious and inauspicious [occasions],
when Rāhu, the lord of the Asuras, is seen within a single lunar fortnight.
The entire circle of the moon and the sun, arranged both collectively and individually,
as well as a great falling of weapons, is seen upon the surface of the earth.
One should always and constantly employ these and other [mantras] at the appropriate times;
for many kinds of terrible obstacles are seen to arise.
When the time of the end of the age had arrived, indeed when the world-vessel was most unrighteous,
the entire moon was eclipsed and entered the constellation Mūla.
If the moon sets during the night, there will be a gathering of troops;
or if the sun sets during the day, it is afflicted.
281) When the sun and the moon set at midnight during an eclipse, they do so out of fear of the shadow of the lord of the Dānavas.
The wicked king residing in his own country will be slain, without a doubt;
he will either face the danger of death from his own side or be destroyed by enemies.
The lord of the Mlecchas will plunder the eastern region;
likewise, all the Udra districts and the lord of the Udras [will do the same].
If the two planets, the Moon and the Sun, should be seen in Aśvinī, or likewise in Rohiṇī and Bharaṇī,
or when they are seen in Kṛttikā;
Various diseases arising from phlegm, bile, and wind,
as well as others that are combinations of these, arise for all embodied beings.
Various outbreaks of disease are seen among all the foolish when [the moon is] in Maghā, Phalgunī, Uttarā, or Pūrvā.
Likewise in Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, and Viśākhā—
whenever the Moon or the Sun is eclipsed during these [nakṣatras], there is no doubt.
First, both the moon and the sun are swallowed by Rāhu;
likewise, the ruler of the eastern region [is seized].
The king of Vaṅga, Aṅga, or Māgadha will be seized by pain in the eye;
or their son will die, or there will be danger from the death of his wife.
Or if there should be a gathering of enemies with malicious intent, then [the following constellations are relevant]:
Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and likewise Āśleṣā.
When Rāhu is seen eclipsing both the sun and the moon in these [asterisms],
the king of Magadha and the people of the Magadha region are then afflicted.
The ministers would experience fear of disease, along with the suffering of imprisonment for the citizens;
under Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā, all these things would be seen, O Lord of the Dānavas.
Then, disease shall arise pervading all the inhabited lands,
as well as various forms of slaughter, imprisonment, affliction, and exhaustion.
282) When these [asterisms] are obstructed by the leaders of men, there is growth;
likewise in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇa, and Uttarāṣāḍhā.
The orb of the sun becomes distorted and the moon assumes a reddish hue;
there is the constant arrival of malefic planets, and famine arises.
When the moon or the sun is eclipsed while situated in the lunar mansions of Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, or Śatabhiṣaj;
They know that when a planet arrives by resorting to a black appearance,
there will be great sorrow, exhaustion, and famine on all sides.
One should know that there will be great danger from kings and thieves throughout all the provinces when the asterism is Revatī or Uttarābhādrapadā.
The lunar and solar orbs are first swallowed by Rāhu;
afterwards, the orb of the sun is seen again after one fortnight has passed.
Every Magadhan king, even the sovereign lord, falls from his kingdom;
these are the signs declared when Rāhu approaches.
In whichever directions one perceives the solar disc eclipsed by the moon,
in those respective regions, auspicious or inauspicious events then arise.
Whatever tremors of the earth have been described as marked by worldly signs,
one should understand that the auspicious or inauspicious results thereof occur specifically during an eclipse of the planets.
If there is smoke for five days at the end of the day, it will cause rain;
thereafter, for half that time, there will be anxiety among the people concerning Tīrabhukti.
All the inhabited lands, which are the abodes of the origin of diseases, shall perish;
and even the king shall perish on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, Himavanta was placed in the womb; Durbhagajvara was stationed there, and the kings were also positioned all around as guardians of the quarters.
Then, on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, that lord of the Tīrabhukti region,
the king, shall die from various sorrows and torments.
283) That lord of men perishes together with his sons and wife;
indeed, one should predict smoke during those lunar mansions in which an earthquake occurs.
In all directions, terrible clouds devoid of rain have arisen;
five days have passed, yet it has always been exceedingly cloudy.
The mutual spheres of mortals born of human lineage would perish;
there, the sight of humans would no longer function toward one another.
One should know that there will be great danger in that case; it shall destroy the king along with his kingdom, wherever such a trembling occurs accompanied by the falling of meteors on all sides.
Furthermore, if two or three [crows] are seen perched upon the searchers' heads at night, or if there is a rainbow, or if a crow appears with white wings, it is indeed terrible.
A white-colored bird appears black, and a black one appears white;
the colors of the birds are reversed, as are the seasonal sounds.
Wherever birds appear to be portending ill omen, there is great danger;
this applies to all beings—whether two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, or footless.
If birds fly horizontally, they portend calamity for living beings; if they do so in the opposite direction, there is great danger.
Likewise, if dogs howl repeatedly with their muzzles turned upwards, it is a sign of fear.
Whether by day or by night, wherever there is great fear,
and wherever many such various kinds [of dangers] have been manifested in manifold ways;
There shall be drought, and the king's wheel [of power] will perish;
for just as the auspicious and inauspicious destinies of living beings are declared by their birth-rites (jātaka), so too is this foretold.
Thus, portents arise from that [karma], producing here both auspicious and inauspicious results;
no sign whatsoever is seen to occur otherwise than through its prior cause.
Obstacles arising from portents do not occur without a cause.

Thus concludes the twenty-second chapter, the detailed exposition on the light of knowledge regarding signs, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
284) Now follows the twenty-fifth detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, again addressed the hosts of planets, lunar mansions, stars, and luminaries.

Listen, all of you! This King of Rituals (*kalparāja*) of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta— comprising the procedures for mantras, tantras, consecrations, and mandalas, as well as the rules for recitation, fire-offerings (*homa*), and the accomplishment of vidyās— is not to be transgressed by the holders of vidyās (*vidyādharas*) who are engaged in this supreme ritual manual.
"You must create obstacles for those who possess knowledge of the lunar days, constellations, movements, and calculations regarding the stars.
All the hosts of gods must provide protection there for those engaged in this teaching. Furthermore, all wicked beings must be restrained, obstructed, and disciplined; none at all shall [prevail]."
They should be caused to be destroyed and established within the regulations of this teaching of the Ten-Powered Ones.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the samādhi called "The Exalted Uṣṇīṣa of All Tathāgatas" for the purpose of warding off all malevolent beings among all sentient beings.
As soon as the Blessed One Śākyamuni had entered that state, all those Tathāgatas [also did so].

Having beheld the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, residing in the palace of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana) situated within the world-systems of the ten directions, they approached him. Having approached,
through the inconceivable empowerment of their own buddha-nature, they addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero! for the arising of the welfare of the worlds, concerning the engagement of all mantras and tantras according to the rule.
This King of Vidyās of great supernatural power, the single-syllable, supreme, and foremost, has been taught by all the Buddhas for this lost time in the Kali Yuga.
The most excellent of all mantras, spoken by all the Buddhas,
is the King Uṣṇīṣa of great heroism, the warder-off of all malevolent spirits.
He is the restrainer of the planets, the constellations, and the malevolent mothers; likewise, he is the subduer of all obstacles and whatever other beings exist in the world with wicked intentions.
For the sake of favoring sentient beings and for the arising of happiness for those who recite [mantras],
he is indeed the foremost in this entire teaching, a universal monarch of great supernatural power.
285) O Uṣṇīṣarāja, of great heroism, the supreme lord over all! O Tathāgata, speak now of that which is the time for this.
When they had spoken thus, those Buddhas remained in silence.

Then, from the assembly of those Buddhas, the entire great trichiliocosm and the world-receptacles of all sentient beings became a single mass of flame, yet there was no suffering for any sentient beings.
By the Buddha’s empowerment, great radiances were seen.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sons of the gods residing there, and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas gathered in the great assembly of the Blessed One.
May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, all the Pratyekabuddhas and Noble Śrāvakas, attend to me! [I take refuge] in the Blessed One,
the single-syllable Vidyārāja, who stands above all the Uṣṇīṣas of the Tathāgatas, whose teaching is unimpeded, and whose strength and prowess are immeasurable.
Furthermore, I shall again proclaim the ritual manual of the Uṣṇīṣarājacakravartin for this time, in this degenerate age.

Now I shall again proclaim the mantra of the Blessed One, whose teaching is difficult to transgress, the teacher of the three worlds, honored by all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, and the accomplisher of the purpose of all rites, in this time of the Kali age.

At the time when the teaching is disappearing, the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣacakravartin will become the protector of the teaching and will attain accomplishment. At all times, and specifically at the moment when the teachings of all the Buddhas are vanishing, this Blessed Buddha will act for the benefit of sentient beings.
This Blessed One is the protector, thoroughly integrated with the Dharma-treasury of all Tathāgatas. Listen, O hosts of gods and all sentient beings! BHRŪM!
This Blessed One, the omniscient one, established by the Buddhas in the form of mantra,
the teacher of great compassion, wanders among all embodied beings.
The glorious lord of mantras, renowned and honored as Uṣṇīṣa,
having come forth from the essence of compassion, stands here as this imperishable syllable.
286) Having emerged from that dharmadhātu, this [body] of the one who possesses all forms stands forth;
for just as the relics (dhātavaḥ) of the Buddhas have proceeded among people from their bodies.
Those who are honored by the world are possessed of worldly gain; those who are free from worldly gain are especially distinguished.
They are declared to be the repositories of the true Dharma, free from worldly gain, and the causes for the welfare of the world.
The great miraculous powers of the Lords of Jinas within the physical body are said to be "with attachment" (sāmiṣā);
whereas the various relics of the Moon-like Sages, being free from outflows (nirāśrava), are said to be "without attachment."
Both with and without worldly attachment, they have issued forth for the sake of the world,
blending the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) out of the power of compassion for sentient beings.
The Lord of the World, the Maker of Light, abides in the form of mantra;
he, the omniscient one who possesses all forms, is indeed seen upon the surface of the earth.
This mantra, which accomplishes all aims, was spoken by all the Buddhas;
this very mantra, when recited according to the ritual procedure itself, is [efficacious] in brief.
It indeed always accomplishes every rite, making one's desires fruitful;
its ritual manual (kalpa) shall now be proclaimed again in brief.
When the Tathāgata, the best of sages, has passed away from the world at the end of the eon,
the accomplishment of mantras is declared to be the accomplishment of the kalpa at that time.

Now, [I shall explain] in brief the ritual manual for the Single-Syllable [Mantra] of the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, which belongs to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin— the destroyer of the application of others' rites, the unconquered victor, the sovereign of all mantras, and the one authorized by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It has been previously set forth in detail.

First of all, in whatever place this is recited, within a distance of one *yojana* along that path, all malevolent planets flee; even all accomplished mantras (*siddhamantra*) have no power there, and all gods abandon their presence—
except by the will of the practitioner for others, whether worldly or supramundane.
It takes away the accomplishment of practitioners; it releases the mantras of others' applications that have been severed, split, or pinned down.

One who desires to effect the severance of a spell himself should take a handful of fresh green kuśa grass, empower it one hundred and eight times with the mantra, and cut it with a weapon while aiming at that spell; thus, that spell is severed.

[It] becomes [effective]. Having made an image with this [substance], one should strike it in the heart with a stake; it becomes pinned down. With a thread over which the mantra has been recited seven times and dyed with safflower, one should tie a knot; she becomes bound. One should cover [the image] with a shallow bowl over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times;
she becomes obstructed.

287) If one cuts the heart in two with a weapon, it becomes split. If one dyes it with mustard seeds colored with poison and blood, it becomes stained. If one strikes it with a *karavīra* creeper, it becomes oppressed.

One performs all vidyās and magical rites according to one's desire. In every case, for a rite of fulfillment, one should perform a fire offering (homa) after bathing [the image] with milk; this brings peace. By a fire offering of ghee, peace and nourishment are brought about for all. By clenching the fist, one paralyzes all mantras; by means of the mind, one releases the mantra.

One who desires to accomplish [a rite] should accomplish it by obstructing with this very [mantra]. If one wishes to accomplish another ritual manual (*kalpa*), one should accomplish that by means of this very [mantra]; it succeeds. By this very mantra, the invocation (*āvāhana*) occurs; again, by this very [mantra], the dismissal (*visarjana*) occurs. By this very [mantra], whoever is protected also becomes invisible. As for the mantra which...

Success is achieved, or else he does not grant a response; one should recite [the mantra] together with this very [mantra]. Success is swiftly achieved, or else he grants a response. If success is not achieved, he provides a response: "He shall die."

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for seven days, directed toward whichever mantra; he over whom it is performed will come under one’s control and will perform whatever task is commanded. Or, I shall grant a counter-instruction: if one desires to bring the gods under control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *devadāru* wood fuel.

Within seven nights, one becomes subject [to control]. One desiring to bring the *nāgas* under control should offer oblations of the three sweets (*trimadhura*); they become subject. One desiring to bring the *yakṣas* under control should offer curd-rice (*dadhibhakta*). With all types of perfumes, one brings the *gandharvas* under control. With fuel-sticks or flowers of *aśoka* and *priyaṅgu*, [one gains mastery] over the *yakṣiṇīs*, *nāgas*, and *nāga-grahas*.

With black mustard seeds one subjugates a king; with white mustard seeds, a Brahmin; with a flower-oblation, a Vaiśya; with curd, milk, and ghee, a Śūdra; with chaff and dust, a woman; with a salt-oblation, a widow;
with a bean-and-jambul-fruit oblation, a maiden; and with an oblation of parched grain, ghee, and oil, one brings all people under one's control.

"Everywhere, for three periods of the day and seven nights"—having spoken thus, the Supreme Victor became silent. Then the seventh among the preeminent sages, who knows the ways of the world, laughed at the assembly of gods regarding the mantra; he was liberated, his mind having attained peace.
Then the supreme sage addressed the eldest son of the Buddha;
he then chose Mañjughoṣa, the bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
288) This ritual procedure has been proclaimed by me as but a single portion for the wielder of the discus;
for the extent of that wise Lord, the God of gods, is vast.
The measure of which cannot be expressed even by the Victors throughout eons—
I shall describe it to you in brief for the sake of bringing about the welfare of human beings.
When this had been said, the glorious Mañjughoṣa, possessed of great supernatural power,
then made a formal request to that Buddha who was stationed above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero! O Perfectly Awakened One, supreme among bipeds!
[Reveal] the arising of happiness for human beings when the time has perished at the end of the age.

How is it that for this one of great majesty and great heroism, the king of mantras is seen to grant success through the cloth-painting? And how is the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting performed so as to bring swift results?

Thus concludes the twenty-third chapter, the detailed exposition on the emergence of the Single-Syllable Universal Monarch, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avatamsaka*.
289) Now follows the twenty-sixth detailed chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [spoke].
He addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī!
There is a concise procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) of the One-Syllable Wheel-Turner of great majesty.
It has been explained at length previously; now it shall be given in brief, for in this degenerate age, sentient beings possess little vigor."
Those of little wisdom and dull intellect are unable to accomplish the application of the cloth's dimensions in detail. Out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I shall speak in brief,
so that those practitioners of recitation may attain the accomplishment of the supreme goal.

One who desires to perform the supreme sādhana should have the Blessed One painted on an unbleached cloth that has its fringes intact, from which the hair has been removed, using colors that do not adhere [to the surface]. He is the King of Dharma, the Turner of the Wheel of Dharma,
