the Lord of all worlds, the Supreme among Men, the Foremost of bipeds, the Jewel of the Tathāgatas, named Ratnaketu.

The Supreme Victor, teaching the Dharma, is surrounded by a mandala of light blazing on all sides; below him are Brahmā and the noble Vajrapāṇi, above him are two sons of gods bearing garlands, and below him is the practitioner.
In front of it, burning agarwood incense at the three junctions of the day, one should recite the mantra one million times; thereafter, the ritual activities will succeed.
Desiring to perform the first wheel-attainment (*cakrasādhana*), one should fashion a twelve-spoked wheel made of flower-metal (*puṣpaloha*).
During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), while burning *agaru* incense before the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day, one should recite [the mantra] one million times.
At the end, on the full moon day, having performed a grand worship and grasping [the wheel] with the hand, one should recite it until—
"Blazing": having taken that [substance], one becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas; together with those by whom he is seen and those whom he sees, he flies up into the air.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the parasol should have a white, variegated, and new parasol made, marked with a golden wheel and draped with silk cloth; having placed it upon his head according to this very procedure, he should recite the mantra, and the Vidyā will manifest of its own accord. Furthermore, he should offer agarwood incense before the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day.

One should recite it one million times. At the end, on the full moon day, having performed a magnificent worship, one should grasp [the object] with the hand and recite until it blazes. Having taken hold of it, one becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*. Month after month, on the full moon, within five fortnights—specifically during the fortnight of miracles—it is accomplished.
290) Then, by the mere accomplishment [of this], all dharmas become manifest before one. One attains all the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
One becomes perfected in entering into all sentient beings, being welcomed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Even in another world-system, he becomes a universal monarch with a retinue of a thousand.

Then, one desiring to accomplish the *uṣṇīṣa* [rite] should fashion a staff one cubit in length out of gold, silver, copper, or gems; one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth. Having grasped it, one wanders at will and teaches the Dharma to sentient beings; one lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).

Now, one desiring to accomplish the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*) should fashion a golden auspicious jar, fill it with all kinds of seeds, jewels, and medicinal herbs, and wrap it in white cloth; one should accomplish it by means of this [mantra]. One should begin the rite during one fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), and it becomes effective during the other. Having placed whatever one desires into that [jar], it is achieved.
One obtains that; it becomes inexhaustible.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the *cintāmaṇi* jewel should fashion a golden staff with a genuine gem and a crystal gem, or a golden [staff] adorned with hanging cloth, and accomplish it according to this very procedure; whatever one thinks of, all that is accomplished. And by holding this among gods and humans, one becomes possessed of unimpeded strength and prowess. Now...

If one recites the mantra of the Blessed One ten million times, one flies up with one's own body and lives for many great divine kalpas. Furthermore, other rites such as those headed by the *Asitātapatra* (Black Parasol) are also accomplished by this recitation of the Blessed One’s mantra one hundred thousand times. Thus, the Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa is unimpeded even when performed according to the procedures of other tantras.

In whatever manner one applies it, in that very way it is accomplished. After being recited one million times, the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣacakravartin—the universal monarch of all vidyā-mantras—accomplishes everything in no time at all.

Then, desiring to accomplish the vajra, one should fashion a single-pronged vajra made of red sandalwood or else made of "flower-metal" (puṣpaloha). Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having performed a grand worship before the cloth painting (paṭa) and lit lamps of ghee, one should wash it with scented water. O Yakṣas...

They become submissive. Having offered oneself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should perform protection by means of this Uṣṇīṣarāja together with his retinue, or by means of Tejorāśi and Sitātapatra.

Having performed the binding of the mandala and having provided protection for his companions, he should take a vajra in his right hand; then, when the first watch has passed, sitting in the second watch with a one-pointed mind, he should recite the mantra until it blazes forth. In the meantime, all the vidyādharas, as well as all the gods, nāgas, and yakṣas, assemble there. And all...

The kings of the Vidyādharas arrive; being praised by them, he goes to the city of the Vidyādharas and becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas. Possessing a body like that of Vajrapāṇi and strength equal to Vajrapāṇi, he goes in a single kṣaṇa, lava, or muhūrta to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, where the gods abound, and remains there for a great eon (mahākalpa).
He beholds the Blessed One, the noble Maitreya; he hears the Dharma; having died, he is reborn wherever he desires. If he so wishes, he arises from the presence of Vajrapāṇi.
Now, one who desires to accomplish the sword-rite should take a flawless sword and remain fasting for a day and night.
Having performed a grand worship of the Blessed One, one should recite [the mantra] until, having blazed forth and attained accomplishment, one flies up together with one's retinue.
With hair curled in locks, appearing like a sixteen-year-old, one does not yield the path and becomes unassailable by all *vidyādharas*, living for an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*).

Now, one desiring to accomplish the rite of realgar (manaḥśilā) should purchase it by means of a "hero's price" (vīrakraya). Having fasted for three nights during the conjunction of Puṣya, he should feed the monks designated for the Saṅgha and cause them to grant his authorization. Once authorized, he should enter the place of practice. Having performed a magnificent worship, he should light a thousand lamps of ghee.

Having fasted for three nights, having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and having offered oneself, one should take realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained. One should first contemplate [the signs] of heat, smoke, and flame. Having applied a tilaka-mark that emits heat as a sign of unmanifested accomplishment, one [subdues] all gods, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, and so forth.

And the beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa become his servants; they become his attendants. He lives for a thousand years. Having applied a mark while smoke is rising, he becomes invisible. If he so desires, he becomes invisible even to the gods; he is seen in a moment, a lava, or a muhūrta, and then becomes invisible again. Among all those who possess the power of invisibility, [he is supreme].

One becomes a king; one lives for three thousand years and becomes a blazing Vidyādhara. One flies up together with one's retinue and becomes a king of the Vidyādharas. Possessing the body of a celestial youth, one is invincible to all the gods, let alone the Vidyādharas;
one remains for an eon and, upon death, is reborn in the Tuṣita realm of the gods.
292) Now, one who desires to accomplish the trident should fashion a trident made of *puṣpaloha* (flower-metal) and recite the mantra for one year.
Then, having constructed a stūpa made of sand measuring one cubit in height, he should perform a grand worship of it.

Having presented a magnificent offering and grasping a trident with the right hand, one should recite the mantra until— having assumed the cross-legged posture— it quivers, blazes, and emits thousands of rays of light. During this interval, the gods headed by Maheśvara arrive, and all the vidyādharas rain down a shower of flowers.

Then, surrounded by them, he flies up together with all those whom he sees and who see him. Having three eyes like a second Maheśvara, honored by all the Vidyādharas, and remaining for a great kalpa, he causes those of evil intent to fall by his mere glance. He becomes unassailable by anyone, let alone by the world including the gods.
One who falls from the state of a *vidyādhara* is reborn in Sukhāvatī.

Alternatively, one may accomplish the *vetāḍa*: having seized a man with uninjured limbs and seated oneself upon his chest—which has been secured with four stakes of *khadira* wood—one should offer an oblation of powdered jewels. Then, the *cintāmaṇi* jewel will appear on the tip of his tongue.

Having seized it, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*. Whatever weapons one thinks of appear by the mere power of the mind. One illuminates a hundred *yojanas* with one's radiance. One passes away according to one’s will.
One goes wherever one desires, even becoming a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas* in other world-systems. When one passes away...
One is reborn in the world-system Vimalā.

The second is the *vetāla*-sādhana. Having seized a *vetāla* with its limbs unimpaired, one should pin it down with stakes of *badara* wood and offer iron filings into its mouth. Its tongue will emerge; having cut it off, one flies up accompanied by a retinue of a hundred. One lives for an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*) and sports and delights upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. When one dies, then—
The king becomes a teacher of only one part.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the goad (*aṅkuśa*) should fashion a goad out of *kuśa* grass and wash it with the five products of a cow (*pañcagavya*) on either the full moon or the new moon day. Having fasted for one night, the handle of the goad should be made to the measure of one cubit (*hasta*).
Having performed a grand worship, one hundred ghee lamps should be lit for Vajrapāṇi.

Having formed a mandala-boundary with a mass of light and having consecrated seven stakes with the *vikaraṇa* mantra, they should be driven into the ground in the four directions. Then, the site will be secured and the location taken possession of.
Thereafter, during the second watch, with a one-pointed mind and having assumed the cross-legged posture, [one should visualize] the hook.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and incense (43,
and having performed the protection rite and paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should take a hook in the hand and recite the mantra.
In the meantime, the sufferings of the hell-beings are pacified.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he rises up as a King of Vidyādharas with unimpeded movement, his hand grasping a hook. Upon seeing him from afar, all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and others prostrate themselves.
They perform [the rites]. When one who abides for the duration of a kalpa dies, he goes to the Vajra-abode and beholds Vajrapāṇi.

If one accomplishes the cloth-painting (paṭa), by means of its blazing, one becomes a vidyādhara. Having grasped the name of whichever mantra one wishes to accomplish for a kalpa, one should recite it one hundred thousand times; at the end, having fasted for one night, one should perform a magnificent worship.

Having prepared a fire with *arka* wood and kindled it, one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, he arrives; he bestows whatever wealth one desires and remains under one's control, as submissive as a servant.

Then, desiring to become Maheśvara, one should perform a great worship of Maheśvara, kindle a fire with *arka* wood at the southern image, and offer eight thousand oblations. A sound of "hā hā" will arise.
One must not be afraid; then he arrives and says, "What should be done? All the *vidyās* of Maheśvara are mine."
"May they be successful! Whatever boon you desire, that shall be granted. Having said, "So be it," he vanished.

In this way, one attracts Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others. This same procedure should also be performed for whomever one desires to summon. The rite must be carried out by one who has performed the protection.

Now, if one desires to summon a yakṣiṇī, one should take her name and offer oblations of aśoka flowers for seven days. She comes and grants a boon; on the seventh week she certainly arrives. Whether as mother, sister, or wife, she does whatever one requests. If she does not go [to him], her head shall split apart.

For one desiring to attract a *nāgī*, this same procedure applies using *nāga* flowers. For one desiring to attract a *yakṣa*, one should offer oblations of curd-rice for three months. At the conclusion, having fasted for one night and performed worship of the Blessed One, and having presented the *yakṣa*-bali and incitements to the *yakṣas*, one should resolve in the mind: "I shall perform the attraction of the *yakṣas*."

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *vaṭa* tree fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. In the meantime, Kubera and other yakṣas will arrive. An offering (*argha*) should be presented to them with red flowers. They will ask, "What must be done for you? and one should say:
294) [He said: "Every day, send a yakṣa who carries out orders. Then they provide one yakṣa each day;
his command must be given. They bring a woman even from a hundred yojanas away, and in the morning, they lead her back to that very same place.
They provide food for him when he is surrounded by a hundred [attendants]. Having mounted its back, he goes wherever he desires; it carries him.
It bestows an elixir (*rasāyana*). When commanded, it performs everything.

Now, one who desires to accomplish Vajrapāṇi should perform the preliminary service fourfold or sevenfold; having performed a most magnificent worship throughout the fortnight of miracles until the full moon,
and having performed worship on the full-moon day itself, he should feed the monks designated for the Saṅgha.
It should be rejoiced in by the noble Vajradhara himself; therefore, having performed a magnificent worship,

when the first watch has passed and the second watch has begun, one should sit cross-legged with a one-pointed mind, forming the resolve, "I shall behold Vajradhara," [and offer] pills of guggulu resin the size of jujube seeds.

One should offer oblations for one watch of the night. Then the garland of the Blessed One will move; the earth trembles; the clouds rumble; and all the *vidyādharas* rain down a shower of flowers. In the meantime, the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi arrives, surrounded by all the *vidyās*, headed by Vidyottama.

Surrounded by the vidyārājas, and surrounded by all the devas, all the nāgas, all the yakṣas, all the gandharvas, the kinnaras, and the bodhisattvas, he arrives. At that very moment, the intense sufferings of the beings in the hells cease. One should offer the guest-water (arghya) with scented water; then, one should remain prostrate.

Vajradhara will say: "What boon shall I grant you? Sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, entry into subterranean caverns, a kingdom, or invisibility—whatever is pleasing to you may be obtained from that very Blessed One. Or, if it is sovereignty over the Vidyādharas that is pleasing, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of all Vidyādharas with a vajra-body.

Like Vajrapāṇi, all weapons arise through mere thought. He remains for a great aeon (*mahākalpa*). When he dies, he goes to the Vajra-abode. This same procedure applies briefly to other vidyādharas as well—those mentioned in the *Vajrapāṇi-kalpa*, those in the *Avalokiteśvara-kalpa*, and those spoken by the Blessed One.

Those [deities] who are to be accomplished throughout the aeons—whether in the aeon of Brahmā, the aeon of Maheśvara, or briefly, in mundane and supramundane aeons—are all accomplished by this very sādhana alone. Great mantras that do not succeed when being practiced will succeed when recited together with this one; if recited for seven nights, it will certainly grant a vision. If, however, it does not...
It bestows [boons] and then perishes. If one recites it before the gods headed by Maheśvara, he grants a vision within seven nights; if not, [the result is as follows].
If one gives [these], the head will split into twenty-one pieces. During a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse,
substances such as ghee, vacā, collyrium, purifying items, wooden staffs, sacrificial threads, yellow orpiment, realgar, and so forth, should be prepared.

Now, for one desiring to accomplish the rite of the substance (*dravya*), one should take realgar (*manaḥśilā*), grind it with human milk, and fashion five pills. Having placed them in a casket of *agaru* wood together with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*), one should perform the practice during a lunar or solar eclipse after having made the offering (*bali*). When the mustard seeds begin to crackle (*ciṭiciṭīyanti*), then—

The first success is that which subjugates all people; by means of it, all worldly beings become obedient, and whatever is commanded is entirely performed. Then, when it smokes, one becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility;
one lives for an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*). When it blazes, then one possesses the body of a divine youth (*devakumāra*) with the brilliance of the rising sun.
One becomes a king of the Vidyādharas and lives for a great eon (mahākalpa).
In this manner, yellow orpiment, green vitriol, and other such substances are to be prepared.

Then, one desiring to accomplish the eye-salve (*añjana*) should take *śrotāñjana*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *kuṣṭha*, and sandalwood (*candana*), place them together in a copper vessel, and recite the mantra during a lunar eclipse until it emits smoke.
With eyes anointed by that, one becomes invisible, able to assume any form at will, and becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the sword rite should take a flawless sword and, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed an elaborate worship of the cloth painting and the offering of oblations, and having established the protection circle, should grasp the sword with the right hand and recite the mantra until it quivers. When it blazes and quivers, [one should remain] alone.

One becomes a vidyādhara. When it blazes, one becomes the king of all vidyādharas, possessing unimpeded strength and prowess; with those by whom he is seen and those whom he sees, he flies up together into the air.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the vajra should fashion a vajra made of *puṣpaloha* iron, sixteen finger-breadths in length and with three prongs on both ends; having anointed it with red sandalwood, beginning from the first day of the fortnight of miracles, one should perform grand worship of the cloth painting and recite the mantra daily, while feeding an increasing number of monks.

Having fasted for three nights, having installed the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*), having performed a grand worship, and having lit a hundred lamps of ghee, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass. Grasping [the painting] with both hands joined like a vajra and a mūdrā, one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth. Taking hold of it, one flies up together with a retinue of seven.

296) He becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas; possessing prowess equal to that of Vajrapāṇi, he lives for a great aeon (mahākalpa). When his body is dissolved, he goes to the abode of Vajrapāṇi.
In this manner, all weapons such as the spear, the discus, the arrow, the javelin, and so forth,

as well as the cloth, the sandals, the staff, the wooden [scepter], the sacrificial thread, and other items, are to be accomplished according to the procedures prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
For all of these, there are three kinds of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

Desiring to perform a rite for pacification (*śāntika*), one should prepare an altar in the shape of a lotus, kindle a fire with sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*), and offer eight thousand oblations of the finest cooked rice mixed with curd, honey, and ghee using a *sruva* ladle. Through three nights, peace is attained for oneself or another; through seven nights, for an entire village.

Or for a city: during an outbreak of a great plague, one should offer oblations of *śamī* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; during a drought, one should offer the "three sweets" (*trimadhu*). In all cases, supreme peace will prevail. Subsisting on alms-food, one should recite [the mantra] three million times. On the full moon of the bright fortnight during the *prātihāraka-pakṣa*, having fasted for three nights, [one should perform this] during a lunar eclipse.
Having consecrated black cow’s milk one hundred and eight times, one should drink it; it becomes a rasāyana endowed with excellent qualities.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *dūrvā* sprouts smeared with curds, honey, and ghee for ten nights;
untimely death is pacified, and one attains long life. One should likewise consecrate banners, conchs, and other such items.

Having seen or heard of an enemy army, one paralyzes it. Having prepared a new jar filled with water scented with all kinds of rice (*vrīhi*), one should touch and bathe someone afflicted by *vināyakas* with that jar over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times. Once consecrated, one becomes possessed of fortune (*lakṣmī*). By means of this consecration, one is liberated from all sins and performs the rites of the mandala.

By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one destroys all poisons with a peacock feather; by that same [mantra], one destroys fever, eye pain, diseases, and so forth. With a thread, accompanied by the mudrā and joined with the mantra, one destroys the mechanical devices of the asuras. [One should offer] fuel-sticks of khadira wood smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One should offer oblations eight thousand times; it bestows a great treasure.

Having descended to a river flowing toward the ocean, one should cause a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with red sandalwood to float away. One obtains a treasure equal in size to that heap of lotuses; it remains inexhaustible as long as it is being given.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. One attains enjoyments.

297) One desiring to bring the gods under one's control should offer eight thousand oblations of *agaru* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, three times a day for twenty-one nights, using rice grains.
One should offer oblations by combining curds, honey, and ghee; the food will become inexhaustible.
For the subjugation of yakṣas, one should offer oblations of guggulu pills smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. With *aśoka* wood fuel-sticks for yakṣiṇīs; with *nāgapuṣpa* flowers for nāgas;
with *agaru* wood fuel-sticks for the noble Vajrapāṇi; and with *damana* wood fuel-sticks for vidyādharas.
With an oblation of *aguru* fuel-sticks smeared with *turuṣka* oil for the *gandharvas*, an oblation of *kunduru* for the *pretas*,

an oblation of *śrīvāsaka* for the *kinnaras*, and an oblation of *sarjarasa* for the *vināyakas*— for all of these, there is an oblation of one hundred and eight [times] for seven days; for the king, one should offer one hundred and eight [times] [oblations] of royal mustard seeds smeared with oil.
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times facing the sun for seven nights at the three junctions of the day, one is liberated from all sins.

Desiring to cause the absorption of all vidyās, one should subsist on cow urine and barley gruel, fashion an image made of uśīra root, worship it with white flowers, and offer eight hundred oblations of milk. One should also bathe it with milk and offer agarwood incense over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times. Thus, it becomes replenished. By reciting it even once, there is protection for oneself.
Protection is accomplished for another by reciting [the mantra] twice, and protection for a substance is accomplished by reciting it three times.
Desiring to perform the restoration of those [mantras] that are severed, split, lost, or pinned down, one should fashion an image out of uśīra root,

worship it with white flowers, and before the cloth painting, offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with curds, honey, and ghee while reciting this Uṣṇīṣarāja. With reference to the vidyā, it becomes unpinned.
Having ascertained that the knowledge [of the mantra] is neither deficient nor excessive, one should write it on a birch-bark leaf with *gorocanā* pigment;

then, having consecrated one's own mantra eight hundred times and performed a grand worship of the Blessed One, one should recite it eight thousand times together with the Blessed One and sleep right there upon a bed of *kuśa* grass. [If it is] neither deficient nor excessive...
Having come in a dream, he speaks.
Now, one who desires to accomplish the lotus should fashion a lotus out of red sandalwood and perform a grand worship.
Having fasted for three nights, he should take that lotus in his right hand and recite the mantra until it blazes forth.
Then, accompanied by a retinue of twenty, he flies up and becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*, possessing unimpeded movement. When he dies...
Then one is reborn in Sukhāvatī.
Now, one desiring to accomplish the vajra should fashion a vajra from clay mixed with anthill earth and sand;
then, subsisting on alms, observing silence, and not looking back, he should take hold of the vajra and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.

A single-pointed vajra should be fashioned. Placing that vajra in the midst of white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), one should remain during a lunar eclipse. One should recite the mantra until the mustard seeds crackle and pop; then the vajra becomes empowered. By grasping that vajra, one performs all rites: it pulverizes mountain peaks and [dries up] the lakes of the *nāgas*.
It dries up [waters]; it causes rivers to flow upstream; it puts the *nāgas* to flight; it renders poisons non-poisonous;

it paralyzes all living beings; it deludes them; it casts them down; it pulverizes mechanical devices; and it paralyzes and pulverizes carts and the like. It performs all such actions as these. This is the power of the single-pointed *vajra*.
The means of accomplishment.

For one who accomplishes the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, no one whatsoever is able to create an obstacle; for even the Lord of Death himself [cannot do so] when it is performed according to the ritual rules, not otherwise. And during the time of reciting this, one should constantly recite the Buddha-locanā both before and after; in this way, gentleness arises.
Siddhi becomes manifest before one.

Then, having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses; Śrī comes and grants a boon, and bestows a kingdom. Then, if one should offer three hundred thousand, one becomes a universal monarch (sārvabhaumika) and becomes the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa. Having installed a painted image (paṭa) before the opening of the cave, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times.

All the mechanical devices fall away. One should enter without hesitation. Having entered, one extracts the elixir of mercury (*rasarasāyana*). Then, while staying right there, the fear of the discus of Viṣṇu arises. If one enters [again], it is reduced to ashes by the mere act of recollecting [the mantra]. One revives it by means of the mind alone. It never enters that [place] again.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should strike the big toe of the Blessed One’s foot with *jātī* flowers that have been consecrated once with the mantra three times a day. When a ray of light issues forth from the big toe and dissolves into the body of the practitioner, at that very moment his hair becomes curled like a ringlet; he flies up together with his retinue and becomes a king of the *vidyādharas*.
Abiding for an eon.

Then, having established the cloth-painting facing west on the shore of the ocean and kindled a fire with *nāga*-wood, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, dedicating them to the ocean. Waves will arise in the ocean;
one must not fear this as a sign of success. This continues until the Ocean appears in the guise of a Brahmin and says:
"What should I do? What should I say? [The practitioner says: "Become subject to me. Then, he performs everything that is commanded.

299) Having drawn a thousand-petaled lotus upon the ground and sat upon it, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. Piercing through the earth, one arises as a king of the *vidyādharas*, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand, born with a lifespan lasting for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
He becomes one who gives without hesitation; by his splendor, he illuminates five yojanas.
During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), one should offer one hundred thousand *jātī* flowers over the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of the Blessed One, the King (*rāja*).

Each flower should be consecrated with a single recitation (*japta*). This continues until a ray of light issues from the crown protuberance and dissolves into the body of the practitioner. At that very moment, he becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijña*). When recited one million times (*daśalakṣa*), it is as follows:

In whatever manner one applies oneself, if this vidyā is recited together with this very Blessed One, she will certainly come. If, while being recited by him, she does not appear in person, his head will split or wither.

And this single-syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin is the Tathāgata himself in person; who else in the world with its gods could be the king of all mantra-vidyās? It is the Tathāgata alone. Sitātapatra, Tejorāśi, and others are his retinue. For all the Uṣṇīṣa kings, the entire procedure for accomplishment (*sādhana*) is to be applied right here. All [of them].

And the Uṣṇīṣarāja is to be accomplished by this [mantra]. One desiring the supreme accomplishment should apply it without hesitation; if one hesitates, the supreme siddhi will not occur. In brief, all the gods are summoned by this. Furthermore, it opens up hidden treasures: having gone to where the treasure lies, one should take an unbaked jar.

Having smeared [the ground] with all kinds of perfumes and having poured white sandalwood water into a jar, one should consecrate it eight thousand times with mantras and establish it as a foundation. If the treasure remains [hidden], then that ground will crack open. If the treasure remains at the depth of a man's height, it should be touched with water; having dug down a cubit’s length, it should be seized.

Then, desiring to accomplish the rite of the lion, one should fashion an image from the clay of an anthill, smear it with *gorocanā* pigment, install it upon a pedestal, and perform a grand worship. One should recite the mantra until it moves.
Once it has moved, success is attained; mounting its back, with one's hair curled into ringlets, one flies up into the air as the fifth person including oneself.
He lives for nine thousand years with the lifespan of Brahmā, having attained the state of all vidyādharas.
In this same way, elephants, horses, and buffaloes are to be accomplished; when they let out a lion’s roar, then the gods tremble from their seats.

300) Having gone to a lotus pond, one should offer one hundred thousand lotuses; one obtains the sovereignty of a vassal king. One should perform a fire-oblation of one hundred thousand buds of red karavīra; one obtains a princess. [One should offer] jāti flowers...
If one causes a hundred thousand [offerings] to flow into a river that goes to the ocean, one obtains whatever maiden one desires;
all those supreme accomplishments (sādhana) will be perfected.
Wherever that Uṣṇīṣacakravartin goes, even Indra offers him his seat.
And all the kings of the gods, upon seeing him from afar, become afraid and terrified. He eclipses the splendor of all the kings of the gods within a range of a hundred yojanas.

"This Tathāgata Cakravartin—this Lord of the Devaloka and all [beings] of the aeon—are under the control of the Blessed One, the Single-Syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin. All mantra-tantras, together with their ritual manuals and in their full detail, are subordinate to him.
Thus spoke the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion, the Supreme among Men.

Thus concludes the twenty-fourth chapter, the detailed exposition of the ritual procedures for the Single-Syllable Universal Monarch (*ekākṣaracakravartin*), from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
301) The twenty-seventh chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana) and those residing there, [spoke].

Then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, along with the entire assembly of gods, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas, once again addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, this treasury of Dharma, which is the very essence of all Tathāgatas and resembles a wish-fulfilling gem, has been taught."

At that time, in this debased age, for the sake of fulfilling the aspirations of the worlds, when the Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa in a void Buddha-field and at the moment when the guidance of the True Dharma is disappearing—
at that very time and at that very moment— for the sake of protecting the treasury of mantras of all the Tathāgatas.

O Mañjuśrī! This One-Syllable Universal Monarch (Ekākṣara-cakravartin), when recited according to the ritual procedure, shall become the essence of all the mantra-tantras of the Tathāgatas and the foremost within your own Kumāra-kalparāja; it will serve as a treasury for your kumāra-mantra-tantras in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja). By means of this—
By reciting this, all the Tathāgatas, the kings of vidyās, become as if recited.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! In your own King of Rituals (Kalparāja), there was formerly a single-syllable [mantra] that was a treasure-trove, the very essence, the foremost, and the most preeminent. In a past time, in a past age, sixty-two eons ago—equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā—there appeared one named Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the worlds, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—
by the mere recollection of whom, and by the mere utterance of his name, the five deeds of immediate retribution are brought to exhaustion; this is certain.

Many beings destined for enlightenment will hear even the mere name; what need is there to mention those who seek the accomplishment of mantras? Furthermore, by all reciters of mantras, this Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarāja, must necessarily be brought to mind first of all.
And it should be spoken with words: "Homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra."

Then, having paid homage to Amitābha, Ratnaketu, and all the Buddhas, the mantras should be recited according to one's desire; they bestow swift accomplishment. For this reason, the proclamation of the names and the salutation of the Tathāgatas' mantras lead to the great increase of merit.

The measure of all Tathāgatas is fixed for him; he becomes one who is destined for enlightenment and is fully perfected in the accumulation of merit. He enters the rank of the Bodhisattvas, and the mantras grant him swift accomplishment.
302) This single-syllable mantra, which is the heart of all Tathāgatas and is esteemed by all mantra-tantras, was [taught] by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra.

O Mañjughoṣa, achiever of all karmic goals! In this King of Ritual Manuals (kalparāja) of yours, there is a supreme secret, most profoundly esoteric, which should be employed by people for their own benefit;
yet it must not be given to one who is not a disciple or to one who is unrighteous.
Likewise, toward one who has no faith in this teaching of the Teacher proclaimed by the Jina,
and toward one who is malicious, arrogant, and a destroyer of the Teacher’s dispensation.
It should never be employed toward those sons of the Conquerors who are not yet serene,
nor toward Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas who are incapable of receiving worship and favor.
One should certainly not give the mantra to such a person, for no success is seen for them;
[the recipient should instead be] faithful, gentle-minded, and devoted to the teaching of the Jina.
In that way, a bodhisattva who is constantly intent upon worship and favor will achieve success in the mantra proclaimed here in this ritual manual.
In the great one-syllable mantra assigned to Mañjughoṣa,
that Lord of the World bestowed this mantra which brings happiness.
It is the heart of all Buddhas and the source of all mantras;
seventy-six crores of verses were sung by the Self-Existent One in the past.
For the sake of the welfare of embodied beings deluded by evil, all mantras have set; they have taken refuge in the image of the Teacher.
Among them, this King of Vidyās, possessed of great supernatural power, is the very essence;
arranged as a single syllable, it proceeds eternally.
This limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi) remains established for the Buddhas who act for the welfare of the world;
relying upon the guide of the Dharma, this single syllable stands firm.
This mantra accomplishes all aims and wards off wicked kings;
it performs a variety of rites and brings all activities to fulfillment.
And it certainly performs eight thousand rites;
likewise, through the ritual procedure as prescribed, it bestows manifold prosperity.
303) This syllable *ma*, conjoined with the mantra, is the heart of Mañjuśrī;
known as eternally present within the syllable *u*, it has been set forth in the world by the Blessed One.
The King of Infinite Life and Wisdom has revealed the definitive meaning;
this was set forth by the Buddha for Mañjughoṣa through the power of his mastery.
Therefore, at the end of this age, when the Teacher has passed into parinirvāṇa,
one shall swiftly attain accomplishment through ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.
The buddha-field named Amitāyus was conceived;
there, that Blessed One, the Buddha, turns the wheel of Dharma.
He remains for immeasurable eons, having empowered his lifespan;
for this very reason, his name became Amitāyurjñānaviniścaya (The Determination of Immeasurable Life-Knowledge).
This Tathāgata, the lord of kings of all worlds and possessed of great supernatural power,
shall bestow the supreme and foremost mantra upon the wise son of the Buddha.
The eldest son of that preeminent offspring was established in a great station of vast supernatural power;
thereafter, this [teaching] was entrusted by that son to Samantabhadra.
Then that son of the Buddha indeed bestowed it upon Mañjughoṣa;
now I, the Tathāgata, shall proclaim its foremost ritual manual.
This indeed is that foremost of mantras spoken by Dharmarāja;
for the sake of the welfare of all beings, he proclaimed this mantra.

Homage to Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha; homage to all Buddhas, beginning with Śālendrarāja, Amitāyus, Amitāyus, and Ratnaketu. Having paid homage to these, the single-syllable mantra should be recited three times. And what is that? *Muṃ*.

This, O worthy ones, was spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, while residing in the world-system Amitavyūhavatī, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings,
out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit of the great multitude and those of the future.

Having observed the people and recognized that the time for the disappearance of the Teaching had arrived, he [the Buddha], for the sake of warding off wicked kings who would harm the Three Jewels at the end of this degenerate age, [appointed] his eldest legitimate son (p.

The [teaching] was given by all the Tathāgatas to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta; through the Buddha’s empowerment, it was given to Samantabhadra; and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra gave it to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. Then, by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—

Out of great compassion for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he established [the teaching] within his own form, residing in his heart. Having foreseen the future time— the period of the lowest eon, at the moment when the teaching is about to vanish— I, the final Tathāgata, [have appeared] for the purpose of protecting my teaching during this wicked age, the Kaliyuga.
He will perform this with the accompaniment of mantras.
I shall explain its ritual manual (kalpa) in brief. Listen, O Kumāra! Mañjusvara! Susvara!
This is your own majesty and the expansion of this ritual manual; I shall explain it in even greater detail for this sovereign king of manuals.
First, having ascended to a mountain peak, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and twenty thousand times; thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished.

One should do so while subsisting on milk, observing silence, with the mind focused exclusively on the mantra, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, and having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

It should be recited by one who has undertaken the vows of the bodhisattva restraint and has been initiated into the observance of the ethical discipline of the *moṣadha*. From that, the rites proceed. First of all, a cloth painting (*paṭa*) must be commissioned. It should be painted by an artist observing the *upoṣadha* fast, using non-adhesive pigments on either a clean piece of cloth or a wooden board.

It should be caused to be painted by a pure painter who eats the three white foods, wears clean garments, and has perfumed himself with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, in a clean place; on the fifteenth day at the time of sunrise when the moon is full and the lunar mansion is pure, it should be painted until midday. Beyond that, one should avoid it. Thus, day after day, until...
"It is completed."

First of all, one should paint the world-system of Amitāyusvatī upon a cloth; on a cloth measuring one cubit, or on a rectangular panel measuring four Sugata-spans, one should depict the world-system of Amitāyusvatī on all sides,
adorned below by mountains of ruby, sapphire, crystal, and emerald, and above them likewise.

Its appearance was adorned with a great jeweled celestial palace, its lofty form graced with banners and flags; in its center sat the Tathāgata Amitāyurviniścayarājendra upon a jeweled lion throne, teaching the Dharma, garlanded with a blaze of universal radiance, slightly reddish-white in hue, and seated upon a jeweled stone at his left side.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, holding a yak-tail whisk in his right hand, gazing at the Tathāgata, with a citron fruit placed in his left hand, and fair-complexioned like the Priyaṅgu flower. (55, p. 305)

On the right side, one should visualize the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, his body adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by a halo of light on all sides; he stands upon a precious stone, holding a yak-tail whisk in his hand,
with his left hand raised and gracefully positioned.

On his right side is the noble Mañjuśrī, whose body is dark green like the *iyaṅgu* fruit, yet white in complexion; he is adorned with all ornaments and a jeweled crown, wears a lower garment of blue silk, and has a pearl necklace and a jeweled sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). He is encircled by a garland of flames on all sides.

The youth standing upon a jewel-stone, his head adorned with five locks of hair and decorated with the ornaments of a young child; golden-hued, clad in a lower garment of blue silk, wearing a sacred thread interspersed with strings of pearls and jewels, possessing the gaze of a Tathāgata, and with a face slightly smiling.
One should have [the deity] painted with a gentle appearance, a beautiful form, palms joined in reverence, and endowed with the excellence of all marks.

Below him, the practitioner should be depicted according to his specific characteristic, dress, and posture, holding a garland of lotuses, resting on his knees and elbows, with his head bowed toward the corner of the cloth painting. Of the Blessed One...

Above, four Blessed Buddhas should be caused to be painted: on the right side, two—Amitābha and Puṇyābha; and on the left side above, two Tathāgatas should be caused to be depicted—Sālendrarāja and Ratnaketu. They are all of golden color, with light radiating in every direction and flames blazing all around.

Endowed with the excellence of all aspects and strewn with every kind of flower, they were seated only upon lotus thrones and not on any other seats, teaching the Dharma while sitting cross-legged, with serene countenances; and above the Blessed One, a form of the Tathāgata— hidden within a cloud, rising up and raining down a shower of flowers— was seen.
The one named Sunetra should be depicted, endowed with all the supreme marks, garlanded with a blaze of light on all sides,
granting a boon with his right hand, and holding the corner of his robe with his left hand.
This is the rite for the cloth-painting of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra. This is the single-syllable mantra of this very Blessed One.
He is the King of Uṣṇīṣas, the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, who rivals [the Buddha], possessing equal vigor and equal power.

The extent of its qualities, power, and majesty is inconceivable; it possesses great supernatural efficacy and great majesty. In brief, it performs all those extensive ritual procedures that have been taught for the Single Syllable, the Great Universal Monarch who is the Crown of All Tathāgatas. Even when not yet fully accomplished, it performs its activities merely by being recited. What need is there to mention [its power when it is perfected]?

It is accomplished. It bestows the attainment of desired fruits. One's wish is fulfilled. Whatever is pleasing to one's mind, by the mere sight of this cloth-painting, one certainly becomes destined for enlightenment.

306) By the empowerment of that very Blessed One, Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, he is called the Heart of All Tathāgatas; he is called the Uṣṇīṣarāja of All Tathāgatas; he is called the Cakravartin.
It is called the Great Universal Monarch; it is called the Heart of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta;

it is called the Single Syllable. In brief, its power is inconceivable. For the empowerment of the Buddhas is indeed inconceivable, and the miraculous display of the Buddhas is inconceivable—even when not yet accomplished.
Even for one who has not performed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), even for one established in the undertaking and consecration of all dwellings,

and even for one who indulges in all kinds of food, liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse— with the exception of those who lack faith and have not generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)— there is no accomplishment for these [latter]. However, for those who have rendered service to the Three Jewels, [accomplishment exists].

And for those who harm their diligent efforts, even minor rites do not succeed for them; what need is there to mention middling or superior accomplishments? For one who engages in the practice of all desired activities and modes of conduct, eight thousand rites—including the minor ones—will succeed when applied to the ritual procedures. And which are they?
First, recited once, it is protection for oneself; recited twice, it is protection for others; recited three times, it becomes great protection.

Even a Mahābodhisattva established on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is unable to disturb it, let alone other beings. One should wrap [the waist] with a five-colored thread over which the mantra has been recited four times.

The binding of semen (*śukrabandha*) is accomplished. Furthermore, he shall suffer no impairment of sleep. However, except by his own will, if he so desires, it may be performed alone during that very night; otherwise, it should be performed day after day. If he does not desire this, he should consecrate ashes seven times with mantras and touch the region of the navel. Thus, for three weeks, the binding of semen is accomplished.
Having meditated upon the Buddha, the Blessed One, and recited the mantra five times, whoever one touches becomes submissive.
During a lunar eclipse, while the moon is eclipsed, having kindled a fire with *arka* wood within the lunar disc (*śaśimaṇḍala*), even without a painted cloth (*paṭa*),
one should face the east and offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) near a royal palace.

In a dwelling of the gods separated by a river, or in a place not separated [by such] where the king resides, the fire-offering ritual (*homakarma*) should be performed nearby. At dawn, the king becomes submissive; he does everything that is commanded.
When he is no longer seen, his mind becomes fixed [on the practitioner], or he becomes sluggish, or suffers from mental distraction.

He recovers. A further restoration must be performed: one should offer eight thousand oblations of milk at whatever time or place. From that point on, he becomes healthy. This rite must not be performed for those who observe the *śrāddha* rites, who have faith in the Three Jewels, or who have generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). If one performs it [for them], it will bring about a much greater [calamity].
One would destroy a mass of demerit;
this should be done toward others who cause harm. One should see those with wicked minds and fierce minds day after day.
And [the gift] must be given. They become gentle-minded; if they do not, they are deprived of great wealth and their lives are left with only a remnant.

Furthermore, there is another ritual: during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood fuel, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter. At dawn, one becomes the sovereign king of the land;
he provides counsel on what should be deliberated upon and reveals the true state of affairs. Within six months, that which was to be instructed will be taught.
He gives a village consisting of a thousand households. If he offers the oblation at midnight, he obtains it in three months;

if he offers it throughout the entire night, he obtains it in one month. If he offers it every single night for a month, he obtains a province, or a village equal to a province, or whatever other wealth there may be. His enemies—
They do not prevail; if they were to prevail, there would again be karma.

During a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *apāmārga* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into the fire of a Brahmin’s enemy. At the conclusion, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *picumanda* leaves smeared with pungent oil. At dawn, the gentle Brahmins shall become the king.
He becomes hated.

There is yet another rite: during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with whatever wood is available, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter. At the conclusion of the homa, one should cast that ash in whichever direction the lord resides; he becomes submissive, whether it be at that very moment or at any other time.

He finds pleasure in [the practitioner's] enjoyments and provides assistance; he bestows a very small or even a large village, or a province. And the accomplishment becomes unfailing and certain within six months.

Then, with a mind full of anger, one of the four castes may go to some place of ill omen, or by means of a strange or prominent sign, he may approach a devotee of another deity among worldly folk; in whichever direction they reside, that very house he enters for him, and he departs for another region. He becomes agitated, or he flees at night, or his household [is likewise affected].
It is split. For the purpose of healing, eight thousand oblations of milk should be offered. He becomes healthy.

There is yet another rite: during a lunar eclipse, according to that same procedure, one who is pure should [perform it] before an image or painting of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, or before a book of the True Dharma, or before a stūpa containing relics (58, p.
Clad in clean garments and having fasted for a day and night, one should perform the rite with water free from living organisms.

One should prepare that location with dry, fragrant flowers, filled with sandalwood and saffron, and perfumed with camphor incense. Where the rite is applied—for an enemy of a Brāhmaṇa, with wood of the *palāśa* tree; for an enemy of a Kṣatriya...

Having kindled the fire with *aśvattha* wood for a Vaiśya, *khadira* wood for a Śūdra, or other woods for those other than these, one should perform that very rite. For a Brāhmaṇa, there are *palāśa* fuel-sticks;
for a Kṣatriya, *aśvattha* fuel-sticks; for a Vaiśya, *khadira* fuel-sticks; and for a Śūdra, *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.

Or one may perform the ritual with whatever other materials are available at the conclusion of the *rājyahoma*. Likewise, O Great King, one should offer fuel-sticks from the root of the *aparājita* plant; eight thousand oblations of clarified butter should be offered, and at the end, one should cast that very same ash in whichever direction the Great King stands, should he approach with a malicious intent.
Or, having bound the single-syllable mudrā of the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, one should cast [the mantra]. Or, having bound the utpala mudrā, he will turn back in terror;
or his wheel becomes broken; or some other great portent occurs;
or there is a great affliction and mental instability by which his speech is turned back.

These or other rites may be performed as desired. Having consecrated a garment with mantras, one should put it on; one becomes fortunate. Having consecrated one's eyes with mantras, one should apply collyrium; one becomes beloved by all people. One should perform the consecration seven times.
Having applied it to the eyes and the face in every respect, one should look into the face of an angry person; that person becomes submissive.

Having consecrated with seven recitations a gentle flower, fruit, or anything else fragrant, one should present it to the king; by merely smelling it, he becomes submissive. Or, whatever other being it may be, that being becomes submissive by the mere sight of it. In cases of pain in all the limbs, having consecrated [the remedy] one hundred and eight times—
One should bathe with warm water; one becomes healthy.
One should not perform these actions toward beings who are suffering,
nor toward those who are destitute, fallen, impotent, or observers of vows within this teaching.
One who has faith in the Three Jewels may perform such a rite;
however, one should certainly not perform the rite upon women, nor upon children, the elderly, or the sick.
One should not perform such a rite for one who is poor, suffering, of little merit, or born of a low womb; rather, one should employ it for a being of great merit.
One should perform such an action against one who is brave, reckless, greedy, possessed of great allies, great wealth, excessively arrogant, and fierce.
309) [These are ineffective] for one who hates the teaching, for one who is angry, for one who steals the property of others,
for one who lacks faith, and for all mantras, medicinal herbs, and yogins.
One should employ these rites against a king who is arrogant, evil-minded, and despised by the world;
one must avoid employing them against those who are righteous.
They say that another rite exists which has been abandoned by the Buddhas;
indeed, the reciter, when enraged, should cast that very ash toward whichever direction he intends.
The enemies stationed there become enraged, and the king perishes as well;
those people also certainly fall into a state of long-lasting exhaustion.
Furthermore, if a great plague or calamity is seen in that region,
one should not perform the ritual even if one has fallen into dire distress.
Within three weeks, all those lords of men there will perish;
once that karma is fulfilled, however, he shall destroy them within fourteen days.
In the first [week] there is distraction of mind; in the second week, illness;
likewise, in the third week, death; therefore, one should avoid it.
In the first [period] they flee; in the second, there is confusion of the region;
and in the third week, there is destruction. One should not perform such a rite.
The leaders of the world have taught that [these beings] are to be disciplined solely through their spiritual strength;
for these Buddhas of pure mind do not [rely] excessively upon worldly prosperity.
Action that obstructs the vital breath is censured by all the Buddhas;
one who recites mantras and desires supreme accomplishment should not perform such an act.
Rebirth in hell is seen only within these very realms of desire;
however, this alone has been declared as the arising of the fruit of black and white karma.
The majesty of the diversity of karma, as it has been seen by the best of bipeds, is capable of bringing about auspicious results constantly; even that which is dark brings auspiciousness to him.
Likewise, mixed karma is taught as being indeed mixed;
thus has this variety of karma been demonstrated by those who perceive reality.
310) The reciter should avoid that which is black or mixed karma;
he should resort to the white, auspicious [karma], which brings about the arising of the fruit of virtuous action.
By obstructing the life-force, the reciter of mantras goes again and again to hell;
therefore, the cessation of that [obstruction] is likewise Dharma—the supreme action of non-violence.
Heaven, as well as the accomplishment of mantras and an auspicious destiny, are attained through meritorious deeds; conversely, that which is contrary is said to result from contrary actions.
I have declared dharma and adharma, and the practice for the state of omniscience; one who always performs auspicious actions and recites [the mantra] should begin with the desire for accomplishment.
The mantras of that reciter are accomplished when he abides in auspiciousness;
for one devoted to white deeds, liberation is indeed irreversible.
The Tathāgatas declare that success comes to the minister through spiritual excellence;
however, the diversity of karma is taught for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
One thousand rites, or even slightly more than eight hundred, will be accomplished as desired;
however, one may perform minor rites, but the supreme one will not be obtained.
The middling [attainment] is accomplished with some effort through recitation and fire-offerings;
the inferior [attainment] is accomplished quickly by means of ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.
Threefold action has been taught: superior, inferior, and middling;
likewise, one who is of excellent form and an ascetic obtains the superior [result].
Likewise, one who recites moderately shall obtain moderate success in their actions;
likewise, one who recites little shall always be occupied with minor tasks.
One attains only a minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*), but shall not obtain any other accomplishment.
Furthermore, the recitation according to the measure of time (*kālapramāṇa*) is seen to be threefold in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Success is seen to be greater than great among those who are middling;
from small and even smaller actions, only minor success is obtained.

Thus concludes the twenty-fifth chapter, the detailed ritual procedure for the cloth-painting of the Heart-Mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, consisting of the Single-Syllable Root-Mantra, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
311) Now follows the twenty-eighth detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, [addressed] Mañjuśrī...

He addressed the Youthful One: "Mañjuśrī! There is yet another procedure for your cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), a means for accomplishment that fulfills the purpose of all rites. This may be performed with this very single-syllable heart-mantra, or with the six-syllable mantra ending in *vāma*, or with your own root-mantra, or with the six-syllable heart-mantra."

With the single-syllable mantra beginning with *oṃ*, this very ritual manual (*kalpa*) is to be performed before the cloth painting. In the future time, in the final age, when I, the Tathāgata, have passed into parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha-field has become empty, when the lowest of ages has arrived,
and when the world is without protection, without refuge, and without resort— this very king of manuals shall become a source of protection.
It has become a refuge, a shelter, and a final resort. And what is that?

First of all, one should first have the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni painted on a previously unwashed cloth that is seven cubits long and three cubits wide, free of hair, with its fringes intact, and treated with saffron and sandalwood paste;
[he should be depicted] seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma, together with Mañjuśrī.

Beholding the Youthful One (Kumārabhūta); on the right side, Sudhana, Subhūmi, the noble Akṣayamati, and Mañjuśrī, all in youthful form with limbs adorned with every ornament, paying homage to the Blessed One; and on the left side, Samantabhadra and the noble Avalokiteśvara.
One should have Bhadrapāla and Suśobhana depicted. The image of the Blessed One should be drawn as somewhat shorter [in stature].

Noble Avalokiteśvara and Sudhana should be made with fly-whisks in their hands. And below them, the Earth Goddess should be depicted, with her hands holding a jewel casket, emerging from the front part of his body. And above—

Two Vidyādhara youths wearing garlands and clouds raining down with lightning should be painted. All the Bodhisattvas should be depicted scattering flowers while gazing at the face of the Blessed One;
they should be adorned, with serene gazes, and shown seated with their upper bodies slightly bowed forward.
Having placed such a cloth-painting in a reliquary shrine (caitya), one should recite the syllables one hundred thousand times while facing westward.

Regarding this Mañjuśrī, one should observe wooden silence, bathe three times a day, change into three sets of robes, constantly maintain the *poṣadha* vows, and subsist on a diet of vegetables, barley-gruel, or whatever alms-food is obtained; having divided the food into four portions, [one should offer] one portion to the Three Jewels...
One part [of the merit] belongs to Mañjuśrī, another to all sentient beings, and the remainder one should utilize for oneself.

With a body that has not yet attained patience, having placed the Blessed One in mind and with a mind focused on all sentient beings as its object, one should contemplate: "I do nothing, nor will I do anything, for my own sake, except for the sake of all sentient beings."
One should perform the recitation (*jāpa*).
312) One should offer bathing water, perfume, flowers, incense, sacrificial food (*bali*), and lamps. [The ritual of] bathing.

One should constantly offer incense, flowers, and a ritual oblation beneath the shadow of the cloth-painting. One should first offer these to them in that very place; thereafter, to the Three Jewels, then to Maitreya, followed by Avalokiteśvara, Ārya Samantabhadra, Ārya Ākāśagarbha, and Ārya Akṣayamati Kumārabhūta.

Having first offered incense, flowers, incense smoke, and an oblation to Candraprabha, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the noble Vajradhara, the noble Tārā, the noble Mahāmāyūrī, the noble Aparājitā, and the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā, [one should offer them] afterwards to the cloth painting (paṭa).
One should give.

Afterwards, in a certain spot outside, one should fashion effigies (*vināyaka*) in the form of camels, donkeys, horses, and elephants using the earth from an anthill, and offer all of these to them without exception. Without forgetting, [one should also offer] oil-cake flour,
sesame preparations, horse-gram (*kulattha*), fish, meat, radish, eggplant (*vārtāka*), lotus leaves, and bell-metal...

One should avoid vessels. Seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, weary from that very [practice], one should cultivate the recollection of all Buddhas. One should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) mentally. Elsewhere, in a secluded place, one should prepare a bed on a spread of *kuśa* grass.
One should avoid excessive drinking, excessive eating, excessive wandering, excessive looking about, and excessive sleeping. Three times a day...

One should cultivate the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) and effect the retention of the seminal essence (śukrabandha). One should not disclose auspicious dreams to anyone else, but should report them to the Blessed One.

Thus, proceeding in due order and with haste, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. At the conclusion, one should recite the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*. During the time of recitation, one should perform the recitation while gazing at the face of the Blessed One or of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, with syllables and words free from confusion. And at the end of the rosary, one should offer a salutation.
Having prepared it, one should offer it.
Having performed the preliminary service according to this procedure, one should place the cloth painting in some healthy location and carry out the ritual where there is satisfaction of the mind.
The ritual for the cloth painting is completed.
Thereafter, one should have an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made of white sandalwood, seated upon a lotus throne, holding the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā in one hand and a fruit in his right hand.
Having placed that [image] facing west in a clean location, one should prepare a fire-pit in front of it.

One should construct it; for all rites, it should be square, measuring two spans in size, and one should place fragrances and all kinds of grains beneath it. Upon that, one should construct [the altar].

313) Having generated the new fire according to this procedure, one should bring all of the following— *aśvattha* wood for the fire, or *aśoka* wood, clarified butter, rice grains, boiled rice, milk, curd, and honey— and place them in a copper vessel.

Having recited [the mantra] eight thousand times, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Afterwards, on another day beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), one should perform the rite: having kindled the fire with *aśvattha* wood and seeing that it is free of smoke, one should invoke the fire: "Come, O tawny-hued one! O flaming-tongued one! O red-eyed one! O tawny-hued one! Grant [me]..."
Cause [it] to be given; svāhā!

With this mantra, one should offer three oblations. Afterwards, one should invoke the Blessed One: "Come, come, O Youthful One! I am intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings; provide me with assistance. Accept this incense, flowers, and perfume. Svāhā!"

Whatever he gives, that should be given by him. To one who has arrived, the guest-offering (*argha*) should be presented with fragrant flowers and water; thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). Having recited [the mantra] seven times, one should cast a single oblation. In this manner, for seven days, one should perform the nourishment rite with ghee, rice, sesame, and barley-gruel.
In the meantime, one will certainly see the noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a youth.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks, each two finger-breadths in length; day by day, this brings one hundred lords of the earth under one's control. If one offers one hundred thousand *jāti* flowers, the king becomes submissive.
It comes to pass: one should offer a thousand lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains wealth.

Having kindled the fire with *śamī* fuel-sticks, one should offer sesame seeds; one becomes a lord of riches. One should constantly offer water into the water; having risen in the morning, one becomes beloved by all people. [With] *arka* fuel-sticks...
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of [grains] smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains a village consisting of a thousand households.

One should offer oblations for the sake of having many sons; one obtains whatever daughter one desires. One should offer oblations of *apāmārga* grass; it pacifies disease. Having kindled a fire with wood from milk-producing trees, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds.

One should perform oblations. Whatever one contemplates while performing them, that one obtains. One who desires a kingdom should offer a hundred thousand lotuses; he obtains a kingdom. By offering a hundred thousand barley grains, inexhaustible food arises. One should offer guggulu and priyaṅgu together with clarified butter; one obtains a son. In a place where *akākolīna* grows, one should offer jasmine flowers into water.
Within seven days, one obtains a village. Taking each flower of the *jātī* jasmine one by one, one should offer them as oblations into water.
Whosoever is given the remaining fragment to smell becomes submissive merely by that scent.
Furthermore, having placed saffron, musk, cloves, and *jātī* flowers in the mouth, one should recite the mantra.

314) Whomever one consults with becomes submissive. Having consecrated *marīca* eight thousand times and placed it in the mouth, even if one is angry, one becomes beloved through one's speech. One should bind the topknot (*śikhā*) with this very [mantra]; one becomes invisible.

Upon seeing Śakra, one should recollect him in the mind; thus, one becomes free from anger. By constant recitation, one becomes beloved by all people. Rising at the break of dawn, one should offer water together with *jātī* flowers upon the ground in a clean place; one then becomes a master of mantras, whose word cannot be transgressed, and in whom fear does not arise when it has arisen in the mind.

One should perform [this]. Fear will not arise. Even toward another who is angry, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and having recollected [the practice], one should look upon them with liberation. One becomes free from anger. One should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with all kinds of fragrant flowers; whoever is the object of this rite shall become submissive. At dawn, one should drink water consecrated seven times with mantras.

One exhausts karma that is to be experienced with certainty. By washing one's face with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, one becomes beloved by all people. By consecrating flowers with the mantra and giving them to someone, that person becomes submissive. Through a single hundred-thousandfold oblation (*lakṣahoma*) of rice grains, one attains the status of a teacher (*ācārya*). Through [the same number of] sesame seeds, one attains the status of a regional ruler (*viṣayapati*). One should offer a thousand lotuses into the fire.

One obtains a thousand *dīnāras*. Having combined together *guggulu*, *sarjarasa*, *gandharasa*, and *śrīvāsaka*—purchased by means of a hero’s price—one should perform oblations on every fifth day for six months. When completed, one obtains a thousandfold return. Having fashioned an image out of all types of perfumes, one should cut it with a sharp, single-edged weapon; having cut it again and again...
One should perform the oblation. By [offering] the right foot of a man or the left foot of a woman, he whom one desires becomes submissive.
One should offer *dhuttūraka* flowers three times a day for seven days; one obtains cattle. With *arka* wood, one obtains grain; with *śirīṣa* flowers, horses; with *aśoka* flowers, gold.

With *vyādhighātaka* flowers, one obtains garments. Whatever one desires, all that is accomplished by means of an oblation of *jātī* flowers. If one offers flowers of whatever color into water at sunrise, one obtains garments of that same color. Having consecrated a vessel with seven recitations, if one goes for alms, one obtains inexhaustible alms.
Having risen during the night and recited [the mantra] over himself, he personally beholds auspicious dreams.

Then, one who desires to bring a king under control should take the dust from his feet, mix it with mustard seeds and oils, and perform oblations for seven days at the three junctions of the day; thus he becomes submissive.

Desiring to bring a queen under one's control, one should combine *sauvarcala* salt, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vārāhī* together and offer them as oblations; after seven nights, performed at the three junctions of the day, she becomes submissive. Desiring to bring a royal minister under one's control, one should fashion an image out of *bhallātaka* nuts, sesame seeds, and *vacā*, and offer it as oblations for seven days and seven nights.
He becomes submissive.
315) One desiring to bring a domestic priest (purohita) under control should combine *brahmadaṇḍī* and *śatapuṣpā* together and offer them as oblations.
After seven nights, performed at the three junctions of the day, he becomes submissive.
One who desires to bring Brahmins under one's control should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee; all will become submissive.
Now, if one desires to bring a Kṣatriya under control, one should offer oblations of boiled rice mixed with ghee for seven days.
For the subjugation of Vaiśyas, one should offer oblations of barley-gruel mixed with molasses; they will become submissive.
One should offer oil-cake as an oblation; thus Śūdra women become submissive.
Having combined all [the mantras] into one, one should offer them as oblations; then all become subject to one's will.
Having offered an oblation at a crossroads or in a solitary house, whoever is afflicted by illness becomes liberated from it.

If one recites [the mantra] while touching the face, the fever departs. By tying a lock of hair with [the mantra] recited eight hundred times, one is completely freed from all diseases. Having tied a lock of hair with [the mantra] for protection against all ailments, one should bind the topknot.

Having performed [the rite], one should sleep; all diseases will depart. One seized by illness is liberated merely by reciting [the mantra]. In the case of throat-obstruction (*galagraha*), one should recite over clay from an anthill and apply it as an ointment; the disease departs. In the case of eye-disease, one should offer oblations of indigo buds; it is pacified.
The ritual for the preparation of the cloth-painting.

According to the previously described procedure, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta should be painted upon an unbleached cloth that is free of hair; he is adorned with all ornaments, red in color, having the form of a youth, and seated upon a lotus throne. On his right side is the noble Avalokiteśvara, and on his left side is Samantabhadra.
Slightly smaller than that of Noble Mañjuśrī; having placed that cloth painting [in a shrine], one should recite the mantra ten million times, and one becomes a king.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks anointed with saffron; one becomes a king.

One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of agalloch wood fuel-sticks anointed with curd, honey, and ghee; one becomes a king. One should offer ten million oblations of jasmine flowers anointed with ghee; one becomes a king.

316) One obtains a heap of dināras equal in number to the heap of lotuses that one offers as an oblation. As long as [the deity] does not accept the recitation, for that long one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the vidyādharas.

If one performs a hundred thousand oblations of *bhallātaka* fruits, one receives a thousand *dīnāra*s. If one performs a hundred thousand oblations of *vyādhighātaka* fruits, one becomes a great lord of wealth. By performing eight thousand oblations with *guggulu* wood-fuel, one obtains grain. By performing oblations of sesame seeds continuously, one obtains an uninterrupted supply of grain. [By performing oblations] of cow-rice...

One should offer a hundred thousand oblations. Together with curd, one obtains a thousand cows. Having placed the fruits of the *bahuputrikā* and the fruits of the *śamī* together, one should offer them; one obtains whatever maiden one desires. One should offer *śamī* leaves; it becomes a granter of all desires. One should offer *agasti* flowers smeared with milk; this is for the subjugation of Brahmins.

One should offer white *karavīra* flowers for the subjugation of a Kṣatriya. One should offer *karṇikāra* flowers for the subjugation of a king. One should offer *dhuttūraka* flowers for the subjugation of a Śūdra.
One should offer one hundred thousand *arka* flowers, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, for [protection] from all diseases.
is completely liberated.

By this very rite, one should offer one hundred thousand fragrant flowers at the base of the feet; one will become eternally happy. Having kindled a fire with *aśvattha* wood, one should offer a thousand *śamī* flowers;
the affliction caused by the stars will be pacified. Having written the mantra with bovine gallstone (*gorocanā*) and bound it upon the head, [one attains protection].

He shall enter into battle; he will not be touched by weapons. Having placed Mañjuśrī at the head of the army upon the neck of an elephant, the enemy force is broken by the mere sight of him. Having fashioned the form of the Youth (Kumāra) at the top of the banner, seated upon a golden peacock throne, one should enter the battle; by the mere sight of it, the enemy force [is destroyed].

There is a break [in the ritual]. One should offer a hundred thousand jasmine flowers at the base of the [deity’s] feet. Right there, one should prepare a bed on a layer of *kuśa* grass. [The deity] will speak in a dream according to one's desire. Having offered a thousand lamps, one should make a single lamp with a wick made of lotus fiber, wrap it with licorice (*madhuyaṣṭi*), light it, and look [upon it].
One sees Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta as he truly is.

The second procedure for the cloth painting is completed. Having fashioned a youth out of gold or silver, with his right hand granting boons and his left hand holding the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, one should place such a figure before him together with a casket containing relics.
Having established [the image], one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. One should perform worship during the day.
Furthermore, young boys and girls should be fed in front of it.
