One should perform singing, instrumental music, and the recitation of books. Upon the completion of the recitation (*japa*), having offered an *argha* with three flowers, one should dismiss [the deity].

One should perform the invocation and dismissal according to the previously stated procedure; having formed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*), one should perform the recitation. The turning of the banner mudrā (*dhvajamudrā*) and the seat [are performed] with the svastika mudrā (*svastikamudrā*).

One should offer the *argha* with the *pūrṇamudrā*, flowers with the *ekaliṅgamudrā*, a lamp with the *manorathamudrā*, incense with the *yamalamudrā*, perfume with the *mayūrāsanamudrā*, and the *bali* offering with the *yaṣṭimudrā*. According to this procedure, one should perform these rites every night until the completion of the recitation (*jāpa*). Afterwards, one should perform the ritual actions (*karmāṇi*).
One should float a hundred thousand *jātī* flowers on a river flowing to the ocean; one obtains a kingdom.

Having made a heap of *jātī* flowers at night, one should sleep before the Blessed One; one sees the Blessed One preaching the Dharma, surrounded by bodhisattvas. Whatever purpose one undertakes, that very task shall be accomplished; it is not for anyone else.

One should perform [the rite]. Having observed the *upoṣadha* fast, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer oblations of *śrīvāsaka* incense mixed with honey; one will obtain a kingdom. If one recites the mantra ten million times, one will see Mañjuśrī himself, who will deliver a teaching of the Dharma. If one converses with him, he speaks face-to-face, and [the practitioner] becomes an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva.
It comes to be.
The third procedure:

One should have an image of Kumāra made of red sandalwood, with Priyaṅkara on one side and Vīramatī on the other, both resting against an Aśoka tree. Having placed it on one side, [one should perform the ritual].
Having fashioned an image of red sandalwood mixed with salt, *sarpapa*, and *rājikā*, one should cut it into pieces and offer them as oblations while reciting the name of a person;
that person becomes submissive. One should offer *udumbara* fruits while reciting the name of a person; that person becomes submissive.
One should offer fruits of the *kākodumbarikā* while reciting the name of a person; that person becomes submissive. [One should offer] *śṛṅgāṭaka*.
For the subjugation of a Brāhmaṇa, one should offer lotus roots; for the subjugation of a Kṣatriya, one should offer *kaśeruka* stalks;

for the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer lotus tubers (*śālūka*); for the subjugation of a Śūdra, one should offer eight thousand offerings of salt and sugar. He whose name one offers [these] at the three junctions of the day for seven days—[he shall be subdued].

One becomes subject [to control]. One should offer oblations of neem leaves smeared with pungent oil, eight thousand times, at the three junctions of the day for seven days, in the name of whomever; that person becomes subject. By means of this entire fire-offering, subjugation is achieved.
One should offer one hundred thousand *bṛhatī* flowers and obtain gold;
one should offer eight thousand *kālāñjanikā* flowers and obtain a large village;
one should offer *pāṭala* flowers and obtain inexhaustible grain.

318) One should offer *śrīparṇī* flowers as oblations; one obtains gold. One should offer *vacā* root smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one becomes a superior debater in all discussions. Having placed [the substance] together with the juice of *brāhmī* and ghee in a copper vessel...

One should recite it as many as ten thousand times; thereafter, one may drink [the water] and will conquer all disputants. If one takes a clod of earth, consecrates it eight thousand times while in a state of anger, and hurls it before someone, that person's anger will be released.
The fourth procedure:

On an unbleached cloth, free from hair, by a painter who has observed the *upoṣadha* fast, the noble Mañjuśrī is to be painted using non-staining pigments; he should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma.

On the right side is the noble Mahāmekhalā, and on the left side is the noble Prajñāpāramitā, engaged in recitation, adorned with all ornaments, and dressed in white garments. Below her is a lotus pond strewn with various kinds of flowers, from which two Nāga kings emerge, holding lotus stalks in their hands.

On one side is the noble Aparājitā, who destroys obstacles and hindering spirits; she has a face like a blazing flame and her eyes are knit in a frown. On the other side is the noble Parṇaśabarī, her hands busy with a noose and an axe, her eyes black and red, mounted upon the back of a peacock, protecting the practitioner. And the practitioner—
Two sons of gods (devaputra) should be depicted above, holding chowries, flower garlands, and drums in their hands occupied with lotus garlands, gazing at the face of the Blessed One Mañjuśrī.
Having placed that cloth painting facing west in a reliquary shrine (*caitya*) containing relics, one should recite [the mantra] ten million times.

At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed a great worship and caused the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā to be recited, one should recite it ten thousand times while gazing upon the face of Mañjuśrī. Thereafter, the cloth painting trembles; one obtains a kingdom.

One obtains the divine eye; one becomes a vidyādhara; by laughing, one becomes a cakravartin; by speaking, one becomes a bodhisattva who has attained the first bhūmi; and one hears his teaching of the Dharma.

In front of that very cloth, one should take cow’s ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, place it in a copper vessel, and recite the mantra until it becomes warm, emits smoke, and bursts into flames. By drinking it while it is becoming warm, one becomes supremely intelligent; while it is emitting smoke, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara); and while it is blazing, one attains invisibility (antarddhāna).

Flying through the sky: Having placed *vacā* root inside a pair of unbaked earthen bowls (*āma-śarāva-sampuṭa*), wrap it with jasmine flowers (*jātī-kusuma*) and recite the mantra until it sprouts. Having eaten that, [one attains the power]. (69, p. 319)

One becomes a possessor of the heard teachings (*śrutidhara*). If one recites another ten million times, one beholds Mañjuśrī directly, hears his teaching of the Dharma, and gains resolute faith in it.

Having had a hundred-petaled golden lotus fashioned and having placed the right knee upon the ground, one should recite the mantra until it blazes. As soon as it is grasped by him, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) among the *vidyādharas*, invincible by others. [Likewise, one may recite over] realgar, yellow orpiment, or collyrium in a casket made of *śrīparṇī* wood.

Having thrown it [into the fire], one should recite the mantra until it makes a *khuṭ-khuṭ* sound. As soon as it is grasped, one becomes the invincible lord of the earth-dwelling *rākṣasas* and *piśācas*. Taking a sword that is endowed with excellent marks and free from blemishes, one should recite the mantra until it stands up like a serpent spreading its hood; having grasped it, [one attains mastery].

One becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*, with a lifespan of an eon and invincible. Having encased realgar (*manaḥśilā*) in three metals and placed it in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra until it makes a *culuculu* sound; then one becomes invisible. As an invisible wielder of the sword, one performs all deeds associated with virtue, with the exception of those associated with sensual desire.

Having taken the heartwood of an *aśvattha* tree growing upon a *śamī* tree, having encased it with the three metals and placed it in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra until it makes a "culuculu" sound. One becomes invincible and lives for a thousand years. Having fashioned a silver wheel, one should recite the mantra before the entrance of an asura cave until the wheel pierces the mechanical devices of the asuras.

He enters. At that very moment, the young women of the asuras emerge. Having entered with them, he remains for an eon (*kalpasthāyin*). Having fashioned an iron trident, he performs the recitation (*jāpa*) at the entrance of that opening;
there, all mechanical devices (*yantra*) shatter. He enters together with as many [companions] as he desires, remaining for an eon.
It occurs; and one beholds the Blessed One Maitreya.
The fifth method for preparing the cloth painting:

having had an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made from white *arka* wood, the size of a thumb, one should offer one hundred thousand *arka* flowers; one will obtain the sovereignty of a neighboring kingdom.
Having fashioned [an image] from the root of the white *karavīra* tree, exactly the size of a thumb, one should offer ten million of its flowers;

the practitioner becomes a minister (*mantrī*). Having had [an image] made from the *karahāṭa* tree, measuring exactly one span (*vitasti*), one should offer one hundred thousand of its flowers; he obtains the position of a commander-in-chief (*senāpati*). [An image] made of white sandalwood...

Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī measuring exactly one *vitasti*, one should offer a hundred thousand *jātī* flowers; one will obtain the office of domestic priest (*purohitya*). Having had an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made from *aśvattha* wood, measuring the size of a single finger, [one should act likewise].

320) One should offer a water-pitcher at a place free from crows; one will become esteemed by many people. Having fashioned [an image] out of all kinds of perfumes and having offered flowers of every fragrance, one obtains whatever one desires.
If the mantra-practitioner offers oblations of *agaru* (aloe) wood fuel continuously and uninterruptedly, he will become honored by many people.

By constant recitation, he dispels the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*). At the time of death, he beholds Mañjuśrī, who delivers a teaching of the Dharma to him. Rising up again and again, if he recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he becomes invincible to all beings.

It comes to pass: having recited the mantra over one's eyes, one should look at the master; he becomes well-disposed. For whomever one performs this rite, [the result is obtained] in seven days if that person is present there, in twenty-one days if they are in another village, in four months if they are in another district, and in six months if they are separated by a river.

By means of the ritual procedure of one's own family and the ritual procedure of other mantras, one performs every action, with the exception of those associated with sensual desire and those involving malevolent magic.
The sixth procedure. Thus was it spoken by the Sage of old for the benefit of beings with little merit, concerning that which is intended for the end of the eon.
When the teaching of the ascetic Śākyasiṃha has disappeared,
one will attain accomplishment during that fierce and most terrifying time.
Indeed, the seventh [chapter] will be spoken here in this auspicious King of Rituals;
I have taught this ritual manual for that most terrible time.
Indeed, this path has been set forth for sentient beings of little merit;
it serves as the cause for the equipment of awakening and flows toward the way of the three vehicles.
At that time, in this age, I manifest skillful means for the sake of sentient beings;
for indeed, sentient beings are deluded by craving and agitated by passion and hatred.
To them, who follow the impulse of craving, I show this path;
yet they remain bound by the fetters of craving, even though their actions may be wholesome due to the cause of karma.
Likewise, the substances to be accomplished for the sake of spiritual attainments, along with the mantras and tantras,
were taught by the Leaders of the World for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings.
"Such is the majesty of this rite for practitioners who recite the mantra.
Having spoken thus, the supreme sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men, stood at the forefront.
321) Having explained in detail the power and efficacy of the mantras and tantras,
one should demonstrate unfailing accomplishment at that time, in this most degenerate age.
Then the Supreme Victor chose the Śuddhāvāsa heaven for the assembly of gods,
wherein this King of Rituals (Kalparāja) was proclaimed in full detail, O worthy ones.
This is the teaching of Mañjughoṣa for the sake of the welfare of the entire world.

Thus concludes the twenty-sixth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual procedures for Noble Mañjuśrī, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
322) Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, [addressed] Mañjuśrī...

He addressed the Youthful Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, there exists in your ritual manual (*kalpavidhāna*) a seventh section concerning the procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭakarmavidhāna*). At that time, in that age, at the end of the eon (*yugānta*), those who shall accomplish it will achieve unfailing success. Their fruits will be fruitful, bringing happiness and a pleasant maturation."
To him there will be success that is to be experienced in this very life, which wards off all miserable destinies, and which is certain to lead to enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke the heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
The six-syllable mantra, whose nature is the liberation from the six realms of existence, is inconceivable, peerless, and unequaled, possessing great supernatural power;
it is the deliverer from the ocean of all states of becoming and from the bonds of the fetters of existence and the suffering of the three types of pain.
Unbearable to all beings, it anoints all the worlds;
unassailable by all beings, it purifies the path of existence.
It brings about the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha, wards off all that is evil,
is rejoiced in by all the Buddhas, and produces every form of prosperity.
The most excellent among all mantras in the teaching of Mañjughoṣa is this one: Oṃ vākyeda namaḥ.

The ritual procedure for this is as follows: subsisting on a diet of vegetables, barley gruel, or alms-food, bathing three times a day and changing one's clothes three times, one should recite the syllables one hundred thousand times. Thus, the preliminary service is accomplished.

Then, on a cloth with ten uncut fringes, a painter who observes the *poṣadha* vows should paint Noble Mañjuśrī using non-adhesive pigments; he should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma, adorned with all ornaments, in the form of a youth, with his upper garment draped over one shoulder, and to his left—
Āryāvalokiteśvara, with a lotus in his hand and a fly-whisk held in his other hand, [should be depicted]; to the right, Ārya Samantabhadra;

above, two Vidyādharas emerging from the interior of a cloud, bearing garlands, should be caused to be painted; below, the practitioner (sādhaka), with a censer held in his hand; and all around, mountain peaks should be caused to be painted.
Below is a lotus pond.
323) Having installed a cloth painting facing west in a relic-containing caitya, having performed a grand worship,
and having lit ghee lamps, one should consecrate each of eight thousand jasmine flowers with the mantra.
One should strike the face of Mañjuśrī. Then, the sound of a great and profound *huṃ* is heard, or the cloth painting trembles.

By the sound of the *huṃ*, one becomes a sovereign king; by the trembling of the cloth painting, one becomes a superior debater among all disputants and the sole knower of the treatises of all the world. Should it not succeed thus—
One becomes capable of performing all ritual actions.
This is the first ritual procedure:

one should offer as oblations throughout the entire night sticks of *agaru* wood, measuring one and a half finger-breadths in length, soaked in *turuṣka* oil, upon smokeless embers of *khadira* wood. At the rising of the dawn, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī.
He grants him whatever boon he desires, with the exception of that which is connected to sensual pleasure.
In front of that very painting, one should recite this [mantra] throughout the entire night while burning sandalwood incense without interruption.
Thereupon, the noble Mañjuśrī comes in person and teaches the profound Dharma. One becomes devoted to it; having become devoted, one is liberated from all diseases and attains mastery.

Having fashioned a lotus made of red sandalwood, six finger-breadths in circumference and with a stalk, and having smeared it with red sandalwood paste, one should perform a thousand oblations by casting [the substance] into the fire and consecrate it a thousand times with mantras. Then, on the full moon day, having placed it upon a lotus leaf in front of the cloth painting and grasping it with the hand, one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth. By that—
Having taken it, one assumes the form of a sixteen-year-old, possesses the luster of molten gold, and has a brilliance that even surpasses the sun;
such a divine youth, honored by all the Vidyādharas, lives for a great eon (mahākalpa). When the body is cast off, he is reborn in the Abhirati realm.

During a lunar eclipse, one should take white *vacā* root, wash it with the five products of a cow (*pañcagavya*), and support it with *aśvattha* leaves; one should recite the mantra until it steams, smokes, and blazes.
It brings all people under one's influence and grants victory over all disputants; when it smokes, invisibility (*antardhāna*) is attained.
He lives for thirty thousand years; when it blazes, he travels through the sky and lives for a great eon (mahākalpa).
Having taken the ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, and having placed it in a copper vessel upon seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree,

one should recite [the mantra] until the threefold accomplishment is attained. By drinking that, one becomes a possessor of the Veda (*śrutidhara*), gains the power of invisibility, and the ability to travel through the sky.

324) Having placed a lotus seed in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra during a lunar eclipse until it makes a *culuculā* sound. Having encased it with the three metals and placed it in the mouth, one becomes invisible; when it is spat out, one becomes visible again.

Having placed the scent of cloves in one's mouth, one should recite [the mantra] six hundred thousand times; whoever he addresses becomes subject to his will. Subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, if one recites it one hundred thousand times, one becomes a *vidyādhara*. Subsisting on alms-food and observing silence like a piece of wood, if one recites it one hundred thousand times, one becomes invisible. If one recites it ten million times, Noble Mañjuśrī teaches the Dharma just as follows:
The Bodhisattva is one who is in his final existence; through constant recitation, there is an increase in all objectives.
Having fashioned an image of someone with all kinds of perfumes, if one cuts it up and offers it as an oblation, that person becomes submissive within seven nights.
If one should offer one hundred thousand pills of guggulu resin, each the size of a jujube seed and smeared with clarified butter, one obtains one hundred thousand dīnāras.

Having descended to a river that flows to the ocean, one should offer one hundred thousand lotuses; one will see a great treasure equal to a heap of lotuses, which never comes to an end. One should offer eight thousand white mustard seeds anointed with saffron; the king becomes submissive. [One should offer] sesame seeds...
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of items smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one becomes a great householder who bestows all things.
Having prepared a mandala with fresh cow dung and having scattered loose flowers upon it, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.

Then, one should have a volume of the True Dharma read aloud; within a month, one becomes supremely intelligent. [Furthermore,] having performed the rite one hundred and eight times with yellow pigment (rocanā) ...

One should apply a *tilaka* mark; one becomes beloved by all people. Having performed the consecration (*japta*) of the topknot (*śikhā*) seven times, one becomes invulnerable to all sentient beings. One should offer ten thousand oblations of *kirīmāla* flowers;
one is liberated from all diseases. If one recites [the mantra] seven times every day, one exhausts even karma that is destined to be experienced.
Then, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at the time of death, one will see the noble Mañjuśrī in his entirety before one's eyes.

Thus concludes the twenty-seventh chapter, the seventh detailed section on the ritual procedures for the cloth-painting of Mañjuśrī, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
325) Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists within your mantra-tantra..."

These are the places of accomplishment for all mantras, headed by the *uṣṇīṣas* of all the Tathāgatas and including the Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*) among the Queens of Knowledge (*vidyārājñī*). In brief, throughout the northern region, the Tathāgata-kings of knowledge attain accomplishment there.
In China and indeed in Mahācīna, Mañjughoṣa himself is terrified of him;
and whatever mantras he possesses will surely attain accomplishment there.
Indeed, the accomplishment of the Uṣṇīṣa Kings is seen everywhere there,
in Kāpiśī, Vakhala, and likewise in Udiyāna in all directions.
In Kaśmīra, in the land of Sindh, and at the junctions of the Himavat mountains—
having emerged in the northern direction— the mantras that lead to the highest good attain accomplishment.
Those songs which were sung by the Buddhas of the past, those now being set forth,
and those yet to be uttered by the future Perfectly Awakened Ones, are the causes of peace.
All indeed attain success there in this auspicious and blessed land arising from the lap of the Himalaya mountains; for the welfare of the people, I shall begin to perform a rite of peace.
Likewise, these mantras born of Padma attain accomplishment in the Middle Country;
success is also seen there in the Gaja and Umā families.
The mantra of the yakṣa Pañcika, that of Hārītī born from the yakṣa womb, and those mantras belonging to the gandharvas— their accomplishment is declared to be identical.
Then, [they were] constantly in the city of Kāśī, throughout Magadha,
as well as in the land of Aṅga, in the east, and throughout Kāmarūpa.
On the delightful bank of the Lauhityā, throughout the regions of Vaṅga,
there shall be the attainment of siddhi for Jambhala, as well as for those born of the Maṇi lineage.
On the shores of the ocean, on islands, and everywhere where there are bodies of water, the city of the Siṃhalas is beautiful; there the mantra-deities attain accomplishment.
326) Bhṛkuṭī, Mahāśrī, Yaśasvinī,
and Sitā— these are all the mantras belonging to the four Kumārīs in the great ocean.
They indeed attain success in that place, throughout the eastern region,
situated within the lap of the Vindhya mountains and all around Agra and Indraprastha.
Then Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī attain accomplishment everywhere—
in the depths of Śṛṅgāra, on Mount Kukṣi, in its caves, and in its forests.
There, the Vināyakas who create obstacles for those engaged in recitation [are present];
they possess the form of elephants, have many tusks, and are of great splendor.
Likewise, she assumed many forms of horses, possessing various shapes;
she was the divine daughter of Īśāna, appearing in diverse ways as a creator of obstacles.
Therein are seen the fields of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) where those mantras have been proclaimed,
as well as Mothers of various forms and most terrible planetary deities (graha).
The realm of the pretas is assigned to those who consume human food and belong to the Nairṛtas;
it is declared that the field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) is assigned to the King of the Pretas.
Therefore, one should designate that as the field of accomplishment for all beings from the beginning;
indeed, those of great heroism who are like the Vajra-krauñca will attain accomplishment there.
The foremost mantras of the Asuras, as well as other worldly mantras,
indeed attain accomplishment there, for they are based in the southern direction.
Likewise, one should always assign [the rites] to Yama, the King of the Pretas;
for then the mantras of the various castes, as well as those of the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas, will attain success.
Cruel mantras, commanded by Vajrapāṇi and others, are ineffective for non-cruel rites, such as those performed in sacred fields and the like; they are intended for cruel deeds.
Having gone to the southern region, those who have committed evil deeds attain success;
indeed, the ripening of inauspicious fruits is seen there in that direction.
Those mantras spoken by Āditya and those proclaimed as belonging to Soma,
as well as the mantras of Indra, are successful in the beautiful western direction.
327) There, the Lord of Yakṣas himself, possessed of great supernatural power,
the giver of wealth to all beings, shall achieve accomplishment for those who are foolish and deluded.
He bestows his heart upon living beings through causes seen in the ritual injunctions;
he becomes successful in the western region, possessing enjoyments and accomplishing all aims.
Renowned here on this earth by the name Dhanada,
he is the Yakṣa Vajrapāṇi himself, a Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
The foremost of mantras, the most excellent boon-granter, himself the sovereign of the ten stages—
by him all mantras born of the Vajra and Lotus families are indeed accomplished.
Likewise, the eightfold mantras are dependent upon the eight directions;
indeed, the mantras born of the Jina are accomplished in the northern direction.
Likewise, in the eastern region, the mantras born of the Lotus family attain accomplishment;
relying on the southern path, those belonging to the Vajra abode are accomplished.
In the western intermediate direction, Gaja is proclaimed, and likewise Maṇikula;
in the junction of the west and north, Siddhi is ordained among them.
Likewise, at the junction of the west and the south is the family of yakṣas;
and in the southeastern quarter are the śrāvakas of great majesty.
Among them, that which is called the "Family" (Kula) is indeed seen; in those places, success is achieved.
In the northeastern direction lies the source of the Pratyekabuddhas and the Jinas.
That which is called the Kula is highly esteemed in the world; indeed, accomplishment (siddhi) resides within them.
Furthermore, in the downward direction, all worldly accomplishments are attained.
The mantras that enter the netherworld (pātāla) are indeed perfected within the eight families;
likewise, the supramundane mantras, such as the Uṣṇīṣas and others, have been proclaimed.
Those [attainments] proclaimed by the Cakravartin Jina lead to success above;
however, for the Vajrin, success is achieved everywhere in all directions.
Likewise, all other kings of mantras born from the Lotus-Born One,
and indeed all mantras that bestow enjoyments, are always successful in every way.
Success is achieved at all times here, even for those of the Vajra and Lotus families;
this is designated as the field, and now that time is proclaimed.
328) At the beginning of the arising of all Buddhas, there was the mantra-siddhi proclaimed by the Jinas;
but in the intermediate period of the Buddhas, it arose from the lotus and the vajra.
For these mantras and for other mantra-holders at this particular time, success is said to occur through the power of time; it is not proclaimed to occur at any other time.
Through austerity, one may attain supreme perfection within three births;
likewise, for those who constantly recite the mantra, whose minds are devoted to it, and who have surrendered their hearts to it.
For those sons of the Victorious Ones who are serene, success is achieved even in this very life;
as well as for those devoted to the Three Jewels and adorned with the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
For one who abides in the vow, possesses great wisdom, and is proficient in the tantras and mantras,
the mantras are accomplished without effort because she is established in the vow of awakening.
The accomplishment of sentient beings' karma is declared to be the accomplishment of the self;
mantras are always already accomplished, yet they appear unaccomplished when sentient beings are deluded.
For this very reason, the Lord of Jinas has proclaimed this King of Rituals;
for the seventh [Buddha], the most excellent of Buddhas, has made the mantra extensive.
Then that chief of sages, the Moon-like Buddha of great supernatural power,
chose Mañjughoṣa, the eldest son of the Buddha, who possesses great majesty.
Listen, O Youth! to the definitive course of the power of mantras, at which time the Buddhas, the leaders of the world, are always sustained.
At that time, the accomplishment (siddhi) of the Uṣṇīṣa and others is proclaimed;
likewise, the Wheel-turning King (cakravartin) is proclaimed as a mass of splendor (tejorāśi).
Many [deities] such as Sitātapatrā and Uṣṇīṣā have been described by the Jinas;
likewise, these and other Uṣṇīṣas will be accomplished at that time.
When, in due time, a universal monarch shall appear in Jambudvīpa,
there shall also abide the Perfectly Awakened One, the King of Dharma, the supreme among bipeds.
"At that time, there shall be the accomplishment of all the mantras as they have been spoken.
This concludes the twenty-eighth [chapter] from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avatamsaka.
The detailed chapter on the rules for fields, times, and procedures is hereby completed.
329) Now follows the thirty-ninth detailed chapter.
Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having once again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, spoke.
He addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī Kumāra!
I shall speak of the previously taught state, the conduct of those possessed by spirits, and the auspicious and inauspicious signs."
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One,

placed his joined palms to his head, and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would speak of the noble, divine [incantations] for those beings who have entered into the bodies of other beings."

The Blessed One knows the mental activities of those such as siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, mahoragas, and others— beings who are human or non-human, whose bodies are fashioned by diverse karma, who rely on various destinies, and who possess many marks of manifold forms; the Blessed One knows them, the Sugata knows them.

"Do now whatever you deem to be the right time. Thus addressed, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta remained silent upon his own seat, having made his request to Gautama, the most excellent of Jinas, the Leader of the World, the best of Conquerors.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, spoke concerning the knowledge of the signs and marks of the mental conduct of sentient beings, as well as the [appropriate] time.
A sentient being who has gone to another world is drawn back by the application of mantras;
some, out of greed for food, seize a human being on earth.
Others, indeed with angry minds, and others due to former enmity—
these most terrible beings seize humans in this world upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, being eternally free from passion and endowed with compassion and equanimity,
they again take birth in this mortal world in auspicious human form.
A woman who is praiseworthy, auspicious, free from physical defects, and superior in complexion to men—
her union with the rising sun is said to be their "entrance" (āveśa).
Their incarnations occur at this time when the sun has set and it is night;
they are seen during the first watch of the night in the bright fortnights.
An incarnation is seen among those men who are always righteous, who perform auspicious deeds, and who are endowed with purity and skill; such individuals are highly praised.

Then mortals are possessed by those who are free from passion and possess great supernatural powers (maharddhika), in a pure place, among people, and under auspicious lunar mansions and stars. (80, p. 330)
On an auspicious day, under a favorable weekday, during the bright fortnight, on a propitious day.
When the lunar day is conjoined with a bright planet and fully endowed with its fullness,
and likewise when the moon is perfectly full, their descent is seen therein.
The sign of one who has entered existence, though free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power,
is that he leaps up from the earth and stands in the sky at the height of a palm tree.
He is seen seated in the paryanka posture within a fixed abode;
there are various divine and incomparable sounds, as well as those pertaining to Brahma and the Sun, which are pleasing to the ear.
That Great Being speaks from wherever he stands with a mind intent on causing affliction;
when drawn forth by the Uṣṇīṣa mudrās, he falls to the surface of the earth.
While standing with his feet not touching the ground, he should immediately offer the *arghya*,
mixed with *jātī* flowers, white sandalwood, and saffron.

The practitioner, having prostrated himself upon the ground, should immediately offer water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya), making this request out of a desire for their welfare: "I pray [you to accept my offerings]."
For when that being, whose mind is free from envy, is entreated,
he utters divine speech that is flawless and pleasing to the ear.
Then, being skilled and confident in the knowledge of mantras, one may ask whatever one desires;
at that time, one must not be afraid, but should instead call Mañjughoṣa to mind.
Having bound the five-crested mudrā and another born from the uṣṇīṣa,
one should then perform the binding of the directions— above, below, and across.
Then he will recount the entire sequence of events from beginning to end—
the start, the middle, and likewise the time— exactly as it occurred and as it will be in the future.
That one of great splendor describes the present exactly as it is;
likewise, with unblinking eyes and motionless, he gazes upon his terrified enemies.
The word uttered by him shall not be otherwise than true;
likewise, he knows the substance to be accomplished through spiritual power, as well as the womb, the accumulation, and the destiny.
331) Pratyekabuddhahood, Arhatship, and Great Enlightenment are certain; it is also certain for those fixed in the lineage of Buddhahood.
Characterized by the samaya, he shall truthfully declare everything: the absence of lineage, the time, and the powerful being who is destined for liberation.
The yogi should speak only of the characteristics [of the moment] and should not look toward any other time;
whatever he may pray for with a well-disposed mind, let it be accomplished in this very instant.
One quickly obtains all that, as well as the complete accomplishment of the mantra;
one shall attain every prosperity, exactly as desired and wished for.
Having quickly dismissed that [deity] and offered the approved *argha*,
the mantra-practitioner should perform the protection of the vessel according to the ritual procedure as seen in the scriptures.
Having indeed considered the fallen body lying upon the surface of the earth,
one should employ the Uṣṇīṣa mudrā and the mantra appropriate for the Jina.
With that very [substance], or with the five-crested mudrā, one should perform protection;
then, with a healthy body, the being [should remain] on the ground with the remains.
This protection has been devised for all beings who are possessed;
indeed, malevolent beings are powerless to harm those who have taken refuge in the worthy vessel.
Indeed, this is a great protection for living beings arising from the vessel;
his speech is proclaimed as being neutral in the Middle Country.
Having resorted to the divine womb, these other signs of those born of form are seen among the gods of the Form Realm, beginning with Akaniṣṭha.
Those who are lords of the desire realm and among the celestial dwellers of the desire realm possess a gait and appearance inferior to that, yet their speech is exceedingly sweet.
Then, having emerged from the earth and standing in their celestial chariots,
those inhabitants of heaven and the yakṣas addressed Kāśīpurī with words full of joy.
Likewise, the speech of the Mahoragas is proclaimed to be that of the Aṅga country;
the eastern speech belongs to those Garuḍas of great majesty.
332) Likewise, that speech which arises as being similar to the language of Vaṅga,
and likewise the speech of the Kinnaras— that speech is considered [as such].
The speech of the Yaudheya people shall always be the perfected lore for those bearing swords;
that same speech belongs to the Vidyādharas as well.
But for the sages who possess all forms through speech, that speech is capable of assuming any form at will;
indeed, that speech of the sages is conceived as possessing the five superknowledges.
That which is the Sāma riverbank speech and that which is the Harikelikā speech—
both the indistinct and the distinct— is indeed dependent upon the syllable *ḍa*.
Speech that abounds in the letter *la* is called the Paiśācī tongue;
it arises in the islands known as Karmaraṅga, where the Nāḍikesara flower grows.
Likewise, among the beings born on the islands of Vāruṣaka, Nagna, Vāli, and Samudrabhava,
as well as those born on the island of Yava and other such islands.
Speech that abounds in the letter "ra," speech that has become indistinct,
unclear, harsh, and full of anger leads to birth among the hungry ghosts (preta-yoni).
The speech of the southern region consists of Andhra, Karṇāṭa, and Drāviḍa;
that of the Kosalas, Aḍavis, and Sattvas; and that which originates on the island of Siṃhala.
Speech joined with the letter 'ḍa' and the letter 'ra' is known as Rākṣasī;
it is also spoken by humans dwelling in other continents.
Having spoken these words, he designated the fifth speech among the highly powerful Mothers as belonging to Vaidiśī and Mālavī.
The Vatsamatsārṇavī is fashioned by speech, as is the Śūrasenī;
there is also the Daśārṇavī, the Pārvatī, and the Śrīkaṇṭhī as well as the Gaurjarī.
By speech, the supreme planet Āditya and others have been designated;
however, the other principal planet has been conceived as Pāriyātrī.
In Arbuda, in the Sahya region, and among the mountain-dwellers of Malaya,
as well as among the people born in the Khaṣa valley— such is the nature of their speech.
333) Such speech is specified as being born from the womb of the *kūṣmāṇḍa* spirits; it arises from the letters ś, ṛ, ṣ, s, and is produced from y, r, l, v, and k.
The speech proclaimed with the syllable "gha" shall indicate the Dānavas;
it originates in the land of Kaśmīra and in the people's abode at Kāviśa.
All those born of the family are born from the Vajrapāṇi family;
the speech of all these foremost mantra-holders is thus intended.
Likewise, those situated in the middle of the lotus, having resorted to the *kulayoni*,
are seen to have speech, movement, and signs arising from the lotus.
Thus, the mantras of the Jinas previously described are conceptualized;
and those signs which belong to those free from passion are the signs born of the Jinas.
In whatever place the speech occurs, the movement and activity situated therein indicate that very being; one should recognize that sign in every respect.
Dwelling within the slopes of the Himalayas on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā,
Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Ṛṣis appear among the people through their speech.
Those creatures who are born in the valleys of the Vindhya mountains, on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā,
as well as those born on the Śrīparvata mountain;
Rākṣasas, Tārakas, Pretas, the deformed ones, and likewise the Mātṛs;
those of terrible form, great obstacles, and most dreadful planetary spirits (grahas).
Greedy for taking the lives of others, she arises from the speech of those people;
whatever are the signs in that region, such are the movements and behaviors in that land.
The speech and the utterances of those possessed by the wicked,
as well as their various movements— these and many others are the manifestations of their actions and gestures.
And having forms of various shapes and marked with diverse signs,
it is seen as the various wombs for the foremost among the various classes of beings.
One should perform this rite, characterized by these signs and marked by the [proper] course of action,
for all human beings, as it brings them happiness.
334) For the sake of protection, the youth Viśvasambhava should be employed;
the reciter should perform this by means of the six-syllable mantra itself.
When joined with Mahāmudrā,
and placed upon the five locks of hair, it will become a great protection.

Thus concludes the twenty-ninth chapter, the detailed exposition of the ritual procedure for the activity of those possessed by spirits, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
335) Now follows the thirty-second detailed chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [spoke].
He addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists within all your mantras an entry into all tantras,
a secret of all vidyās, which brings about the arising of the fruits of various qualities and portions over many times, as well as the signs of its continuity."
I shall now explain the means of accomplishment according to their measure. That is to say:
accomplishment may be attained in another birth; accomplishment does not depend on the cause of time.
As for the application of that measure, it arises from what was previously connected.
Success comes from being attentive to what is beneficial; it arises from rational investigation.
The principle of taking refuge in your son is seen by all embodied beings.
In this context, previously performed karma is designated as "reasoning" (yukti).
Through its application, the wise person shall attain supreme accomplishment by means of reasoning.
An unaccomplished action is brought to completion; there is no accomplishment without action.
When joined with both the object and the agent, accomplishment is conceived through their union.
He attained the supreme state through the cause of acting according to the prescribed rule;
he did not choose counsel from a minister, for one who lacks counsel would become like a non-minister among ministers.
In the practice of the ritual of silence, one attains abundant success;
the reciter, through the collection of seed-syllables, brought forth the highest wisdom.

One who is free from worldly attachment shall attain the first goal, the most excellent state of space; through the absence of attachment to space, being established in one's own self, one shall attain the wealth of immortality.
In brief, for one who desires success at the wrong time,
there is no success in the mantras— regardless of their signs— even for Śakra himself.
Furthermore, for one who acts harmfully toward living beings and advances at the wrong time,
no success is seen, even for a high-souled Brahmin.
Overcome by lethargy and thirst, possessed by intoxication and pride, characterized by laxity and arrogance, he is constantly devoted to vulgar company.
336) For one who is lazy and joined with a wife, how could there be success? If [the mantras] belong to the teachers of the gods, then they belong to the asuras.
They too are unable to accomplish the mantra if it is devoid of the prescribed rules;
likewise, a ritual action lacking the proper procedure causes confusion of the mind.
Therefore, one should not mutter that mantra without the proper application or the prescribed rite;
such [practices] produce a delusion of vision in the ignorant.
But the deluded fools fall from there into a most miserable state;
therefore, those who hold the mantras rescue them from that once again.
Then, in due order, they bestow accomplishment and an auspicious rebirth; thereafter, those mantras establish that reciter upon the immovable mountain of Śiva.
Thus, the Tathāgatas have declared that the recitation of mantras is unfailing;
even when the mind is deluded by false views, it is employed solely for the sake of bringing about grace.
These indeed are the spiritual friends; these are those who are affectionate toward sentient beings.
For them, the auspicious equality of the three vehicles is taught as the accomplishment.
Therefore, with all effort and with a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra;
for mantras employed by mantra-reciters through improper application [are ineffective].
Liberation from saṃsāra is held to occur only after a long time;
it is seen that the accomplishment of mantras is achieved only after a very long period has passed.
For mantras employed according to the prescribed rules indeed attain success quickly;
one perceives the accomplishment of their fruit, for a mantra is not said to be fruitless.
In this very life, the mantras are perfected, arising together with their fruits;
there is no accomplishment without the action that brings the fruit, nor is action ever intended to be without fruit.
The fruit arises from the conjunction with karma; thus karma is said to be fruitful. That which is born from it is produced by recitation, arising in the sky as a non-existent manifestation.
Those of peaceful disposition are liberated through the auspiciousness pointed out by the world;
such is the greatness of the destination attained by those who follow the path of the Buddha.
337) Even in this age of adversity, success is seen for him as well;
success may occur in this very life, or it may manifest at the end of the birth.
Until there is the ultimate peace, the unconditioned path of Śiva—
that most stainless state of Śiva which is pointed out by the world.
Buddhahood, however, is luminous and revealed in every way by all beings;
the attainment of mantra-siddhi is said to be its very limit, indeed its end.
The non-existence that is unmanifest, which arises within each individual,
has been described in the world by the Moon-like Sages of great supernatural power as being [revealed] through mantras.
Direct accomplishment is ordained for embodied beings even in this very life;
when the mantra enters one who knows reality in the empty field, it brings about Buddhahood.
When the time of the Kali age has arrived and the Knower of Reality has attained peace,
mantras will not quickly bring success for those who desire their goals.
At that time, one who knows the mantras and tantras should accomplish [the goal] through application and ritual action as seen in the rules, according to the teaching spoken by the Sage.
When the Tathāgata remains, supreme accomplishment is swiftly attained;
likewise, during the intermediate period, middling accomplishment is proclaimed.
When the time of the end of the age has arrived, it is called the lowest accomplishment;
whereas in a beautiful age and at an auspicious time, there is likewise the power of flying through the sky.
The accomplishment of all mantras has been taught by the Leaders of the World;
at that time, that foremost of the families of the Lords of Jinas will be successfully accomplished.
In the middle age, accomplishment belongs to the Lotus family; at the end of the age, however, it belongs to the Vajra family.
By the power of their past aspirations, certain mantras are accomplished at all times.
Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, and the King of Yakṣas—
all the yakṣas who move among humans— attain accomplishment at all times.
Those mantras and others that are employed by all the deities,
as well as those worldly ones clearly marked [by specific signs], attain accomplishment in the time of the Kali Yuga for those possessed of passion.
338) It was proclaimed by gods and humans, by lords of the Dānavas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
and also by ṛṣis, garuḍas, piśācas, hosts of bhūtas, and grahas.
Both human and non-human beings, belonging to the realm of desire—
those possessing great supernatural powers and merit, as well as those of cruel deeds and most terrible nature.
By Śakra, Brahmā, and likewise by Rudra, by Īśāna and others,
and by Viṣṇu along with all the beings, mantras of great supernatural power have been proclaimed.
Even they attain accomplishment for those who recite mantras at that end of the eon;
likewise, accomplishment in fierce rites occurs at that time of great terror.
On this earth, the accomplishment of subjugating, attracting, or [dealing with] flesh-eating spirits is seen to be fruitless and is condemned as leading to the next world.
Therefore, at that time of great terror, the Lord of Jinas,
intent on benefiting sentient beings, was instructed by Mañjughoṣa.
Then those beings who recite mantras will perish,
even though they have faith in this teaching and are worshippers of the Three Jewels.

Thus concludes the thirtieth chapter, the detailed exposition on the rules, regulations, and timing, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
339) Now follows the thirty-third chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [spoke].
He addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "In your *Mañjuśrī-kalparāja*,
which is fully proclaimed as the *Dharmadhātukośa-tathāgatagarbha-dharmadhātu-niṣpanda-anucarita*,
in this detailed exposition of the chapter on the supreme jewel of the Great Sūtra, authorized as the supreme secret of the Tathāgatas, and wherein the mantra-rites are being accomplished."

The various sounds of all beings, which serve as the means for accomplishment, are separated by signs, knowledge, marks, time, and measure; they are the resonances of the perceptions of both non-sentient and sentient beings.
It is said that there is verbal knowledge, and non-verbal knowledge is likewise proclaimed;
furthermore, the practice of mantras through reasoning is mixed—thus the activity is threefold.
Endowed with divine sounds, employed for the sake of impermanence,
forever free from incorrect words, and adorned with the meaning of refined linguistic usage.
In all established doctrines, the noble mantras are proclaimed;
they are eternally devoid of referential objects, yet they are divided into three types.
Adorned with heavy, light, and medium syllables,
that mantra-deity shall indeed be embellished with vowels and meters.
The discourse on the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as the meaningful and the meaningless, according to others;
likewise, the meaning of the elements, the logical reasoning, and that which is adorned with the meaning of the mantras of the destinies.
The speech of all worldly mantras is abundant in conceptual construction;
it consists of one or two syllables, follows metrical rules, and possesses the accents of svarita and ālaya.
The accomplishment of the letters is held to occur at the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, as well as the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth [vowels].
These syllables, which are the causes of all letters, are joined with ten vowels;
indeed, these syllables are seen on the surface of the earth as being multiplied tenfold.
From one hundred syllables down to twenty, and even unto a single syllable—
by these measures of letters is the perfection of mantra composed.
Mantras endowed with four lines accomplish all purposes;
for those mantras spoken by the Jina are the most excellent, preeminent, and noble.
340) But those [teachings] are middling and inferior... at that time;
however, those which were spoken by their own sons, the sons of the Conquerors, are indeed the middling ones.
Those mantras which are indeed spoken by all worldly beings are inferior;
those mantras spoken by the Nairṛtas are said to be base.
The measure of these mantras spoken by the Noble Ones and the Victors is ten, eighteen, twenty-eight, twenty, or even up to more than a hundred.
The number of syllables in these mantras, as proclaimed by the Bodhisattvas, ranges from one or two syllables up to five hundred syllables.
The application of mantras is declared to be arranged within those syllables;
the meters are joined with vowels and adorned with the meanings of verbal roots and their significations.
Indeed, even a well-employed statement endowed with the principles of tantra may sometimes result in success, provided it is not devoid of the correct phonemes and accents.
Accompanied by mudrās and sounds, [the practice] proceeds from the head to the end of the sibilants (ūṣman) and the palate;
the sound emanates from the teeth, lips, and throat—this is the ritual of accomplishment.
But that which is well-applied is declared to be free from the unmanifest;
one who employs it correctly will accomplish the word as a complete utterance.

A mantra that deviates from the prescribed rules, is devoid of ritual action, and is separated from its proper sounds and meanings, will not achieve success quickly; it requires a long period of time.
For that reciter, success is never fruitless; his recitation is not performed in vain.
Even in another birth, the granting of boons through the perfection of mantras is seen.
Through the power of that mantra, and because it has been recited for a long time by those who chant it,
the mantra makes the ritual action unfailing for people who know the mantras and employ them with the mantra.
It is inferior to all mantras— those that are worldly or human,
those spoken by all spirits, and those that are characterized by envy.
Their syllables are said to be one, two, or three in number,
expressed through various Mleccha languages as well as those proclaimed in the divine tongue.
They are always composed as strings, arranged in sequences, and intermingled according to their sounds;
they range from one thousand, eight hundred, eight, down to even a single syllable.
341) That which has four feet or half a foot is declared to be prose and verse; it is described as consisting of *ślokas*, *daṇḍakas*, and so forth, along with *gāthās*, *skandhakas*, and *pañcikas*.
The reasoning of the counter-argument, adorned with thousands of meanings,
discriminates between words in Apabhraṃśa and Saṃskṛta that are devoid of meaning.
When the unmanifest is joined with that which is devoid of manifestation and devoid of measures,
the accomplishment of mantra is said to occur through the dissociation from [specific] destinations and locations.
This is the characteristic of all mantras:
those mantras which abound in the letter *śa* and are adorned with the meaning of the syllable *oṃ*.
Success will certainly be attained for those who abide by the tantra characterized by the letter *ta*;
likewise for those mantras which begin with the syllable *oṃ* and end with the letter *ma*.
That which is joined with the letter *śa* is fruitful and likewise auspicious;
it has the form of the square letter *ta*, and is devoid of the final letters of the *pratyāhāra*.
The syllable *takāra* joined with the letter *repha* (ra), together with the mantra, is the rite of accomplishment;
it is the first, abounding in two *rephas*, arising from the quality of the *huṃ* syllable.
Within the square enclosure of the letter *va*, the phonemes are capable of accomplishment;
it consists of the letter *ka* joined with *ra*, ending in *ma*, and interspersed with the vowel measures (*mātrā*).
The mantra that begins with the syllable *ma* followed by the syllable *na* is said to be the most excellent;
it is seen in all tantras to abound with the syllable *ta*.
That mantra is said to be Saumya; that which is adorned with the syllable *huṃ* is Yāmya;
and that which abounds in the syllable *bha* is said to be Aindrāvāyavya.
They say that the letter *ca* belongs to Varuṇa and is beneficial and nourishing in this world;
a mantra in which the letter *va* predominates is seen to belong to Mahendra.
The mantra that proceeds with the initial going for refuge to the Three Jewels,
as well as the salutation, brings about peace and bestows happiness.
That other [mantra] is employed for the purpose of paying homage to all the deities;
one's own mantra and the Lord of Mantras—that mantra performs all rites.
342) Any mantra that abounds in the syllable *ḍa*, and which is uttered with *phaṭ* and *huṃ*,
these mantras are extremely fierce, radiant, and possessed of great power.
Because it immediately obstructs the vital breath when employed against cruel beings, one should not perform sinful actions, especially those that are particularly harmful.
The reciter should avoid that, because it has always been avoided by the sages;
for even in both matters, the mantras for pacification and nourishment are accomplished.
In an instant, they accomplish all actions as many as have been spoken;
for these mantras, when well-recited, are powerful and possess great supernatural efficacy.
One should perform peaceful rites with those spoken by the Jina;
however, one should perform all enriching rites within the Kokanada family.
All evil deeds are employed in the rite of sorcery;
however, one should perform all rites of sorcery by means of the Vajra family.
Prohibited by the Lords of the World, yet revealed by the Lord of Yakṣas for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, it arises from the majesty of mantra.
The threefold [teaching] has indeed been explained everywhere within the three families;
those which are declared as the eight foremost families by the Sage himself—
Among them, accomplishment (siddhi) proceeds in three ways; it is declared to be of three kinds:
superior, middling, and inferior, and thus it is divided into these three.
Pacifying (śāntika), enriching (pauṣṭika), and also subjugating (ābhicāruka) rites are intended;
the application of mantra alone is declared to be the application of tantra.
The power of the movement of mantras is employed for malevolent rites (*ābhicāruka*);
however, this action is inferior and is censured by the omniscient ones.
One should not perform an action that obstructs life, even when fallen into distress;
however, the greatness of action has been described here only in brief.
The procedure for the application of tantras through mantras, with its extensive elaboration of ritual actions,
is taught here in the *Karmarāja*, though it is also seen in other tantras.
343) However, one who possesses the proper method among all mantras does not employ that which is devoid of ritual action;
this applies to as many worldly mantras as there are, whether they be *sakala* (with parts) or *niṣkala* (without parts).
All [these] are indeed supramundane, and their qualities are always immeasurable; the accomplishment of mantra is likewise proclaimed to be immeasurable.
Although it has been stated that [the numbers] begin with the single count up to twenty, nevertheless,
thereafter thirty is mentioned in brief, as well as another forty.
Then, they say there are sixty-three, and likewise seventy;
another ten, and another eighty in number.
They say that ten times ten is ninety; a full hundred is ten times more than that.
The count of a hundred is established, and ten times that is a thousand.
Ten thousand is an ayuta; ten ayutas are a lakṣa;
ten lakṣas are a vilakṣa; and ten vilakṣas are a koṭi.
Ten arbudas are said to be a nirarbuda; ten of those are intended to be a khaḍga.
Ten *khaḍga* is a *nikhaḍga*; ten *nikhaḍga* is considered a *kharva*. Ten *nikharva* is a *padma*, and ten *padma* is a *mahāpadma*.
Ten padmas constitute a vāha; likewise, ten vāhas make another unit called a vivāha;
ten vivāhas make a mahāvivāha; and ten times that is said to be a māya.
The tenth stage of that is Mahāmāyā; beyond Mahāmāyā is the next stage, Samudra, which has been designated by the Leaders of the World as the knowledge of calculation.
After that, one should complete the Mahāsamudra for twenty-five [verses];
thus indeed is the Mahāsamudra described, followed by the Sāgara with ten [verses].
They say that by adding half of twenty, one reaches the *mahāsāgara*;
and by multiplying ten *mahāsāgaras*, it is thus called the *pravarā*.
Ten *pragharas* are said to be one *ghara*; that is proclaimed as such. Ten *gharas* are also called by the name *nāma*, and all of that is described in its entirety.
344) When the *aśeṣa* is multiplied by twenty-five, it becomes the *mahāśeṣa*;
that is declared by the Leaders of the World to be the measure of the *asaṅkhya*.
They say that ten times the number is "asaṅkhya" (incalculable); that asaṅkhya multiplied [tenfold] is "parārdha.
Beyond that, it is likewise... [repeated].
That world is proclaimed to be a thousandfold greater than Amitā;
beyond that world is Mahāloka, which is multiplied [in extent] by the same factor as Mahāloka.
Then, that which is called "complete darkness" is expressed by *tamas*; light is expressed by *jyotis*.
Having multiplied the light by ten million, that great mass is called *mahārāśi*.
From a great heap comes what is called a "great heap"; from a heap, the profound is said to arise.
They say that the profound is stable; from stability, one should proceed to even greater stability.
Beyond that, by means of great understanding, the highly esteemed state is described; those who are devoted to the knowledge of calculation call it the "state beyond the state."
From there, one should go to Mahāsthāna; Mahāsthāna is considered to be "the measured place. Having made the measured equal to the measured, it is proclaimed as being of great significance.
From Mahārtha, one should go to Suśrutasthāna, and from there to Mahārṇava;
they say that Mahārṇava is the first, for it is indeed more primary than the first.
They say that from the first comes the "Excellent" (śreṣṭha); from the Excellent, it is said to end with the "Eldest" (jyeṣṭha).
From the Eldest comes that which is named "Wine of the Temple" (mandirasa), which is proclaimed as inconceivable.

The inconceivable is the most excellent among those seeking the inconceivable; from the terrible, the kingdom is desired as more terrible. Beyond the kingdom is the one who is cast down, and beyond the one who is cast down is auspiciousness.
Beyond the auspicious, the Great Consciousness (mahācetaḥ) will be cognized as the Great Consciousness;
that which is the distraction of the mind is called "consciousness" (cetas), and it is described as being expressible.
The expressible and the inexpressible are indeed called "with sound" (svara);
that which is beyond the universe is the Great Universe (mahāviśva), and it is said to be "without sound" (asvara).
From Asvara comes Mahāsvarasthāna; likewise, from Kharva comes Adhigarvita.
Those who have reached the further shore of calculation have declared Śreyasa and Śānti to be the [next] stations.
345) From that, Mahādhṛṣṭa is the Dhṛṣṭa; this is here called Odaka.
Odaka is the state of mental distraction, and there is another supreme station.
Beyond the highest [level], the Buddhas do not perceive the domain of lower stages;
for humans, however, the calculation of the world's formations is impossible.
Beyond that, the sphere of the Buddhas is considered to be nothing else;
it is described as a Buddha-field [as vast as] the sands of the river Ganges.
The Leaders explained this by breaking down atoms;
for this is made into an illustration, as it is within the scope of logical knowledge.
A substance is established by its cause; it cannot be [fully] enumerated by others.
This is the measure [of the Buddhas], whom I attended in the past.
Having propitiated them during this thoughtless aeon for such an immeasurable length of time, I was previously a bodhisattva.
Having fully awakened for the sake of sentient beings, one should enter into Buddhahood;
in various places, I have taught tantras and extensive ritual manuals.
This is the supreme and foremost ritual manual; this is the wisdom that has been spoken. This is the authoritative standard taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones as an ancient tradition.
Now, O Prince! at this final time of birth, I have proclaimed all the worldly mantras and the beautiful Kalparājas.
Whether supramundane, divine, or human— including those of the gods and asuras—
the application of the tantras has been proclaimed for all mantras.
This King of Rituals, possessed of great supernatural power, is authorized everywhere;
through the performance of its ritual procedures, Mañjughoṣa brings about accomplishment for them.
By this very method, Mañjubhānin,
the powerful one, has declared the accomplishment for all of them.
How much more so in the human world those who are other mantra-deities;
all supramundane mantras, as well as mundane ones possessing great supernatural power.
346) By means of this ritual procedure, the sovereign of rituals, one attains accomplishment;
mastery over all mantras is proclaimed as the result of all rituals.
Mañjuśrī is indeed authorized in this supreme king of manuals regarding whatever worldly arts and sciences are recognized by the world.
The omens of knowledge of signs are characterized by the knowledge of astrology;
the auspicious and inauspicious results of the conduct of those who know signs are indeed found in their cries.
And indeed the cries of all beings, conduct marked by the mind,
the element, the most extensive, and the substance...
They say that bodily gestures and omens, as well as mining, metallurgy, and agriculture,
along with mathematics, grammar, the sciences, weaponry, sequence, and ritual procedure [are the fields of knowledge].
Inner science, medicine— which brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings— and likewise logic, as well as other fields such as grammar, were set forth.
The classification of perfumes, as well as the art of incense—
these have been proclaimed by me, a Bodhisattva, for the benefit of sentient beings.
In the past, I was a bodhisattva for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings;
previously, I spoke thus to those dwelling in the ocean of saṃsāra.
I have indeed dwelt for a long time in the dense wilderness of saṃsāra;
I act therein according to the needs of those beings who are to be disciplined.
In whatever way sentient beings indeed undertake beneficial action,
in that very way I perform for their benefit action that is the abode of virtue.
The various states of beings, which are sources of benefit, are made manifold by their diverse karma;
they are fashioned in diverse ways, corrupted by the source of diverse objects.
Just as they are described in the treatises, endowed with various karmas and possessing diverse purposes,
so do I likewise fashion for them a manifold perfection of form.
I shall likewise assume various guises with diverse limbs, both my own and those of others;
out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I manifest manifold forms.
(97, p. 347) In the past, I likewise created Maheśvara, Śakra, Brahmā, and the others, as well as Viṣṇu, Dhanada, and Nairṛta, along with the various forms of the planets.
With minds permeated by great compassion, I shall gradually establish those beings, who dwell within the sphere of their own inclinations, in the state of auspiciousness.
I wander through saṃsāra, which has been entered for a long time;
for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, I have taught [this] in the form of mantra.
The knowledge of the mind and the ritual manual of mantras have been set forth in due order;
after wandering for a long time through births, I have now taken my place within the lineage of the Buddhas.
I have no creator, nor even a master;
having relied upon my fixed lineage, I am the Buddha who has awakened to supreme enlightenment.
I have attained security, the ageless, the peaceful, the sorrowless, the stainless, and the auspicious;
I have reached extinction and tranquility, and I am liberated from the bond of birth.
Now that the wheel has been set in motion, resting upon the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
I shall indeed demonstrate this ritual manual (kalpa) for the discourse on mantras in full detail.
The practitioner of recitation should not perform the ritual procedures in detail in vain;
for all worldly mantras and their ritual manuals have been declared in this same manner.
All of them are to be honored and revered, and contempt for them must be avoided;
therefore, the minister should not despise them, providing them with detailed ritual manuals.
One should not perform these signs, the application of knowledge, and the astrological calculations proclaimed by the knowers of the stars in vain; they are declared for the sake of auspiciousness.
Thus, the attainment of substances for the sake of supernatural powers and the like is merely for the present life;
it is tainted by worldly gain and is a lure for success. Therefore, such success is called an ill omen.
It is consecrated with the praises of the Jinas and adorned with verses of auspiciousness,
on excellent and preeminent days of the bright fortnight clearly marked by favorable signs.
One should begin the practice of mantra when conjoined with the most excellent of the bright planets;
thus, one should employ such auspicious conjunctions and avoid those that are inauspicious.
(98, p. 348) This was previously taught by me alone; therefore, it should be accepted by those who recite [mantras].
Whatever skill in the knowledge of astrology there may be in this world—
Or others there who are experts in policy, possessing the causes and reasons thereof,
well-connected with the treatises on logic, acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
All of that has been told by me alone; it is to be grasped by those who recite mantras.
This path, which is the cause of accomplishment, has been shown by the seers of reality.
For whatever has been taught as the complete and exhaustive doctrine that is the cause of liberation,
by that very means one should establish the path of mantras, which are the causes of accomplishment.
The reciter should never perform the application of mantras in vain,
for all worldly mantras are proclaimed to be supreme.
One should employ all supramundane and divine [mantras] in every case;
one should not cause the mind to be false, nor should one ever corrupt the mental faculty therein.
Indeed, all mantras are to be honored; they are proclaimed as those who know the samaya in this teaching, which is the equal benefit of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
The sons of the Victors are established, drawn in, and introduced into the mandala of the Moon-like Sages; they are declared here to be knowers of the samaya.
Those [mantras] brought forth by the Viśas through their spells are always fruitful;
one should not bow down before the mantras of others, nor should one treat them with contempt.
Those mantras which are indeed non-noble are proclaimed to be fruitless;
as many as there are worldly mantras, they are inferior and arise from mere recitation.
Those [deities], including those with afflictions and ending with those who have seen the path, are not fruitless for those who recite [mantras].
One should not allow the mind to be made vain by being joined with anger toward the wrathful [deities].
One should neither offer praise nor show devotion to that which yields fruitless action;
for it is dependent upon that [worldly state], one should never yield one's mind to it, nor ever bow down before it.
But one who is established in reason, focused, and constantly performs the recitation with a single mantra,
obtains the entire fruit exactly as described by the rule of the ritual procedure.
349) Having made the mind steady, one should recite that single mantra.
For one whose mind is focused on a single object, mantras that accomplish all aims are perfected.
For one whose mind is distracted and whose self is deluded, success is not seen;
however, by attaining the complete accomplishment of the fruit, one shall reach the vast state.
"Success is declared to be desired for one whose mind is eternally pure, who truly has faith in the teaching, and who is devoted to the Three Jewels. Thus,
from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The thirty-first chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction of the knowledge of signs for the performance of ritual actions, is completed.
350) Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon that abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī!
Your mudrā-tantra, together with its secrets, is the most supreme secret."

It is not to be revealed to those who lack faith in the teaching of the Tathāgata, who have no devotion to it, who are not authorized by the samaya, who do not act to ensure the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels, who are under the influence of non-virtuous friends, who desire merit [only for themselves],
who are mired in the company of wicked people, who are possessed by evil associates, and who have become distant from the Buddha-dharmas.

O Youth! since this eon has become fruitless due to the lack of instruction from teachers, you have been consecrated in this most supreme secret mandala. It must not be revealed to those who have not seen the samaya, nor to those outside the family of the Tathāgatas, nor to people who are not universal, nor to those who follow your mantras but lack faith in the Buddha and Dharma; for such people are far removed from enlightenment.
One should not cause her to receive the mudrā, nor should one show her the tantra;
if, out of negligence, delusion, confusion, or greed, one should cause it to be given, [the fault is incurred].
The tantras and mantras indeed do not succeed for one who recites them erroneously;
they will bring about the absence of the deity's presence through the mudrā, and the mantras likewise act otherwise.

One does not quickly attain accomplishment and may even be deprived of one's body [if one acts] toward those who are gentle, whose minds are devoted to the ancestral rites (śrāddha), who abide by the observances, and who perceive reality.
One should reveal the *mudrā-tantra* to those engaged in the *tantra-mantras*,
as well as to those who worship the Three Jewels and have faith in the teaching of the Jina.
One should reveal the mudrās of those [deities] observed in the ritual applications,
which are adorned by the *bodhicitta* for those who know the procedure of the *bodhicitta*.
One should reveal their mudrā to those who constantly abide on the path to enlightenment,
who are engaged in the application of tantra and mantra, and who have perceived the higher and lower within the samaya.
One should reveal the mudrā of those who aspire to great enlightenment,
as well as that of the sons of the Conquerors, the Śrāvakas, and the Pratyekabuddhas, provided they are devoted to them.
One should reveal the mudrā to those for whom the fruit is visible in this very life—
those who have non-conceptualized dharmas and are faithful yet free from envy.

351) One should reveal the seal (*mudrā*) to those who understand the words and reasoning of the Teacher; for these are indeed sealed by the seal, established as authoritative, numbering one hundred and eight.
Neither exceeding nor deficient, they were revealed directly by the Buddhas;
indeed, the mantras in the Mañjuśrī-kalpa are equal to them.
It was said that there are one hundred and eight mantras;
likewise, the best of sages declared in the past that there are one hundred and eight mudrās corresponding to them.
This is the measure of the eon for the emergence of mudrās and mantras;
it is declared to be the treasury of all Buddhas, the treasury of mantras.
Endowed with mudrās and mantras, when joined together, they bring about swift action; for without a wheel, no movement occurs in a chariot, however well-constructed it may be.
In the same way, among all mantras, those devoid of mudrās do not perform their function;
mantras joined with and accompanied by mudrās accomplish their tasks swiftly.
For these indeed cause even the three worlds, including the gods and asuras, to revolve;
how much more so in the world of humans, regarding other conditioned activities?
For the fruit of these is seen in this very life within the mudrās and mantras;
when combined with both and shown according to the prescribed ritual, they are pure.
They cause the beings to turn toward the state of being sons of the supreme Victors;
the mantra, the mudrā, and the austerity—these three types of action reside in the hand.
Just as the reciter may obtain all perfections according to his desire,
so too are the mudrās sealed by the mantras, and the mantras are likewise sealed by the mudrās.
A mantra devoid of mudrā is ineffective, and a mudrā bereft of mantra is likewise powerless;
however, when mudrā and mantra are joined together, they are united and efficacious for all ritual actions.
For these are mutually the fruits of one another, arising as mutual fruits;
when applied with skill by the practitioner, no karma exists alongside them.
All mantras of those possessing form are indeed accomplished when joined with mudrās;
for a mantra applied according to the prescribed rite is empowered when accompanied by its seal.
352) There exists no place where one who is drawn [into this practice] does not achieve success;
from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, one traverses the entire world-system.
There is no being whatsoever to be found who, once possessed by [this resolve], could not be drawn back, nor who is impossible to save.
Even Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are drawn in by the chanting of the ritual;
even Bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages are rendered powerless.
Whether to break through protective rites or to obstruct the accomplishment of ritual acts,
those who rely upon mantras and mudrās are invincible to all beings.
For whoever among all beings relies upon the mantra,
these applications of mudrās indeed arise as protection.
The manifestation of all mantras is seen within all mantras;
from the mantra, all mudrās arise, mutually dependent upon one another.
The procedure for the recitation of forms is employed on the path in the rite of fire-offering;
therefore, such accomplishment as is born from this is seen within the mantras and mudrās.
For one who recites constantly, is ever-diligent, and always remains established in those [practices], all mantras indeed attain accomplishment; the word of the Munis is never in vain.
The speech of all the Buddhas has been acted upon otherwise by those who seek welfare;
yet by whomsoever the rite has been performed through mantra and mudrā, they are liberated without exception.
O Youthful Mañjuśrī! I declare this again and again.
The liberation from all mantras without exception is the mudrā; therein lies the arising of benefit.
I pay homage to that which brings about the attainment of fruit and delivers one across [samsāra] in this King of Ritual Manuals.
