The most secret and beneficial *mudrā-tantra* has been extracted from that [source];
therefore, he is endowed with skillful means, glorious, patient, and possesses the form of a child.
With a slightly smiling face, the youth who is the source of the universe,
the Bodhisattva of great heroism, has attained the ten stages.
353) Bestow [this] upon the Buddha, the foremost of sages and kinsman of the sun;
for this, O Blessed One, is the cause of mantras that has been proclaimed in the world.
That was taught to me long ago by previous perfectly awakened ones;
for what purpose has it now been revealed by the Lion of the Śākyas?
This doubt has arisen in me; explain it, O best of sages!
How is it that the wise one, possessing the voice of a kalaviṅka bird, was born from the thundering of Brahmā?
But he spoke to the Bodhisattva established on the ten stages:
"In the past, as I wandered through saṃsāra for many eons..."
This sovereign king of kalpas was obtained from the sage named Saṅkusumita;
in various places, I have performed much benefit for sentient beings.
Having come under the sway of compassion, I then made this vow:
"When I indeed become the supreme Buddha in this most degenerate age."
Having indeed fulfilled the purpose of the teaching by turning the wheel of Dharma,
I shall enter final nirvana on this earth during the very last period of time.
I shall now point out this sovereign king of ritual manuals (kalparājendra) in your presence;
for even when I have passed away and the world called Jambudvīpa is empty, [this shall remain].
When the treasury of the Teacher’s Dharma has become distant in the Kali age,
this King of Kalpas will act for the sake of destroying [the obstacles] of sentient beings.
This king of rituals, in its full detail, is bestowed upon you alone;
at that time, you shall be intent upon the welfare of sentient beings.
At that terrifying time, sentient beings will be most unrighteous;
kings, with wicked minds, will always remain unstable.
Both humans and non-humans alike, all those who are hostile to the teaching,
will destroy my entire treasury of Dharma that has been proclaimed by me.
For the sake of their discipline, this treasury of mantras has been proclaimed;
O Youth! this was your vow in inconceivable past eons.
354) "As many Buddhas as there may be, those friends of the world who have entered parinirvāṇa, for the sake of their teaching, I shall act in age after age."
Taking the form of a young boy, I shall wander everywhere;
through the form of mantras, I will discipline sentient beings from time to time.
"O youth! This very vow was indeed made by you in the past;
it has now been attained, O child! Therefore, I shall instruct you accordingly."
Then, in a void buddha-field where there is no refuge for people,
you, though appearing as a fool, shall instruct sentient beings by means of mantra-forms.
You shall discipline many beings, bestowing all forms of prosperity;
you are the granter of boons to all sentient beings in that time of the debased age.
For when I have passed into nirvāṇa and the surface of the earth has become empty,
you yourself, in the form of a child, will perform the work of a Buddha.
"Then, in that delightful great forest situated in the lap of the Himalayas,
on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī, my final liberation will take place."

The thirty-second chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction for the ritual of inciting mudrās as requested by Mañjuśrī, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, is completed.
105. (p. 355) Now follows the thirty-fifth chapter.
Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having once again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [spoke].
He entered the samādhi called "The Stirring of the Treasury of the Tathāgata’s Great Seal.

Immediately upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s entering it, a great ray of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows. That web of light was accompanied by a retinue numbering many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of rays. That web of light [illuminated] many...
Having illuminated the Buddha-fields and exhorted all the Buddhas, they vanished once again into the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

And immediately upon being thus exhorted, all the Blessed Buddhas entered the meditative absorption known as the "Nature of Space" and stationed themselves in the expanse of the sky above the Pure Abodes.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having paid homage to all the Buddhas, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī! This is the ritual procedure for the chapter on the treasury of mudrās, which is empowered by all the Buddhas of the future."

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and bowed to all the Buddhas, addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni: "It would be well, Blessed One, if you would explain the chapter on the treasury of the mudrās of all the Tathāgatas, which is most supremely secret; do so now, if you deem it the right time."
It will come to pass for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit,
and happiness of the great mass of people, and for the arising of happiness and the ripening of happiness for all beings, both gods and humans.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having been requested by the Blessed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
looked upon all the Buddhas, took hold of all sentient beings in his mind, gladdened all the bodhisattvas, and pacified all the pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas.

Having exhorted those whose minds were intent upon the meaning of all mantras, having warded off all the wicked, having comforted all who were afraid, and having established all who were in distress in the secure, auspicious state of nirvāṇa, he spoke this ritual procedure for the chapter on mudrās for the sake of the happiness of all who suffer.
Listen, O youth Mañjuśrī! I shall explain the chapter on the mudrās;
first, there is the five-crested [mudrā], which is considered the Great Mudrā (Mahāmudrā).
One should know the second to be the Triśikha, and the third the Ekacīraka;
the fourth, the Fully Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds, call the Utpala.
The fifth is seen as the Svastika; the sixth is called the Dhvaja.
Those well-adorned with the knowledge of mantras say that the seventh is the Pūrṇa.
The eighth is designated as the staff by the Lords of the World who have conquered their enemies;
the ninth is designated as the parasol, and the tenth is called the spear.
The eleventh, however, the Perfectly Awakened Ones designate as Sampuṭa;
the twelfth is called Phara, and the thirteenth is likewise Gada.
The fourteenth is indicated as the sword, and the fifteenth likewise as the jar;
the sixteenth is said to be the noose, and the seventeenth is remembered as the goad.
The eighteenth is Bhadrapīṭha, while the nineteenth is Pīṭhaka;
the twentieth is said to be Mayūrāsana, and the twenty-first is Paṭṭiśa.
The *ekaliṅga* consists of twenty-two; the *dviliṅga*, twenty-three;
the *mālā*, twenty-four; and the *dhanus* likewise consists of twenty-five.
It is declared that twenty-six [units] are prescribed for the *nārāca* [joint],
while they say twenty-seven are employed in the *samaliṅga*.
The twenty-eighth is the trident (śūla), the twenty-ninth is the mallet (mudgara),
they say the thirtieth is the lance (tomara), and the thirty-first is the right [hand].
The thirty-second is the speaker (vaktṛ), the thirty-third is said to be the cloth (paṭa),
the thirty-fourth is the jar (kumbha), and the thirty-fifth is the skull-topped staff (khakhara).
The thirty-sixth is said to be the *kalaśa*; the thirty-seventh is the *mauśala*;
the thirty-eighth is the *paryaṅka*; and the thirty-ninth is the *paṭaha*.
They say that forty [links] are declared to be the Dharma-conch;
that same forty-first is proclaimed as the Śaṅkalā.
The second is said to be highly esteemed; the third fulfills one's desires;
the fourth is seen as the Mother, the measured Prajñāpāramitā.
The perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds, call the fifth the "bowl" (pātra);
the sixth is said to be the "arch" (toraṇa), while the seventh is the "excellent arch" (sutoraṇa).
357) The eighth is that which is designated by sound, while the ninth is the word of recitation (*japa*).
The fifty are said to be the *bherī* [drum], but the *dharmabherī* (Dharma-drum) exceeds them.
They say that "dvipañcāśat" (fifty-two) refers to the elephant; likewise, the three excellent hands [form] "catuḥpañcāśat" (fifty-four), which should be known as the mudrā moving within it.
They say the fifth is the banner (ketu), and the sixth is likewise the arrow (śara);
the seventh is designated as the axe (paraśu), and the eighth is honored by the world.
In brief, the *bhiṇḍipāla* should be known to be fifty-nine [in measure],
while the *lāṅgala* should be sixty in measure.
Then, sixty-one is called the Lotus; sixty-two is called the Vajra;
and sixty-three is said in the world to be the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
Likewise, the Puṇḍarīka should be known to consist of sixty-four [fingers] when fully extended;
one should know that the Varada, the supreme mudrā, consists of sixty-five.
Likewise, the sixty-sixth is proclaimed as the Vajra-mudrā;
and the sixty-seventh in the world, the wise call the Kunta.
Likewise, one should fashion sixty-eight [spokes], which is declared to be the Vajramaṇḍala;
similarly, sixty-nine would be that which is celebrated as the Śataghnī.
From that, one should know the seventy-first [mudrā] as Nādāmudrā in brief;
they call the seventy-first the auspicious Vimāna, the excellent mudrā.
In brief, the chariot is described here as having seventy-two [parts],
and the bed of the Lords of the World is briefly said to have seventy-three others.
The seventy-fifth and likewise the seventy-fourth are declared to be the two mudrās known as the Half-moon and the Lute.
The seventy-sixth mudrā in the world is Padmālayā;
the seventy-seventh, the most excellent, is Kuvalayodbhavā.
The seventy-eighth is declared to be the mudrā of salutation;
the ninety-ninth is the ninth [in this sequence]; both of these mudrās are most auspicious.
The *sampuṭa* and the *yamala* mudrās constitute the ninety-first;
they say that the ninety-second is declared to be the *puṣpa* mudrā.
The second is the bracelet mudrā, while the third always performs the incense offering;
the fourth is the fragrance mudrā, and the fifth is known as the lamp offering.
One should know the means [of accomplishment] through the sixth [case]; the seventh is traditionally taught as the seat;
the eighth is declared to be the invocation; and the ninth is the dismissal.
One should know that a full hundred is the "all-action" mudrā;
more than a hundred, they say, is known as the "great mudrā" (mahāmudrā).
The crown of the Lords of the World always resides upon the Guru;
that is declared to be the first mudrā, while the second arises from the white one.
The third is seen as the root mudrā of Mañjughoṣa; the fourth, abiding in the treasury of Dharma, is characterized as the Dharma mudrā.
The fifth is said to be the Saṅgha, and it is also the Mahāmudrā;
the sixth, however, is the pacifier of beings, arising from the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
The seventh belongs to the Bodhisattvas, while the tenth belongs to those who have entered [the stages];
it is the lotus garland seal (mudrā), which the wise know as the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
The bestower of boons among all mudrās and mantras, including those of the mundane world;
she of great power, the most excellent mother, the eldest, worshipped by the three worlds.
One should employ the eighth mudrā, the Abode of the Three Worlds;
the number of mudrās taught in this great and eminent tantra is [as follows].
One hundred and eight is the number prescribed for the mudrās;
this measure was formerly proclaimed on the earth by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
When the Teacher’s teaching has vanished, it will circulate among embodied beings;
first, however, it shall rest in the hand, with both tips held in the hands.
Then, having interlaced the fingers of each other's hands and joined them together,
both hands are marked with the five-crested sign (pañcacūḍā).
359) Then, with those fingers inverted, the five-crested mudrā is to be known at their tips; it is indeed the five-tufted [ascetic’s head-dress].
Renowned as Mahāmudrā, it is likewise the crest-jewel of the Bodhisattvas; this seal of great power, when applied, accomplishes all activities.
One should always employ the mantra of Mañjuśrī, or his heart-mantras, or indeed the mantra of Keśinī, or the root-mantra.
Or again, one should apply [these] among all mantras according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform all rites, for this word of the Sage is never fruitless.
In that same manner, one should place the two hands together to form a hollowed palm (karasaṃpuṭa);
therein, with the fingers interlaced, one should form the three-pronged gesture (triśikha).
When both hands have their thumbs in the form of a void and are supported [against each other], and the middle and ring fingers are likewise braided in a reversed manner;
This should be known as the "Three-Pointed" (*triśikha*), and furthermore as the "Form of the Three Rags" (*tricīrākāra*);
this is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the wise Mañjughoṣa.
One should perform all rituals exactly as prescribed by the rules;
one should apply these [rules] to all the mantras of Mañjuśrī.
For those who recite it, this quickly accomplishes the goals desired in this life;
likewise, one should place the hands [in that position] and form the single-crest mudrā.
The middle fingers joined together shall certainly form the single crest;
this is the Mahāmudrā, as proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Mantras entrusted to Kumāra, as well as others belonging to the worldly realm,
when joined with this [practice], become effective and swiftly accomplish their tasks.
By this, the supreme mantras spoken by the Victors are accomplished;
for one quickly achieves all aims through ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.
That same [mudrā], with the hands joined and the fingers arranged closely together,
with both index fingers bent, resembles a needle and an añjali.
360) When the two thumbs are placed together and the two middle fingers are extended,
while the ring fingers are curled around, it is called the *utpala* [mudrā].
This is observed to be the root mantra of the Bodhisattva;
indeed, it encompasses all the rites that have been taught in the *Pañcacīraka*.
One should perform all that quickly; one should accomplish it with the blue lotus.
This is the boon-granting mudrā, which swiftly brings about enjoyments.
When joined with the root mantra, it will swiftly accomplish one's purpose;
likewise, both hands should always be joined and held palms upward.
Having formed that very same *sampuṭa* mudrā with the fingers on all sides,
it is placed so as to have a beautiful form arising in the shape of a *svastika*.
When the little fingers are placed level with the middle of the middle fingers,
and the pair of thumbs is set [atop them], this mudrā is called Svastika.
This mudrā, which accomplishes all aims, is employed in rites of pacification;
when joined with the six-syllable heart mantras, it indeed performs all activities.
When those very two hands are joined together with the fingers interlaced,
those who have attained the excellence of knowledge regarding the [mudrās] call this the Pūrṇamudrā.
Having formed the añjali gesture from the hollow of the palms with the fingers slightly spread apart on all sides,
the Perfectly Awakened Ones have declared this to be the "Full Mudrā" for those who recite mantras.
This [mantra], which pacifies everything,
when impelled by the root mantra, quickly makes one who is suffering from the pain of poverty wealthy with riches.
Those who are well-versed in worldly knowledge and conduct call this another mudrā;
having positioned both hands in that manner, one rests upon the left index finger.
Having placed the right hand upon it with the fingers positioned together,
when the index finger and the middle finger are extended, it is called the *dhvaja* (banner) mudrā.
Known as the Dhvaja-mudrā, it is raised up like the banner of Śakra;
with this mudrā, one should perform the sequence of rites such as the bali offering and the homa.
361) For this [mudrā], when impelled by the root mantra, performs all rites. It is formed by placing the two hands together with the fingers joined in a hollowed gesture.
That mudrā, when performed in the manner of a *sampuṭa*, shall be the destroyer of all obstacles;
arising from the union of mantra and gnosis, it accomplishes the ritual action in due order.
Indeed, when employed according to the prescribed ritual, mantras quickly accomplish their purpose;
specifically, those mantras of Mañjughoṣa that arise from the location of his heart.
Joined together, it performs all actions marked by worldly convention;
that same [mudrā] has the hands placed such that the left hand rests upon the right.
Grasping the right index finger while raising the left index finger—
this is known as the *yaṣṭi* mudrā, which wards off Śakra.
It pacifies all obstacles, even those that are cruel and most terrifying;
it has been prescribed for the purpose of slaying all malevolent beings for those who recite mantras.
Accompanied by the root mantra, it quickly accomplishes many purposes;
that very hand, when placed and raised in the shape of a staff, [is likewise effective].
Extending the right hand, it is called the "Umbrella" (chatra) mudrā;
with this mudrā, one should perform self-protection starting from the head.
With all mantras, one should perform the rite designated as protection;
one may cover the mouths of enemies or paralyze them as desired.
One may cause a wicked person, even one accompanied by humans, to act according to one's desire;
indeed, all obstacles perish upon seeing this mudrā together with the parasol.
One should form that very same hand-gesture, beautiful with its arranged form,
joined by the tips of the two thumbs and extended by the middle fingers.
The ring finger, with its tip bent upon the middle joint of the middle finger—
that very gesture is designated as Śakti, the warder-off of all evil-doers.
This protection, which destroys the grahas, was proclaimed by the Lords of the World;
it was arranged by the wrathful King Yamāntaka.
362) One might more swiftly bring about a terrible evil arising in the world—
a deed that obstructs life and is shunned by all the Buddhas.
One should not perform such an action that is forbidden by the highest people in the world;
therefore, one should employ the supreme power through mantras that are all-pervading.
Whatever worldly mantras there may be, as well as those spoken by the Jinas—
one who is well-composed should employ them with this mudrā and with power.
Upon seeing the formidable and supreme mudrā, all the Nairṛtas,
Piśācas, Tārakas, Pretas, Pūtanās, and the Mātṛs perish.
The deformed child-seizing spirits and those who afflict children—
all wicked beings whatsoever who perform cruel deeds shall indeed perish.
That very hand, when placed so as to produce the form of a spear (śaktikā),
has its fingers interlaced with one another in the shape of an inverted casket (sampuṭa).
The Fully Awakened Ones, free from all enmity, call that very [mantra] the "enveloping" (sampuṭa).
By means of this single-syllable mantra, one should perform the ritual action.
One should seal all directions; that is called the "binding of the quarters.
This great protection of the mudrā remains as it encloses [the practitioner] within its embrace.
Indeed, all the wicked ones and whatever others are harmful are destroyed;
it protects the entire body and the retinue within its range.
The Wheel protects everything wherever the reciter always dwells;
for him, no sin whatsoever nor any harm shall arise.
There will be security, abundance of food, and freedom from disease; whence could there be fear of a foreign army?
One should clasp both hands together and then turn them over.
Having placed the right hand below and the left hand above with the palms joined together,
these two hands thus interlaced are called the *pharaṃ* by the supreme Victors.
She wards off the arising of evil from wicked enemies;
having brought [it about], she is endowed with syllables and supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
363) Endowed with these mantras of a single color, this [rite] indeed swiftly accomplishes its purpose;
it performs various meaningful actions that eliminate the evils arising from enemies.
When employed as a root mantra, it destroys the poison of those who possess it,
and it eradicates other defects caused by magical applications in embodied beings.
This supreme mudrā has been proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the best of bipeds;
it is formed by placing the two hands together with the fingers interlaced.
Then one should form the shape of a mace (gadā), encircled by the root [finger];
it is well-encircled by the two little fingers in the middle of the two thumbs.
One should form a beautiful hollow shape with the six fingers;
this mudrā is called the mace (gada), which destroys all dānavas.
The Daityas who are evil-minded perish upon seeing one whose mind is gentle,
when the mudrā is raised or even when the mace is well-worshipped.
When employed with the root mantra, this auspicious [mudrā] swiftly accomplishes one's purpose;
likewise, it is designated as the "sword" when the tips of the ring fingers are well-contracted.
In that same manner, one should form the hands with the tips extended and slightly curved,
making them equal in shape to a shallow bowl by means of the fingers on all sides.
The Buddhas know that bell; they have revealed it for the sake of embodied beings.
Having joined both hands together, one should form the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭa*).
Having indeed interlaced them with the middle fingers, one should form the shape of a circle; that shall then become the shape of a noose.
Then, with the index fingers placed upon the middle joints and well-joined together,
this mudrā known as the "Noose" (pāśa) is manifested by the Buddhas.
For the sake of those to be trained, he is liberated from the most terrible bondage of sentient beings;
as are the wicked and cruel planetary spirits and all the rākṣasas.
For when she is impelled even slightly, she binds one here along with one's mother;
indeed, when told "Bind! Bind!", she binds here even Śakra himself.
364) How much more so in the world of humans, regarding those flesh-eating, meat-consuming *kravyāda*s?
Having placed both hands together and made them equal, one should perform that very [rite].
The right hand is likewise placed upon the left;
its middle finger and index finger are shaped like a hook.
Clinging to the middle joint, one should form a hook with the index finger;
this hook, empowered by the root mantra, is thus directed.
Reciters shall swiftly accomplish whatever rites they desire in this life;
they can even quickly summon the lords of the gods, including Brahmā and others, along with Śakra.
The excellent and most auspicious supreme mudrā is the drawing-in of the hook;
it consists of the two hands joined together in a reversed form like a ball.
Having bent the middle and ring fingers resting on the left hand,
[one should likewise bend] both the index and little fingers of the right hand.
Indicated by the right hand, the middle and ring fingers are bent;
they are then placed reversed and joined, with the thumbs made to touch.
That very same auspicious seat is declared to be the excellent and virtuous mudrā;
it is the throne of all Buddhas and the warder-off of the wrathful *śakra*.
When employed with all mantras born of the families of the foremost Victors, it is perfected.
All the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power have been established [therein].
It indeed makes the entire world, including the gods, motionless;
that very [mudrā] is the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), resting upon the middle fingers.
The middle fingers are placed upon the upper positions and thus variegated;
that very [arrangement] is designated as the *pīṭha* by the lion-like sages who have conquered their enemies.
Then, with both hands joined together, one should intertwine the fingers;
thereafter, one should form the needle of the little finger like a braid.
Having quickly contracted [the fingers] from the middle, one should always place the two thumbs joined together, arising from the expanse of the lotus petals, in the *sthita* (standing) position.
365) This is declared by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, free from all hatred, to be the Peacock Seat of the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa.
This mudrā, which is always like a child’s plaything for the best of sages,
has indeed been declared by the self-arisen ones of old to possess great power.
Impelled by the charming mantra, she performs a variety of actions;
she destroys the wicked, the flesh-eating and corpse-consuming demons.
Furthermore, twenty mudrās in their entirety are considered to have been taught by the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds and the leaders of the world.
Hereafter, I shall explain the origin of the ritual procedure for the mudrās,
performed with hands that are auspicious, pure, stainless, and cleansed by water.
Having sipped water mixed with white sandalwood, camphor, saffron,
and many varieties of fragrant scents, which has been dried by the wind;
With pure hands, using ointments and even firm goads,
one should perform that very mudrā for the One Worthy of Veneration, the Supreme among Bipeds.
Śāla, Saṅkusuma, Amitābha, Ratnaketu,
Amitāyurjñānaviniścayendra, Lokanātha, and Divaṅkara.
To Kṣema, Lokanātha, Sunetra, Dharmaketu,
and the one renowned as Prabhāmālī— the eldest, the most excellent, the peerless, and the supreme.
Having paid homage to one of these Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds,
and having become pure in a pure place, one should bind the mudrā at the conclusion of the recitation.
But having seen such a teacher from whom one is liberated from doubt regarding the meaning,
one who is perfected in proper conduct should bind the mudrā with him as is convenient.
Having thoroughly cleansed it and made it secluded, one should consecrate the site with mantras;
neither angry, nor impure from food remnants, nor reviled by another.
One should never bind the mudrā upon charcoal or in the midst of ashes;
nor, at that time, should one be attached to the wives of others or to the property of others.
366) One should not form the mudrā that brings about bliss while standing or sitting;
nor should one do so facing south, nor while rising with one's face turned toward the west.
One should not perform the binding of the mudrās above nor below;
rather, one should do so facing north or east, or indeed in those intermediate directions.
One who knows the mudrās and mantras should bind the mudrā while recollecting the Mantra of the Holder of the Discus; this is considered the best method among all mudrās for binding.
Hereafter, I shall explain the twenty-first mudrā:
one should join both hands together, with the fingers interlaced.
Then, one should indicate the middle void with the fingers,
placed upon the middle joint, with its tip at the void and joined by the little fingers.
The knower of mantras should always form [this mudrā] by resting the two thumbs upon the curved fingers;
joined in the shape of a trident, the wise know this as the *paṭṭiśa*.
This supreme mudrā swiftly cuts through the mantras of others;
likewise, it shatters the supreme mudrās employed by wicked beings.
It causes all spirits, grahas, mātṛs, and pūtanas to tremble;
it performs a variety of rites and swiftly brings about auspiciousness.
Those mantras which were spoken by Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā himself—
the knower of mantras cut them off through a rite prescribed by rule.
When joined with this very mudrā and the great *paṭṭiśa*,
and established in union with the mantras originating from the mouth of the Jina;
It performs a variety of actions, such as cutting and splitting;
it utterly destroys, without exception, that evil committed against other beings.
Having thus folded the hands, with the middle and ring fingers raised,
both palms joined together, they take on the form of a *liṅga*.
The Liṅgamudrā is considered to be joined with four fingers;
Maheśvara, the son of the gods, [taught] his own mantra along with the mudrā.
367) In the *Tantra*, the Sage of old indeed taught,
in full detail, the mantras and mudrās of others as well as his own, for the purpose of summoning.
Drawn forth at this time, he revealed this supreme and foremost mudrā during this most excellent kalpa; it is indeed proclaimed among worldly beings as the best.
Whatever mantras have been proclaimed by Rudra upon the surface of the earth,
this single mudrā, embraced [by the deity], is indeed their sovereign and foremost.
Through the power of the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa,
the one who accomplishes the ritual action has been brought into the maṇḍala.
Whatever malevolent beings roam upon the surface of the earth—
planets, flesh-eaters, those who feed on meat, mātṛs, and kaṭapūtanas— [all these are subdued].
Indeed, for the purpose of warding them off when obstacles are created by Rudras,
this excellent mudrā has been taught during the rites of bali offerings at night.
Or, through the miraculous power of the Buddha’s empowerment, he performs all activities;
likewise, having performed such [a rite], he is designated as possessing both genders.
In the same way, when the *mālā* is placed upon the finger, it is proclaimed as *mālā*;
likewise, by contracting that very *mālā*, it takes on the form of a *sampuṭa*.
Joining both index fingers together, one should form them like a bow;
pressing the two thumbs within the fists, that is recognized as the Dhanur-mudrā (bow mudrā).
In this way, one should form the *aṅkuśī* [gesture]:
the right hand is extended, while the left index finger is pressed down upon the joint within the fist.
The *nārāca* mudrā has been described; now I shall speak again of the *samaliṅga*.
Having then placed both hands together, with the fingers interlaced and joined.
Those skilled in this teaching and ritual manual know that when the thumb of the right hand is raised, it constitutes the arising of the *liṅga*; they recognize that as the "Equal Liṅga."
Having joined both hands together with the fingers interlaced,
one should join the two index fingers and form the shape of a trident.
368) This is declared to be the *śūla* [mudrā], the instruction for those whose beings are corrupted. Then, having extended both hands and formed fists once again...
Having placed the two thumbs in a standing position, it is declared to be the Mudgara [mudrā];
that same Mudgara should be moved slightly within the hollow of the joined palms.
This supreme *tomara* mudrā, which destroys Śakra, has indeed been described;
then, one should form the *utpala* [mudrā] with the ring fingers at that time.
Placed below between the two thumbs and not shown [to others], this is called *daṃṣṭra*; when it is opened, it is called *vaktra*.
Then, having made the fingers equal on all sides and placing the left hand upon the chest, one should cast [the flower]; this is called the *paṭa* [method].
Having formed both hands into a hollowed casket (sampuṭa), with the beautiful [hands] placed [together],
the fingers should be joined to one another, their tips touching each other.
Having raised [the hands] and contracted them, it is called the *kumbha-mudrā*;
joining those very same hands into fists, with the two index fingers raised again, [is another].
One should form the shape of a *khakhara* (a type of staff) arising in the form of a braid;
this mudrā is declared, O destroyers of enemies, to be the *khakhara*.
That very same [mudrā], when slightly bent like a hoe (khakhara) and beautifully formed with the thumbs placed [within], is here called the *kalaśa* [mudrā].
Having raised it again,
one should form the shape of a pestle with the four fingers, arising from the index finger and the middle finger.
Those endowed with knowledge of the mantras call this mudrā the *muśala*;
it is formed by placing the middle and ring fingers downward upon those very hands.
Above those [fingers], it is always placed, encircled by the right-hand wind;
having wrapped [it] around, the little finger and the index finger are placed upon the two thumbs.
The Tathāgatas call the form of the full lotus posture the *mudrā*; this is known throughout the world as the "full lotus *mudrā*."
369) Furthermore, one who is endowed with this mudrā and likewise joined with the mantra—
[specifically] with all those spoken by the Jinas that arise from the Vajra and Lotus families—
Employed with these mantras, this auspicious [rite] performs all actions;
and likewise, those mudrās which have been described, such as the mace (muśala) and others originating from the trident (śūla).
All these fierce weapon-wielders within this teaching of the Wrathful King Yamāntaka are indeed emanations created for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
Then, through the power and supernatural might of the Bodhisattva,
Kumbha and the others performed everything that was spoken by the seal for the sake of those wicked ones who were to be disciplined.
That same hand, positioned so as to take the form of a drum,
should be bound together with all the fingers joined and provided with a thumb-loop.
Then, having formed a braid with the thumbs and placed it upon the hand again,
one should position the forefinger in the middle and cause its tip to be raised upward.
This is designated as the drum; the mudrā wards off the wicked. It is the same [as before], with the two hands placed together in a well-applied añjali.
Having contracted both index fingers so they are beautiful in the shape of earrings,
place the thumbs below them and bend both thumbs.
Having entered and remaining within the middle casket, the conch becomes beautiful;
this is indeed the excellent Dharma-conch mudrā as it has been revealed.
Joined with the mantras spoken by the best of sages, it accomplishes all rites and performs a variety of actions against all fanged venomous serpents.
Employed with the root mantra, it destroys them all;
one should fill a conch shell that has been consecrated by recitation with the highly powerful kings of vidyās.
Any creature who is fainting from poison shall quickly become free of poison.
These forty mudrās are proclaimed as supreme and possessed of great supernatural power (maharddhika).
Henceforth, I shall explain the origin of the characteristics of the mudrās: O Lord, the two hands are placed together with the tips of the fingers joined like a reed.
370) One should further exert effort to tighten it and cause it to turn counter-clockwise;

This is the most excellent of supreme mudrās, which binds all wicked beings;
it is joined with those mantras spoken by the foremost of sages for their sake.
It binds all beings afflicted by grahas, mātṛs, and kaśmalas;
having contracted the hands in that same manner, one should release and raise them like a braid.

Having bound that very [mudrā] according to the prescribed rule, one should again join the middle joints of the thumbs and middle fingers with another [hand], while keeping both palms joined at their tips.
Having offered [the oblation] facing the fire and being well-joined with the fire-mantra,

This is the Mahāmudrā, revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones;

Raising the right hand, one should form the gesture of granting fearlessness;

Touching the middle finger with the index finger,

This supreme and most excellent mudrā was proclaimed by the primordial Buddhas;
having bound this mudrā, the reciter bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
When joined with the mantras according to the teachings of the sages, it swiftly accomplishes one's purpose.
That same [mudrā], when the two hands are joined together in a beautiful hollowed-out form (sampuṭa), [is used for that purpose].
The mudrā *Tadgatacāriṇī* consists of the two middle fingers extended upward;
likewise, having encircled [the hand] with the fingers, the two thumbs are placed on top.

Both index fingers joined together with their tips interlaced,

That very same mudrā, when pointed with the axe [gesture], accomplishes all aims;

Thus one should raise it so that the tip of the index finger forms a needle;

All those weapons, when joined with mudrās and impelled by mantras,

373) This mudrā, which arises from the weapon, utterly destroys all those chief rākṣasas who terrify all children.
This characteristic of sixty mudrās has been fully proclaimed;

When those very hands are placed together, raised in the shape of a lotus,

Both hands joined together with the middle fingers raised;

This indeed is the Wheel of Dharma, proclaimed here as the King of Mudrās;

374) Then Municandra, the seventh, chose the Peaceful Wheel (*śānticakra*);

Those who possess the wheel and the uṣṇīṣas, Locanā, and the supreme Vidyā;

All worldly mantras spoken by Viṣṇu and Īśāna are accomplished when joined with the King of Mudrās, the Dharmacakra.
Having seen that [seal] joined with the mudrās of those who recite,
this supreme and most excellent mudrā has indeed emerged from the *dharmadhātu*.
It indeed performs all actions according to the desires of sentient beings;
this mudrā was proclaimed by the King of Dharma for the sake of peace.
In this most excellent and supreme eon, this mudrā known as the Dharmacakra is the accomplisher of all rites within the teaching of Mañjughoṣa.
One should employ the foremost of all mudrās in rites of pacification;

Those same hands, placed together in the form of a hollowed casket (*sampuṭa*),

This mudrā, which accomplishes all aims, is to be known as the Puṇḍarīka.

Joining the two hands together in the form of a hollowed casket,

then, having placed both hands so that they are hollowed out on all sides.
Then, having formed the añjali gesture and placed it upon the seat of the horse,
this is known as the Bherī mudrā by those who desire the welfare of the three worlds.
It delivers all beings from the great ocean of saṃsāra;
indeed, having offered that very [gesture], both palms of the hands are joined in añjali.
Those who follow the path of beings above call this the *vimāna-mudrā*;
that same gesture, with the hands drawn together, is here called the *syandana* (chariot).
The departure by means of the three vehicles is supreme; for it is said that those who delight in it are praised by the reciters, as it leads all beings who chant to the perfection of mantra.
Having relied upon the supreme vehicle, they went toward that state of the Buddhas;
then, having released both hands and joined them together once more, they proceeded from there.
One should form a pure, variegated palm-base arising in the shape of a pedestal;
this is the most excellent and supreme mudrā, highly honored by the Lords of the World.
This bed of all the Buddhas has been proclaimed by the sons of the Conquerors;
it is there that the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past, relying upon it, attained peace.
Resting in the realm of nirvāṇa, following the inclination of those who have ascended [to it], this is known as the Mudrā; it is the resting place of the Leader of the World.
In that same manner, having placed the two hands together with the fingers joined evenly,
they are set in a hollowed, casket-like form, with only the right index finger extended.

376) One should form a half-moon at the front by bending [the fingers]; that is called [the half-moon mudrā]. Then, having again formed both hands into fists with the right thumb [inside], [one forms the other mudrās].
Having formed a fist with all the fingers of the left hand properly joined at the tips of the hand, it is mixed with the right thumb.
With the right hands joined together with the fingers hollowed out,
having extended the little finger, this is declared to be the vīṇā mudrā.
Again, having made both hands hollow with the fingers slightly separated,
both middle fingers should rest between the two thumbs and touch both index fingers.
This is the six-fingered mudrā taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones in the world;
its two thumbs are always raised, O Kuvalayodbhava.
This mudrā has been taught in the world by the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds;
thus, having formed the añjali gesture, one should pay homage to the Teacher of the World.
This is the mudrā of salutation, renowned throughout all worlds;
it is formed by fixing the two hands together in a joined position.
This is the Yamala-mudrā, renowned throughout the three worlds:
the two hands are slightly joined at the base, and the two thumbs are firmly pressed together.
That shall be the *sampuṭa* mudrā, which destroys sorrow, fatigue, and disease.
These are the mudrās that have been described, all of which arise from weapons.
Those named Puṣpa, Śayana, Vādya, and those named after the planets—
all of them are capable of performing every action when joined with all the mantras as spoken [by the Buddha].
Neither the lunar day nor the asterism nor fasting is prescribed;
when combined with the mudrās and mantras, they shall swiftly accomplish all rites.
The wise reciter, endowed with austerity, by the mere act of recitation,
and through the application of mudrās and mantras, finds nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Again, having joined both hands together in the añjali gesture with the fingers interlaced,
the little fingers, ring fingers, and thumbs placed on the sides is declared to be the incense mudrā.
377) By means of the joined palms as a support, one should slightly bend the two index fingers;
this is the general *bali* mudrā, which was brought forth by the Protectors of the World.
In the center, flowers are arranged according to what is available from various sources;
this is offered in all the ritual offerings (balikarma) for the mantras.
Having formed the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with the right hand,
the right hand should indeed be grasped by the left hand using the wrist-connection (*maṇibandhana*).
This is declared to you as the fragrance mudrā for all mantras:
always place those two thumbs and middle fingers within the fist of the right hand.
Then, having formed the shape of a needle, it is declared to be the lamp mudrā;
it is established from the ring finger and the thumb as the rosary.
Constantly extending the little finger, placing the middle finger behind it,
and setting the index finger in a curved position— this is called the *akṣamudrā*.
Then, having placed the *garbhāñjali* [mudrā] and the rosary,
that knower of mantras should recite the mantra as desired, which swiftly bestows the boon of accomplishment.
This is always the prescribed method for all beautiful mudrās:
one should form the tip of the right hand in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) toward the southeast.
Having placed it facing forward in the fire, one should always bend the index finger;
having placed the thumb upon the hand, it should remain bent in the middle.
This is taught as the invocation mudrā for Jātavedas:
the tips of the index fingers are bent and the two thumbs are joined together.
The dismissal (*visarjana*) is observed in all rites within the blazing fire;
one skilled in the ritual of *homa* should perform it for all mantras.
When fully endowed with these mudrās and properly applied to the mantra-fire,
one should perform a salutation with joined palms, with the fingers interlaced on all sides.
One should perform it in reverse, however, with the two thumbs joined together,
the two index fingers bent outward, and resting upon the middle fingers.
378) This is indeed declared to be the supreme mudrā when employed in rites of worship;
it is the salutation to all mantras, to the Lord of Mantras, the Son of the Jinas.
One should cause the purification of all mantras and the offering of a seat;
even in the absence of flowers, one should apply them by forming the mudrā.
For when these mantras are worshipped according to the ritual procedure, they accomplish all aims;
by performing the binding of mudrās for the sake of worship, it becomes auspicious.
But the second is the mental worship, which is like that arising from flowers;
this method of worship has been proclaimed by the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds.
In the absence of flowers, however, a two-fold worship is prescribed;
for the sake of accomplishing all mantras, one should employ it in all rites.
This mudrā, which performs all actions, has been taught by all the Buddhas;
it is to be used during sitting, lying down, bathing, drinking, and eating.
In a beautiful, illuminating place, with the mantra as the cause for the mandala,
this is the convention for all mantras for the sake of the empowerment of practitioners.
This mudrā, effective for all rites, has been taught by the Lords of the World;
this rule concerning one hundred complete mudrās has thus been proclaimed.
Hereafter, I shall explain the mudrā that has attained the status of the eighth:
having placed both hands in that very same manner, one should then [proceed] further.
Having formed that very [mudrā] with the index finger as the middle one and joined with the needle [finger],
the two [thumbs] are made to touch at the third part below the nail.
Having encircled the sheath and brought it forth, one should form the shape of a needle;
this is the mudrā of the Great-Souled Śakrin, the Lord of Mantras.
These very same [fingers], with the index fingers moved together and the middle fingers level,
have the needle-like [tips] placed upon the nails, and the ring fingers joined together.
This is indeed the Uṣṇīṣa mudrā, proclaimed by the Lords of Jinas;
it is formed by placing the hands together with the middle fingers interlaced.
379) When the little fingers are joined together, this is the *mitamudbhavā* mudrā;
having made the middle fingers equal like needles, the fingertips are brought into contact.
Released from its coiled form, it is called the Great Seal (mahāmudrā);
that very [seal] is held with the tips of the index fingers slightly joined together.
Then, having placed [the hands] on the middle needle with the palms joined below,
the two thumbs are placed on the third joints of the index fingers and pressed by the nails.
This is declared to be the excellent mudrā of the wise Mañjughoṣa;
it is formed by placing the two hands together in the gesture of reverential salutation (añjali).
The two middle fingers are placed together and extended with their tips pointing like needles;
the two thumbs, touching the middle fingers, rest upon the three joints of those fingers.
Having formed a needle with the little fingers, [the other fingers] are extended and raised;
this is the excellent and supreme mudrā, which has attained the state of being the treasury of the Dharma.
Those very hands, placed according to the prescribed rule and brought together,
with all the fingers fully extended, are thus positioned like a sheath.
One should open both hands, covered by eight fingers;
[the mudrā] consists of eight, representing the knowledge of the eight principles of the person, and has reached the fourfold union.
The perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds, declare that very [reality] to be the Saṅgha;

This is the supreme and most excellent mudrā, which accomplishes all activities:
having joined both hands together, they are positioned in the form of an añjali.
Extending a single index finger emerging from the right hand—

This is known as the supreme mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all rites.
It is formed by placing the hands in that same manner, marked at the tips by the interlacing of the fingers.

These eight seals are the Great Seals;

Sixty crores of Vimbakas, along with eighty [crores] arising together,

"For when applied according to the prescribed method, these will swiftly accomplish one's purpose.
Having spoken thus, the Lion of the Śākyas, the foremost of sages and the best among men, [departed].
Then, the one of great supernatural power [addressed] Mañjughoṣa, the Bodhisattva Vajra;
this [is] the origin of the mudrās in the ritual manual (kalpa) of Mañjuśrī.
This very person was entrusted by you alone for the sake of protection within the teaching on earth,
when the end of the age has arrived and I myself have entered final nirvana.
For the sake of protecting my teaching, all of this has been told by me;
indeed, the characteristics of the mudrās and the mantras have been explained in detail.
This secret of all the worlds, and even that which is called the mystery,
has been proclaimed in this Sūtra, the sovereign of ritual manuals, extensively expanded with a wealth of qualities.
The emergence of the qualities and praises of mantras is manifold;
the application of mantras and the application of tantras are explained in many ways.
The doctrine of the power and qualities of those who recite [mantras], the arising of their causes,
the auspicious emergence of their fruits, and the destinies and wombs of sentient beings have indeed been explained.
"O Kumāra! [This] has been employed as the cause for the accomplishment of your mantras.
Thus addressed, the youth Mañjuśrī remained in the sky.
381) Having bowed his head to the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of the World,
the Maker of Light, he sighed deeply and, moistened with compassion, wept again and again.
Having requested a boon from the Bestower of Boons, they stood near the Buddha;
for when the Blessed One had passed away, the treasury of mantras on this earth was lost.
"How will the greatness of the destiny of sentient beings come to pass for him?
Thus addressed, the Perfectly Awakened One then spoke to Mañjughoṣa.
Listen, child Mañjuśrī, O Kumāra! If you ask, [it is because] when I have passed away and the world has become empty upon the surface of the earth...
When the treasury of Dharma has been destroyed and the Śrāvakas have long since entered parinirvāṇa,
one should indeed fashion an image of the Teacher, the Supreme among Bipeds.
Having performed worship with honor, using incense, perfumes, and ointments,
as well as various excellent garments and other ornaments such as jeweled earrings;
Having prepared various kinds of foods and edibles as an offering for Him who assumes whatever form He desires, [one should present] that which is endowed with diverse forms.
Likewise, having repeated the mantra, he brought about an auspicious rebirth from the womb of a sentient being,
reaching the most excellent city for the sake of the highest state and origin.
Standing at the foot of the Bodhi tree, they attained peace in the western direction.
Thus addressed by the Perfectly Awakened One, Mañjuśrī was pleased and urged on.
Then the wise Bodhisattva of great supernatural power, being thoroughly satisfied,
[spoke] all of this which had been sung of old while stationed above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
"In the presence of the Buddhas, he who sets in motion the wheel of the Buddha's Dharma then chose the wheel of mantras that has continued for a long time. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the thirty-third chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual of mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists a most supreme secret."
Your root mudrā, together with its retinue and the characteristics of the mudrās, is to be employed in all rites;
it bestows all prosperity, is fruitful, follows all mantras, and accomplishes the purpose of all activities.
Listen briefly, Mañjuśrī!
First, with the palms extended in *añjali*, the index and ring fingers are inserted individually into the middle joints of [the thumbs].

This, O Mañjuśrī, is your renowned Root Mudrā; it is effective for all rites. Likewise, having joined the hands together, the ring fingers are pressed together, as are the index, middle, and little fingers.

On the tip of the thumb situated upon the upward-pointing line—this, O Mañjuśrī, is declared to be your other face-mudrā. Having formed fists with the fingers interlocked, releasing the middle fingers and making them like needles, one should place the pair of index fingers, bent at their sides, at the ends; this, O Mañjuśrī, is your mudrā.

This is the *daṃṣṭrā* [fang] mudrā. One should place the pair of thumbs on the sides of the mudrā. O Mañjuśrī, you yourself are this very mudrā! In that place, within those joined palms, you abide through your commitment (*samaya*) and grant your presence.
Having released the index fingers from two fists whose fingers are interlocked, with the pair of thumbs in the middle—this is [the *daṃṣṭrā* mudrā].

O Mañjuśrī! This is another mudrā of yours, the *cīraka* (rag) mudrā. Having extended the fingers of the joined palms, with the ring fingers and the tips of the index fingers positioned between the middle fingers—this, O Mañjuśrī, is declared to be your very own fundamental (*mūla*) mudrā. By extending the index finger of this same mudrā, this is that [other mudrā].

Mañjuśrī, this is your eye-mudrā: the little fingers and ring fingers are joined like braids and placed in the middle of the hollowed palms; the middle fingers are outside [the palms], with their tips bent over the index fingers; and the tips of the thumbs are joined together. This other mudrā of yours, Mañjuśrī, is your face-mudrā, which is effective for all rites.

In this manner, by this sequence, release each finger one by one; then, with all fingers joined together including the two thumbs, extend them one by one. O Mañjuśrī! This, with the right thumb raised, is your Uṣṇīṣa mudrā. Having contracted the right [hand] and raised the left, it becomes your Lalāṭa mudrā.
O Mañjuśrī! Upon seeing her, all malevolent grahas flee away.
(133, p. 383) Thus, the ears, neck, arms, heart, hands, throat, waist, navel, thighs, shanks,
feet, eyes, face, and tongue— these are likewise raised in succession by the ten fingers.
The characteristics of the successive mudrās are as follows: one performs the successive rites.
With the face-mudrā, there is the binding of the mouth; with the fang-mudrā, the liberation from malevolent grahas;
with the tongue-mudrā, the warding off of evil speech; and with the heart-mudrā, the destruction of a king’s wrath or that of any other being.
It becomes the destroyer of anger for those possessing form who have resorted to various states of existence, such as gods, asuras, humans, and non-humans.

In this sequence, one performs all rites in every respect. In this manner, there are incalculable mudrās according to this order. And you, Mañjuśrī, perform incalculable rites; indeed, in every way, all rites are contained within all the mudrās.
That Mahāmudrā was bound by those countless great heroes, the Tathāgatas,
as well as by the great heroes who have attained the great stages.
Therein are groves of *nimbaraka* trees numbering thirty-six, eighty-four, nine, five, sixty,
and so forth, in the count of *nayutas*, each succeeding one surpassing all the worlds.
All mundane activities whatsoever are included within all mudrās;
by means of any one of these mudrās, one should accomplish all goals.
Indeed, they should be bound with both hands during the time of practice, in the mandala,
or again during the fire-offerings and recitations by one intent upon the preliminary service.
Seated or even standing, the observer of the vow should recite as long as desired,
by means of this great rite of protection for oneself or for another.
One should perform all rites at all times within all mudrās. Thus it is said.

Thus concludes the thirty-fourth chapter, the second detailed section on the ritual of mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
384) At the end of this work, following the conclusion of the fifty-third chapter-section,
another chapter-section named the Mahāmudrāpaṭalavisara, the thirty-fourth, has been written.
It is perceived. Since it must be a specific variety of the thirty-fourth [chapter] of that which has passed, for this reason it is applied right here.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes, [addressed] Mañjuśrī—
He addressed the Youthful Prince, all the bodhisattvas, and all the beings assembled in the gathering:

"Listen, O hosts of spirits! All you sons of gods possessed of great supernatural power! There exists within the extensive ritual manual of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince..."

This is the manual for the practice of the *samudrāpaṭala*, which serves as the cause for the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment for those beings who have entered into the conduct of all mantra-tantras. It explains how all mantras are accomplished most swiftly,
how all rites are drawn forth from every source for everyone, and how there are mudrās by which, when sealed, [beings] are brought under control most swiftly.
They exist. Listen to that, sirs; for the benefit of all sentient beings, I shall speak. These are the mudrās of all mantras.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the samādhi called the Ocean-Seal of the Tathāgata’s Greatness of Qualities Adorned with the Seals of All Buddha-Dharmas. Immediately upon the Blessed One having entered [that samādhi], all the Tathāgatas [manifested] the pledge of all seals.
He spoke. Having arisen from that samādhi, he proclaimed the extensive section on the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), which is sealed with the seals of all the Tathāgatas and pertains to all mantras.
First of all, there are heart-mantras for all the mantra families. One should recite them twice, seven times, or once.
Then the mudrās must be bound; it is not otherwise. And what is that?

The heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas is *jinajik*. O worthy ones! This is the heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas, effective for all rites. Within the Tathāgata family, all mudrās should be bound; thereafter, one should commence the ritual activity. *Āroliku* is the heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara, effective for all rites. While binding all mudrās within the Lotus family, this mantra should be recited.

O Vajradhṛk, this is the heart-mantra of Vajrapāṇi, which is useful for all means of accomplishment in all rites. O noble ones, when reciting it within all the Vajra families, the mudrā must be bound. *Surāraku*. This [mantra] is to be employed in all rites by one who binds all the mudrās of all the gods.

(135, p. 385) *Sarvadevānāṃ hṛdayaḥ* (The Heart of all gods). *Yakṣātak*. *Sarvayakṣāṇāṃ hṛdayaḥ* (The Heart of all yakṣas). *Pinādhṛk*. *Rudrasya hṛdayaḥ* (The Heart of Rudra). *Ṣṭhoṃ*. O venerable ones, this is that single-syllabled heart-mantra.
Of all mundane and supramundane beings—including all bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, pūtanas, kravyādas, and so forth;
the constellations, grahas, mātṛs, kumāras, and kumārikās;
and all beings such as humans, non-humans, all those enumerated among the vidyādharas, ṛṣis, and others.

For the sake of all sentient beings— those bound by the karma of the threads of all destinies, those who are liberated and free from passion, those of great and small supernatural powers, those who have pacified the three faults, and those submerged in the three muds— this single-syllable mantra serves as the heart-essence for them all.

One performs all rites. All mudrās should be bound. While performing recitation, the recitation must be done with this very heart-mantra. One is constantly sustained by the empowerment of the Buddha. This [mantra] possesses great power and great benefits for all rites, including those concerning mudrās, ritual vessels, procedures, and the accomplishment of the paṭa.
The *sattva* should be applied in succession; it accomplishes everything that is desired by the practitioner in his mind.
From that, there are one hundred and eight mudrās;
first, one should perform the uṣṇīṣa mudrā for the Victor who wields the wheel.
Beyond that, in the supreme world, it is called the Lotus Mudrā;
the third, however, is the Vajra Mudrā, which belongs to Vajrapāṇi.
One should designate the fourth as the deity-seal, the svastika;
the fifth is said here to be the sword-seal (khaḍgamudrā) of the rākṣasas.
The sixth is proclaimed as the gadā-mudrā of the yakṣas;
the seventh, for the mantras of the asuras, is declared to be the vajra-muṣṭi.
The eighth is taught as the Śūla-mudrā for all the Krodhas;
the ninth is proclaimed as the Puṣpa-mudrā for the Yakṣas and Yakṣīs.
One should know the tenth to be the mallet (mudgara), the eleventh the supreme [discus] (phara),
and the twelfth is designated as the spear (śakti) of the child Kārttikeya.
One should employ the renowned utpala of Mañjughoṣa;
the number thirteen has been specified by the sages who teach for the sake of sentient beings.
The fourteenth is the conch (śaṅkha), while the fifteenth is known as the kettle-drum (bherī).
The sixteenth should be understood as the hand-drum (paṭaha), and the seventeenth is the other, the war-drum (dundubhi).
Eighteen [finger-breadths] is likewise called the "firmly bound" (baddha), nineteen is called the "instrument" (karaṇa),
and twenty is specified as the "axe" (paraśu) according to the measurement of their respective counts.
Likewise, a white umbrella is proclaimed as the crown (uṣṇīṣa);
the robe is designated as the bowl (pātra), and the mendicant’s staff (khakkhara) is considered the supreme [attribute].
Compassion, loving-kindness, as well as wisdom, meditative concentration, and likewise ethical discipline—
the sixfold set beginning with patience and generosity— has been taught by the Leaders of the World.
For these six perfections have been taught by the Buddhas through hearing;
thirty mudrās for the Wheel-turner have been taught, O Hero among Men.
Of the single-syllable Hero, the Lord of Mantras,
the All-pervading Sovereign of the World, and the Vidyās, twenty-eight [mantras] have been taught.
The goddess known as Sitā, Mahāśvetā, as well as Ṣaṇḍaravāsinī, Bhṛkuṭī, and likewise the goddess [named] Buddhadattā, are born from the hearts of the Buddhas.
The mudrā of Tārā is said to be the lotus;
however, the mudrā of the formidable Hayagrīva is known as the "mouth."
O Vajrapāṇi, there are likewise thirty-one mudrās;
all of them are his weapons, established in various forms for battle.
The four great mudrās are also proclaimed within the maṇḍala of Māra; they are designated as the trident of Rudra... [incomplete].
The rosary of Brahmā, the discus of Viṣṇu,
and likewise the mace— this entire array of mudrās belonging to all the gods, all the lords of yakṣas and men, and all beings, is the refuge of all sentient beings.
The supreme realm exists in three ways for those with passion and those free from passion;
it encompasses all the world in three ways, consisting of the stationary and the moving.
387) Among those beings who speak of the truth regarding the innumerable realms designated by the elements,
it is said that for all of them, everywhere, there is but one mudrā and so forth.
Thus, one hundred and eight [names] have been proclaimed;
now, the detailed qualities and the power of these are being described here.
Just as success may be achieved for humans when joined with mantras,
so too does it act through other applications, beautifully adorned by the fingers.
Placed between the two hands, this supreme [mudrā] quickly grants wealth;
I shall first describe it for you, so listen, O you who desire prosperity!
First of all, in a pure place, wearing white garments and clean clothes,
performing pure deeds with constant devotion in a pure location;
Facing the east, one should stand before the stūpa and perform the binding;
it must not be given to one who is not a disciple or to one who engages in fierce deeds.
To one who grants fearlessness, who has entered into the covenant,
and who is devoted to the sons of the Conquerors as well as to the teaching of the Buddhas.
For those who have not yet generated the [awakening] mind, the perfection of the mudrās is not to be accepted,
even by devoted sons of the Conquerors and wise Bodhisattvas.
One should always give to Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who have been honored;
such a teacher, firmly established in the conduct of awakening, is always highly esteemed.
In all applications of mantras, it is always supreme;
therefore, the mudrā should then be given to the disciple who is free from doubt.
Likewise, the preceptor should be one who knows the application of mantras, is pure, skillful, and of noble lineage; he should be righteous, wise, consecrated, and one who has beheld the maṇḍala.
The mantras have thus been shown; the disciple who knows the tantra should be accepted.
The disciple should likewise show love for the guru as he would for the Buddha.
Otherwise, there is no accomplishment of the mantras or among any of the mudrās at any time.
388) First, having become pure and facing east, one should rub the hands with white sandalwood; first of all:

The *samayamudrā* should be bound. This is the *mudrā* of the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣa: both hands are joined in the hollowed-palms gesture (*añjalipuṭa*), not hollowed out, slightly curved, in the form of a bud, with the faces of the hands like unopened lotuses. This is the *samayamudrā* of the Blessed Buddha. That same gesture, with the hands extended and held together in a hollowed position, in the form of a blooming lotus, is that of Avalokita.
The Mudrā: Having encircled both hands as before, one should press down the little fingers with the index fingers while they remain inside. This is the Utpala Mudrā of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Contracting those same little fingers as before, the hands remain in the same position with the index fingers joined with the thumbs.

One should display the shape of a blue lotus bud; this is the mudrā of Tārā, with all fingers bent. Contracting that very same [mudrā] and forming the shape of an eye, this is the mudrā of Ārya-Bhṛkuṭī. One should place that very same [mudrā] upon the forehead; this is the Eye-mudrā of the Goddess Devī. Again, contracting those two [thumbs] with the middle fingers—

Having formed the shape of a pair of tongs, one should place it above the head; this is the single-syllable great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) of the Blessed One, the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), which performs all rites. Placing that same [mudrā] on the forehead is the heart-mudrā (*hṛdayamudrā*) of the Blessed Buddha. One should place it on the eyes; that same [mudrā] is the eye-mudrā (*netramudrā*) of the Universal Monarch. That same [mudrā] on the mouth...

One should place [them]. That itself is the face-mudrā of the one-syllable Universal Monarch, the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyādhipati*). In this way, up to the mantra-practitioner’s arms, knees, shanks, feet, and so forth, there are twenty types of mudrās; eight of these are the great mudrās (*mahāmudrā*). They are to be employed in all ritual actions. That same [mudrā] is the hollowed palms joined together (*karasaṃpuṭa*).
Having entwined the two middle fingers and formed the two little fingers into needles,

with the tips of both thumbs positioned like barley grains, the two index fingers extended and joined to the needles, and both ring fingers tucked inside and their ends bent, well-arranged— this is the Great Mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma of the Blessed Ones.
Bending the two thumbs and extending them in the middle—this is the *mudrā* of the Buddhas for the defeat of the four Māras. One should display that same *mudrā* placed above the head;
it is the great *mudrā* named "The Destroyer of All Defilements of All Buddhas. One should place that same [mudrā] upon the forehead.

That which is called Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the seal (*mudrā*) of all Buddhas. Placing that very [seal] upon the heart is the Great Seal named "Extraction of the Arrows of All Views. One should place both hands in that same seal;
this is the Great Seal named "Accomplishment of All Vidyās. One should place that same seal upon the neck.
The Great Seal named "The Pacifier of All Misfortunes" is as follows: one should rotate that very seal in every direction.

The Great Seal named "The Attainment of Great Protection" is likewise. In this manner, there are eight Great Seals that accomplish all aims; they are the seals of the Victorious Uṣṇīṣa. That very [seal]...
The two hands, like sprouting leaves, extended from the left and placed obliquely toward the right; this is the *sitātapatra* (White Parasol) mudrā.
Those same hands, likewise positioned upon the head, constitute the mudrā of the Blessed One’s *uṣṇīṣa*. Both palms...

Having formed the *sampuṭa* (enclosed) gesture, it is placed upon the head in the form of an *uṣṇīṣa*; this is the seal (*mudrā*) of the Blessed One Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa. One should then open that same seal; this is the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of Jvālāmālinoṣṇīṣa, effective for all rites (*sarvakarmika*). It should be employed in all fears and in all ritual actions. One should place that same seal upon the chest.

This is the great mudrā of all the uṣṇīṣas. With the hands folded and held firmly together in that same manner, it is the great armor mudrā of all the Tathāgatas, to be employed against all obstacles. With the hands held in that same manner, with the tips of both [hands] positioned so as to form the shape of a book, one should place them at the center of the chest. This is the mother of all Buddhas.

The Perfection of Wisdom is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā). One should show it to all sentient beings; it pacifies all obstacles and all misfortunes, accomplishes all aims, and generates mindfulness. Placing those very hands upon the forehead is the Dharma Great Seal, the consecration of all Buddhas, for all consecrations.
It should be applied to all sentient beings. One should place those same two hands upon the forehead in a variegated form;

this is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) named "The Dispeller of All Māras. Those same two hands, with fingers contracted, joined together in a contracted manner, positioned in the shape of a needle, and with the middle fingers extended.

With the two thumbs marked by needle-like signs and grasped [by the fingers], this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Blessed One, the Mass of Radiance (tejorāśi). Placing that same seal above the head, this is another Great Seal of the Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣa, the Mass of Radiance.
Placing both hands on the forehead in that very same manner, this is the third seal of the Blessed One, the Eye Seal (netramudrā).

With those same hands, both made beautiful and placed one above the other for the sake of making an offering—or else held in the form of a hollowed cup with the left hand—the thumbs and little fingers of each are interlaced. This is the root mudrā of the Great Vajra Seat of all Buddhas. With those same hands, they are displayed at the crown of the head.

The seal of the root of the Great Bodhi tree: with those same hands joined and turned back, it is called the seal that destroys all Māras of all Buddhas. With those same hands interlaced, one should place them at the neck;
this is called the seal that subjugates all spirits. One should hold those same [hands] at the throat; this is the seal that surveys all spirits.
This is the Mahāmudrā named Sarvadurgativiśodhanī (Purifier of All Evil Destinies). One should place that very same [hand] upon the knees.
This is the Mahāmudrā named Sarvadevotpattisannicaya (Accumulation of the Arising of All Deities). One should throw that very same [hand] upward.
Both hands in the gesture of fearlessness is the Mahāmudrā named Śani (Saturn), which is the sphere of all enjoyments.

One should place that very same [mudrā] upon the crown of the head with the palms joined; this is the Great Seal named Sarvabuddhakṣetrākramaṇī (Traverser of All Buddha-fields). One should place both hands at the ears in the manner of blossoming flowers; this is the Great Seal named Sarvanāgadamanī (Subduer of All Nāgas). One should join both hands together in a hollowed cup and hold them at the tip of the nose.
The Great Seal named "The Object of Support of All Buddhas" (sarvabuddhānāmālambana):
one should place that very seal upon the crown of the head. This is the Great Seal named "The Uṣṇīṣa Exalted Above All Buddhas."
In this manner, there are incalculable mudrās belonging to the uṣṇīṣas of all the Tathāgatas.

By means of the incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, there is an incalculable lineage of Cakravartins and incalculable Cakravartins. Their sovereign is the Single-Syllable Cakravartin, the Lord of Mantras.

There are also innumerable Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-kings and innumerable ritual expansions (*kalpavisara*) for all mantras. Of these, I shall speak briefly; here there is but one single mudrā for all, and the heart-mantra is the single-syllable Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*). Its very root-mudrā, as prescribed among the mantras, is now described here.
Possessing great majesty and immeasurable power, by the mere binding of which all mantras become manifest,

and all the Blessed Ones in battle grant their accomplishments; and they empower the practitioner of the vidyā-rite simply by the recollection of the Lord of Mantras, the peerless single-syllable [mantra], like a universal monarch.

One becomes one who has acquired the roots of merit of ten million Buddhas. Even for a monk who has committed the four root downfalls, that karma which would lead to rebirth in the great hells goes to destruction through mere recollection;
what need is there to mention recitation? The five deeds of immediate retribution also go to destruction; what need is there to mention others?

Since they are unwholesome, this sovereign king of vidyās, the Single Syllable, should therefore be remembered, recited, meditated upon, brought to mind, worshipped, and constantly propitiated with every effort.
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām*. *Bhrūṃ*. This, O noble ones, is [the essence] of all the uṣṇīṣas.

This is the root mantra spoken by the Tathāgata. By means of this very sovereign of mantras, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin born from the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, one should perform all rites. When accompanied by the mudrā, it is certain to succeed in all mundane and supramundane mantras throughout the various ritual manuals (*kalpavisara*). And here is the mudrā:

One should hold those very hands above the head in the form of a *uṣṇīṣa*, with the palms joined, the middle fingers extended, the tips of all the fingers positioned inward, and the shape curved like a coil, slightly tilted upward. This is the great root-mudrā for the One-Syllable Universal Monarch (*Ekākṣaracakravartin*).

One should perform all rites with this [mantra]. One should employ it in the supreme means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and so forth. It should also be applied for the sake of protection, shielding, and guarding. One who employs it in minor accomplishments and such applications becomes ignorant of the ritual commitments (*asamayajña*). For such a mantra-master, the mantras will not be successful, except in the case of protective rites and for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*).

For the purpose of destroying evil, it should be recited constantly in a pure place—on mountains, at the banks of rivers, streams, or oceans—and not in other locations; for this reason, this King of Vidyās possesses great power and should not be recited in other places. One should recite it with a mind exalted by its power, pervading all sentient beings with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
And here is the mudrā (141, p. 391):
having formed the two hands in the shape of hollowed palms with the fingers kept separate, [one should join] the middle fingers...
In the third part [of the hand], one should slightly incline it; one should fashion it in the shape of a *uṣṇīṣa*.

This is the great mudrā of the Blessed One, the King of the *Uṣṇīṣas*. Having joined the two hands together in the hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*) as before, one should slightly incline them; this is the third great mudrā of the Blessed One’s *Uṣṇīṣa*. Oṃ godare vīra svāhā. This...
This is the heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas; it accomplishes all activities, fulfills all aims, and wards off all misfortunes. By merely recollecting it, one becomes empowered by all Buddhas.
One is liberated from all sins. It stands above all mantras. The Buddha himself should be regarded as being directly present.

It should be employed together with this mudrā; it performs all rites most swiftly. While this is being recited, all mantras become as if recited. In whatever manner it is applied, in that very manner it accomplishes the rites.
According to the wish of the reciter, it becomes effective for all purposes. Then, one should place both hands, held in the hollowed-palm position, upon the head.

In the form of a triple-pronged needle. This is the second heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*) of all the Blessed Buddhas. And here is the mantra: *oṃ gerure vīra svāhā*. This is the heart-seal of all the Blessed Buddhas; it performs all activities, wards off all misfortunes, and accomplishes all goals.

Possessing great power, it is to be accomplished in all mantra rituals; no doubt should be entertained here. In whatever manner it is employed, in that very manner it succeeds. Furthermore, with those same hands placed in the hollowed-cup (sampuṭa) gesture, one should firmly encircle them with the inner fingers and extend both index fingers.

One should slightly contract [the fingers] and display them while placing them above the head. This is the great mudrā of all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas. And here is the mantra: Oṃ ṭrāṃ bandha svāhā. This is the root mantra of all uṣṇīṣas, effective for all rites; it should be employed in all directions and in all bindings. It accomplishes all activities.

One performs it. At the time of the recitation for accomplishment (*sādhana*), during fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth, whether for one's own protection or the protection of others—in all substances and in all ritual manuals of mantras (*mantrakalpa*), both mundane and supramundane—whatever protections have been taught, they should all be performed by means of this alone. Thus, a great protection (*mahārakṣā*) is established. It should be employed with all mantras; it succeeds in all rites.

The chapters on the vehicles and accomplishments, as well as the mudrās and mantras— beginning with Tejarāśi, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, and so forth— of all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas, the great universal monarchs and lords of vidyās, should all be applied in their entirety and in detail, including all those that are mundane and supramundane.
There are extensive chapters on the details of mantra and tantra, as well as infinite mudrās. And herein are the mantras: *Oṃ jvalitogradeha vibhinda hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (This is 142, p. 192)

The supreme heart-mantra of the Blessed One, the Buddha Tejorāśi, which is effective for all rites in all tantras, should be employed. That very [mudrā] is formed by joining the two hands with the middle fingers extended and the index fingers encircling them in the shape of a bracelet, both being wound like a noose and forming the expanse of a maṇḍala. And this—
The *khaṅkhara* mudrā belongs to the Blessed Buddha. And here is the mantra: Oṃ dhuna jitāraṇa hūṃ.
This *khaṅkhara* mudrā-mantra of the Blessed Buddhas is to be employed in all rites;
