it awakens all mantras as desired and brings all spirits (*bhūta*) under control.

It provides consolation for all sentient beings, inspires all substances, accomplishes [all aims], and completely dries up all evils. In whatever way this eight-syllable mantra of the Tathāgata is applied, in that very way it accomplishes all activities. Having performed the hand-gesture by interlacing the hands, [one should recite it].

It has the form of a bowl. This is the bowl-mudrā of all the Tathāgatas; it should be understood as the "Tathāgata Bowl. One should hold it at the region of the navel; it becomes capable of performing all rites. And here is the mantra:
Oṃ, empowered by the world-protectors, hold, hold, maintain, O you of great majesty, Buddha-bowl, svāhā! This...
The mantra of the Tathāgata’s bowl-seal of the Blessed Buddhas, when joined with this,
shall be capable of accomplishing all rites.
It performs a variety of actions honored by the greatness of their destinies;
it accomplishes all rites spoken of in all mantras.
By the will of the practitioner, it accomplishes [this] quickly here; of this there is no doubt.
This applies even to those mantras of the Tathāgatas and those of Avalokiteśvara.
The principal mantras known as the Vajra, which are worshipped by various deities,
all attain accomplishment when uttered from the vessel of the Buddha.
Indeed, there were various groups of preeminent female messengers, as well as groups of male and female servants;
and there were the leaders of various attendants, including yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kaśmalas.
They were sent as messengers for all counsel and likewise as performers of all tasks by the eminent kings,
who were well-known and born of the lineages of gods and gandharvas.
The mantras were [revealed] by the accomplished Vidyādharas, as were the world-protectors of great supernatural power,
along with Śakra and the others, and the foremost of the gods led by Brahmā, who are all wise.
Whatever mantras may have been spoken by the Kinnaras and the Garuḍas, who possess great supernatural powers, they are always effective in performing all rites.
393) All of them attain accomplishment when united with the vessel of the Buddha,
having drawn forth all mantras that depend upon their movements and forms.
He is the king of mantras, the master, the lord, the most excellent, and of great splendor;
he is designated by the seers of reality as the foremost of all mantras.
That mantra, residing within a worthy vessel, is like a wish-fulfilling gem in three ways;
it performs a variety of actions according to the desired will of the practitioner.
It produces a greatness of diverse qualities and a supreme power that is difficult for all mantrins to overcome through their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
One who is unworthy becomes worthy when the mantra resides within him as described by the best of sages;
indeed, one who is worthy is empowered by the application of the mantra and endowed with the mudrās.
It produces a manifold expansion of virtues arising from karma;
it destroys diseases from all sides and brings about abundant enjoyments.
"Joined in all rites, it shall swiftly bring about prosperity for the beings belonging to the three realms of existence, as well as for gods, daityas, and lords of men. Thus,
one should place those very hands, formed into the shape of hollowed palms and bound with various braided locks, against the region of the forehead.
Citrahasta, that indeed is the great mudrā of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇiratna*) of the Blessed Buddhas. And here is the mantra:
*namaḥ sarvabuddhebhyaḥ oṃ tejojvāla sarvārthasādhakaṃ sidhya sidhya siddhicintāmaṇiratna hūṃ*.
The Cintāmaṇi-ratna mantra accomplishes all aims;
it shall bring about desired objects, as well as the mantras in their full detail.
It brings about the greatness of one's virtues and accomplishes even that which is contemplated;
it also makes the wealth of the well-spoken words of mantra and tantra bear fruit.
One should accomplish the ultimate goal, which is likewise fixed upon Buddhahood;
thus, by his own will, he performed the application of karma and was born as such.
One shall immediately accomplish all the various forms of prosperity, whose fruits arise from one's own efforts,
as well as the perfected results of all mantras and tantras.
394) Furthermore, [he beholds] the state of a deity, or the state of Śakra, or even the embodied state of Brahmā; likewise, the Sudarśanas who resemble the forms of the Ābhāsvara gods.
"Through this practice, one attains a physical form consisting mostly of gods, reaching the Suraśreṣṭha, the foremost Surā, the Bṛhatphala, and the Akaniṣṭha realms."
Indeed, *cintā* is said to be the foremost of mental states, which extensively explains the meaning of mantras;
it is abundant among the *mudrās* and accomplishes the goals of the Dharma and one’s destiny.
The accomplishment of the purpose of all phenomena, the realization of the purpose of all mantras,
for the sake of all qualities and enlightenment, having the dharmadhātu as its support.
This which is worshipped as the jewel and the tip of thought has been taught in the form of mantra;
through it, one shall especially attain the very support that is the nature of heaven.
Through this practice, one shall attain heaven and the extensive path of the meaning of the mantra.

In that same manner, both hands are placed upon the shoulders, with the right and left held half-way up, interlocked and joined at the bases of the palms. This is the *cīvara-mudrā* of all the Buddhas. There is also a mantra for this: *Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhitā me cīvara svāhā*. This is the *cīvara-mantra*.

Having consecrated one's own robe with mantras, one should wear it; one becomes invincible to all spirits. A consecrated Kṣatriya great king, who has been anointed on the head and brings comfort to all, should consecrate his own garment seven times and enter the battlefield; upon seeing him, all enemies become paralyzed and retreat.

Or, all beings become submissive upon merely seeing him. His pride, intoxication, and arrogance have departed, and no weapon falls upon his body. He has no fear of humans or non-humans; neither poison nor fire falls upon his body. He has no fear of disease, nor does he have any fear of untimely death. Nor does he...
One is not slain by the armies of an enemy; nor can one be harmed by ḍākinīs, bhūtas, piśācas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or gandharvas;

nor by various hosts of spirits who steal vitality, those with fierce minds, flesh-eaters, all carnivorous beings, or violent ones who torment other sentient beings; nor even by kings who practice evil deeds.

To cause injury—how much less so to break through it without protection? In all rites and with all substances, it is impossible to deprive one of life. Indeed, there exists no being, nor any class of beings, nor mantra, nor mudrā, nor poison, whether stationary or mobile, nor weapon, nor various implements of attack that can prevail against it.
Whether it be a *rākṣasa* or a *rākṣasī*, a *yakṣa* or a *yakṣī*, a male elder *yakṣa* or a female elder *yakṣī*,
a male attendant *yakṣa* or a female attendant *yakṣī*— the same should be applied in detail for all beings.

This is not possible. Therefore, by means of the Tathāgata’s seal, robe-mantra, and the performance of protection, or merely through recitation or remembrance, no one else is able to break it—not even by the mantras of the Tathāgatas or by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—except by the will of that very practitioner himself. Thus...

This mantra possesses great power; it accomplishes all rites, achieves all aims, destroys all that is evil, is endowed with all auspiciousness, fulfills all purposes, purifies all miserable rebirths, eradicates all afflictions, and brings the qualities of a Buddha to perfection.

In that same manner, with the hands as before, one should form the two middle fingers bent downward, the tips of the ring fingers placed [upon them], the thumbs bent around [the fingers] so that they do not separate from the third joint, and the little fingers bent; having made these into the shape of wheels, complete with spokes and a hub, one should place them at the position of the head. This is...
This is the Dharma-wheel mudrā of all the Buddhas. And here is the mantra: Oṃ chinda chinda hana hana daha daha dīptacakra hūṃ. This is that mantra of the Dharma-wheel of all the Buddhas;
it destroys all afflictions and cuts through all the miserable rebirths and downfalls caused by unwholesome means. [It bestows] all the qualities of a Buddha.
It kindles [the light]; it illuminates the darkness of all afflictions;
it dispels all suffering; it accomplishes all rites; it liberates from all miseries; it inflames all substances.
This Blessed Wheel of Dharma [is effective] against those wicked beings who have practiced supreme mantras and offer up living beings as sacrifices.

Indeed, by the will of the practitioner, he cuts, rends, cooks, dries up, and destroys the harmful, fierce, and deformed mantras; he uproots them, liberates them, and establishes them in their proper state.
In whatever manner this Blessed One is employed, in that very manner he performs the ritual actions.

Excluding those rites of malevolent magic (*abhicāruka*) and those associated with sensual desire, it should be employed in all rites of pacification (*śāntika*). It should be employed for the benefit of all sentient beings in every respect through great protections and the like. In all accomplishments, both mundane and supramundane, regarding mantras and mudrās as taught in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*), and in all activities of pacification and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*).
This great protection should be employed by means of this very [mantra].

That very [form] has its two hands engaged in striking; the left hand, with its palm turned upward, threatens with the index finger of the right hand; the corners of the mouth are compressed by the application of the knuckles of the clenched fists; the left foot rests upon the knees while the right foot is extended and slightly lowered as he sits in a somewhat upright posture.
396) This is the great mudrā of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā. And here is the mantra: Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā. [This is] of Aparājitā.
This mantra of all the Buddhas is the destroyer of all Māras,
the pacifier of all obstacles, and the increaser of longevity and health.
It is the most excellent among all mantras for the performance of protective rites,
and it is the supreme producer of good fortune for men, women, and youths.
Humans and non-humans, and whatever other beings have malicious intentions— rākṣasas, uccāṭakas, pretas, skandas, apasmāras, and guhyakas.
The hosts of Mātṛs, Bhūtas, and Grahas, as well as those produced by the power of yoga and mantras; afflictions, diseases, and various ailments arising from the humors (dhātus).
Snakes, mice, spiders, insects,
and boils shall not afflict his body, except as a result of past karma.
In disputes regarding travel, and in the face of kings, thieves, water, or fire, one shall obtain victory, security, auspiciousness, and peace; of this there is no doubt.
Having written it on birch bark, or on cloth, or elsewhere,
one should carry it on the head, or on the neck, or on the waist, or on the arm, or in the hand.
Whoever constantly wears this garland of knots, having bound it as a cloth-tie or a topknot-tie, for him there shall be well-being.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this while sleeping,
shall pass away in happiness and remember seven lifetimes.
Possessing beauty, endowed with virtue, and having a mouth with the fragrance of a blue lotus,
he will be beloved and his words will be accepted in birth after birth.
And here there are effective mantra-words known as mantras that accomplish their stated purposes, as follows:
*bhañjane stambhane dhā dhā dhā dhatsa yā yā yā yate hā hā hā hate parakarāṇi vīryevīrye guṇatejabhūtakari bhadrakari raudrakari kumbhavati*.
397) O you who possess the jar of poison, O you who possess all power, O you who possess the power of spirits! Protect, protect me from all poisons and from all obstacles!
That is to say: Siddhakari, Siddhārthe, Siddhamanorathe, Siddhakārye, Phurunurūpe, Svaste!

O Praśastā, Siddhā, Siddhārthā, Dhairyavatī, Samanā, Tapanā, Śaraṇā, Bhadrā, Bhavati, Śāntā, Dāntā, and Śivā, protect me! Grant me refuge! Grant me acceptance! Grant me protection! Grant me peace! Grant me well-being! Grant protection for me and for all sentient beings! Svāhā! This is the heart-mantra.

Of Aparājitā: first, the root-vidyā. The practitioner must necessarily be intent upon the side of virtue (*kuśalapakṣa*). It should be recited three times a day. Even before that, one should recite it once from a book or by oral transmission; this alone constitutes the side of virtue. And here is the *upahṛdaya*: *namaḥ saptānām*...
By the splendor and supernatural power of Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Enlightened One together with his community of disciples who have transcended all enmity and fear; likewise by that of Śikhin;
by the wisdom of Viśvabhū, and by the strength of Krakucchanda.
Through the training of Kanakamuni, the virtues of Kāśyapa,
and the heroic power of Śākyasiṃha, may there always be auspiciousness for me.

It is as follows: *Jaye vijaye aparājite mārasainyapramardanīye svāhā! Sarvārthasādhanīye svāhā!* This Blessed Lady, the accomplisher of all aims, performs her activities exactly according to how she is employed. She should be applied in all protective rites; she must certainly be kept in mind by the practitioner.

It destroys all obstacles; it disperses all the activities of Māra; it brings all mantras to manifestation; it fulfills all the qualities of a Buddha; it draws forth all mantras, both mundane and supramundane; it completes what is deficient and removes what is redundant; it accomplishes all hopes; [and it subdues] all the wicked.

She wards [off obstacles]. In brief, she accomplishes everything according to the practitioner's wish. At the time of death, she grants him a vision of her face. She dries up all miserable states and evil destinies. By constant recitation, one exhausts the five deeds of immediate retribution. Even the four root downfalls she makes thin. Merely by remembering her—
By recitation alone, one uproots [all obstacles]; one establishes oneself in rebirth among all gods and rebirth as a human;

one engages in all the practices of a bodhisattva; and one fulfills all the qualities of a Buddha. Thus, O Blessed Lady, you possess immeasurable virtues and benefits, great power, and have been proclaimed from the mouths of all the Buddhas.
It was spoken by all the Tathāgatas for the total destruction of all Māras; it dries up all afflictions (kleśas). (148, p.
398) It is unimpeded in all activities and should be employed for all forms of protection, shielding, and guarding. [It belongs] to all the Buddhas.

This is a thunderous roar; this is the great lion’s roar; this is the basis for all conduct; this is the awakening of all Buddhas; this is the outflow of the great samādhi; this is the great miraculous power;
this is the preeminent excellence of all things; this is the state of total peace; this is the station of all Buddhas; this is the state of nirvāṇa.
This is the word for auspiciousness; this is the word for the ineffable; this is the word for the limit of reality;
this is the word for the nature of non-existence; that is to say, it is the word of mantra, the word of the empowerment of all Buddhas.

Placing those very hands joined in a hollowed cup (*karasaṃpuṭa*) with the middle fingers of both hands pointing upward, one should place them at the region of the forehead. This is the second mudrā of Aparājitā; when applied together with the root mantra, it fulfills all desires. When placed at the location of the heart and conjoined with the heart mantra, it destroys all demons.

It destroys all states of woe and miserable rebirths. This is the third heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*) of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā. With those same hands, hanging down from the region of the navel with the palms turned downward, this is the fourth subsidiary heart-seal (*upahṛdayamudrā*) of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā. All rites are to be performed with the heart-mantra.

It is regarded as all-auspicious, bringing all peace and well-being. By consecrating water with mantras and performing an ablution therewith, one brings about supreme good fortune, removes misfortune, generates prosperity, and bestows glory and success. One should place the hands at the region of the face; this is another great mudrā of the Blessed Aparājitā.

The great seal (mahāmudrā) is the fifth. In this manner, there are thus innumerable seals. It should be employed among all the *parājita* mantras. That very same hand, thrown out to the right and slightly joined with a loose fist, while the left hand forms a firm fist—this is [the seal] of all the Buddhas.

The Mahāśaktimudrā. And the mantra for this is: *oṃ vijaye mahāśakti durdhari hūṃ phaṭ vijayine phaṭ maṅgale phaṭ svāhā*. This Tathāgata-śakti mantra should be employed against all wicked beings. Furthermore, when great dangers have arisen, it should be employed together with the mudrā, whether in a village or elsewhere.

In all rites, and during afflictions caused by planets and constellations; for those seized by any *vetāḍa* or *graha*, and for one possessed by any *yakṣa*, *rākṣasa*, *piśāca*, *marut-graha*, *brahmarākṣasa*, and so forth—the mantras should be employed after forming the mudrā. At that very moment, one is liberated. And [this applies] to all entries into great cremation grounds.
It should be employed. All obstacles flee and run away; they cease to exist in every respect and in all ways.
It accomplishes various such manifold purposes of all rites through the majesty of the mantra and tantra.
It provides protection, defense, and concealment from all things, destroys all malevolent spirits, and is purifying, increasing longevity and health.

399) That very [mudrā] consists of the two hands joined in a hollowed cup (*karasaṃpuṭa*), with the middle fingers slightly bent, the little fingers encircled by the ring fingers, shaped like eyes, and pressed down by both thumbs; this belongs to the Blessed Ones.

This is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of the Tathāgata-eye of the Buddhas. Displayed in the region of the eyes, it is the measure of the supreme qualities of all Tathāgatas; it is the mother who gives birth to all Tathāgatas, the illuminator of all vidyās, the fulfiller of all aims, and the purifier of all wrong views.

She who generates right view in all sentient beings, the mother of the family of all Tathāgatas, the sustainer of the family of all mantra lineages, the fulfiller of all mundane and supramundane mantras, the fulfiller of all aims, and the source of consolation. And here is the mantra: Oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha.

*Siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā*. This is the Great Vidyā of Tathāgatalocanā. *Vacana vacana vacana oṃ buddhalocane svāhā*. This is that Vidyā of Vajrapāṇi, which performs all rites (*sarvakarmikā*). Having formed the hands in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭākāra*) as before, the middle fingers are bent downward.

With the tips of the little fingers extended and slightly bent downward, both thumbs encircled by the index fingers, and the ring fingers joined and slightly curved— this is the *ūrṇā* mudrā of the Blessed One and of all Buddhas. Placing the same hands with both fingertips against the forehead constitutes the *ūrṇā* mudrā of all Tathāgatas.

With those same hands, having formed both tips into loops, one should place them in the region of the forehead in the shape of a circle; this is the third, the *ūrṇāmaṇiratna* mudrā. With those same hands, having bent both [hands] inward and wrapped the little fingers around [the thumbs], with both thumbs joined together—this is the fourth, the *ūrṇā* mudrā. Those same [thumbs] are then bent downward.

One should display it in the form of a *citra* on the forehead; this is the *ūrṇā* of all the Tathāgatas. These five great mudrās are equal in power, equal in majesty, and are effective for all rites. And here is the mantra for them all: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo ’rhadbhyaḥ samyaksambuddhebhyaḥ. He he.*
Bind! Bind! Stay! Stay! Hold! Hold! Restrain! Restrain! O *ūrṇāmaṇi*, svāhā!
These mantras of the Blessed One accomplish all rites for all *ūrṇāmaṇi* mudrās.
This *tathāgatorṇāmudrā* is unimpeded in all rites and should be employed in every application. [One should apply] a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with *gorocana*.
Having performed the mantra and recited it, one should enter the battle with the *ūrṇā* of the Tathāgata. All enemies will be paralyzed;

upon seeing him, they will flee. They will become free from anger, and all sentient beings will become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), a mind of benefit, and will find complete relief upon seeing him having applied the *rocanā* tilaka.
All flesh-eaters and the like are unable [to approach];
upon seeing that Great King, the Great Being of great renown and great energy, they behold him as if blazing.
[He is the subduer] of all the wicked and malicious, and of all yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, all grahas, bhūtas, and kaśmalas.
Those with fierce minds become possessed of loving-kindness;
they depart from that place, and one is liberated from all calamitous activities and from those seized by all malevolent spirits.

In cases of possession by all types of *mātṛs*, children, *grahas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, and so forth, one should consecrate yellow orpiment (*gorocana*) with mantras and, having applied it as a mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead, show it [to the afflicted]. Upon merely being seen, they all release [the victim], flee, and run away. They will not affect him at all in any way, nor will they seize him again. If they do seize him, they will utterly perish.

In this manner, it should be applied in all cases; whatever various [practices] are taught in the rituals of the mantra-tantras, whether mundane or supramundane—such as the prescriptions for maṇḍalas, cloth-paintings (paṭas), and ritual accomplishments—all of these are to be accomplished by this very [method], and they are accomplished more swiftly. Having empowered yellow orpiment and applied it as a tilaka...
One may enter into the midst of enemies; they will become free from anger and will not be able to overcome one.

One may enter into the midst of a great multitude while reciting [the mantra]; all will become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*), their words will become acceptable, and one will be invincible and unassailable by others among all beings everywhere. Having empowered *gorocana* with the mantra...
Having applied a *tilaka* with this mantra seven times, one should enter the great cremation ground (*mahāśmaśāna*).
All flesh-eaters will flee; all *grahas* and *mātṛs* will perish. One becomes invincible.
Seeing him as if blazing with the splendor of all men, those who steal vitality (*ojas*) will depart. Therefore...

Even the lands do not grant them a sight; how much less can they take away their vital energy (*ojas*)? They do not remain stationary for even a moment. Having abandoned the great cremation ground, the hosts of spirits who dwell there depart. From here and from there, they cannot even be looked upon; how much less can they take away their vital energy?

Or even to cause harm. Nevertheless, this great spell of all knowledge, possessing great supernatural power, which is called the *Tathāgatorṇa*, remains present; it has been spoken by incalculable Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and it has been spoken and approved. Now, by Śākyamuni, [it is] correctly...

It was spoken and approved by the Perfectly Awakened One; those who will become Perfectly Awakened Ones in the future time will also speak it. Thus, it has been praised and highly extolled by the Blessed Buddhas of the past and the future, and it is likewise now praised and highly extolled by me, Śākyamuni.

Having been granted permission, they will accomplish all things for all sentient beings according to the ritual rules. In whatever manner one applies oneself, in that very manner one performs all rites—excepting those of malevolent sorcery (*abhicāruka*) and those associated with sensual desire (*kāma*).
Then, having joined the two hands in the gesture of a hollowed casket (*sampuṭa*), having interlaced them and made them variegated, [one places them] in the middle upon one's own chest.
One should place [it]. This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Blessed One’s Samādhi-vajra.
Having bound it, one becomes irreversible and established in the certainty of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

And here is the mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ vibhide cūrṇaya cūrṇaya vajradhik vajradhik hūṃ hūṃ jaḥ jaḥ samādhijaḥ hūṃ haṭ svāhā*. All of this should be applied in detail, even if it is brief. And its benefits are immeasurable. This is the Blessed One, Samādhivajra.

Of all the Buddhas. One should place that very same mudrā at the region of the throat; this is the lotus-lotus mudrā of all the Buddhas. One should place this very same [mudrā] on the left side; it is the utpala mudrā. One should place this very same [mudrā] on the right arm;
this is the mudrā of the Blessed Buddha’s compassionate focus and loving-kindness (*kṛpālambanamaitrī*). This very same [mudrā] with both hands...

With both hands encircled and the middle fingers extended, forming the shape of a circular expanse, they are placed at the center of the heart. This is the second Maitrī-mudrā. It performs all rites for all Tathāgatas;
it is unimpeded. In this same manner, by this very procedure, the third is placed on the forehead, and the fourth is placed facing upward all around.

The fifth is the *maitrīmudrā*, which consists of rotating [the hands]. It should be employed at the time of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) upon an object. Then, no humans will cause him harm; neither humans nor non-humans—nor any *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *kaṭapūtanas*, and so forth—will produce any affliction in his body. And all...
The Māras perform their demonic deeds, yet all obstacles become non-obstacles. And here is the mantra:

*oṃ prasphura prasphura kṛtālambanamantrātmaka hrāṃ*. This loving-kindness (*maitrī*) of the Blessed One should be employed. Then, having interlaced the two hands and formed them into the shape of a braid, one should place them upon the mandala.

One should place the two index fingers, standing upright, at the region of the forehead. This is the Mahākaruṇā mudrā of the Blessed Buddha. And here is the mantra: Oṃ viśve svāhā. It performs all rites and should be employed for the sake of sentient beings; they become possessed of the nature of compassion. Then, having rotated those same hands...
The two hands are depicted standing in the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*). This is the Great Sealed Gesture (*mahāmudrā*) of the Blessed Buddha.
And here is the mantra: *oṃ munimuni gagana svāhā*. This Blessed Lady accomplishes all rites;
she fulfills all [desires] and should be employed with a joyful mind. She performs everything—whatever [rites] exist in all the mantra-rituals.

It accomplishes all those actions pertaining to both the mundane and the supramundane without exception. One should display that very same [mudrā] with both hands joined at the forehead, the thumbs placed together and made prominent;
this is the Blessed One’s Tathāgata-prekṣā mudrā, which performs all rites and accomplishes all aims. And the mantra for this is:
It is as follows: *Oṃ mahadgate upekṣayā sarvadharmān viśvātmane viśvamūrti jvala jvalaya sarvabuddhadharmān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. And for the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), there are six mudrās.

Those same hands, with the gesture of granting boons (*varapradāna*), constitute this Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Generosity (*dānapāramitā*). Those same hands, slightly contracted and placed at the region of the navel, constitute this Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Ethical Discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Those same hands, turned downward and positioned by placing them within the armpits, constitute this [Mahāmudrā] of the Perfection of Patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
The Mahāmudrā: one should place those very hands upon the upper arms, touching them in a reversed manner.

This is the Mahāmudrā of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). One should place those very hands above while forming the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), binding the left and right [hands] together above; this is the [mudrā] of compassion for all sentient beings while seated in the cross-legged posture.

The gaze directed toward the object of meditation is the *mahāmudrā* of the Blessed Lady’s perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). That same seal of the perfection of meditation, without breaking the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), takes the form of teaching the Dharma; this is the *mahāmudrā* of the Blessed Lady’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). One should break that very cross-legged posture, with the left hand resting upon the lap.

Placing the right hand on the ground and touching it in the form of a vajra-seat, this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of all Buddhas for their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; this indeed is the Great Seal of all Buddha-dharmas. The mantras for all of them are as follows: Oṃ dāne.

*Dada dadāpaya jvala jvala sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite hūṃ hūṃ jaḥ svāhā!* This is the great mudrā of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). *Oṃ śīla śīlāḍhye śāntikaraṇi śive praśaste sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā!* This is the great mudrā of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). *Oṃ śānte śrīkari kṣānte*...

*Kṣāntikari svāhā*. This is for the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). *Oṃ vīrye vīryam iti sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā*. *Abhāvasvabhāve svāhā*. *Vajrākramaṇi svāhā*. This is for the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). *Oṃ śāntikari dhūdhūdhūrdhari dhairye vīrye gagane ramaṇe dhyānavati svāhā*. This is...

Of the perfection of meditative concentration: Oṃ dhīḥ dhūḥ. This is the perfection of wisdom. Oṃ, protect me, O Blessed One, you who are honored by all Buddhas, you who are without objective support, whose nature is space, who have entered the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), you who create light! Dispel, dispel the darkness of all afflictions! Dry it up! Deliver me! Amūrttije hūṃ hūṃ.

*dālaya sarvakarmāṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra of great awakening belonging to the Blessed Buddhas; it accomplishes all activities, fulfills all aims, wards off all misfortunes, brings to completion all Buddha-qualities, destroys all afflictions, and [surpasses] all mantras.

It is the destroyer of those who perform the works of others, the disperser of all Māras, the accomplisher of all mundane and supramundane mantras, the dispeller of all evils, the burner away of all miserable rebirths,
and that which establishes one in all the Buddha-dharmas among all gods and humans. In brief, in whatever manner—
In whatever way one applies oneself, in that same way one performs actions.
403) It is not possible to fully describe the greatness of its qualities even in ten million eons, nor by means of incalculable [eons].

It is impossible for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to speak of or describe the empowerment of their miraculous power, the transformations of their conduct, and the sustaining force of their supernatural faculties. Likewise, it is impossible to fully elaborate upon the six perfections, which constitute the manifestations of the boundless extent of the majesty and qualities of this Blessed Lady. In brief, these are her power of instruction, her conduct, and her supernatural faculties.
The conduct established upon the lineage of qualities (guṇagotra) is to be known in its entirety, as is the attainment of excellence.
The nature of phenomena is like the sky, a state beyond the investigation of existence and non-existence;
it employs syllables throughout every eon for the accomplishment of all activities.
The wise have declared it to be abundant, arising swiftly from the manifestation of its fruit;
it is the meaning of the mantra whose nature is space, adorned by the clarity of the syllables.
When properly applied and well-examined, they bear fruit in many ways in due time;
thus has the mudrā-tantra been explained in detail by those who act according to reality.
The course of mantra and tantra, as well as time and the observances, are well-joined;
recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth should be known as leading to the fruit that arises from reality.
The movement of substances toward their support is clearly characterized by its defining marks;
the mantra-knowledge, one's own mantra, and the arising from the source of the family [are likewise defined].
For the time of accomplishment is indeed indicated by the appearance of signs and mudrās;
the mantra-practitioner, established in the reality and composed in mind, should recite the mantra.
One should show the family deity (kuladevatā) who reveals the accomplishment of the causes of success;
these are declared to be the excellent mudrās and the highly renowned mantras.
"Those who are engaged in the prescribed ritual attain success according to their desires within the mind-born [lotus]. Thus it is said.

That same [gesture], with the fingers interlaced, the right thumbs bent down and resting beneath the left thumbs—this is the heart-mudrā of all Buddhas, spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and it accomplishes all rites. And here is the mantra: Oṃ trailokyapūjitāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
They perform all rites; they should be employed in all mandala rituals for the great protection and other purposes of all sentient beings.

With both hands joined at the tips and the middle fingers bent upward, this is the root mudrā of all the Blessed Buddhas. And here is the mantra: Oṃ da dadātu daṇḍa hūṃ | Oṃ sarvasattvāmṛtapradeśikaraṇāya svāhā | [This is for] both the staff and the water-pot.
These are the root mantras. By means of these, one should perform all rites. They should be employed everywhere in all mantras;

they grant all accomplishments and should be applied in all protective rituals. One should place those same hands, joined at both palms with the fingers interlaced like a braid, at the position of the head. They should be employed for specific purposes. And there is a verse on this point:

The mantra is: *oṃ jvala jvala sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā*. By means of this, one should perform all rites within the Tathāgata family. Alternatively, the intensification (*uttejana*) of a substance should be performed with the mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī using red oleander (*karavīra*), jasmine (*mālatī*), or other flowers. It should be applied in every case using the root mantra of Mañjuśrī; indeed, in all respects.
It should be employed in all rites. One should place those same two hands, formed in the shape of two interlaced braids, at the position of the head;
this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Uṣṇīṣa of all Buddhas. And the mantra for this is: JRĪṂ.
This King Uṣṇīṣa performs all rites. One should form those same two hands into the shape of a lotus and place them at the heart.

This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Avalokita in the Lotus Family, which performs all rites. The mantra for this is: *jrīḥ*. Keeping the hands in the shape of a closed lotus bud (*kuḍmala-padma*), one should place them at the center of the navel. This is another Great Seal of Avalokita, named "The Pacifier of All Obstacles. The mantra for this is: *jiḥ*. This...

The *sarvakarmika* [mudrā] should be employed for protection from all fears. Having formed the two hands in the shape of a hollow bowl with the fingers interlocked against one another, one should place them upon the forehead; this is the great mudrā of all Buddhas named *prabhāvamānasodbhava*. And the mantras should be employed here as follows:

There are four single-syllable [mantras]: *tāḥ*, *vāḥ*, *droḥ*, and *hāḥ*. These four single-syllable mantras were spoken by four hundred million Buddhas; they are the Uṣṇīṣa-kings of all Buddhas, the majestic powers of all those possessing great supernatural faculties (*vidyā-maharddhika*), and the basis of all phenomena through the four supernormal powers (*catu-ṛddhi*).
Having five feet, established in the four noble truths, with their heads inclined toward awakening,

they are to be cultivated by all through the four liberations, the four dhyānas, and the samādhis; they are unshakable by any mundane or supramundane mantras and tantras, and are the supreme lords among all vidyārāja universal monarchs.
She is the eldest of all mantras, inconceivable among all the distinctions of samādhis, and has attained awakening.

Thus, she is the sovereign of the three worlds for the great beings; she is inaccessible through the mantras and tantras of all families, and is unassailable by all bodhisattvas, noble śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. In this way, she is inconceivable, devoid of intrinsic nature, and insurmountable.

"Having the sky as its intrinsic nature, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as its untroubled foundation"—in brief, this should be applied in all ritual actions.
By this very [mudrā], one should perform all rites, especially those prescribed in the ritual procedures of the *Mūlakalpa* of Noble Mañjuśrī.

One should display that same pair of hands in the shape of a hollowed casket at the position of the head. This is the Great Mudrā named "Destroyer of All Poisons" within the family of all Tathāgatas; it should be employed in all rites concerning poison. *Ṭroṃ*.
This mantra, spoken by the Buddha, when joined with this mudrā,
quickly renders all beings, both stationary and moving, free from poison.
It renders non-venomous even those serpents who are intent on striking and arrogant with their poison;
likewise, it destroys all defects born of passion and hatred.
And this mantra, when joined with the mudrā, overcomes even those born of delusion;
it performs various rites arising from poisons and living beings.
In brief, this mudrā,
when applied according to the Mantra vehicle, performs various rites arising from poison;
it subdues his karma and brings the poison under his control at will.

Thus, with [the mantra] recited one hundred thousand times; that same [gesture], with both hands in the form of the Samaya-vajra, having three prongs on each side, with the left hand placed below and the right hand inverted above it, should be placed at the location of the head.
That itself is the heart-mudrā of Vajrādhipati, effective for all rites. And the mantra here is: HŪṂ.

This is a rite for all purposes, accomplishing every aim; it should be employed against all cruel planets, and no doubt should be entertained otherwise. *Oṃ bhadre bhadravati karaṭe ratna viratna svāhā*. First, its recitation (*jāpa*) should be performed eight hundred times; then Mañjuśrī will be accomplished. In that very same way, [one should perform] the hand-gestures (*hasta*).

Placing both hands with the fingertips slightly curved upon the crown of the head—this is the great mudrā of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. It should be employed in all rites; it is effective for all protections and accomplishes all goals.
In the sādhanas of Mañjuśrī, one should first perform this [mudrā] and afterwards carry out the ritual action.
"The commonality of the three families. One should place that very same mudrā on the forehead of Noble Samantabhadra;

it is the great mudrā (mahāmudrā) of Ākāśagarbha. And here is the mantra for all rites: *svaṃ*. One should place that same mudrā on the region of the throat; this is the great mudrā of Vimalagate. And here is the mantra:
*Sarvakarmika*—*laṃ*. One should place that very same mudrā at the center of the chest; this is the *mahāmudrā* of Maitreya.
And here the mantra is: *maṃ*. One should place the hands in that same manner as before at the region of the navel.

This is the great seal (mahāmudrā) of Kṣitigarbha. And here is the mantra for all rites: *kṣiṃ*. One should apply that same seal to the region of the waist and cast it upward; this is the seal of Gaganagañja. And here is the mantra for all rites: *gaṃ*. Having placed that same seal on both arms, one should rotate it over the head by means of a dancing gesture (*nṛttayoga*).
This belongs to all bodhisattvas, noble śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. And here is the mantra: *ghruḥ*.
This [mudrā] possesses an extensive power of action and immeasurable benefits through its connection with the greatness and qualities of that which is to be seen from every direction.
Having looked upward at that very mudrā and brought it down, one should cast it upward by means of the yoga of dance. This...

For all the gods residing in the three realms, for all sentient beings— above, below, across, and in every direction— contained within infinite world-systems, including yakṣas, yakṣīs, rākṣasas, and rākṣasīs, this Great Seal named Sarvatratalayā should be employed in all rites for all of them in detail.
It should be employed in all rites, including the summoning and dismissal [of deities], the ritual procedures for the maṇḍala sections, and all practices for accomplishment.
And here is the mantra: *oṣṭrai*. One should place both hands in the form of the joined palms (*añjali*) upon the head;
this is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Great Obstacle-Remover (*antarāvaṇa*) among all mantras. It should also be rotated at the region of the waist.

And there is a mantra for this: *Gyaṃ jaye kumāri śuklabandhani svāhā*. One should tie a thread spun by a maiden, over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times, around the waist. Thus, the binding of semen is accomplished. One should gaze in all directions; all obstacles will be paralyzed, and there is protection from all sides.

Therefore, the practitioner should first perform this application of the binding of the mudrās in all rites; afterwards, the specific ritual actions are to be performed. In this way, there are one hundred and twenty-eight mudrās.
The practitioner may, according to his desire, employ any one of them in all rites, or employ all of them.
In this manner, by means of this application, there are incalculable mudrās and incalculable mantras. In that same way, both hands, positioned in the form of hollowed palms with the fingers—
both joined and separated— adorned by the two thumbs, assume the form of five prongs.

In the formation of the fist, one should place it upon the head at the position of the crown. This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Noble Mañjuśrī called the Five-Crested; it performs all rites. By the drawing back and casting forth of the thumbs with the fingers contracted, there is summoning;
by their being cast forth, there is dismissal. Thus, through all applications performed mentally, one accomplishes all rites.

Whether joined with the root mantra, the heart-mantra, or the subsidiary mantra (upahṛdaya) of Mañjuśrī, or indeed with all mantras, it accomplishes all aims. That same [mudrā] in the shape of a three-pronged needle is called the "Three-Crest" (triśikhā) of Mañjuśrī. That same [mudrā], when formed with the little fingers in the shape of a single needle, is to be understood as the "Single-Row" (ekacīra).
407) Both hands joined in a hollowed cup, bent inward on all sides, with the fingers well-arranged and placed,
firmly attached and positioned at the head— this is the mudrā of Mañjuśrī named *Sarvaśirobhyudgata* (Rising Above All Heads).
The Mahāmudrā: with those same hands, the tips of the fingers raised and palms facing upward, one should hold them in the middle of the face;

this is the Mahāvaktra-mudrā of Mañjuśrī. Lowering those same hands, one should place them in the middle of the heart; this is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Hṛdaya-mudrā. With those same hands positioned halfway down and slightly inclined toward the forehead—
This is another heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*). Raising those same hands, the middle fingers are bent downward; the ring fingers have their tips shown while bent;

they are encircled by the index fingers and extended along the sides of the thumbs. This is another great root-seal of the Crooked Fang (*vakradaṃṣṭramahāmūlamudrā*), which should be employed in all great fears. The two [hands] are likewise [joined] very gently.
This is another, the *utpala* mudrā of Mañjuśrī: those same [fingers] bound together, lowered, and coiled.

This is the peacock-throne mudrā (*mayūrāsana-mudrā*) of Mañjuśrī: those same [fingers], with the index fingers pressing down on the little fingers, positioned obliquely on both sides in the shape of a seat. This is another, the auspicious-seat mudrā (*bhadrapīṭha-mudrā*).

That same hand, with the fingers made into a fist and the index finger raised alone, is this other *yaṣṭi-mudrā*. With two [fingers] raised, it is the *dhvaja-mudrā*. With three raised, it is the *patākā-mudrā*. With four raised, it is the *ghaṇṭā*. That same hand, with the index finger positioned on top, is the *chatra-mudrā*. When all [the fingers] are bent downward, it is the *phala-mudrā*. Hūṃ.

The *aṅkuśa-mudrā* is formed when the index finger is positioned at the tip of the hook-like finger. That same [gesture], with the index finger held firmly within the fist, is the *muṣṭi-mudrā*. That same [gesture], with the two index fingers positioned horizontally at the tips of the needles, is the *śūla-mudrā*. When joined with both index fingers, it is the *mahāśūla-mudrā*. With one thumb raised, it is the *ekaliṅga-mudrā*. That same [gesture]...

One should place the mudrā at the heart with the heart-mantra; this is the Manoratha-mudrā. Making those same hands joined in the shape of a hollowed cup, placed one upon the other, is the Yamala-mudrā. Making those same hands joined in the shape of a bud and opening them, placed one upon the other, is the Yamala-mudrā. Having opened that same bud-shaped form, one should cast it over the head.

The *utpala* mudrā. That same [mudrā], when full and having the form of space, is the *pūrṇa* mudrā. When that same [mudrā] is placed at the crown of the head and formed below with the fists, it is the *mañjuśrī-yaṣṭi* mudrā. Again, when the two hands are made variegated, it is the upward-pointing *svastika* of Mañjuśrī; it should all be bound with red *mālatī* flowers. That same [mudrā] is the hands.

With the hands crossed and the tips of the middle fingers extended, this is another *śakti-mudrā* of Mañjuśrī Kārttikeya. The bell and banner are to be understood as before. Having joined those same hands in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭīkṛta*), one should open them;
this is another *padma-mudrā* of Mañjuśrī. Those same hands are positioned crosswise.

One should form the shape of a *svastika* with the two well-formed hands. With four fingers positioned in the four directions and well-extended, with the middle [fingers] properly placed [within], this is another *svastika* mudrā of Mañjuśrī. Those same hands, shaped like sprouts (*karapallava*), are joined together with the fingers [interlaced].
408) This is another *pallavamudrā*. Those same two hands formed into fists constitute this other *sarvabuddhāspadamudrā*.
For Mañjuśrī, those same hands joined together with a hollow space in the middle constitute the *dharmabherīmudrā*.
Wrapping the ring fingers with the index fingers, the two thumbs are placed upon the palms of the ring fingers and bent, forming a mark in the shape of a conch.
This is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Dharma-conch mudrā.
The wheel is as before; having the form of a wheel of Dharma, this is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Dharma-wheel mudrā. That same [mudrā]...

Having placed the mudrā on the forehead and performed the yoga of the third [finger], one should cast it with the yoga of the left side. This is another great mudrā for miraculous play; it should be employed against great fears by means of the root mantra itself, and they will perish without exception.
In this manner, by this application, there are incalculable mudrās;

and incalculable mudrā-kalpas, mantras, and tantras; and incalculable [deities] are to be beheld, arisen from the self-existent one who has emerged with great power. All of these are to be employed here in this extensive ritual manual.

And all [of these] should be employed while wrapped within clean garments. In this *kalpavisara*, all [of them] should be employed while wrapped within clean garments, so that they are not seen by beings who do not know the pledge (*samaya*). Thus are they of great power; otherwise, it would be a transgression of the pledge. These are the means for accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Hand gestures (kara-mudrās) placed upon the hands become manifold through the application of dance and song; likewise, they are explained sequentially according to the specific cries of sentient beings. Now, the great mudrās (mahāmudrās) suitable for the practice of the maṇḍala are presented.
Likewise, the stūpas of all Buddhas on the ground consist of relics;
those of Bodhisattvas are likewise lotuses, and those of Śrāvakas are circular.
The square [mandala] is said to belong to the Pratyekabuddhas; it consists of three circles and is adorned with various vehicles and diverse ornaments.
Furthermore, for gods, yakṣas, and grahas, it consists of various weapons;
for men, it is a man’s [form]; and for sages, it is a staff and a water-pot.
In these mandalas, one should briefly perform the mudrās corresponding to whatever is the constant weapon of a deity, or whatever serves as its vehicle or ornament.
Then one should visualize the sun and moon as mandalas above the [other] mandala;
in brief, whatever ground belongs to whom, that very thing one should summon with the mind.
Various living beings were then described; one should assign them to their respective [deities].
Many types of beings are mentioned, and many mudrās are proclaimed.
409) One should fashion their [emblems] according to the ritual procedure within the maṇḍala:
the lotus of Brahmā, the thunderbolt of Śakra, the noose of Varuṇa, the trident of Rudra, and that of Durga.
The spear of the Ṛṣi, the water-pot of Yama, the staff of Dhanada, the mace of Kubera, the sword of Hutāśana,

the sacrificial fire-pan of Agni, the jar of the Earth— recalling all these according to the prescribed rite, just as their respective weapons and ornaments were seen in the world today, he beheld them all everywhere.

They should be employed in all maṇḍalas, or they should be drawn according to the procedure declared in the ritual manual (kalpa). All maṇḍalas should be drawn with a mind characterized by the altruistic intention for the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, out of compassion for all sentient beings,
having generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and out of sympathy for all sentient beings.

[This should be performed] by those consecrated in all mandalas, or by those consecrated in the great mandala; or by one who has seen the mandala and received consecration from Noble Mañjuśrī. Otherwise, one must certainly draw all the mandalas. Noble Mañjuśrī should be kept in mind. For what reason? Because I have been consecrated by all the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

"You shall teach the Dharma through the method of the profound reality-meaning of all mantras; appearing in the form of a youth or a child, you shall act for the benefit of sentient beings by means of the form of mantra."
One should not perform that which is joined with mantra and mudrā while being distracted from the Dharma;
one should not do what is harmful here, nor should one do what is beneficial if it is not desired as such.
When joined with mudrās and mantras, it wards off that which is harmful;
it always brings about everything beneficial and likewise wards off that which is harmful.
Every mantra should be effective when sealed by the mudrā;
however, a mudrā without a mantra does not act, nor does a mantra likewise remain unsealed by a mudrā.
Combined with the meaning of the mudrā, it will accomplish its purpose;
a mantra joined with a mudrā is fruitful, for it brings about the fruit of the mudrā.
One should accomplish the expansion of rites through meditation equal to the mudrās;
those mudrās which belong to pacification, and likewise the mantras for pacification.
Through the union of mantra and mudrā, one should undertake rites of pacification (śāntika);
and in the case of mantras for enrichment (pauṣṭika), one should bind the arising of the mudrā.
They say that when joined with mantras as previously described, this is the *mudrā* for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
In rites of pacification (*śāntika*), one should perform pacifying acts by means of the *mudrās* and mantras taught here.
410) By means of the Victors, the preeminent mantras of the Victors, and also by means of the mudrās,
one should accomplish all rites in all seasons during the cool periods.
The mantras arising from the Lotus family have been taught for the sake of nourishment;
likewise, the mantras and tantras are [accomplished] by means of the fierce mudrās proclaimed by you.
By means of renowned and proclaimed mantras, as well as highly efficacious mudrās,
which have been prescribed for the lotus-family (abjakula), and which are pure and radiant.
With auspicious rites that are highly praised and abundant in health and prosperity,
as well as with wrathful mantras and those described with ritual gestures (mudrās).
With those [offerings] prescribed for the attainment of enjoyments and wealth— pure, beautiful,
white, marked with white seals, and accompanied by the appropriate mantras and mudrās.
One should accomplish the mantras that bring about prosperity and enjoyment in this life;
when accomplished by means of such mantras and mudrās, they yield fruitful results.
Likewise, the wrathful mantras beginning with *mantra* are said to obstruct the vital breath;
they were taught in the *Vajratantra* and in the *Jinābjasamudbhava*.
The fierce executioners of the Tīrthaṅkaras, who subdue wicked beings, are appointed to the killing of living creatures; a wise person should not perform such an act.
The mudrās are the staff, the taming [noose], the vajra, the trident, and the battle-axe;
likewise, there are various weapons and great spears for Yamāntaka.
Having quickly joined with ministers and certainly brought about the destruction of life,
the wise man should not perform that which obstructs all vital breaths.
One who knows the mantras and tantras should employ a fierce [rite] marked by fierceness;
the mudrā employed in fierce mantras is said to be even fiercer than the fierce [rite].
Just as it is accomplished by cruel beings who engage in cruel deeds,
so does that evil-minded person here undergo various sufferings of hell.
One should not perform malevolent rites against those of evil conduct using cruel mantras;
likewise, people should not bestow cruel mantras or mudrās upon anyone at all.
411) Since one experiences undesirable fruit again and again, then that practitioner of mantras does not find happiness; he is cruel... (?)
It is seen in the threefold attainments (*siddhi*).
The sacrifice is dependent on the desired fruit; therefore, one should avoid performing rituals for cruel deeds during the *iṣṭa* [sacrifice]. One should abandon such dharmas.
The best of sages [taught] those yogas...
the mantras in the Vajra family are proclaimed to be threefold:
inferior, superior, and [intermediate].
These were previously taught by the supreme Victors, and now they are proclaimed here.
Thus concludes the thirty-fourth detailed chapter on the Great Mudrās from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which belongs to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-ava-taṃsaka*.
Now follows the thirty-seventh detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there is [a teaching] in your own *Mūlakalpa*."
Furthermore, there is another mudrā that is most supremely secret; it is the ritual procedure for the tantra of all mudrās,

approved by all mantras, and when combined with all mantras, it accomplishes all activities, purifies the path to perfect enlightenment, destroys the paths of all worldly existence, and provides sustenance for all sentient beings.

It fulfills all hopes for long life, health, and sovereignty; it perfects all factors conducive to enlightenment; it brings satisfaction to all sentient beings; it makes fruitful the aspirations and desires of all sentient beings; it accomplishes all activities; it grants success to all mantras; and it is accompanied by all mudrās and mantras. Listen!
O Kumāra Mañjuśrī!

First, there is the characteristic of the uṣṇīṣa: with both hands extended and palms joined, one places the ring fingers within the center of the hands, with nail against nail, and they are pressed down by the tips of the thumbs.
The two little fingers are joined at their tips in the shape of a needle; likewise, the middle fingers are joined at their middle parts with the tips of the nails touching.
This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) named Uṣṇīṣa-mahālakṣaṇa, which has the appearance of a needle on all sides. And there is a verse on this point:
The mantra is: ĀḤ MAḤ HAṂ. Having moved those same two index fingers, one should touch nail to nail.

This is the Great Dharma-Wheel Mudrā called "the Burning Away of the Arrows of Wrong Views and Perversions" by means of needle-like [fingers] in the form of a circle. And the mantra for this is: OṂ DHUNA PĀTAYA CHINDA CAKRE VAJRIṆI.

HŪṂ. When the index fingers are extended toward the region of the Samayirava, this is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) named Vajravīrācalācalamahīkleśāsanī, the couch for the enemy of the four Māras. And the mantra for this is: OṂ VAJRĀNANI HŪṂ PHAṬ.
Furthermore, when the mudrās and mantras are combined for all ritual activities,
all obstacles are indeed destroyed, just as clouds are by autumn.
Whatever obstacles created by the four Māras, as well as those involving gods and asuras,
are indeed destroyed merely by seeing this supreme, excellent mudrā.
Aiming equally at the outside, with the third finger extended and the tip of the index finger slightly contracted, this auspicious fist is known as the Tathāgatī.
The great mudrā for the entire triple world is named Mahāmaheśvaragabhastimālinī. And the mantra for this is:
Oṃ vijaye haḥ. There is also the Tathāgatamuṣṭi mudrā. By means of any one of these mudrās—(163, p. 413).

Having bound [the hands] with both hands at the time of practice or during the preliminary service, one should recite it once and then chant as much as desired, whether seated or standing. In this way, all obstacles and impediments find no opportunity to enter,
and accomplishment becomes manifest.

Having moved those same index fingers so that their tips are joined above the middle fingers, one forms the *Udgatoṣṇīṣa* mudrā. And the mantra for this is: *oṃ jvalojjvala dīptodgatoṣṇīṣa dhuna dhuna hūṃ*.

Moving those same index fingers so that they are always joined at the tips of the nails with the middle fingers, this mudrā—shaped like a ring with bent ankles—is the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa. And the mantra for this is: Oṃ ma ma ma ma hūṃ niḥ.
Raising those same two index fingers equally upward from there and joining them with the middle fingers forming a needle, this is the *tejorāśi* mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ tathāgatoṣṇīṣa anavalokitamūrdhni tejorāśi hūṃ jvala eka eka dara viara cchinna bhinda hūṃ hūṃ sphaṭ sphaṭ svāhā*.
When those same [fingers] have their middle fingers joined at their tips like a needle, [forming] the shape of a circle, it is the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: Oṃ jayoṣṇīṣa jvala jvala bandha bandha dama dama ṅra& ṅra& ṅra& haḥ hana hūṃ—the Jayoṣṇīṣa mantra.

Moving the tips of those same index fingers and joining them at the third part above the nail of the middle finger, this is the *cakravartin* mudrā. Oṃ, homage to the invincible Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa, whose crown is unobservable;
O *cakravartin*, hūṃ! Blaze, blaze! Burn, burn! Shake, shake! Tremble! Terrify! Slay! Destroy! Strike!

*Hana aṃ aṃ aḥ aḥ kaḥ kaḥ proṃkhini proṃkhini kuṇḍalini aparājitāstradhāriṇi hūṃ phaṭ!* Moving those very same [fingers] so that the tips of the index fingers (*pradeśinī*) are joined with the third part below the nail of the middle finger (*madhyama*), which acts as a needle— this is the mudrā of the Lord of Mantras, the Cakravartin. Moving those very same [fingers] so that the tips of the index fingers...
Moving those same index fingers so that their tips are joined beneath the nails of the middle fingers is the mudrā of the Lord of Mantras.

Moving those same index fingers so that their tips are joined between the nail and the joint of the middle fingers is the mudrā of the Great Cakravartin. Moving those same index fingers [so that their tips are joined] with the middle finger...

414) On the third joint at the base, joined in the shape of a coil, is the mudrā for the Great Cakravartin. Those same [fingers], having moved the tips of the index fingers so that they are joined between the two joints of the middle finger's needle-like [finger], form the mudrā.

This is the mudrā for the Great Universal Monarch, the Lord of Mantras. Those same [fingers], with the tips of the index fingers bent at the third joint of the middle phalanges and joined beneath the middle joints by the middle finger acting as a needle, constitute the heart-mudrā of Aparājita-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin. And the mantra here is: Oṃ.
O Aparājitā, shame!
One should perform all rites using that very same [mudrā], ending with the *uṣṇīṣamūla-mudrā*, arranged together with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).

By moving the tips of the thumbs and stroking with the ring fingers, one should effect the invocation (*āvāhana*). And the mantra for this is: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya ehi ehi bhagavan! Dharmarāja!*

May I accept the water for the feet (*arghya*), fragrance, flowers, incense, the food offering (*balya*), and the lamp. And may you protect me, O you of unimpeded strength and prowess—*svāhā*. The invocation is performed with white flowers.

Then, in one's own form, [the deity] receives the water for the feet, the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the seat, and sits upon it. At that time, by this very [mantra], [one offers] in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as below.
And one should bind it upward.
One should wipe those very two ring fingers with the tips of the thumbs and then bend them; touching the middle joints, one should lift them up.
With the *visarjana-argha* [offering], one should rotate [the mudrā] counter-clockwise for one’s own deity. Thus the binding and releasing of the directional mudrās are accomplished.
And there is a mantra for this: "Homage to the Unconquerable Uṣṇīṣa! Go, go, O Blessed One!"

O Dharmarāja! Accept from me this water for honor (*arghya*), fragrance, flower, and incense; and protect me with your unimpeded strength and prowess through this dismissal-offering (*visarjanārghya*) accompanied by mudrās and mantras.

Those same two index fingers, joined at their third joints below the needle-like middle fingers, with the thumbs together and the little fingers pressed into the fist, form the needle-like middle fingers. And here is the mantra:
*Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya oṃ oṃ hrauṃ bandha hūṃ phaṭ*. O Unassailable Uṣṇīṣa, Mass of Splendor!
The mudrās and mantras are employed for all bindings and so forth; they are effective for all ritual actions.

Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent, joined at the third joint of the needle-like middle finger, constitute the *vikaraṇoṣṇīṣa* mudrā. And here is the mantra: *namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya vikaraṇa dhuna dhuna hūṃ vikaraṇoṣṇīṣaḥ*, the Lord’s Great King of Vidyās, the Sovereign of Vidyās.

In the Uṣṇīṣa Tantra, it is employed in all rites, such as the destruction of all obstacles and Vināyakas, consecrations, self-protection, the binding of the directions, and the binding of the maṇḍala.

415) Those same two index fingers, with their tips opened and slightly bent, moved and drawn back, perform the invocation of Agni; subsequently, one performs the oblation. This very same gesture, with the index fingers spread apart, constitutes the dismissal.

This is the Jvālāmālinyoṣṇīṣa mudrā. It is unimpeded in all rites. And here is the mantra: Homage to the Blessed One, the Unimpeded Uṣṇīṣa! Come, come, O you who wear a garland of flames, to Agni! Svāhā!

Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent, are joined at the third joint of the middle finger—specifically, between the joints of the middle finger—to form the *Balotkaṭoṣṇīṣa* mudrā. And here is the mantra for this: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya, imaṃ gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ dhūpaṃ baliṃ dīpaṃ ca pratīccha hara hara*.
Svāhā to the one empowered by all Buddhas, the foremost King of Dharma, who is free from obstruction!

Regarding the mantras for perfumes and so forth: with the ring fingers reversed, the third [fingers] bent, and the index fingers joined at the tips of the thumbs, this needle-shaped gesture is the Vajratejoṣṇīṣa mudrā. It is unassailable by all Vināyakas. With it, one should perform the subjugation of companions, as well as of directions and times. Thus, by means of these mantras and mudrās, protection is provided during the time of recitation.
At the time of the ritual practice, all activities should also be performed within the mandala. And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvavighnavidhvaṃsanakarāya troṭaya svāhā*.

Placing the thumbs at the base of the two ring fingers in a circular fashion, and likewise making the two index fingers needle-shaped, this is the Aparājita-uṣṇīṣa mudrā, which is unimpeded everywhere. And the mantra for this is: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvatrāparājitāya samaye śānte dānte dharmarājabhāṣite*.
"O Great Vidyā, accomplisher of all aims, svāhā! One should perform rites for pacification and nourishment during oblations of ghee and the like."

With the ring fingers [forming] two earrings and the index fingers with their tips bent, this is the Apratihatoṣṇīṣa mudrā. And the mantra for this is: *namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣa oṃ śaṅkare svāhā*. It provides protection in all rites.
The tips of the two thumbs are placed upon the third joints of the two ring fingers; likewise, the two index fingers are joined like a needle.
This is the Vajrāpratihatasamayauṣṇīṣa mudrā, which is common to all samayas. The mantra for this is:
*Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya | oṃ saṅkare samayaṃ svāhā*.

The tips of the two thumbs are pressed against the middle joints of the two ring fingers; the two index fingers are bent at their tips and joined to the middle joint of the needle-like middle fingers. This is the Unobstructed Great Samaya Uṣṇīṣa Mudrā, which is employed among gods and asuras when established in the samaya.
And here is the mantra: *namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya oṃ śaṅkare mahāsamayaṃ svāhā*.
Having performed the binding of the maṇḍala with this, one should recite: "O Universal Monarch, abide, abide in the pledge! (*tiṣṭha tiṣṭha samaye*).

He also surpasses other universal monarchs (*cakravartins*). By performing recitation (*japa*) in that very place, he is unimpeded in causing the mutual destruction of the power, influence, and strength of all mundane and supramundane mantras among all those who recite in a single location. Such are the primary [powers].
The Uṣṇīṣa Kings are innumerable. The entire family of all the Tathāgatas should be set forth in detail.

For here, Mañjuśrī, in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), there are immeasurable mantras and various kinds of mudrās. I shall speak of them in brief; for if I were to explain them in full detail, it would be impossible.
It cannot be grasped or retained by all humans and non-humans, even in the measure of time of a thousand eons. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, I shall speak in brief; listen attentively to this summary.
First, O Sage, the most excellent mudrā of the Heart is taught here;
thereafter, indeed, is the mudrā of the Cakravartin, the God of gods.
Then the mudrās of the wise Bodhisattva Avalokitacandra and of Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Yakṣas, are proclaimed.
Then, [he taught] all the other great mudrās of immeasurable power,
as well as the entire host of male and female messengers (dūta-dūtī), and the supreme male and female servants (ceṭa-ceṭī).
Yakṣas and yakṣīs, as well as gods and goddesses, likewise nāgas and other nāginīs,
and kiṅkaras and kiṅkarīs, as well as piśācas and piśācīs.
She is the one of great supernatural power among the rākṣasīs, as well as among other celestial women,
the wives of the daityas, and all the siddhas and vidyādharas.
The mudrās for all non-human beings, as well as for all human beings, have been taught individually according to their births within the three realms of existence.
Mantras, moreover, are of various forms and are effective for diverse ritual actions;
in royal lineages as well as in brahmin lineages, their mudrās are each distinct.
For Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, both mudrās bring about beauty;
for all Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, they likewise do so.
417) The mudrā and the heart-mantra are each proclaimed [for use] even within the divine yakṣa family, which is honored by ṛṣis and gandharvas.
The mudrā associated with the Gandharvas is said to belong to the seventh family;
likewise, the mudrā belonging to the [other] families is proclaimed in the eighth.
All mudrās have been fully explained, as well as others called by the name of the Sugata,
each belonging to their respective mantras, both worldly and Buddhist.
A mantra accompanied by a mudrā becomes radiant in ritual activities;
the Vināyakas do not follow one who is skilled in the casting of mudrās and other such practices.

Now, indeed, follows the definition of these [mudrās], beginning with the Mahāmudrā. The definition of the heart-mudrā (*hṛdayamudrā*) of the Blessed Buddhas is as follows: having interlaced the fingers of both hands with one another, one should show the two thumbs.
This is the heart-mudrā of the Tathāgatas. This same [mudrā], however, with the right thumb...

By displaying each one individually, there is the mudrā of Padmadhara. Having first formed a fist with the left hand and the other, release the pair of middle fingers and extend them together into the shape of a vajra;
this is the mudrā of Vajradhara. Bending down a single index finger, this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin.

Raising them once more, one should form the shape of a circle; this is the mudrā of Gajagandha. One should bend a single joint of both [index fingers]; this is the mudrā for the Maṇi family. For all the jewel-walkers (maṇicarāḥ), such as Jambhala, Jalendra, and others, one should employ it with their respective mantras. [The two index fingers] have two joints.

The fingers are curled with the nails joined to one another; this is the mudrā for the Yakṣa family, for the great-iddhi Yakṣas such as Pañcika and others. One should hold the thumbs with their nails joined to one another above the [other] nails.
Having positioned the hands exactly as before, one should raise the pair of middle fingers so that they take the form of a needle.

Having performed [this], this is the mudrā of all the gods of the divine lineage, beginning with Akaniṣṭha and the other celestial dwellers. Furthermore, likewise joining the hands and forming a fist, one should show the two thumbs;
this is the mudrā of the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas.
Thus, these eight mudrās are encompassed by the eight families;
however, one single mudrā for all the sons of the Victors shall now be described.
With the palms joined and extended, then slightly contracted again—
this is declared to be the mudrā of the most exalted Bodhisattvas.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the water-strainer, the saṅghāṭī robe, the alms-bowl, the monastic garment,
and the hand displaying the fangs and the gesture of fearlessness— these seven are the mudrās of the Sage.
The Sugata stands with the web of light-rays of his loving gaze and the tuft of hair between his brows;
this too is that supreme mudrā of the Jina, born from his own body.
These two groups of seven and these five mudrās have been remembered by me;
together with the heart-mantra of the Sage, they are said to be twenty, including the self-arisen [mantras] and others.
Indeed, these mudrās were previously taught by the primordial Jinas;
thus, the retinue of the Cakravartin is declared to consist of twenty.
The supreme [mudrās] are reckoned as those based on mantras and mudrās.

Having raised [the hands] and coiled them, it is the *cintāmaṇi-mudrā*. Holding the fists at the shoulder region on the left and right while in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), it becomes the *khakharaka-mudrā*. With the palms joined together facing one another...
The *saṅghāṭī* mudrā is as follows: the bowl is held with the hands joined like a hollow vessel; the robe is held by the left hand;
the fang is formed from the heart-mudrā with the left thumb raised; the hand of fearlessness (*abhayahasta*) is slightly bent downward;
the robe hangs from the left side; and in the hand of fearlessness, the two middle fingers are joined in a hollow while the two index fingers are extended outward.

One should place the middle fingers and thumbs in a contracted position; this is the *buddhalocanā* mudrā. In that same [mudrā], one should make the index fingers curved at the first joint on one side; this is *buddhamaitrī*. Having formed the *añjali* with fingers spread apart, one should conceal the index and ring fingers with the three-pointed needle [gesture]; this is the *māmakī* mudrā. Having formed the *añjali*...

One should join the third joints of the index and middle fingers, bending them outward; the two thumbs should be held separately in the shape of a finger, forming the Bhogavatī mudrā. With the left hand, one should hold the Vijayā with the index and middle fingers, while holding a three-fingered vajra at the hip region with the right hand.
In this very way, having personally bound the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) upon one's head—the seal of the King of Vidyās—one should perform all rites.
One may scatter flowers at the time [of initiation] or within the mandala; one may act according to the previously prescribed rule or by this present method.
One should perform all rites as desired. These are the pledges (samaya) proclaimed by the vidyā-mantras.

They are sealed by mudrās and possess the power of mudrās. If one should suddenly bind a mudrā in an improper place, that itself constitutes a violation of his samaya. That which is a vajra is a trident (śūla); there is no difference between the trident and the vajra.
That which is positioned above becomes the mudrā of Vajradhara.
419) And below Maheśvara; in the middle, for the teacher, the preceptor, those worthy of offerings, and for all human beings, when one finger is raised, [this is the height] for all human beings.
It is the seal (*mudrā*) for all beings established in various forms—whether two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, or footless.

With [the fingers] raised twice, it is the seal for all *yakṣas* and *yakṣīs*. With [the fingers] raised thrice, it is the seal for all *vidyādharas* and *vidyādharīs*. With [the fingers] raised four times and placed evenly with the palms joined, [it is the seal for the Buddhas].

It becomes the mudrā for the women of the *asuras* and *suras*. With the hands placed in the manner of the *añjali* gesture and positioned in a beautiful form, it becomes the mudrā for all the gods who dwell in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Those same hands [in that position] become the mudrā for the gods who dwell in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Those same hands...

The two hands, joined hollow-together like a tube and bound in a fist, constitute the mudrā for all beings dwelling in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), beginning with the lords of the desire realm and including humans, animals, pretas, and those of the world of Yama.
By releasing a single finger from that very same mudrā, it becomes the mudrā for all male and female piśācas.

With two fingers extended, [one subdues] the *rākṣasa*s and *rākṣasī*s; with three fingers extended, all the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) and so forth, including the *graha*s, *mātṛ*s, *kūṣmāṇḍa*s, and all other flesh-eaters, as well as all the *ḍākinī*s, *vyantara*s, and so forth; and with all four fingers contracted, one subdues all those possessed by *kaśmala*.
This is the mudrā. With the mudrās drawn in, there is attraction; with the mudrās raised up, there is dismissal. One should perform all rites by means of one's own mind.

With these very mudrās, one should employ each respective mantra as desired. One should not employ others, nor cause other rites to be performed. One should apply each mudrā to that specific rite for which the mantra is intended;
for these mudrās are not to be transgressed, being empowered by all the Buddhas.
Indeed, all sentient beings are truly incapable of becoming angry even upon seeing the mudrā.

By transgressing the mudrās, they meet with destruction. From the destruction of the mudrās comes the violation of the samaya and the transgression of all vidyās; in the end, those who create obstacles incur a most severe rebirth in the Raurava hell, or even in the Avīci hell, among the great hells. And those who...

They consecrate the mudrā-samaya; for them, there arises long-lasting and abundant happiness, as well as rebirth among the great gods. At the end of their course, they will certainly be destined for enlightenment. In brief, many kinds of mudrās have been revealed by the primordial Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power. Not...

It is impossible to reach its limit or to perform a calculation of its number, nor can it be fully grasped by all sentient beings. In brief, within the family of the Victorious One, this single-syllable sovereign king of vidyās serves as his seal for the sake of protection.

420) Having first formed a fist with the right hand, one should release the pair of middle fingers and extend them together; then, one should bend one joint of both [the middle fingers]. The pair of index fingers should be bent at two joints.

One should join the nails of the hands together and place them upon the nails of the thumbs; this is the Cakravartin-mudrā, the most excellent of all mantras, taught by the Protectors of the World as effective for all rites. When combined with the previously mentioned One-Syllable Cakravartin [mantra], it becomes effective for all rites. By accomplishing this, everything—
The Tathāgata family and all mundane and supramundane mantras become accomplished;
by reciting this, all mantras are recited.

Furthermore, the practitioner must necessarily first perform eight thousand recitations of this supreme mantra as enjoined in this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*). In this way, all these vidyās become manifest before one and swiftly bestow accomplishment;
they quickly grant boons, and one will certainly be destined for enlightenment through the Padmadhara mudrā.

When conjoined with the single-syllable heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara, it performs all rites. Or, when conjoined with the mantra or mudrā of Pāṇḍaravāsinī, it likewise performs all rites.
