When conjoined with the mudrā of Vajradhara and his very same single-syllable heart-mantra, it likewise performs all rites. Or [with] Māmakī...
By means of the Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā).

Thus, in the royal family, one should perform all rites with the single-syllable heart-mantra of the Bodhisattva Rājagandha and with its corresponding mudrā. Likewise, in the jewel family, the yakṣa family, the divine, and the noble families, all rites should be performed here with their respective single-syllable heart-mantras and those very same mudrās. In this manner, everywhere, all rites should be performed with all mudrās and all mantras.
One should perform the empowerments of the knowledge-mantras according to the proper method; rituals must not be performed otherwise.

Thus, the hand placed on the right side with the *svasti* gesture belongs to the Brahmin Sahāmpati; the single-fingered seal (*ekaliṅgamudrā*) belongs to Maheśvara; the discus-seal (*cakramudrā*) belongs to Viṣṇu; the hollowed palm with fingers slightly spread (*añjali*) belongs to Garuḍa; likewise, the hand raised for a curse is the seal of the Ṛṣis; and likewise for the Gandharvas, along with the Suras and Asuras.
With the left hand, the thumb placed inside with its tip shown, held in the posture of a staff—

this is the mudrā of the Four Maidens; by that same mantra, one should likewise [perform it] for Kārttikeya with the Śakti-mudrā, and similarly for all others, such as Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Mahoragas, and so forth.
For all beings dwelling in the three realms of existence, for those included within all states of rebirth,

and for all those dependent upon the realm of sentient beings— including the *graha-mātṛs*, carnivorous spirits, the *kaśmala*, and so forth— there are seals (*mudrā*) prescribed for them from every side, as well as mantras from every side.
When applied in successive order and step by step, everything comes to be; it does not arise from anything else.

(171, p. 421) First of all, O Mañjuśrī, in this King of Rituals (kalparāja), the practitioner must rely upon the auspicious Tathāgata-gati, the Mahāmudrās, and the mantras that are their limbs— namely, those belonging to the Noble Samantabhadra, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and Vimalagati.

The Utpala mudrā and the mudrās of these bodhisattvas must certainly be performed by the practitioner who, having risen at dawn, being pure and situated in a clean place, stands facing east toward the sun;
having bound one of these mudrās, he should cast it upward over his own head.

One should recite any one of these mantras eight hundred times; one becomes liberated from all diseases, attains long life, and is not overcome by any obstacles. One becomes invincible to all beings, and all mantras become manifest before one; they swiftly bestow accomplishment.

He becomes empowered by all the Buddhas; he is destined for enlightenment as his ultimate goal; and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta becomes his spiritual friend until he reaches the seat of awakening. And what are those mudrās and mantras?

First, the Mahāvīra-mudrā will be explained. Having joined the two hands in a hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*), with the fingers interlaced, the two thumbs raised and bent at the third joint like a mountain peak—this is the Mahāvīra-mudrā as taught by all the Tathāgatas. And here is the mantra: *Āḥ vīra hūṃ khaḥ*. With this mantra...
This mudrā, when joined [with the mantra], performs all rites.

Having formed those same two hands into a hollowed cup (*sampuṭa*) and then opening them wide with the fingers expanded on all sides so as to take the form of a vajra—this is the mudrā named Vikāsinī, the supreme one revealed by the primordial Buddhas. And here is the mantra:
*oṃ gaganasambhave dīpta dīpta jvālaya jvālaya buddhādhiṣṭhite vikāśaya*.

"Vikāśaya sarvabuddhān | Hūṃ hūṃ vikāsini phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. This is the Vikāsinī mudrā. When joined with this mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites. It causes those possessed by grahas to speak and makes those seized by grahas, or those seized by flesh-eating demons (kravyāda) and impurities, or those unconscious from poison, speak according to their nature.

In whatever manner it is applied, it accomplishes all that accordingly. This is the vidyā that, when joined with the mudrā of Vidākāsinī, accomplishes all purposes in brief; even if not yet perfected, it swiftly brings about the desired result.

Having formed the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭa*) with both hands, one should make the fingers equalized within; this is the heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*). Having empowered the heart [mantra] seven times, it should be released. Thus it is in all cases. And here is the mantra: *oṃ godare vīra svāhā*. This is the Heart of the Tathāgata.

422) That same *hasta-sampuṭa* [mudrā], with the fingers interlaced so that there is a hollow space between the tips of all the fingers, is the *uṣṇīṣa-mudrā*. And the mantra for this is: *oṃ droṃ bandha svāhā*. This is effective for all rites.
Having formed a fist with the right hand while leaving the thumb free, this is the *khakharaka* mudrā. The mantra for this is:
*oṃ dhunājitaraṇa hūṃ*. This *khakharaka* mantra is effective for all rites.

By joining with this very mudrā and placing the left [hand] so that it touches the robe, one forms the *cīvara-mudrā*. Herein is the mantra: *oṃ rakṣa rakṣa sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhitātmacīvara svāhā*. This is the Tathāgata’s robe.
By means of this very mudrā, one performs all rites. Having consecrated his robe with this, he may wear it and become fortunate.
Great protection is thereby established. All grahas, mātṛs, piśitāsanas, kravyādas, and śakaśmalas, as well as all obstacles, flee upon merely being seen.

Having joined the left thumb and the right little finger together, with the palms facing downward as a support, this is the bowl mudrā (*pātramudrā*). And here is the mantra: *oṃ lokapālādhiṣṭhita dhara dhāraya mahānubhāva buddhapātra svāhā*. This mantra, when combined with this very mudrā, is effective for all rites.
It should be remembered at the time of eating; then no poisons or venomous toxins will have power over one.
When the two hands are joined with fists formed, and the two index fingers are bent at the middle joints—this is the Cintāmaṇi-mudrā.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ tejo jvala sarvārthasādhaka sidhya sidhya cintāmaṇiratna hūṃ | Cintāmaṇiratna. United with this very mudrā, it is auspicious and performs all rites. By means of this...
Having consecrated all kinds of excellent ornaments and decorations with this mantra, one should bind them on oneself; thus a great protection is established.

One becomes supremely fortunate. Having adorned oneself and consecrated one's armor with the mantra, one may enter into battle, and no weapon shall fall upon one's body. One becomes invincible to all enemies.
He protects his own army and attacks the enemy army.
One performs these and other such immeasurable rites while remaining unaccomplished.
Having taken any one of the specific jewels, such as ruby or emerald, and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times,
one places it at the top of a banner, upon one's own head, or on the shoulder of an elephant.

Having descended with the head of the battle, one must not engage [the enemy]. Upon seeing the opposing army, it will certainly suffer a rout even without fighting, or it will become utterly paralyzed. Or else, their troops will flee in disarray, and their commander-in-chief will be lost.

423) Having formed fists with the fingers interlocked, and having bent the two middle fingers at their third joints so that they rest against each other, this is the Dharmacakra-mudrā. And the mantra for this is: *oṃ chinda*.
Bhinda hana daha dīpta cakra hūṃ! Dharmacakra!

With the left foot extended and the right knee placed on the ground, leaning with support upon the right hand which is raised behind with a striking gesture and accompanied by the sound "hūṃ"—this is the Aparājitā mudrā. And here is the mantra: Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā. This is Aparājitā.
This is the mantra of the Invincible Wheel of Dharma. When combined with these very mudrās, it becomes effective for all rites.
In brief, it cuts through all sufferings; in whatever way it is employed, it performs all activities accordingly.

Placing the hand in the same way upon the lap of the braid (*veṇī*), with the right hand in the gesture of teaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanāhasta*), there is the Tathāgata-Śakti-mudrā. And the mantra for this is: *oṃ vijaye mahāśakti durdhari hūṃ phaṭ vijayini phaṭ maṅgale phaṭ*. This is the Tathāgata-Śakti. When conjoined with this very mudrā...

It is effective for all rites. It paralyzes all obstacles, all malevolent beings, all enemies, and even all gods. This [mudrā] possesses boundless qualities; in whatever way it is employed, it performs all activities accordingly.
Likewise, with both hands turned upward, the fingers interlaced, and the tips of the two index fingers joined in the shape of a needle.

One should place it inverted and facing downward upon the forehead. This is the Ūrṇā-mudrā, revealed by the primordial Buddhas for the Blessed Buddhas. And here is the mantra: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo 'rhatsamyaksaṃbuddhebhyaḥ | He he bandha bandha tiṣṭha tiṣṭha*.

Dhāraya dhāraya, nirundha nirundha, ūrṇāmaṇi svāhā! This is the mantra of the Tathāgata’s ūrṇā. When combined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites. Having made a mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead with *gorocanā*, one who recites [this mantra] may enter into the midst of enemies; he becomes invincible and is not harmed by any wicked beings, even in the midst of battle.
Or one may enter [the rite]. Having seen the defeat of an enemy army, one performs it; not having seen it, one does not perform it. And it has been spoken by immeasurable, blessed Buddhas.

Having formed a continuous añjali with the fingers mutually interlocked, one should bend the two index fingers toward each other at their middle joints, and likewise the two thumbs. This is the Tathāgatalocanā mudrā. And the mantra for this is: *oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā*.

424) This mantra of the Tathāgata’s Eye, when joined with this very mudrā, becomes effective for all rites. Having consecrated one's eyes with it, one may enter into the midst of enemies; upon merely being seen, they become free from anger and possess minds of loving-kindness.

They become well-wishers; they attain friendship. Or, having consecrated his own eyes at the front of a battle, he should gaze upon the enemy army; they become peaceful in mind, incapable of striking back, and withdraw without fighting, even offering their assistance.

Both hands are likewise formed with the fingers arranged in the shape of a book, with their tips joined to one another and held horizontally. This is the *mudrā* of Prajñāpāramitā. And here is the mantra: *namo bhagavati cārudarśane oṃ tha*.
This Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, when conjoined with this very *mudrā*, becomes effective for all rites.

Having recited the mantra, one should touch the heart; thus one becomes possessed of mindfulness. Reciting it in the midst of wicked enemies, one steals away their minds. Or, in the midst of battle, one bewilders bipeds, quadrupeds, and other beings who are adversaries, or causes their minds to become distracted—in short, this Blessed Lady acts as described.

In whatever manner one applies it, in that very way one performs all activities. In brief, its qualities are limitless, and its ritual manual (*kalpa*) is likewise limitless. The seals (*mudrā*) and mantras of the Tathāgatas are also limitless. Just as it is stated in the *Sannipātaparivarta*, all the retinues of the Tathāgatas are here [represented by] these seals.
And the mantras should be employed; furthermore, there are incalculable kalpas [of them]. Those mudrās and mantras should be applied within this King of Ritual Manuals (kalparāja).

Thus, in the Lotus Family, it is accompanied by the lotus mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ jiḥ jiḥ jināṅgabhṛdbhayabhedine svāhā*. This mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, when joined with the lotus mudrā, is effective for all rites. By reciting this, the entire Lotus Family [is accomplished].

It becomes recited. By means of this accomplished [mantra], the entire Lotus Family (padmakula) becomes accomplished. Or, by means of the Great Vidyā Pāṇḍaravāsinī. And the mantra here is: Oṃ kaṭe vikaṭe nikaṭe kaṭaṅkaṭe kaṭavikaṭakaṭaṅkaṭe svāhā. One should employ it with the mudrā itself, or with the lotus mudrā; it performs all rites.
It comes to pass; and protection must be performed by one who has gone to every cremation ground.
In this way, Tārā, Bhrukuṭī, Candrā, and Hayagrīva— as described in the chapter on the assembly of the Vidyārājas—
all these and the entire immeasurable Padma family should be employed with their mudrās, mantras, and extensive ritual manuals.
Thus, the banner family is accompanied by both vajra seals. And the mantra here is: HŪṂ. This is Vajrapāṇi himself;
when this is accomplished, the entire vajra family becomes accomplished.

By reciting this, everything becomes recited. When joined with the previously described double-vajra mudrā, it performs all activities according to the practitioner’s wish—even those that are contrary to the teachings of the supreme Victors—by virtue of the necessity of disciplining sentient beings.
This great yakṣa is even more fierce than the great vidyā-mantra of Māmakī or Kulandharī.
It performs all rites. And the mantra for this is: *oṃ kulandhari bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ*.

This great vidyā named Māmakī, which accomplishes all rites, has been taught by all the Buddhas; when joined with the previously employed mudrā of the great vidyā Māmakī, it becomes effective for all rites according to the practitioner’s wish.
In the introductory chapter previously described, the entire Vajra family without exception, together with its retinue headed by Vajrapāṇi,
should be employed here through the conjunctions of mudrās and mantras.

Thus, the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gajagandha of the Elephant family is: Oṃ gajāhvaye hūṃ khacare svāhā. When joined with the previously described mudrā, it is effective for all rites. In this manner, as before, the entire Elephant family becomes accomplished.
Thus is the mantra of Samantabhadra: Oṃ samāsamajinasuta mā vilamba hūṃ phaṭ.
The mantra for one who has attained the great station: Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha! O you who have gone to the great station, awakened one, remember the pledge! Hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
The mantra for Vimalagati is: Oṃ vimale vimale vimala muhūrtaṃ dhaka dhaka samayamanusmara svāhā.

The mantra of Gaganagañja, when conjoined with the mudrā of all bodhisattvas, is effective for all rites. These are the mudrās of the innumerable great bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages, such as Apāyajaha, Sadāprarudita, Kṣitigarbha, Ratnapāṇi, Maitreya, and others.

And the mantras are innumerable; they are to be employed in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja). With full detail, there is the superiority of all mundane and supramundane matters; and the extensive ritual of all mundane mantra-seals (mudrā), which has entered into the great pledge (mahāsamaya) and the non-pledge, and all conceptualizations of rituals—these have been taught here, as well as those things to be accomplished (sādhya) here.
All mantras.

In this same way, they should also be applied within the families of Maṇi, Yakṣa, and the divine Ārya families. All mantras and mudrās of all tantras, though dependent upon the three times, constitute only one single family and no other; that is to say, the Tathāgata family. And you, Mañjuśrī Kumāra, are to be seen as belonging to the Tathāgata family.

Maintain that all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all mundane and supramundane mantras—whether with outflows (*sāśrava*) or without outflows (*anāśrava*)—and the various mudrās have entered the Tathāgata families.

"Mañjuśrī, there exists no secret of all the mudrās, tantras, and mantras that has not entered the family of the Tathāgata and the commitment of the Tathāgata. Mañjuśrī, O Youth, remember that it has indeed been entered!
Because the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme, therefore the family of the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme. Thus, then—"
Mañjuśrī! This king of manuals and this jewel of the foremost family was revealed,
taught, established, and expounded by the Blessed One Saṃkusumitarāja,
the Blessed One Śālarājendra, the Blessed One Saṅkusumitagandhottamarāja, and the Blessed One Ratnaketu, as well as by other primordial Buddhas.
By the Blessed One Amitābha, by the Blessed One Puṇyābha, Kusumottama, Saṅkusuma, Supuṣpa,
Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, Krakutsanda, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, by the Blessed One Konākamuni, and also by me, Śākyamuni, at this present time.
They have been revealed and they will be revealed.

Thus it is, Mañjuśrī Kumāra! This King of Rituals (Kalparāja), which has come down through the succession of Buddhas, is like a supreme jewel at the head of the Tathāgata family; it possesses great benefits, is certain, and is based upon the Dharmadhātu.
It is not possible to describe its benefits even in a thousand eons, for its expansion of great qualities is vast.

To speak of it— to describe those [deeds] to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and those leading toward awakening in future lives (*sāmparāyika*), for all sentient beings to hear, or for those like you to explain— thus there arise immeasurable fruits consisting of the expansion of great virtues,
both pertaining to the present life and to future lives. Whoever, being faithful and free from doubt, should uphold [this teaching],...

One who is devoted to this tantra should recite it; whether one seeks to accomplish a mantra, or should mutter it, or should even bind a mudrā, one should remain constantly devoted to it. Upon seeing these very phenomena, one obtains eight qualities and benefits.
One becomes unassailable by all adversaries, and moreover, no fear shall arise for such a person.
Poison does not affect his body, and weapons do not fall upon his body. He is sustained by the blessing of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. He becomes long-lived, happy, and wise.
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta becomes his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Furthermore, he receives a sign at night.

He grants a vision in dreams; all mantras protect him; and they reveal mudrās to him in his dreams. He becomes invulnerable to hostile kingdoms and to malevolent beings who wish him harm. He is destined for awakening as his ultimate goal.

These eight benefits are to be seen for one who has faith, is free from doubt, and is diligent—whether a householder or a renunciant, a woman or a man—who assists in the teaching of the Great Beings. They are not for others who are engaged in evil deeds; for them, there is a perverted state below in the Raurava hell and other such realms.

427) As it was stated: "In the forenoon, the binding of mudrās brings long life and victory. Therefore, O Mañjuśrī Kumāra, one should honor the mudrās such as the Heart-Uṣṇīṣa and Ālocanā, together with the retinue of the Tathāgata mantras.

Indeed, these [mantras] possess equal potency and equal power with your own mudrās and mantras, as it has been said: "by one who is pure and situated in a pure place. The place is a central area of ground, free from thorns or obstructions, smeared with cow dung that has not fallen [from the animal], and strewn with fragrant white flowers. Standing there, one should recite the mantra.
One should form the mudrā; one should recite [the mantra] together with the mudrā, and not otherwise, nor should one recite any other [mantra] alone.

As it has been said regarding "purity": when the sun has set, one should bathe with pure water that is free of living organisms; wearing fresh garments and having performed protection by means of a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), one should avoid sexual intercourse with village women, being devoted to purity, cleanliness, and the preservation [of the vow], O auspicious one.
Having performed protection with the *uṣṇīṣa* and following the binding of the wheel,
one should meditate there upon the Tathāgatas during the watch of the night that has passed in a dream.

Having taken a thread spun by a maiden or by a Brahmin woman who has not yet given birth, and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with this mantra— *oṃ hara hara bandha bandha śukradhāraṇi siddhārthe svāhā*—
one should recite the mantra while employing the Māmakī mudrā. Then, one should tie the thread around the waist.

Having encircled [the organ] with the three threads, the retention of semen is accomplished. Even the Lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātveśvara*) is unable to cause mental disturbance in a dream; how much less so the obstructing spirits (*vināyaka*) of dreams? Whether by the proper method or not, neither for one with passion nor for one free from passion—even for a seer (*ṛṣi*) who is the Lord of the Desire Realm—are the daughters [of the gods] capable [of causing such disturbance].
They assume various forms to produce mental distress for those possessed by passion; how much more so, then, other women, whether born of humans or non-humans?
Having thus arisen in the morning according to the prescribed rite, having discarded the tooth-stick and rinsed the mouth,

and having bathed with pure, water free of living organisms, one should, standing facing the east, form the mudrā according to the previously mentioned rite and recite the mantras. One will then become long-lived and capable of performing all rites.

One is liberated from great diseases. One becomes beloved by all people. One becomes like a counter-spell (*pratyaṅgira*) to enemies. As soon as they are seen, all *grahas*, *kravyādas*, *kaśmalas*, and the like flee away. It paralyzes the enemy force.
Merely by being seen, it accomplishes all rites—whether one is pure or impure, and whether performed according to the rules or not.

428) Thus, this king of manuals is surrounded by an incalculable multitude of mudrās and mantras; it has been spoken and will be spoken by incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and by me as well, Śākyamuni, at this present time.

This was spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in the midst of a great assembly. You too, O Youthful Mañjuśrī, have been appointed by me for the sake of protecting the teaching and for the sake of long-term preservation of the dharmadhātu after my parinirvāṇa, as you abide at the limit of reality (dharmakoṭi).

This was spoken by me— whose mind is impelled by great compassion even while abiding in the peace that culminates in the limit of reality— for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, at a time when the most terrifying end of the age is occurring,
in order to restrain wicked kings and evil beings who cause harm to the Three Jewels.
And this King of Rituals has been spoken in detail and with full analysis for the sake of discipline and for the benefit of all sentient beings.

Thus concludes the thirty-fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the rules of mantras and mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
429) Now follows the thirty-eighth detailed chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having once again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [spoke].
He addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī!
[I shall explain] in brief the characteristics of the mudrās and the mantras in detail, as well as, in brief, the ritual procedure for the maṇḍalas and the observance of the commitments."
It is the secret of all mantras, the mandala among all mantras.
All of this was previously proclaimed by all the Buddhas of great supernatural power;
the majesty of the course of mantras has been taught across all families as well.
In the past, the primordial Buddhas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
set in motion both the wheel of mantras and the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Following the wheel of peace, they have gone and taken refuge in the limit of reality;
all those Buddhas, possessing great supernatural power in the world, have attained peace.
All this was previously proclaimed by the Tathāgatas of the past;
I too, O Mañjuśrī of noble wisdom, shall teach it to you in this final age.
Having done this, then one should speak these words to the Buddha of great splendor;
indeed, the youth Mañjughoṣa stands before him with palms joined in reverence.
He spoke to the Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers and the supreme among bipeds:
"O one of great wisdom! Speak the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of the worlds."
"In summary, without elaboration, [this is] the arising of the fruit of the greatness of qualities.
Having been addressed thus, Mañjuśrī remained silent.
Then the glorious Brahmeśvara, whose voice was like the song of the kalaviṅka bird,
explained all of that which is established within the mudrās and maṇḍalas.
At that time, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men, staying above the Pure Abodes, taught the mantra and the tantra.
Listen, O youth Mañjuśrī! To the origin of the ritual procedures for the mudrās, and the extensive greatness and qualities of the mantras and the applications of the tantras.
430) First, one should [know] the sign of every Tathāgata, as well as [the state of] beings and non-beings;
likewise, their form, conduct, gestures, and all their bodily movements and speech.
With both hands and feet, the head, and the joining of the fingers of one hand—
all that was declared by the ancient primordial Buddhas to be a *mudrā*.
The water-pot, the parasol, as well as the lotus, the banner, and likewise the flag;
the fish, the thunderbolt, as well as the conch, the jar, and likewise the wheel.
Whatever various weapons are proclaimed to exist in the world,
they all take the form of the utpala-lotus seal within the maṇḍala of seals.
Standing here in successive order, these are likewise declared according to the prescribed rule;
one should always depict all of them with forms and essential natures that are identical.
Having stated that the mudrās are in the maṇḍala, those mudrās are proclaimed as being properly arranged in their respective places throughout all the common [maṇḍalas].
In all mandalas indeed, one should apply one's own form;
likewise, the universal monarch [should apply] the wheel in the white emergence at the uṣṇīṣa.
One should draw the white parasol as the principal [deity] in the mandala;
likewise, the Dharma-wheel of the Buddhas and the lotus for the Lotus family.
The vajra is prescribed for the Vajra family, the elephant for one born of the Gaja family;
likewise, one should employ the pitcher in the Maṇi family throughout the entire mandala.
One should draw the two preeminent divine and noble families, Śrīvatsa and Svastika;
one should draw the fruit arising from the source of fruits in the most excellent Yakṣa family.
Having drawn a swan for Mahābrahmā, one should also draw Śakra with his vajra;
for Maheśvara, one should draw a trident and likewise draw a bull.
Having also drawn the trident and the sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa) along with the javelin of Skanda,
and the discus and maces of Viṣṇu together with the Dānavas.
One should always depict in their midst gods with various weapons, seated upon diverse thrones, and possessing various types of vehicles.
431) One should draw one or another of these reflections, which have undergone a transformation of form yet remain as they truly are, in every mandala.
The mandalas taught by the supreme Victors are joined in groups of one or two, or from three onwards up to an incalculable number; the rows of altars are equal in measure to them.
One should place in the center that person for whose sake the mandala was proclaimed;
or one should draw a Buddha within the womb of the Jina family in the very middle.
Then one should also paint the image of the Teacher situated within;
second, that which is placed in the Lotus family, and third, one should paint the Vajra family.
Having thus drawn all those gods and asuras in succession,
one should thereafter draw the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans upon the entire ground.
Then, having drawn the heretics in their proper order as they are situated,
one should likewise draw the guardians of the directions and all those who have come from various origins.
In brief, one should draw the maṇḍala starting from a single dot, increasing from two up to an incalculable number, extending as far as the very limit of the directions above.
At that time, the surface of the earth within his mandala was indeed said to be immeasurable,
extending from a single point to the limitless expanse of the terrestrial plane.
The ritual procedure for the mandala has been declared and specified as being of three kinds;
namely, it is proclaimed as the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
In the highest [level], the highest accomplishment is declared; in the middling, the middling is proclaimed;
and in the lowest, the minor accomplishment was taught by the supreme Victors of old.
The Supreme Victors have declared that success is threefold according to the mental dispositions:
great success for those of great capacity, and middling success for those of middling capacity.
The third is for minor beings; it is taught as a minor rite. When the mind is serene, Buddhahood arises as the supreme and fruitful result.
A sentient being who has attained a state of equanimity at that time will certainly attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha simply by beholding the maṇḍala.
432) The others are said to be fixed in the state of a Śrāvaka due to their lack of reverence;
however, the greatness of the fruit is not in vain, and peace is declared to be the ultimate goal.
He will certainly attain heaven even without seeing the mandala;
likewise, he shall obtain all the supreme mudrās and the mantras in their full detail.
The mudrās and maṇḍalas are declared to be of three kinds and three types, bringing about happiness; now the benefit of the mantras is being told.
Starting from a single syllable and so forth, up to whatever number according to its measure— however many words are stated in a mantra, that many are proclaimed [to be its parts].
Idle chatter, weeping, laughing, and likewise crying,
as well as all talk and prattle, shall become beneficial for all mantras.
Those mantras are of three kinds and are declared to be of three types;
just as they are known in the mandala, so indeed are they in the case of mudrās and mantras.
This method, joined with the ritual procedure, has been taught by the Leaders of the World;
in that very way, it proceeds in three ways, in many ways, and even in a thousand ways.
It is threefold, of three kinds, and likewise in three ways, and indeed it is innumerable;
for mantra is dependent upon the mind, and there is no mantra devoid of the mind.
One who is joined with the mind-mantra (cittamantra) and properly united will accomplish [the goal],
whether those mantras belong to the Tathāgata family or likewise to the Padma family.
And those songs which are sung in the Lotus family and in the other families by others—
all worldly mantras whatsoever have indeed issued forth from here.
That mantra which was spoken by the Victors and the sons of the Victors for the sake of sentient beings—
whosoever, being diligent, recites it, shall certainly become a Buddha.
Those mantras which are indeed neutral, he who recites them is declared to be a Pratyekabuddha by virtue of his lineage.
Those who are indeed engaged in other mantras spoken by Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats,
as well as those worldly beings intent upon the recitation of mantras;
433) He would certainly be established in the lineage of the Śrāvakas of great supernatural power;
even there, one should apply effort toward the superior, the inferior, and the middling [levels].

In rites for pacification, there shall be the enlightenment of a Buddha; likewise in rites for enrichment, that of those who possess the sword [pratyekabuddhas]. By other minor mantras, however, the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka is proclaimed.
Therein, too, the mind is to be observed; it is divided into three ways, and it is further divided manifoldly, even into incalculable divisions.

Thus concludes the thirty-sixth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for all activities concerning the mudrās and maṇḍalas, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
434) Now follows the thirty-ninth chapter.
Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and all [the beings therein]...

Having surveyed the world-system with his Buddha-eye, he beheld all sentient beings and again addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists within the extensive section on your mantra-tantra mudrās that which enters into all mundane and supramundane samaya-maṇḍalas."

In the accomplishment of the practice of general injunctions, within the basis for the entry of beings, they briefly explain the practice that teaches the treasury of all mantras, all mudrās, all maṇḍalas, and all beings who have entered into all mantras, characterized by inconceivable activity.
Let that be heard.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, made this request: "May the Sugata grant me his favor for the sake of compassion toward us and for the benefit of the world; that will be for the welfare of a great multitude of people."

For the benefit, happiness, and out of compassion for the world, may the Sugata speak to me regarding the procedure conducive to the practice of entering the commitments (*samaya*), the subsequent instructions, and the means of accomplishment for all mantras— including recitation, fire-offerings, nourishment, worship, observances, all tantras, and mudrās— within all maṇḍalas.
The extensive section on the chapters concerning the methods and specific applications for all mundane and supramundane rites.
When this had been said, the Blessed One, the sweet-voiced omniscient one, remained silent for that interval.
The wise Mañjurava, pleased and knowing the Sugata, accepted this;
and all the Buddhas, gathered from all places throughout every realm, [did likewise].
Indeed, all Bodhisattvas, as well as all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
and all beings whatsoever within the beginningless wheel of existence, are of three kinds.
Those who are bound by birth from a womb and joined to the five destinies,
as well as the lords of all hosts of beings— rākṣasas, uragas, and humans.
The Daityas, Dānavas, and Yakṣas; the Kūṣmāṇḍas and Kaṭapūtanas; the chief gods, the leaders of the Gaṇas, and the Mothers of great supernatural power.
All the hosts of planets in the world, as well as the moon and sun,
Brahmā, Indra, Kubera, the Rudras, Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Virūḍhaka;
435) Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Kubera, all the Vasus as well,
and all beings everywhere who are dependent upon the realm of sentient beings.

Bound by the threads of their destinies through actions bearing auspicious and inauspicious fruits, they are both liberated and unliberated everywhere; having arrived at the proper time, they remain established.

Through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment, those born from auspicious wombs and those born from inauspicious ones, established here in three ways, hear [the teaching] by means of supernatural power.
Then all the Buddhas indeed heard that noble Dharma of the Sugata, which brings about the arising of the auspiciousness of the supreme teaching, in the city of Śuddhāvāsa.
It is proclaimed as being invariably endowed with the three— mantra, mudrā, and samādhi—
and it is the path of the Noble Eightfold Way, which is secure and most auspicious.
The path of action is taught as threefold—excellent and leading to the city of Nirvāṇa:
namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration; thus the path is shown in three ways.
The Blessed One said: "O All-Knowing One, initiate the practice of the limbs of the mantra path;
O Wise One, with a slightly smiling face, look upon Mañjughoṣa."
And then all the hosts of beings, hearing this speech endowed with auspiciousness and resonant like the voice of Brahmā, stood there, gentle and confident.
May there be no falling away from your commitment; may it not be in vain, for by being ignorant of the Buddha’s word, it will be harmful to you for a long time.
"O child, you will fall into blinding darkness and become far removed [from me].
Therefore, for your own welfare, these mantras and mudrās have been proclaimed to you."
O worlds, you shall always exercise both favor and restraint;
consider that this is joined with my own action, for my wrath is indeed like the Ender, Yama himself.
He will undoubtedly always exercise restraint in this age;
first, indeed, in a secluded and solitary place strewn with flowers.
Having mentally and through meditation encompassed the mandala to be constructed on all sides,
the wise one should first meditate upon the lotus of all the Buddhas.
436) A second lotus rises up with the great splendor of the sun itself;
situated thereon is the glorious Mañjuvara, marked by the form of a youth.
With five tufts of hair on his head, knees, ears, and elbows prominent,
his body covered in down, and with palms joined in reverence, the boy questioned the Sugata, the Knower.
And uttering auspicious speech within the abode of the Sugata,
one indeed beholds the great lotus of all the Buddhas, arisen from crystal.
A lotus made of beryl, with filaments produced from gold,
a stalk of great emerald, and a pericarp together with gold.
It possessed a great mass of branches and was adorned with great jewels,
featuring buds made of rubies that were beautifully decorated in many forms.
Having meditated upon a vast lotus resting in the sky, adorned with divine sprouts made of emerald, for the best of sages.

Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats Śrāvakas by visualizing a lotus that is smaller than that, well-proportioned, marked with equal signs, and very beautiful.
Therefore, one who possesses an intellect focused on effort should mentally make the third lotus smaller;
they know that the fourth lotus, which is the swirl, is even shorter than that.
One should always meditate upon the fifth lotus, which is shorter than the short,
possessing an equal form and radiance, and wherein all darkness is established within the void.
One who knows [the ritual] should fashion for him a lotus situated on the seven [spokes], by means of the mind;
likewise, the lotus of Vajrapāṇi should be like the rising sun.
To the right of Vighnāntaka is Mañjughoṣa, always upon a lotus;
beyond that is a smaller lotus belonging to the great-souled Lokīśa.
The third is indeed the "Lotus" for one who has attained universal illumination;
the fourth is indeed the "Lotus" for the state of inexhaustible eloquence.
O you of slightly pure gait, there is a short lotus belonging to the fifth principle;
from that, the sixth lotus is the noble one known as Adharma.
Furthermore, one should visualize the great ocean below and all around; from it,
the great nāgas Ananta, Nanda, and Upanandaka emerge halfway out.
All-white great elephants, adorned with every ornament,
born from the ocean, with smiling faces and gazes fixed upon the sky.
With seven heads and great coils, adorned with jeweled earrings,
they are divine in human form, while others likewise have half the coils of a serpent.
The seven folds of skin are gentle, and the eyelids are slightly raised;
to the left are the excellent sages, and five [Buddhas] are situated upon the lotus of the uṣṇīṣa.
The Wheel-Turning [Mantra] has such beginning and end; it is sharpened by the weapon of Śakra.
The Single-Syllable Wheel-Turning One is a mass of splendor, white and lofty.
One should clearly visualize above Jayoṣṇīṣa, the King of Vidyās of great supernatural power,
and below him, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Yakṣas.
In these [deities], the wise one who knows the mantras and is a king of mantras should always and at all times yoke his own mind and intellect to those with form within the womb.
One should meditate upon the Self as being situated there, established in restraint, seated indeed upon a lotus leaf, and seated cross-legged below.
Always confess all misdeeds in the presence of the sages;
remaining there, embodied by the power of his observances, he should entreat the most excellent of the best of sages.
May those born of the Sugata remain turning the wheel of Dharma;
with a mind intent on recitation, I rejoice in their incomparable merit.
White *mālatī* flowers, *punnāga*, *nāgakesara*,
*campaka*, *aśoka*, *tilaka*, *tagara*, and likewise *mallikā*.
One should cast a divine handful of flowers, beautiful on the left side,
whether they are actually present or mentally visualized, endowed with a focused mind and most auspicious.
They should perform various excellent offerings and the enchanting vidyā-mantra,
as well as various superior incenses, perfumes, and ointments.
438) One should perform that with the mind alone, being truly established in the middle state;
having offered it with the bali-mantras, one should then place lamps as well.
Possessing various forms, with diverse and variegated foods,
and consisting of many kinds of preparations including curd-rice and non-glutinous rice.
Having offered barley, wheat, and mung beans, well-adorned with various kinds of food and edibles,
to the Sugata with devotion, one should offer even one's own self.
That by which the mind is disciplined according to reality and not otherwise—
this faith is taught by me as the worship among all forms of worship.
By meditating upon me, all practitioners of recitation will certainly attain awakening;
the accomplishment of the mantra will become fruitful, of this there is no doubt.
In this very life, those lacking in strength succeed with the mantra-deities;
or else, some human beings achieve success in another future birth.

In the past, there was a manifold abundance of enjoyments and also an ample variety of distinctions; likewise, there were diverse [expressions of] time, mind, and speech, as well as threefold meditation.
By means of Buddhas, hundreds of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas,
those illustrious ones attain the threefold enlightenment.
The accomplishment of mantra in this world is said to be of these three types, categorized as sattva, namely:
superior, inferior, and middling.
Action is taught to be threefold:
that which is sublime is said to consist of meditative absorption, while the middling is known as being born of ethical discipline.
The gift born of giving is the lowest, while that which is primary is likewise threefold:
the gift of Dharma is the most excellent, and that which has gone [to its destination] is the middling.
"Speech is indeed declared to be the gift of material goods (āmiṣadāna) for the youngest [son], while ethical conduct (śīla) is also said to be threefold; thus spoke the Sage of old."
The supreme morality is known as that which is dedicated toward Buddhahood;
the middling leads to Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, while the inferior arises from the state of a Śrāvaka.
439) This is supramundane ethical discipline (*lokottara-śīla*), whereas mundane (*laukika*) discipline is now being explained;
that too should be known as threefold, and it is the cause for the arising of outflows (*sāsrava*).
Those who arise from the direct knowledge of the knowers, through devotion and the realization of those seeking liberation,
are always described by the best of sages as the most excellent and the eldest in the world.
The wise declare this to be the foremost morality in the world;
O son of a god, the middling should be known as such, while the lowest, O best of kings, is [as follows].
And that [karma] is also threefold, applied in three ways among the types of action;
it is further described as being of three kinds, of three types, and again released in groups of three, two, seven, and five.
That [number] is twenty-one, and it is further divided threefold;
thus the sprout has appeared, and from the sprout, that which is born of meditation arises in this very manner.
Furthermore, the two lords of the gods [are described] as three, and again as adorned by eight times eight;
just as was previously specified, it is likewise stated regarding the meditations themselves.
Thus, it is divided like waves, yet it proceeds like a flame;
it should be known as having the form of bubbles, fragile and arising in every moment.
In this very way, by the initial application, they are divided again into a hundredfold;
and it should always be known that they extend to thousands and are uncountable, beginningless, and beyond definition.
The supreme action born of meditation, arising from the mind, is accomplished;
therefore, one who possesses meditation should direct the mantra and the mind toward awakening.
By this very method, they shall attain accomplishment in the deity of the mantra;
therefore, those who desire accomplishment and recite [the mantra] should apply every effort.
One should always perform mental worship of the Buddhas in every respect; for one who is constantly devoted to meditation, accomplishment is attained even in this very life.
For this restraint of ethical discipline born of meditative concentration is unimpeded everywhere;
through concentration comes liberation, and through ethical discipline arises the birth of the best of gods.
The taking up of the meditations of arising, [and so forth]...
this has indeed been stated in brief for the sake of mantra-attainment by those who recite.
440) Having understood this, all practitioners of mantra will undoubtedly attain success in mantras quickly,
and they will swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
From the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvataṃsaka*, the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*,

this is the first chapter on the detailed exposition of meditation (*dhyānapaṭalavisara*), concerning the reality of accomplishing all ritual purposes through the means of supreme practice, from the thirty-seventh extensive section of the Great King of Ritual Manuals (*mahākalparāja*).
Thus it is concluded.
441) Now begins the fortieth chapter-section.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists within your Great King of Rituals (Mahākalparāja), in the detailed exposition of the chapter on that which is born of meditative concentration, which is untainted, supremely auspicious and peaceful, and has entered the ultimate limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)."
It has followed the guiding principle of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas; it has entered the path of supreme nirvāṇa;
it has become secure and peaceful through the noble path; it has entered the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the selflessness of all phenomena;
and it has entered the meditative absorption that follows the entry into the reality of all mundane and supramundane things.

[It is] accompanied by the playful drama and the manifestation of the conduct of a child—a summary of the rules for accomplishing the practice of all mantras—which brings satisfaction to those who follow the conduct of beings. And what is that?
Listen, Mañjurava! This glorious meditation, which conforms to all sentient beings, should be known as the source of omniscience and the means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras.
It is the fulfillment of all mantras and the purification of those who have committed evil deeds;
by meditating upon whom, all people shall attain unclouded accomplishment.
Having attained the three types of enlightenment— superior, inferior, and middling— they shall possess the inconceivable bliss of meditative concentration endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
People shall praise his incomparable accomplishment of mantra,
which is the means for accomplishing all aims in the world and the source of fame, renown, and the arising of happiness.
They will swiftly attain long life in this world, the exalted state of the gods, and the fulfillment of all their hopes; of this there is no doubt.
Those who contemplate through meditation shall attain the unsurpassed enlightenment that transcends dualistic proliferation;
it is proclaimed among all mantras as the supreme benefit for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, through the mere recollection of the mantras in all the tantras,
the accomplishments (siddhis) of those who seek success quickly become bound to their expectations.
Mortals on earth who have made aspirations go again to those deities;
here, they bring [their offerings] to the divine city within the abodes of the gods.
All the kings of mantras abide in the mouth of one who meditates upon them;
and having returned, they all [bestow] the form of the deities and mantras.

442) They speak according to reality regarding the arising of the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious for the practitioner who is awakened to speech, whether in a dream or through direct perception.

Whether it be karma resulting in auspicious fruit or even a deity manifest before their eyes, all those who have entered the dream state perceive it, or else they see it through the power of the mantra-practitioner.
Furthermore, practitioners of worldly mantras who recite them do not perceive the other [result];
yet through meditation, evil is destroyed, as is through abundant recitation.
All the kings of mantras are accomplished without delay for that practitioner,
through the power of the yoga of meditation, which possesses inconceivable and wondrous activities.
When he had been addressed thus by the steadfast Śākyasiṃha, the ascetic,
Mañjughoṣa then remained silent in the city of the Śuddhāvāsa gods.
All the principal hosts of gods, residing in the three realms,
released this excellent, pure speech to the Guru, the Lord of all Mantras.
Excellent, excellent, O Great Hero! Excellent, O Lord of Dharma, O All-pervading One! For you, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings who recite mantras—
The meditations have been explained according to their true nature as previously described;
now, however, O Great Hero... [text missing].
Thus addressed, those gods— foremost indeed, most excellent, and beneficial—
then became silent in that city of Śuddhāvāsa.
Thus spoke the greatly steadfast sage, whose splendor was [immeasurable],
with auspicious and divine speech, revealing the true meaning of the principles of the world.
The Perfectly Awakened One spoke with a voice produced from sweet syllables:
"Listen, all you hosts of beings, who abide in the three types of abodes!"
And being composed in meditation, they speak of the exposition of existence—
that which is of manifold meaning yet non-dual, the selflessness that is the vision of reality.
For the sake of the success of all mantras and their purposes, as well as for various worldly aims,
those who are masters of all dharmas in the world arrive when they are well-visualized.
443) And for the sake of the swift accomplishment of the purpose of the mantras for all reciters,
one should first meditate upon the Great Hero, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu.
Seated upon a mountain of jewels within a cave radiant with gems,
he beheld a divine, exceedingly lofty great lotus made of ruby.
The Blessed One sat there upon the cross-legged seat, teaching the Dharma,
as the Great Hero meditated, being indeed born from the lotus.
One should meditate upon the Perfectly Awakened Padmottara, the wise Padmābha,
and the five excellent sages, as well as the Tathāgata Ratnābha.
It should be known as well-proportioned and firmly established within the five secret places;
it may be entirely made of stone along with its mountain, or in some cases made of ruby (*padmarāga*).
In some places it has the luster of a broken sapphire, in others it resembles crystal;
its height has the brilliance of emerald, and its measurement is eight hundred [units].
Extending for a thousand yojanas and sixteen hundred thousand in width,
the perfectly awakened Buddhas, the supreme among men, reside above in infinite numbers.
Thus, above, below, and in all directions and intermediate points,
everything has been attained by the excellent sages, the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds.
And it shines with moon-like radiance upon seats of white lotuses,
possessing the luster of swans, cow’s milk, conch shells, jasmine, the moon, and snow.
"All this is pervaded by the Perfectly Awakened Ones— above, below, and across the seven directions"—
thus [it was proclaimed] in the true sky by the foremost of gods from all sides, with showers of flowers and other offerings.

One should always contemplate oneself seated in the cross-legged posture, with invisible bodies identical in form [to those of the Buddhas], having come together from the sky above and remaining below.
He always beheld his own principal body, stainless and resting upon a lotus petal,
being consecrated from all sides by streams of water.
By countless sages, the foremost of sages, the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds,
who always extend their right hands with fingers pointing outward on all sides.
444) With many streams of white water flowing upwards from all sides and everywhere, one should contemplate the form as indeed one's own self.
With streams of water possessing eight qualities— fragrant, soothingly cool,
clear, and unpolluted, as well as removers of all diseases.
One should also contemplate oneself as being drenched by such streams of water, which destroy old age and death and resemble split crystal.
Having consecrated oneself and reflected upon it, with a mind nourished by those [visualizations],
the meditator shall then become happy through streams of water from all sides.
With a contented mind, the wise one should then perceive knowledge as his seat;
desiring concentration within the mind, he whose intellect is focused should contemplate the five superknowledges.
Thus disciplined, the yogi will then himself perceive phenomena;
likewise, he will attain divine hearing and the knowledge that recollects former births.
The play of supernatural powers, celestial light, the unobstructed divine eye,
the movement of others' minds, their thoughts, and the basis of all sentient beings.
Then the Lord of Yogis, concentrated through yoga, will know everything;
his realization in the unsurpassed state is irreversible forever—of this there is no doubt.

By means of non-conceptualization, this practitioner of constant recitation shall attain the qualities pertaining to the stage of Buddhahood on the first [bhūmi], becoming irreversible from the state of immortality.
Without any effort at all, the mantras are correctly accomplished in every respect—
those which are supramundane and all those proclaimed by the Abhimukhis.
But as for the Bodhisattvas, those who are born from the lotus and those born from the vajra everywhere,
as well as the worldly mantras spoken by Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra—
Together with all the hosts of the chief Yakṣas,
the groups of Mātṛs, Bhūtas, and Grahas, and the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras.
Then by the gods, nāgas, and garuḍas, as well as by the siddhas and vidyādharas,
and also by the kūṣmāṇḍas, vyantaras, and the wretched flesh-eaters.
445) And even by Rākṣasas who take away the lives of others, by Pretas and evil dreams,
by Piśācas, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, and those born of many different forms;
Whatever mantras have been spoken in the world, when they are awakened, they lead that yogin toward even slight enlightenment.
The mantras that accomplish all aims quickly attain success;
indeed, for one who perceives the true meaning of reality, his very speech becomes mantra and swiftly bears fruit.
The sages and the gods who have arisen from human birth, as well as the principal beings— women, men, and eunuchs— who act with forceful resolve.
All those of great supernatural power— whether superior, inferior, or middling—
as well as all worldly mantras honored by the world.
Furthermore, through those mental recitations and mantras,
all those born of mantra spoken by the foremost of sages bring accomplishment to the yogin.
Furthermore, the medicinal herbs contained within tantras and mantras, as well as jewel ornaments—
all the excellent mantras, whether superior, inferior, or middling— belong to him.

When even the imperishable syllable flows away for the sake of attaining all desires, it is indeed accomplished for that practitioner who is thus disciplined; for the practitioner who is thus disciplined.
For one who has been thus addressed, especially for the wise,
the primary signs and marks are the causes for the accomplishment of mantras.
A most excellent body is born, radiant like a lotus and a source of happiness;
moreover, there is coolness of the limbs and a fragrance like that of sandalwood and blue lotuses.
The fragrance of camphor, agallochum, and saffron, along with the color of lotus filaments and campaka flowers,
emanates from his mouth and the pores of his skin.
The *jātī*, *yūthikā*, *puṇnāga*, *nāgakesara*, and *vākula*; the *dhānuṣkārī* along with the *saugandhī*; and that which is produced from the *jāti*, *mallikā*, and *kola*.
Various excellent incenses, or various kinds of flowers;
various excellent perfumes, and various kinds of substances.
446) Various scents pervading everywhere, produced by virtuous deeds—
surpassing all those, his heart-pleasing and excellent fragrance wafts forth.
It wafts forth, surpassing in the world the divine scent of the māndārava flower, along with its filaments and its pollen, together with the fragrance of musk.
Then, having recognized these signs— namely, coolness in the body, one-pointedness of mind, and a face born of discernment— [one knows that the fire has been kindled].
Having fully understood the mind born of the first dhyāna,
as well as pleasure, pain, equanimity, and even detachment within that state of cessation;
In the second [dhyāna], the reciter impels equanimity and purity of mindfulness;
the third is dhyāna by way of the mind, and the fourth is by way of the basis, for the practitioner.
Just as the meditation taught by the best of sages is auspicious in every respect,
so too should the practitioner engaged in mantra recitation meditate with a one-pointed mind.

Those which have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, those of the present, and those yet to come, as well as those proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones and their disciples— these are the sūtras that have been celebrated.
In those yogas, the knowers of mantra should practice meditation in successive order,
turning away from the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and that which arises from the Pratyekabuddhas.
Having brought forth great compassion and likewise great loving-kindness with effort,
one should cultivate the mind in whatever way it accords with its spiritual lineage.
Loving-kindness is the mind intent on the welfare of others; compassion is tenderness toward the suffering of others;
sympathetic joy is delight in the success of others; and equanimity is the overlooking of the faults of others.
Thus spoke the highly fortunate, perfectly awakened one, the supreme among bipeds:
"The reality of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and emptiness is the auspicious state."
The leaders of the world have pointed out the secure, auspicious, and supreme state;
all conditioned phenomena are momentary, and the three types [of existence] are inactive within the ultimate realities.
Those very unconditioned phenomena are established as threefold within awakening;
they alone are declared by those intent on awakening to be the most auspicious in the world.
447) The selflessness of persons and phenomena was described as being like a sharp fall;
that does not exist on the auspicious, secure path taught by the Buddha.
In this dharma that is ultimately supreme and rests upon the limit of reality,
you are equal to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), free from existence and non-existence.
Awakening occurs within the auspicious source of phenomena (dharmodaya), which is endowed with three modes and is based on manifold distinctions, yet ultimately culminates in liberation.
When the knower of mantras stands upon this auspicious path— which is well-applied, well-expounded by all the Buddhas, well-taught, and the remover of all sins— then [success is attained].
Whatever phenomena, whether auspicious or inauspicious, have arisen dependently according to all the supreme sages—
all these should be meditated upon by those following the path of the sages when joined with the [proper] births.
But for the śrāvakas, the training proceeds as higher ethics (adhiśīla) and that which is higher mind (adhicitta), the knowledge which is the cause for the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Those who recite [mantras] should always personally know that which is without sound as being with sound;
likewise, the rhinoceros-like practitioner should understand the training pertaining to the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
Thus, the one known as Sarvasattva uttered this melodious sound, which was proclaimed by the Jinas as following the reality of the path and arising from the three heavens.
Meditative concentration is both with-outflows and without-outflows, as is restraint which brings about excellence;
it is established within the trainings according to its mode of activity and according to its characteristic mark.
By practicing those dharmas, the reciter attains the accomplishment of mantra;
and the merit born of meditation is the merit that arises from the auspiciousness of Brahman.
His success should always be known to arise from meditations and augmented merits;
the practitioner of mantras, devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, remains observant of vows while gathering [the necessary power] from all sides.
One should meditate upon the foremost son of the Victors, who possesses great supernatural power,
the great hero Mañjughoṣa, whose splendor is equal to the appearance of saffron.
The deity has a face with a slight smile, possesses a left-hand mandala of light,
is of serene form, stands upon a lotus, and is illuminated by rays of light radiating from him on all sides.
448) In the previously described place, consecrated by one’s own form,
above the stars of water, in the abode of the supreme Jinas.
One should meditate upon that auspicious Mañjurava seated comfortably there,
the Lord who is auspicious, with his gaze directed upward toward all the Buddhas and accompanied by a gesture of salutation.
In her left hand she holds a beautiful blue lotus;
in her right hand, it is said, she holds [a gesture] in a pure place that is always auspicious.
The practitioner of mantra should always meditate again and again upon that son of the Sage, who is ever accompanied by reverence and whose conduct is slightly less than that of a fool.
Remaining there, the wise one born of meditative concentration beholds those who are afflicted;
by the mere sight of the mantra-practitioner, they are all liberated from their disease.
And looking downward, he beholds the netherworld (pātāla) and all treasures hidden within the earth;
he becomes a master of all mantras and a constant exorcist of those who employ incantations.
Whoever should behold from above those perfected ones (siddhas) moving through the sky will bring everything under control in the world and obtain all perfected substances from every quarter.
Then one should always behold the northern direction and the lords of the yakṣas,
namely the kūṣmāṇḍas, the givers of wealth, and the lord of wealth (Kubera) of great supernatural power.
Īśāna, Bhūtapati,
and all the medicinal herbs born of gold, as well as Rudra together with Umā.
The kinnaras, gods, gandharvas, sages, and likewise the garuḍas—
those who are the refuge of all beings, as well as those in the northern intermediate directions.
And in all directions, as well as everywhere among both the stationary and the moving,
all beings come under the control of the reciter merely by being seen.
Thus it should be known regarding the west: Varuṇa, possessed of great supernatural power, always sees everything with the great nāgas, and they go forth in a state of intense rapture.
Thus did Yama, possessed of great supernatural power, [conquer] the worlds of Vaivasvata,
as well as all those wicked Rākṣasas who were of terrible form and great supernatural power.
449) Birds that snatch away the lives of others, accompanied by their offspring and flocks of servants;
flesh-eaters in human form, always followed by those of terrifying appearance.
The Vyantaras and the Kaśmalas, the Pretas and those of great supernatural power (maharddhika), the Piśācas, the Bhūtas, the Kravyādas, and the Vyālas of great supernatural power.
Possessing forms of many kinds and born from wombs of many kinds,
beings with forms as swift as thought indeed roam the earth.
Fierce with the scent of blood, they always return from all sides for a hundred yojanas, and even for a thousand, O son of the Sun, following after him.
Afflicting human beings, they roam upon the surface of the earth;
some seek food, while others follow for the sake of sport.
All shall come under the control of the reciter merely by being seen;
thus it is in the eastern direction and likewise in all other directions, following the presiding deities of the quarters starting from the east.
Savitar, along with all the constellations, the luminaries, the planets, and the moon; the great portents and secondary omens; Sattva; Virāja; and likewise the Lord of the Quarters.
Whether it be a king with his sons and retinue, or even an armed enemy from all sides—
all of them come under one's control, subdued and won over by meditation.
And he saw everywhere in all directions,
on this earth, the best of gods, the gods themselves, and men and women, and so forth.
All beings in the world— humans and those born of non-humans—
all those beings, including the three classes of immovable creatures, come under one's control.
But those born of the elements— whether primary, intermediate, or inferior—
all come under the control of the meditator, whether invisible or visible.
The karma born of meditative absorption is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Having attained supreme enlightenment through the superior [karma], the meditator turns back from [the cycle of] rebirth.
The unsurpassed, peaceful state is attained individually by those who possess the sword-like path; the inferior enlightenment of the Śrāvakas is attained in dependence upon others.
450) The supreme among men speaks thus regarding those phenomena that arise dependently, which possess the characteristic of being produced from causes, and which are likewise subject to cessation.
Arhatship is to be realized through the four chapters;
knowledge that understands fallacious reasons arises from emptiness and suffering.
The state of arhatship, which is established in the selflessness of phenomena, is ultimately born from the limit of reality;
it should be known as being like cessation and the path, and is also the lowest [of the fruits].
It is the uprooting of the *ālaya*, the cutting off of the path, and the speaking of selflessness;
it is the quenching of thirst, the drying up of the counter-flow, and the severing of the path for embodied beings.
In this beneficial path born of meditation, the arrow of sorrow for embodied beings— along with the river of desire— is blocked on all sides by meditative absorption together with craving.
Likewise, action is of three kinds, marked by manifold aspects;
and for those who are preeminent, awakening is proclaimed to be threefold.

In the past, the supreme Victors taught that the enlightenment of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats who are like rhinoceroses is always designated as the lowest in this world, while that of the middle [vehicle] is also taught.
The supreme goal is always awakening, the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
through such preliminary practice, the sequence of ritual action is threefold.
There it is divided a hundredfold, then a thousandfold, and even beyond number;
it should be understood as being like the sprout of rice, and always like the sprout of a field.
Then, like a seed and its sprout, action is proclaimed to proceed eternally in a continuous stream; one endowed with pure qualities is like a medicinal plant produced from a seed.
Furthermore, through the continuity of the consciousness of sentient beings, it becomes like a boat upon the water;
the wise one should again meditate upon the phenomena born of meditation.
Just as a yogi absorbed in meditation perceives purity in every respect—
threefold, of three types, and arising in manifold forms.
Accomplishment, the application of mantras, and meditative concentration are proclaimed;
for Bodhisattvas, these three alone are declared to be the dhāraṇīs.
451) Mantras endowed with many excellent forms are indeed well-honored,
both those that are mundane and preeminent in the world, as well as those that are always supramundane.
Having followed the path of the Sugatas, meditation and a succession of meditations are accomplished;
indeed, all mantras are mastered for the sake of perceiving the welfare of all sentient beings.
All people who meditate upon him, who is beneficial in every respect,
shall obtain fame, renown, longevity, and the destruction of all diseases.
O best of men, being constantly absorbed in meditation, may you attain the knowledge that reveals the true meaning of the path, as well as a most abundant life.
This yoga was previously taught in brief by the best of sages;
now, this composed method of yoga has been declared by me.
When I too have attained unsurpassed awakening in the state of immortality,
they shall be well-honored by these very same unions and mantras.
The Blessed One has declared that unsurpassed gnosis, which is Buddhahood, is attained through meditative absorptions that are divine, auspicious, and characterized by the activity of dhyāna.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another [method]; listen as I speak it, which is born from the hundred rites of play for the sake of the play of all mantras.

Listen, O people of Mañjuśrī’s voice: by means of the very practice born of meditative absorption, the practitioner should always know what is beneficial and harmful, as well as the miraculous transformations of the mantra-reciters.
By means of yoga born of meditative concentration alone, one should perform [this] for those of dull intellect;
first, one should always meditate upon the great serpent rising in the water.
Indeed, the great ocean surrounds it on all sides; it is adorned by the king of mountains, possesses lofty jeweled peaks, and is auspicious, extending to the four quarters.
There he saw the Great-Souled One, the Buddha renowned throughout the three worlds,
the one with beautiful eyes, preeminent in the Dharma, Amitābha, the supreme Victor.
The Son of the Victors, ever white, the renowned Lokeśa,
the Great Being Padmaketu, who arises from great compassion.

452) One should always perceive the Youthful One in the form of a child, possessing beautiful eyes, situated in the station of the best of sages, with a charming voice, and endowed with various auspicious marks.
In his left hand he holds a blue lotus, and in his right he holds the image of a Sugata;
in this water there is a great nāga known by the name Ananta.
Thus, being entirely white and always adorned with seven radiant heads,
the reciter, having meditated upon him, should contemplate him as decorated with various ornaments.
One should also contemplate his face as receiving [the teaching] from the Sugata;
likewise for the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, who possess great supernatural power.
Rising to that same height and increasing twofold on all sides,
there are Ananta, Karkoṭaka, and the highly powerful Padma, who are equal [in stature].
Kulika, Śaṅkhapāla, and Kapila according to their colors;
then Mahāpadma, the lord of nāgas, and Padmābha, who are always like creepers.
Vāsuki and Takṣaka are to be known as having the color of the filaments of a lotus; they both possess the luster of a lotus and are adorned with various forms of ornaments.
And Śaṅkha the great nāga is auspicious, white in color;
Śaṅkhapāla the jewel-nāga is slightly white in color;
and there is the great nāga Sāgara and the renowned Mucilinda.
Then the Kṛṣṇa-nāga is proclaimed to be entirely black in color;
all of them are equal in size, while Nanda and Upananda are exceedingly lofty.
Then there was Elapatra, the lord of the Nāgas, possessed of great coils and world-renowned;
and Sāgara, the sovereign of the serpents, whose deeds were inconceivable and marvelous.
Understand that he performs various white deeds;
however, one should never cause a corpse or one who is unconscious from poison to be cast into the ocean.
Having indeed enveloped it with a garland and performed meditative yoga with a wise mind,
the deceased rises quickly from his place in the ocean.
One should always step upon the one who is asleep from poison with the foot of a cow and stir him;
by placing him in a place by the ocean, he becomes free from poison at that very moment.
In this way, one should likewise [subdue] the fever-demons, flesh-eaters, and the auspicious Vyantara spirits.
[He destroys] the Rākṣasas, Pretas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Mātṛs,
as well as the Grahas that always seize the lives of men in the world.
Having assumed human bodies, they remain on earth among men.

One should contemplate those beings who seize the powerful through this meditation; one should contemplate the lords of the nāgas of the ocean as rising up before one's very eyes from that which is conceived.
One should meditate upon the being as the mother; it quickly releases even one like Vāli. Thus it is for men bitten or not yet bitten by insects or spiders.
It constantly cures ringworm, scabies, leprosy, eczema, itching, and psoriasis, as well as other eruptive skin diseases and fistula-in-ano.
Plīhameda and Udara, as well as Padma and Supadmaka;
likewise, Padmaka among the Yakṣas, and Padmottara and Kṛśa.
All those afflicted by the disease of fever, including the Vādhyantas and the Nṛjabālisas,
you should all place within the ocean, O best of serpents.
One should indeed cast away all various miseries and sufferings, and the pains of every disease and affliction,
into the ocean-like state, by means of that which is established through meditative reflection.
The Naga, accepting the command of the Sugata, shall swiftly release [them];
and likewise by all the serpents, who perform every task and are auspicious.
Then the entire expanse of the ocean was pervaded on all sides by the lords of serpents,
the most excellent and possessed of great supernatural power.
Knowing the commitments of Mañjughoṣa, they are intent on his command and initiation;
always resorting to gods and yakṣas, they bring about the arising of auspiciousness for human beings.
But through mixed actions and knowledge, there arises a mixed result;
those who uphold the rain [the clouds] always support a righteous way of life.
454) From all sides, with streams of water... [the rain] bears fruit as a cause for the growth of crops, medicinal herbs, and grains once they have been brought to maturity.
Embraced in the form of clouds, they wander upon the surface of the earth;
possessing great supernatural power and great majesty, they endure for an eon and are of great prosperity.
Their city, named Bhogavatī, is situated upon the ocean;
it is there that mortals everywhere throughout Jambūdvīpa are devoted to dharma.
Then the great Nāgas and their retinues indeed remained there,
desiring victory after having experienced that battle between the gods and the Asuras.
They remained situated upon the Jambu tree in the center of Jambudvīpa;
yet, being beyond the range of perception everywhere, they repeatedly entered among men.
One should apply all virtuous deeds toward those nāgas;
for those nāgas dwelling in the water who have fallen from their vow perform [evil] at the appointed time.
Taking sides with the asuras, the nāgas released from all directions every kind of poison, both stationary and mobile, like a swarm of insects.
Pramāthin, Jhalujhala, Kapardin, Mahodadhi,
Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Durmukha, and likewise Bahumukha.
These and other great serpents are exceedingly arrogant and conceited;
they are constantly established in dark karma, or others in mixed karma.
When the mortals dwelling in Jambūdvīpa become most unrighteous, they will be known as "Mehas," possessing terrifying forms and being hostile toward one another through poison.
Then they shall cause great fear, most terrible poison-induced fainting,
vomiting, and dizziness, along with many afflictions of a great pestilence.
In this world, they release wicked serpents that bring about misfortune;
likewise, those great nāgas cause various kinds of calamities and inauspiciousness.
"Those who delight in what is harmful, bringing about drought after drought,
one should undertake this meditation for the destruction of their pride."
[He is] Mañjughoṣa, the greatly steadfast Bodhisattva of great supernatural power,
holding a blue lotus in his left hand and bestowing the boon with his right.
It has the luster of split gorocanā and rivals gold and saffron.
One should meditate on the Son of the Sugata mounted upon Garuḍa, the king of birds,
at the heads of those fanged creatures, [thereby neutralizing] all their virulent poison.
Then, their hearts pierced and their minds terrified and agitated,
they turned back once more and went away, entering the abode of Rūpa.
Having seen various kinds of portents, as well as inauspicious ones accompanied by sounds,
the knower of mantras, being composed, should thus meditate upon Mañjughoṣa.
O knower of mantras, one should prepare various kinds of snake-fangs;
for those who bite, there are egg-born [fangs] of many forms and shapes.
I shall explain, with correct understanding, according to the rites seen in the scriptures:
those born of that lineage, the serpents, indeed bite human beings on earth.
O Garuḍa, one should perform all the rites for embodied beings by means of that very scripture prescribed by the King of Birds according to the injunctions.
The Nāgas such as Kṛṣṇa, Śukla, and others, who roam throughout the entire earth within the terrestrial mandala, move across the world for embodied beings in the form of the sun.
Then, having understood what is curable and incurable, as well as the four beneficial [treatments] for poison,
and [the conditions] involving pitta, śleṣman, and those mixed with vāyu.
They say that due to phlegm (śleṣman) it is called Vāruṇī, being white in color and circular in shape;
whereas that which arises from the unknown source (ajñeyaja) is known as Pitta, appearing triangular in form.
Always fire-colored and slightly reddish, with arms that are somewhat tawny;
it is square, well-proportioned like a noble lineage, reaching to its limits, and variegated.
That which is known as Māhendra should be understood as being black in color and very tall;
they say that elephants are born of phlegm (kapha), while those born of bile (pitta) arise from hatred.
That which is born of wind should be known as delusion (moha), variegated and black in color;
