that very same [element] associated with phlegm (kapha) should be understood as characterized by goodness (sattva), white in color.
456) A silver [vision] is to be known as belonging to one with a predominance of bile (paittika), appearing yellowish-red;
a dark [vision] is to be known as belonging to one with a predominance of wind (vātika), characterized by a variegated or pale appearance.
One should observe that the gender is mixed everywhere, even among all the intermediate beings, such as insects, pustules, and the like, as well as among reptiles.
One should clearly contemplate Mañjughoṣa there, appearing black, rising up,
seated comfortably upon Garuḍa, in the form of a youth, and the source of bliss.
One should contemplate him as surrounded by wicked Vyantaras at the joints of the human fingers;
then one should contemplate the divine Kumāra in the form of a child in the space between them.
He was the great-souled one of universal form, seated upon Garuḍa;
that illustrious being had enemies as pale as autumn reeds.
The wise one should contemplate [the element] from the thighs up to the navel as rising toward the sky;
the meditator should contemplate it as having a yellow luster, situated in the chest, and pertaining to deep sleep.
One should meditate upon Mañjughoṣa, of great heroism, whose vehicle is the king of birds,
as the inconceivable one bearing the banner of Garuḍa stationed at the head.
Then one should contemplate [the deity] as white in appearance, seated upon Garuḍa, and situated outside;
in the case of the Sāttvika poison, there is fainting, and the victim vomits phlegm from all sides.
One should know that a person bitten by [a snake] who salivates incessantly and sinks down repeatedly is afflicted by a sattvic poison; it will be beneficial during the bright fortnight.
When the Lord of All is in a state of paralysis or agitation, one wanders and trembles;
furthermore, when there is a toxic condition arising from bile, fainting occurs and a terrible burning sensation arises.
In the rājasa state, there arises this activity characterized by fangs and biting;
in the tāmasa state, delusion, fainting, and sleep are produced.
When mixed, however, the activity becomes mixed and terrible;
when it is in *sattva*, it appears white, and in the human state, it is in the fangs.
The rajasic [person] should be known as having a somewhat yellowish complexion;
furthermore, the deluded one (mohātman) has a dark complexion, and his complexion becomes such.
In the mixed [state], it is smoke-colored, and in some places likewise pale-white;
it arises from the white fortnight and from the twice-born of both *sāttvika* and *rājasa* nature.
Those born from snakes who are dark-complexioned are of a tamasic and mixed nature;
for these belong to that family-lineage, O excellent Lord of the Chiefs of Serpents.
Clinging to the side of the Asuras, they roam upon the surface of the earth;
among them, the most unrighteous species of Nāgas bite humans in this world.
In this world, some are cruel and others even more cruel, always intent on the pursuit of food;
some are fanged for the sake of inflicting harm, while others are snatchers of life.
For the purpose of destroying poison for all those who subsist by means of fangs,
this supreme and primary meditation is according to the characteristics [of the deity].
When one renounces the thoughts of living beings, that poison is quickly released;
one should always, at all times, employ this in the case of all diseases.
Established in meditative absorptions alone, she destroys all calamities;
as are the nāgas, so too are sentient beings, rākṣasas, grahas, and mātṛs.
Furthermore, those humans who take the lives of others and possess wicked minds,
as well as those afflicted by all manner of diseases in the world, one should employ [the rites] specifically upon the lingas.
One should always contemplate meditation, the object of meditation, liberation, and likewise action;
[one should contemplate] the form of Kumāra, which is auspicious, pure, and the destroyer of sin.
Mañjughoṣa, the great hero, the son of the Victor, possessed of great supernatural power,
seated comfortably upon Garuḍa amidst the rising solar disc.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, the Master of Mantras, who is supreme in every respect;
when contemplated everywhere, he destroys all diseases through meditation.
One should perform all rites at all times toward all sentient beings;
for this [mantra] paralyzes everything and makes everything auspiciously beautiful.
All the mantras of the worlds, when understood within this meditation, quickly attain accomplishment; even those proclaimed in other kalpas do so here.
458) And those mantras of the Tathāgatas, as well as those of the Vajra and Lotus families; [those] of Āditya, Vasu, and Indra; and of the lunar mansions, planets, and luminaries.
Of the Garuḍas, Uragas, and Yakṣas, as well as the chief Ṛṣis together with Pūtanā.
All mantras are accomplished for one who meditates upon this ritual manual (kalpa), whether according to the procedures of other tantras, or by means of one's own tantra, or internally.
One should indeed accomplish the success of one's actions quickly by means of focused meditation;
having meditated upon the one who possesses universal forms as he rises within the solar orb.
Then [he saw] the Youth, appearing as a child, adorned with the ornaments of infancy,
blazing upon the orb of the sun, mounted upon Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā.
Having seen such an unmanifest form, even when well-visualized within the *mūrdhan*, the paralyzing of the enemy's forces arises according to one's intention.
And all those who are bitten become paralyzed and dance with one another; all embodied beings, afflicted by the seizure of the grahas, laugh while being distressed.
Those afflicted by fever and those who have fainted rise up from there quickly;
crying out in various ways of distress, they indeed let forth a terrifying sound.
A practitioner of mantra, being composed, should then recognize those humans on earth who have been seized by the planetary spirits, the Mothers, and the Kūṣmāṇḍas by these signs.
By his will, he can quickly effect the transference of poison;
then, out of a desire to play, the yogi causes the spirits to frolic.
The solar channel (nāḍī) should be employed when one is unconscious from poison;
by the application of the solar channel, one should cause all living beings to move.
While asleep, one becomes free from all poisons, whether stationary or mobile; thereafter, one who has been rendered unconscious by poison quickly awakens—of this there is no doubt.
And another person on this earthly surface quickly perishes from the affliction of poison;
yet again another, and once more another, or even someone else besides them.
459) By means of hundreds and thousands of such methods in all cases,
one should digest the elements through the application of the channels for as long as it takes.
Likewise, in a cloth, a wall, a jar, our water, or fire,
one may in an instant move the channel (nāḍī) and the poison situated therein.
Indeed, all those who were afflicted become healthy at that very moment upon the earth;
by means of such an initial application, one should perform eight hundred rites.
One should perform an incalculable rite, or else with the blood of another's mantra;
this is the practice in brief, for it has been taught as the meditation for those who recite mantras.
The entire dependent nature (paratantra) should be understood as being like Garuḍa;
the Śaiva doctrine is said to be born of resolve (saṅkalpa), and this is especially true for the [Vaiṣṇava] view.
And all worldly mantras should be employed within the extensive meditation;
in this Mañjurava-kalpa, they are especially [effective] through meditation alone.
When well-honored with the applications of all tantras and also with mantras,
those mental formulations intended for ritual procedures (kalpa) should always be employed here.
O Haha! In this divine yoga proclaimed in the King of Ritual Manuals (Kalparāja), all should be engaged through meditation within the stainless state by means of logical reasoning.
It is subtle, pertaining to the domain of the mind, the basis for the accomplishment of mantras,
pure as proclaimed by the son of the Sage, and rejoiced in by all the Buddhas for their own sake.
For one who constantly recites and meditates, all perfections are fully abundant.

Thus ends the instruction on the chapter of meditations for all rites, which serves as the means for accomplishing the ritual procedures for the play of Tārā according to the reality of all worlds; this is the thirty-eighth [chapter] from the *Mahākalparāja-paṭalavisara*, the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*.
The chapter is completed.
460) Now begins the forty-first detailed section.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods,
addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists [this teaching] which is approved by all the Buddhas,
belonging to the great expansion of your own Great King of Kalpas, which follows the practice of the great mantras, and which has entered into all the samayas."

O King of Birds, Garuḍa, you have entered the foundation of the Great Root Ritual Manual; you possess the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom that understands the cries of all beings, and your sphere of activity is the inconceivable wisdom that understands the cries of all beings— this is for you, among all mantras, the supreme mastery of the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom that understands the cries resulting from following the practice of your own mantra.
He alone shall explain to you the own-pledge (*svasamaya*) of all worldly beings who have entered into their respective rituals throughout all eons,
as well as the knowledge of the sounds and the conduct of all those belonging to the animal realm and all the Garuḍa kings of birds within the scope of all mantra rituals.
Then, indeed, from that assembly circle, Vainateya Garuḍa—
surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of garuḍas through the empowerment of the Bodhisattva— rose from his seat,
circumambulated the assembly circle, and approached Mañjuśrī.

With palms joined in reverence at the feet of the Mahābodhisattva, he addressed Mañjuśrī: "O Mahābodhisattva! For the sake, welfare, and happiness of sentient beings, I shall proclaim a hundred varieties of ritual actions, together with their secret mysteries, within this Great King of Kalpas. Therefore, O Mahābodhisattva, it is well; please grant your approval."
Then Mañjuśrī said this to Vainateya: "Speak, speak, O Mahāsattva! Out of compassion for sentient beings!
Then Vainateya, through the empowerment of the Buddha, sat upon his own seat and, with a joyful mind, spoke the hundred-and-one rites of supreme action together with their secret instructions.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ, Śakuna! Great Śakuna!
You of outspread wings! Destroyer of all serpents! Khakha khāhi khāhi! Remember the pledge! Hūṃ! Stay! The Bodhisattva commands: Svāhā! He spoke this hundredfold supreme rite.
The summoning of nāgas, the subduing of nāgas, the restraint of nāgas, the causing of possession by those bitten or unbiten, the invocation of snakes by means of speech,

the effecting of the restraint of snakes, and the playing with poison— the expulsion of all poison [is achieved] by one who observes the *poṣadha* vow and has fasted for three nights on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, through speech, mind, or intellect.

461) On the bank of a river, in a pure location, having prepared an eight-cubit mandala with a five-colored thread established with eight lotuses, one should draw the Blessed One in its center, teaching the Dharma. Of that...
To the right, one should depict Ārya Mañjuśrī with palms joined in *añjali*, gazing at the face of the Blessed One.

To the left of the Blessed Buddha, one should depict Nārāyaṇa with four arms, holding all manner of weapons in his hands. Near him, one should depict a Garuḍa of deformed appearance; immediately following that, one should depict Vinatābharaṇa.

Behind Noble Mañjuśrī, one should depict Noble Akṣayamati, Sudhana, and Subhūti with their palms joined in reverence. Thus should the inner maṇḍala be drawn. Outside, at the eastern gate, one should draw a vajra with white ash; to the south, a sword with black pigment; and to the north, a mace with yellow pigment.
One should draw [it]. To the west, one should draw a noose of red color.

Thus, having performed the invocation of all the deities from the outer mandalas with the root mantra, having worshipped them with all kinds of flowers and all kinds of perfumes, and having offered incense of *guggulu* and an offering (*bali*) consisting of the three sweets, [one should remain] in front of them.
Having kindled the fire with fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood, and having established a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings,
one should sit upon a serpent-throne and offer eight thousand oblations of snake-venom thorns smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Then, as a sign of success, snakes will arrive. An offering (arghya) should be given; in this way, success is achieved.
Reciting one's own mantra, one should say: "Having granted me success, depart. Then they go away.

Then, having performed the dismissal with the root mantra itself, one should sprinkle [the area] with water. Thereafter, one should commence the ritual action. One should cast all the offering substances for the *bali* into the water. Afterwards, by mere speech alone, one performs all rites concerning poisons.
One who desires to create enmity should offer twenty-one oblations of serpent bones smeared with poison; enmity will arise.
Desiring to destroy [an enemy], one should offer twenty-one oblations of fragments of snake sloughs; he is destroyed.
One should offer twenty-one oblations of crow feathers; immediately one wanders like a crow.
For the subjugation of women and men, one should offer twenty-one oblations of mustard seeds smeared with ghee.

They become submissive. For the subjugation of a king or a high official, one should offer twenty-one oblations of excellent food mixed with ghee; he becomes submissive. Having consecrated a clod of earth with mantras, one should throw it into the fire; it will not burn. Release [from its effects] occurs by means of a blade of grass. By the aforementioned method, fish are not caught. By a snap of the fingers, any being, whether sentient or insentient, [is subdued].
He draws [them] forth.
462) By sprinkling water upon one afflicted by every disease, he becomes healthy. Having consecrated a staff with mantras, one should strike the door.
It becomes opened. Taking that very staff covered with a blue cloth, one should go into battle;
upon merely seeing it, the enemy army breaks apart. By tying a knot in one's own garment, all mantras become paralyzed;
when it is released, there is liberation. One should fill the mouth of a snake with ashes; whoever one mentions by name while performing this, he [is affected].

One becomes mute. One should strike a boil with water over which the mantra has been recited once; the boil shrivels and the rival spell falls away. Bind [the enemy] with this; likewise, one releases them. Having consecrated a brick and turned it around, one should recite the mantra;
it causes the knots tied by others to burst. Likewise, one who desires to cause rain should perform the previously mentioned rite of the mandala.
Having performed the worship of the written [mantra] and established the fire, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *varuṇa* fuel-sticks;

it rains an *āḍhaka*. In this manner, it rains up to ten *āḍhakas*. Having consecrated a *pippala* leaf and grasped it with the hand, in whichever direction one throws it, food descends there. This same procedure applies even in cases of fire-conflagrations.

The descent into the water should be performed in this manner: one drives away the *nāgas*. Having fashioned a snake out of clay, one causes whichever [snake] one desires to bite. This is the same procedure for a snake made of charcoal. Furthermore, one effects its release.
One should scatter mustard seeds over which the mantra has been recited seven times in the four directions; the snakes will come. A boundary circle (*maṇḍala*) must be established.

Having sprinkled with water, one should dismiss [the deity]. By sprinkling with water, by throwing a clod of earth, or by reciting the mantra over dust and casting it into water, snakes become free from poison. Taking a bow and four arrows made of non-metal, one should shoot them in the four directions; the snake, stirred by the arrows, will come forth. That nāga should then be addressed as follows:

"Drink this poison!"—when he drinks it, the one who was bitten rises up. Then, in order to pierce snakes, having sprinkled water upon water, his arrows fall upon each [snake], yet the snake remains unhurt. One should fashion four mongooses out of clay from an anthill; having gone there, one should sprinkle water over them after consecrating it with mantras.
The snakes depart. When they have returned, one should say to them, "Drink the poison! They drink it, and the deceased person rises up.

Having consecrated charcoal and drawn a line, one should strike with an *arka* branch; then the snake comes, being dragged along by executioners. Saying, "Drink the poison," it drinks; the one who was bitten becomes free of poison.
One should consecrate a banner or a parasol; all those who have died or drunk poison, upon seeing it, become free from poison.

Having consecrated a musical instrument, one should play it; upon hearing it, they become free from poison. Having drawn a mandala with five-colored dust, the sound of a palm-clap should be given; then the nāgas [will appear].
Snakes come from the four directions; they enter the mandala. One must not be afraid.
One should perform the binding of the topknot and the protection of oneself.
Having consecrated one's eyes with mantras and looked at two angry persons, one should press the left thumb; they fall down at that very moment.
One makes everyone appear as one wishes by means of form. Upon release, there is liberation. Likewise, by means of speech, one causes [the poison] to enter or releases it, whether bitten or unbitten.
Having consecrated the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings (*viṣṇunirmālya*), wherever one throws them—whether on a street or into a house—at that very moment, [the effect occurs].

A snake bites a human; when sprinkled with water, they become free of poison. By raising the hand, there is a paralysis lasting six months. Having consecrated oneself with mantras, one may allow oneself to be bitten by snakes at will; the poison does not affect him. One adorns oneself with bracelets, armlets, and earrings. Having consecrated dust, one should mutter it over the ear.

By means of water, a fan, or even the mind, having recited the mantra, one should cast dust upon the ground; the deceased then rises. Incense made of *mahāmāṃsa* (human flesh) together with ghee effects nourishment (*puṣṭikaraṇa*).
Incense made of powdered human bone and the wings of a crow and an owl effects killing (*māraṇa*). [Incense made of] *madana*, chaff, and seeds [effects]...
Incense for eradication [of enemies] is as follows: incense made of mustard seeds and *rājikā* causes fever; the excrement of a cat and *kodrava* grain causes hatred.
Having combined the powder of a skull with the powder of *madhūka*, this incense, when used with honey, is for eradication.
*Moraṅgī* and castor stalks are an incense for eradication. Cow-bile and human bone, mixed with clarified butter, [are used for the same].
This incense is for the slaying of an enemy:
fish roe, *prasannā* liquor, and cotton seeds combined together;
this incense brings back quickly a man who has gone to another land.
Split lentils and the flesh of a hen’s egg—this incense should be offered to one who is entering; after this, the summoning (ākārṣaṇa) follows.
One should combine the seeds of *bhallātaka* with sesame oil;
this is an attracting incense that brings about attraction. One should offer *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter;
this incense destroys diseases. Having offered incense made of sesame and mustard seeds, one should sacrifice those very same seeds for seven nights at the three junctions of the day.

By whose name [the rite is performed]: one should offer eight thousand oblations of salt and *rājikā* (black mustard) at the three junctions of the day for seven nights; this is the subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) of a great man. Having empowered skull-powder (*kapālacūrṇa*) a thousand times, whoever one desires, by touching that person with the powder, one brings them under control. Together with cremation-ground ashes, whomever...

One grinds [the ingredients] into powder, causes the fever to seize [the victim], and then releases it. If one burns incense made of mongoose hair, mustard seeds, and a snake’s slough while reciting the name of a person, that person becomes hated by all the world.
With sesame seeds, one effects subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and brings about the acquisition of wealth. With sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with ghee, one brings a woman under one's control.
One should offer oblations of barley, sesame, and the fat of a frog at the site of a *nāga* for three nights; this causes the gods to send rain.
Having fashioned an image of Garuḍa out of clay and holding it with cupped hands, one should descend into water reaching up to the shoulders.

One should recite [the mantra] at midnight by the name of whomsoever; that person becomes submissive. Having scattered rice grains in a cremation ground and established the *devahṛdaya*, one should recite the weapon-mantra (*praharaṇa*); this provides a livelihood for [the practitioner] along with his retinue. The incense made from the hair of mongooses and rats, and cotton seeds, brings all spirits under control. Poison...

Incense made from *bhallātaka* together with honey is a means of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Incense made from the shells of hen's eggs together with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) is a means of subjugation. Incense made from *palāśa*, the seeds of *surasā*, and *madanapuṣpa* flowers is for subjugation. Incense made from *śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, the dung of a frog, and that of a sparrow [is also for subjugation].

The purpose is subjugation (*vaśya*). For subjugation, an incense made of barley, sesame seeds, and *dūrvā* grass with cow’s urine is used. For rendering mute, an incense made of yellow orpiment and *kākajihvā* with blood is used. For causing disease, an incense consisting of human hair and cow meat mixed together with oil is used. For eradication (*uccāṭana*), the feathers of a crow and an owl with *nimba* oil are used.

This incense of *guggulu* resin mixed with clarified butter and *sīdhu* liquor brings delight to all sentient beings. An incense made of *patraka*, cinnamon bark, and *turuṣka* binds all sentient beings; it becomes obedient to one’s command. *Turuṣka*, sandalwood, camphor, and collyrium together effect the subjugation of kings. Having performed the ritual of worship and offerings, [one should proceed].

Having offered eight oblations of *mahāmāṃsa* above an image of Viṣṇu, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for three nights; whatever substance one desires shall be obtained. Having fashioned an effigy with cremation-ground ashes and offered incense of *mahāmāṃsa*, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and recite it eight thousand times at night.
In a cremation ground, he brings whoever he desires and makes them obey his command. For the purpose of expulsion (*uccāṭana*), one should offer oblations of cotton chaff with crow feathers;

expulsion occurs in an instant. Having kindled a fire in a cremation ground with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, one seated upon a skull-cup should offer snake skins as oblation; food becomes inexhaustible.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of cremation-ground bone powder mixed with mustard seeds while reciting the name of a person; that person will come from a hundred *yojanas* away. This should be performed for all desired aims. One should visualize the deity with outstretched wings, adorned with all the ornaments of the *nāgas*, fierce and sharp, with a distorted face and deformed claws, seated upon a lotus.
One who observes the *poṣadha* vow should have a craftsman fashion a wooden block, a small piece of wood, or a wall-slab with its surface sloped downward.
Having made it one *vitasti* in length, one should perform all ritual actions before it.
For one desiring nourishment, [the wood] should be of *palāśa*; for the sake of subjugation, *bilva*; for one desiring a son, *udumbara*; and for one desiring cattle, [the same].

One who desires material wealth should have [the image] made of śirīṣa wood or madhuka wood according to the rules. One desiring fruit [of success] should use boar meat. Through horse meat, offspring are obtained. For one seeking prosperity, or for one desiring extensive renown, or for one desiring a wife or the earth, tiger meat [should be used].

465) One who desires victory in legal disputes should offer human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*); one desiring clothing, elephant hair; for subjugating a king, *atibalā*; for subjugating a royal minister, one should offer *aśvagandhā*. For destruction, one should offer elephant hair.
Picumarda is for malevolent rites; these are declared to be the primary woods.

The preparation of the cloth occurs as follows: the practice for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) is with gold from the element; with silver and so forth, it is for the increase of fame. With the homa of crow feathers, one destroys; with vulture feathers, one kills; with owl feathers, one causes enmity;
with peacock feathers, one causes enmity; with peacock feathers, one should bestow wealth; with partridge feathers, [one effects] a woman.
With peacock feathers one [achieves] sons; with crow feathers, gold; with *ṭiṭṭibha* feathers, enchantment.
With dog flesh one causes destruction; with buffalo flesh, one performs attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). In rites of sorcery (*ābhicāruka*), one uses human flesh;
in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), deer hair. One desiring a maiden uses owl hair; one wishing to destroy a region uses throat hair; for inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), [one uses] throat hair.

Human hair is used for malevolent rites (*ābhicāruka*); human hair is used for the destruction of enemies. For all of these, there is a seven-day fire offering (*homa*) performed at the three junctions of the day. By mere recollection, I perform all poison-rites;
by constant recitation (*japa*), I accomplish all activities. O Blessed One, whoever [recites] my mantra in this King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*)...

To whoever shall recite this at the three junctions of the day while practicing [this rite], I shall provide a remedy for all afflictions caused by poisons and I shall follow behind them as their protector.

Then, at that time, he meditated upon the Svarūpa-mudrā: having joined the two thumbs so they encircle each other, the remaining fingers should be positioned like wings; this very Garuḍa-form mudrā was taught to me by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Upon seeing this, the nāgas flee, afflicted by fear;
with their faces cast downward, the fingers [are held] by the knower of mantras with this mantra.
Oṃ jaḥ.
Known as Nāgadamanī, she destroys the pride of the serpents;
her fingers, resembling the buds of a lotus, are positioned at her sides.
Placing the two thumbs in the middle and pressing the fingers together with effort, this is known as the *nāgadamanī* [mudrā], divine among divine rites.
The ring finger and the index finger are well-positioned with the middle finger;
the two thumbs are placed at the opening, while the remaining fingers are situated on the sides.
Renowned as the Garuḍanāda, she terrifies all nāgas;
and whatever has been taught by me regarding the accomplishment of all mantras, [it is contained therein].
466) Regarding worldly *gāruḍa* treatises,
all of those should be performed by him alone out of compassion for all sentient beings.
All [rites] whatsoever, without exception, which accomplish the purpose of the Root Tantra,
are eternally contained within this supreme tantra, which describes the welfare of all sentient beings.
All purposes of ritual action, which are well-established and abundant in benefit for all sentient beings,
should indeed be employed within the extensive rites of the preeminent mantra.
In this supreme kalpa, at its root, your foundation is established upon the surface of the earth through all beings and by means of the qualities arising from the flow of mantras.
Known in detail through universal vision, it is for the compassion toward all sentient beings;
it is well-established for those desiring accomplishment, being based upon logical reasoning.
Embodied beings shall achieve success in all mantras in every respect;
and all sentient beings shall be present at will within the ritual manuals.
Through the conjunction of mantra, mudrā, and breath, they recount history, ancient events, the present, and the future.
This mantra is invincible and draws in all beings;
it is Rudra, the lord of all beings, who is worshipped by the gods.
Tumbaka, who is to be known by the three-syllable name, dwells for an eon upon the surface of the earth;
he is the eternal Maheśvara, the Lord of Umā, whose abode is the Himālaya mountains.
He should be known as the trident-bearer, the wielder of the sword, the bearer of the Pināka bow, and the one whose banner is the bull;
he is the lord of the Gaṇas, the wielder of the spear, the one called Maheśa, and the possessor of great supernatural power.
They call him the Imperishable, the Unchanging; he is Kapardin, whose weapon is the mace.
This mantra is of great significance, causing all beings to tremble for the sake of their welfare.
One should perform all rites; he is the means for accomplishing all actions.
This Great-Souled God is indeed celebrated as Mahādeva.
Renowned for the purpose of all rites, always bestowing both fruit and cause—
listen, you who desire the welfare of beings, as I shall proclaim its mantra.
467) Oṃ sthaḥ! Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded, who are the teachers of the three worlds, and who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms.
O Śivodbhavodbhava, you who are worshipped by the three worlds! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ!
This mantra is a great mantra that instills fear in all enemies.
For the sake of the longevity of all beings, the rites of pacification and nourishment—
indeed, in all ritual actions— one should employ those born of the mind.
The knowledge of the cries of all beings, the activity of the knowledge of supernormal powers,
the mastery of supernormal powers, and likewise the equal knowledge of all treatises.
One shall obtain abundant wealth arising from the cause and fruit [of one's actions],
as well as all worldly mantras in their most perfect form.
A wise practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall attain all of them—
however many worldly mantras there may be, as well as those of Śiva that are highly honored.
The mantras for Garuḍa also lead toward the fruit of the accomplishment-homa;
all worldly mantras, moreover, originate from Indra and Rudra.
All these kings of mantras are bound according to the rules of procedure:
those of Yama, Agni, Vāyu, and Varuṇa; Kubera, the Mothers, and Dayā.
This number is indeed twelvefold, fulfilling Brahmā and Īśāna;
it is the perfect worship of Savitṛ, the gods headed by Śakra, and the Grandfather.
All those who are known as lords of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), including the mantras and the gods who roam therein,
all come under control when the name of the Lord of Mantras is uttered.
And those who dwell in the mansions of the cardinal directions, as well as those who roam in the intermediate quarters.
Furthermore, above in the vault of the sky and below in the abodes of the netherworlds (pātāla),
there are hooded serpents of great supernatural power who have taken refuge upon the paths.
Situated within the lap of the Himalaya mountains and resting in the embrace of the Vindhya range,
she dwells upon that famous great mountain, a wondrous peak abounding in excellent minerals.
468) On Mount Sumeru, which is crowded with various hosts of gods, frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*,
resounds with the singing of throngs of *apsarases*, and is as radiant as the sun.
Those nāgas who reside here, those who take refuge among the hosts of spirits,
those of various forms, or those who have gathered from elsewhere— [all these are present].
All those who are joined with this mantra come under one's control,
including the divine hosts of mantras that instill fear in all beings.
All of them come under one's control when joined with this mantra,
even in mountain caves, difficult terrains, and various interior recesses of ravines.
On the surface of the earth, various captivating people who are lords over hosts of all living beings dwell in temples that resemble gold.
They were the presiding lords over hosts of divine beings, possessing diverse and wondrous forms.
And all the hosts of spirits wander upon the surface of the earth,
possessing various principal forms and assuming diverse appearances as their basis.
Abiding in various forms of contemplation and adorned with diverse garments and ornaments,
they all beheld him on the path by means of the supreme mantra.
He is the leader of all mantras, both worldly and of great supernatural power;
he is the subduer of all spirits, the supreme Lord who causes them to wander.
He is the foremost lord of all mantras, superior even to Yama, Vāyu, Indra, and Vāsava;
he is the preeminent Lord of Mantras and the supreme leader of all worldly beings.
He upholds everywhere the mantras and the most abundant ritual manuals (kalpas);
this god is the Lord of Mantras, the sovereign, and the king of all mantras.
The Lord of all obstacles, the Mantra-master, should be remembered by all who recite mantras;
he alone is proclaimed as the fierce sovereign of all fierce mantras.
In every Śaiva tantra, indeed, one should always mutter the conduct and even the cries of all beings, along with all worldly activities.
469) Those seeking success should indeed employ this at all times along with their ministers.
Then the bird Vainateya, having bowed to the daughter of the Supreme Victor, [spoke].
Then that mighty king of birds spoke these sweet words to Mañjuśrī, as well as to all the sons of the Buddhas, at all times.
Speak, speak, O Great Being! You who are well-ascertained in the profound meaning!
You who are established in the supreme dharma of the reality of the selflessness of phenomena!
I have spoken at length regarding the ritual procedures, the value, the mantras, and their scope;
however, it should be understood that this summary is the most preeminent among all mantras.
This mantra, which is praised and taught by me, should be employed for all accomplishments among worldly mantras alone; it is not an internal (esoteric) word-mantra.
By the sons of the Conquerors, the great heroes, and by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
no other more excellent mantra than this is applied with their intelligence.
With a face slightly smiling, the steadfast one then spoke with a gentle voice;
he then uttered sweet words, adorned by the foundation of both sound and meaning.
This is the one described to you as Suvarṇa, the Lord of Dharma, the supreme among men;
he who intends to release all mantras and is the teacher of the selflessness of phenomena.
The world-teacher, the heroic Māyāvīra, the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun;
the promulgator of all mantras, the excellent and supreme lord of mantras.
The Lord, whose sole purpose is the welfare of others, the Sovereign of the Dharmadhātu, the Guru,
acts for the sake of compassion toward all sentient beings and for the arising of our own happiness.
Having reached the limit of phenomena, he is the ultimate, the limit of reality, and free from attachment;
this one of great splendor quickly proclaims [the truth] to all your mantras.
The thirty-ninth chapter, the Section on the Garuḍa, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the forty-second chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists [this]!"

In the ritual procedure for the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) which serves as the means for all your accomplishments, there is the secret of the pledge (*samaya*) regarding the chapter on mudrās in all mantra-tantras; by those who do not transgress the pledge common to all [tantras],
they enter into that which is impelled by the pledge within all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas.

In all mantra-tantras that serve as general means of accomplishment, these have already been taught; they are the most supreme secrets, the most supreme fortunes, and the most supreme wonders and marvels. Without them, it is impossible to propitiate or accomplish any mantras. Previously, all the Tathāgatas spoke them, and now I too [do so].

I shall speak for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit of the great mass of people, and for the purpose of causing all reciters of mantras to enter the cloud of Dharma of the Mahāyāna— the inconceivable selflessness of phenomena, which is the eternal, eager, and wondrous treasury of great mantras within the realm of reality (dharmadhātu).
And I shall speak whichever one among them is most excellent.
Listen, Mañjurava! To this which is accompanied by all the secret mudrās;
it is to be spoken by oneself in such a manner as was sung of old by the best of sages.
Indeed, this supreme collection of all mudrās should always be employed at all times in every ritual action within the maṇḍala by those who seek the secret mantras.
Then the glorious Mañjurava, the lotus-eyed one, smiling,
gazed upon the Sugata, the most excellent, the Lord and Master of all dharmas.
With palms joined in reverence, the heroic son of the Jina, possessed of great supernatural power,
spoke sweet words adorned with divine sounds and meanings.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! You who speak for the Lord the mantra of the true meaning of the reality of Dharma, which follows the Wheel of Dharma.
Having thus spoken to the Sugata, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men,
the glorious Mañjurava then remained silent in that interval.
Thus spoke the Blessed Buddha, the Lord of the Dharmadhātu, at that time:
"Listen, all you hosts of spirits! O assemblies of gods of great supernatural power!"
471) For those mortals on earth who draw mandalas on the ground— whether they be poor or suffering—
you shall be present for them as the mudrās drawn upon the earth.
And those mudrās which have been taught by the best of sages for all the Buddhas, for the Pratyekabuddhas, the Arhats, and the Khadgins, as well as for the Śrāvakas—
The mudrās of all worldly beings belong to the Victors, the Lotus family, and the Vajra-holders;
indeed, all mudrās are to be employed everywhere in all ritual actions.
I shall now describe for all practitioners of mantras, in brief,
that mantra which was previously taught for all mandalas and ritual activities.
One should likewise employ the site, the fire-oblation, the recitation, and the ritual action;
first, this seal fashioned by the Buddha is to be drawn upon the mandala.
Then there is the white parasol of the Buddhas, blazing all around,
adorned with ornaments and encircled on all sides by five-colored powders shimmering like jewels.
Resplendent with various colors, supreme, and possessing a radiance like that of Indra’s bow—
this is the seal, the great seal, the excellent crown-projection of the Buddhas.
To its right is the bowl, encircled by garlands of light;
immediately following that is the *khakhavaraka*, and beyond it the *daṃṣṭrā* and *jīvaraja*.
The Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the discus, and the water-pot are described; they say there is also the book, the banner, and the flag within that interval.
The bell is the mudrā born of the west, as declared by the leaders of the world;
the parasol is on the left, the lotus is there, and between them is the jewel mudrā.
In that interval, they call it the Vajra, which arises in the form of a triple-pointed needle;
the Utpala, however, is the Gata-mudrā, the water-element, which rests upon the water.
And at the end of that is indeed Water (Toya), situated within a stream of water;
at its end, the two Kuṇḍalas should be known, as well as the two beautiful Bhūṣālas.
At its end, a great mountain made of four jewels should be drawn, radiant and bright;
at its end, the great ocean should be depicted, variegated and brilliant with colors.
472) Then, at its end, there is a great tree, bearing fruit and adorned with leaves;
this tree is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), born from the left side and reaching to the end.

Now, the Sitātapatra is said to be the mudrā of the Buddhas; it is declared to be the most excellent among the foremost. In the mantra of the Khaḍgins, it should be known as the boon-bestower of the Pratyekajinas.
The robe is indeed declared the supreme seal, the source of all śrāvakas;
it is praised as the very fang of the noble Arhats in this world.
The *śrīvatsa* is intended as the seal (*mudrā*) for that which has attained its fruit in the world;
the *khakharaka* is the *mahāmudrā*, and another is born from the solitary *jina*.
Then the Dharmacakra Mudrā indeed shatters all views;
it is declared that the Dharmamudrā arises from the casting away of the agent.
In this world, the Perfection of Wisdom appears as the Conqueror’s relic, a seal, and a book;
it is proclaimed as two great mudrās, the banner and the flag, worshipped by the world.
The two of great heroism are for the attraction of all; both originate from the uṣṇīṣa.
The bell is the final mudrā, with hair like that of a Pratyekabuddha or an Arhat.
The Buddha-mudrā is indeed on the left, with the lotus born from Lokeśvara;
likewise, the Sage-mudrā is to be known for one who has attained Samantajyoti.
The vajra is the mudrā of the wise Vajrin;
the utpala belongs to Mañjughoṣa, and the earring to Kṣitigarbha.
The mudrā called Mahātoya is taught in the Gaganālaya;
then there is this Mahāśaila mudrā, which destroys all evil glances.
O son of the Sugata! The Great Ocean is likewise a mudrā;
the Great Tree is likewise proclaimed as a mudrā, renowned throughout the world.
Furthermore, one should draw all the sons of the Victors within this seal in the abode of the three realms,
in the place near the bell, as described by the Supreme Victor.
The seal of all seals, arising from a square shape,
variegated, endowed with colors, beautiful in hue, and resplendent.
473) Blazing with garlands of flames, radiant, shining with five colors, and auspicious.
Rising in the form of a *piṇḍikā*, auspicious and resembling the sun and moon—
this is the mudrā of great power, the auspicious abode of all mantras,
for the three types of mantras: the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
This is the primary position taught for the mudrās, which accomplishes the purpose of all rites;
within this [space], one should draw the maṇḍala that contains the great mudrās.
Whatever mantra is prescribed for a particular maṇḍala that is renowned in the world,
that very [mantra] should be drawn in the center, like a royal parasol upon the surface of the earth.
In the center of that mandala, there should be either an image or a mudrā;
the images should be depicted as granting boons, and likewise, the arising of Mañjughoṣa.
Indeed, all the lords of mantras and the meanings of all mantras always [reside] on earth; otherwise, one should not draw the mudrās performed according to the ritual rules.
The wise say that when those two [hands] are placed upon it with full jars, it is called "Victory" (vijaya);
moreover, the practitioner should draw the mudrās within the mandala and also on the outside.
In the second maṇḍala, the reciter [should perform the recitation] in all the aforementioned previously specified locations, throughout all directions and intermediate directions.
The wise one should draw the mudrās of all the gods, sages, yakṣas, and garuḍas, as well as those of the piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
He [overcomes] the established doctrines of the heretics, as well as the Kinnaras, Kaṭapūtanas,
and the Kravyāda Vyantaras, along with the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Dūṣakas, and those who exert power in the hells.
All beings, including those of the form realm, the formless realm, and the desire realm,
as well as those born of the gods of the formless realm, are eternally present in the second mandala.
One should draw the foremost of mudrās, which arises in the form of a triangle;
extending toward the eastern direction, it is a radiant line that embraces [the other two].

474) This is said by the primordial Buddhas to be the seal born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) belonging to the foremost gods of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) who possess great supernatural power (*maharddhika*).
Then, O Lotus-born Brahmā, the lines to the north likewise are said to be the mantra "rūpāvacaram" within the abode of the three worlds.
That same line extending from the center of the maṇḍala toward the south is the excellent Mudrākāmaja,
situated in the southern direction.
This mudrā was taught by the foremost sages for the supreme lord of the desire realm; it has been fashioned in the world within the abode of all the gods.
She who is the source of Viṣṇu and the sages, who is naked,
who is the medicinal herb of Arka, Vāsava, and Mausa, and who is marked by the signs of the Sun and Yama.
One should likewise draw all those world-protectors (lokapālas) outside, each in the direction of their respective temples,
and one should likewise apply the appropriate mudrās.

Whichever vehicle is renowned for a particular deity, that [deity] is likewise indicated by those honored by the world as possessing that very vehicle, along with its specific weapon and attire, and its corresponding mudrā.
This group of mudrās has indeed been taught as entirely supramundane and auspicious;
it is effective for all mundane purposes everywhere and in all ritual actions.
The principal mudrās and all the mudrās for practitioners of mantra have been taught;
they should be drawn upon the ground by mortals who recite mantras and desire spiritual accomplishments.
"One who desires to obtain the essence of awakening."

Thus concludes the "Method for Accomplishing All Rituals," from the forty-second chapter of the *Mahākalparāja-vistara*, extracted from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the forty-third detailed chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Dwellers (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists within your own ritual procedure for the maṇḍala—"

In all rites—whether summoning, dismissal, recitation, observances, fire-offerings, accomplishments, or protective rituals—and in all tantric mantras and practices, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) alone is the single Great Hero. It has been spoken of and rejoiced in by countless millions of Buddhas. And what is it?
Listen, O Mañjurava! O glorious one, whose intellect perceives the profound meaning and the supreme reality!
By binding this [mudrā], all practitioners of recitation—
The Mahāmudrā is of great merit, esteemed as the greatest auspiciousness;
its merit is equal to that of Great Brahmā, purifying and destroying all evil.
The supreme state of great security, the unshakable station of nirvāṇa—
auspicious, peaceful, most excellent, cooled, and the ultimate refuge.
It is known as the Lord of All Mudrās, the foremost among all mudrās;
it is renowned as the Lord of All Tantras within the abode of the three worlds.
And the threefold divine majesty, as well as those [signs] which are both terrestrial and divine—
these are the marks of the All-pervading One, the refuge of all beings, who is like the Buddha manifest in person.
The King of Mudrās, who is eternally nourished within the three worlds by all mudrās,
is for the constant protection of practitioners of recitation and of mantra-holders in all their rites.
This celebrated antidote is a destroyer of demons, auspicious, and a dispeller of sins;
it is preeminent in all rites and a warder-off of malevolent beings.
This Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is presented in the world as the tamer of the difficult-to-tame;
it is indeed joined with all mantras for practitioners who have passed through three births.
He destroys all obstacles for practitioners in every rite everywhere;
he instantly invokes the mantras residing in the three wombs.
It leads that world back again and indeed destroys it;
it causes everything to fall everywhere across the entire surface of the earth.
476) Furthermore, one should fix the mudrā through actions such as binding and obstructing;
likewise, there are the mudrās of pressing, uprooting, drying, and destroying.
Furthermore, he is renowned in the three worlds as the "Reviver of Life" for practitioners;
this Mahāmudrā is employed in rites of pacification.
It is the splendor of all mantras, pure, stainless, and the destroyer of sins;
it accomplishes all aims in the world and is renowned as supreme among all.
The supramundane mantras are likewise the foremost among worldly mantras;
they are the most excellent for all ritual purposes, as well as for rites of pacification and enrichment.
The mudrā known as Kṣemaṅgama is eternally employed by all mantra-practitioners;
indeed, this eternal one is called Aparājita when joined with all mantras.
Abiding in the lineage, abiding at the limit of reality, the lord of the realm of phenomena, self-arisen;
he is both beyond syllables and expressible, yet the imperishable, eternally imperishable.
Abiding in the selflessness of phenomena, unarisen yet the source of what has arisen;
free from passion, immovable, established in emptiness by its very nature.
Likewise, Akaniṣṭha is the eldest; it is auspicious for those going to nirvāṇa, the path to unsurpassed awakening, and the source of the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
Likewise, he is the cloud of Dharma, tranquil, and the source from which the waters of the army have emerged;
he knows the ultimate reality and the supreme truth, fulfilling the purpose of both.
The Great Seal, possessed of great majesty, arisen from all the Buddhas;
of great purpose and great heroism, the solitary hero of great supernatural power.
Endowed with many excellent forms, arising from many forms.
This state of omniscience is to be known as entirely complete and final;
it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, the great transcendence, proclaimed by the Victorious One, the Best of Sages.
Worshipped by all beings and gods, honored by each of the Arhats,
this is the supreme Dharma of the Great Seal, the unshakable, most excellent state.
First of all, in a pure place— whether at a solitary tree, on a great mountain,
or on the delightful shore of the great ocean— one should resort to a consecrated sacrificial ground.
477) On a riverbank, at a well, or on a sandy shore; in a beautiful temple of the God, or even in the abode of the Enemy of Māra (Śiva), or in a monastery, a dwelling, or a palace.
In a secluded place, sprinkled and swept clean, adorned with heaps of flowers,
drenched with fragrant scented water, and perfumed with excellent incense.
For rites of pacification (śāntika) and enrichment (pauṣṭika), one should face either the east or the north;
for fierce rites (raudrakarma), one should always face the south, as that is avoided by the Jinas.
For the sake of prosperity, good fortune, and subjugation, one should always perform the goat-sacrifice without cause;
thereafter, one should bind the supreme and excellent Mahāmudrā with the face turned backward.
When a practitioner, holding high views for the sake of attaining a physical body in the Buddha-field, ascends,
he shall go down to the netherworld (Pātāla) and attain the status of a lord of the asuras.
With pure bodily conduct, possessing pure mantras and knowing the mantras,
one should then employ the excellent mudrā, having bathed, sipped water, and performed recitation with a focused mind.
Both hands should always be washed with clean water that is pure, free from insects and small creatures, and scented with clay, cow dung, and fragrant substances.
When both hands, pure and washed with fresh water, have been thus purified and honored,
one should join them together in the form of a hollowed casket, held within the grip of the fists.
Slightly hollow on all sides, six finger-breadths in height,
situated between both thumbs, and bent by the little fingers.
Then, having placed it upon the region of the heart covered with a white cloth,
one should display it in all ritual actions during the practice of accomplishment.
Indeed, for all beings, whatever is desired is quickly accomplished merely by drawing [this seal];
this is the Mañjurava mudrā, the accomplisher of the purpose of all rites.

Thus concludes the second chapter from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, specifically the forty-first section concerning the methods for accomplishing all supreme rites, titled "The Chapter on the Great Mudrās."
478) Now follows the forty-fourth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having once again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, spoke.

It is sealed with the seal of the countless Victors, reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is the ornament of the inconceivable array of excellent qualities of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas; it is the sign of all sentient beings, the most secret chapter on mudrās,
and that which has been conceived through the rituals and methods of all mundane and supramundane mantras and tantras for the welfare of all sentient beings.
It is that which serves as the path for proceeding toward the vision of ultimate reality,
which is common to all mantras and all designations, and which fulfills every aspiration of all sentient beings in this very life.

For the purpose of propitiating all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, for the sake of the supreme happiness that is the cause [of liberation], and for the sake of fulfilling the accumulations for enlightenment—

[this includes] summoning and dismissal, perfumes, flowers, incense, all garlands and offerings, the entry of ignorance and knowledge, visions, the accomplishment of all purposes and goals, and [the invocation of] all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and yakṣas...

It bestows the states of Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Kūṣmāṇḍas, as well as fierce and gentle dispositions; it is the sovereign over all beings, including the presiding lords of spirits; it reveals all undertakings; it possesses the wonders of blazing forth, traveling through space, invisibility, and subjugation; it is the marvelous and extraordinary source for the equipment of awakening; it is in accordance with the purpose of all mantras and tantras; and it is honored by all the kings of vidyās.
It accomplishes all vidyās, is invoked by all the Buddhas and their mothers,

fulfills the desires and aspirations of beings according to their wishes, brings to fruition the causes for the present life of all mantras, and, in brief, is effective in whatever way it is applied and in whatever way it is practiced.

In that very way, one accomplishes it. O Mañjuśrī! I shall speak this supreme secret of the ultimate truth of all Buddhas, which is the most profound secret of the ultimate truth. It was spoken by all Buddhas in the past, and the Blessed Buddhas of the future will speak it; now I shall speak it—let it be heard.
"O Mahāsattva! I shall speak; listen to that, O Mahāsattva! I shall speak. Pay close and thorough attention, Mañjurava! I shall speak—I shall speak to you who possess such charming eloquence."
The Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men, the perfectly awakened one, the supreme among sages,
having realized the welfare of beings, perceives the ultimate reality.
O bull among sages, you indeed speak of the secret mudrās for the sake of the mothers,
in the delightful city of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, which is inhabited by beings of pure essence.
Then, when the King of Rituals, which reveals the reality of Mañjubhāgīna, was being spoken within that most excellent and supreme great assembly— the abode of those free from passion—
479) Then the sons of the Buddha, those ministers who were wise and knew the ultimate truth, said to the assembly: "Listen to this discourse!"
"The eldest son of the Buddha, who follows the supreme dharma of the Mahāyāna,
is indeed named Samantabhadra"— thus he spoke these excellent words.
You are described by the Jinas as the youth who possesses both the form of a child and a great form;
born of the Śākya clan, skillful and glorious, you are beheld as a Buddha.
For you, O one of universal great wisdom, out of a desire to favor the world,
have indeed [expounded] this extensive collection of your ritual manuals sealed with mudrās.
Entreat him, O Great Hero! Son of the Buddha, possessed of great supernatural power!
[The teaching] which is the essence of this eon and endowed with great supernatural power.
Thus addressed by the heroic and wise son of the Buddha,
Mañjughoṣa quickly manifested himself in the form of a child at play.
Having prostrated before the Sugata, the Protector, the sole eye of the world,
he spoke these sweet words with a voice resonant and moistened by compassion.
May the Blessed One, the Buddha, who knows the reality of the power of wisdom,
explain how all mantras are certainly accomplished for those who recite them.
How indeed do they go unfailingly for living beings without conceptualization?
They would be accomplished even when merely cast away or muttered, without being applied to any specific purpose.
From the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell,
and all those living beings who dwell within these three realms of existence— whether they be humans or others.
They are summoned, restrained, and made to enter while all look on,
by means of causes for satisfaction and nourishment, joined with all ritual actions and purposes.
Those who abide on the ten stages and stand upon the path of the Sugata— the Bodhisattvas, the fully awakened ones, and those who rely on the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha— [all pay homage].
The great-souled ones who have transcended passion are summoned when they are well-honored;
they are joined by practitioners through the pledges and sealed with these mudrās.
480) Yogis speak of past events, whether they have occurred or not, as well as those in the present, according to reality, independently, and with direct vision.
The discourse on the heavenly realm is inconceivable, whether it concerns one's own body or another;
likewise, the future is described with such accuracy that it serves as a vivid illustration.
When impelled by mantra and mudrā, they speak according to the proper rule; likewise, when worshipped with mudrās, they bestow accomplishment swiftly.
Endowed with ministers who are experts in mantras, and having been well-honored with offerings and oblations,
the Buddhas and likewise the sons of the Buddha will very swiftly bring about accomplishment.
Even the great-souled Arhats, the Khaḍgins, are always bestowers of success;
so too are the worldly mantras and those others that are supramundane.
And those who are accomplished ones, as well as yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
asuras, gods, and always sentient beings—all sentient beings are established in three ways.
In these infinite directions and within the various world-systems,
there are sentient beings throughout the five realms of existence who are always engaged in what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
They shall swiftly attain accomplishment when well-sealed with these mudrās;
this is known as the Immaculate [Mudrā], proclaimed by the Sugatas, the mantra-knowing sages.
The *viṭaka* should be known according to the prescribed rule, as well as the *visara*, the supreme chapter;
these have been proclaimed by all the Buddhas in the world for the sake of the highest good.
They call this mudrā the "Five-Crested," revealed by all the Buddhas for the sake of the welfare of beings, belonging to the wise Mañjughoṣa.

The hair growing from all sides should be known as that which grows from the head; it belongs to the Tathāgatas. It should be known as the bestower of all aims and the fulfiller of the treasury of Dharma.
For the sake of fulfilling the mantras and mudrās, there is that which possesses great supernatural power,
which is always the most excellent among all mundane and supramundane [practices].
In the Mañjughoṣa tantra, however, this [practice] is considered the foremost, indeed the most excellent;
by its power, one shall swiftly accomplish all activities according to their intended purpose.
481) Having become pure, one should bind the supreme Lord mudrā in a pure place;
first, indeed, having made the two hands hollow and joined like a casket.
With the thumbs slightly separated from the palms and the thumbs placed [together], it is indicated by "tha";
when the five fingers are arranged like five needles, it becomes the Pañcaśikhā mudrā.
Always placed at the location of the head with one finger and a thumb's breadth,
the single-cloth mudrā is applied to the positions on the crown of the head.
The little fingers are placed together, the two middle fingers are likewise closely joined,
and both thumbs are pointed forward.
From the union of the three needle-like forms, the triple-crested mudrā is proclaimed;
it is formed by all the fingers joined together, hollowed out with the openings [of the thumbs].
When this mudrā is always placed at the location of the head, it becomes the Śiravarā;
it is that same [mudrā] with the two fingers raised slightly and their tips bent.
That Mahāmudrā should be known as the Great Heroine of great supernatural power;
these five Mahāmudrās were [taught] by the excellent Jinas in the past.
The two wise ones have explained all the mudrās;
they declare that the eldest is the foremost of mudrās, [and] it is sealed by... (mudritām).
Indeed, all these five great mudrās— both those that are supramundane and all those that are mundane— are the applications that serve as the causes for accomplishment.
These are indeed well-accomplished and most perfected; they are declared to be the eldest [daughters] of Mañjughoṣa, whose power and miraculous deeds are extraordinary.
As many as there are mudrās of the Sugatas, they are all causes for accomplishment;
the mudrā is renowned as "mudrā," and it is the glorious one born from the sprout.
The hair of Mañjughoṣa’s head is most meritorious and auspicious;
by binding it, great beings will certainly attain awakening.
One should always perform one's duties according to the rules, being devoted to that great chief ornament, faithful, with unimpaired faculties, and ever joined with wisdom through sacrifice.
482) But when this mudrā is well-joined with such a being who is endowed [with the necessary qualities], it indeed accomplishes all desired aims in abundance.
However, through instruction, those who are wise, discerning, and effective in achieving their goals—
such disciples approved by the teacher should always be accepted in this world.
In this world, by a person who has observed the ritual actions and is endowed with devotion,
this mudrā is always employed by those who have entered the Mahāyāna.
When applied to mantras in three ways,
all these mudrās are indeed the foremost and most excellent in the world by virtue of their power.
For the sake of accomplishment for those desiring success, these [mantras], when well-conjoined with other mantras,
quickly bring about one's purpose and bestow the fruit of all happiness.
Mañjughoṣa himself abides in meditative equipoise through these mudrās;
in whatever place one performs these, Mañjurava himself is always present.
The Son of the Jina, possessed of great supernatural power, should indeed arrange this supreme protection;
he is a Great Being in the form of a child, possessing all forms and great supernatural power.
He appears in many forms for sentient beings, and in the form of mudrās for embodied beings;
yet for those foolish beings who wander in the ocean of saṃsāra, [he appears as their protector].
Acting for their benefit, he quickly remains in the form of a mudrā;
born from the head of Mañjughoṣa, he is established upon the crown of every head.
For by merely reciting these, joined with the root mantra or with that which follows the heart-mantra, they bring about the accomplishment of all goals.
All those mantras belonging to the Lotus family,
as well as those of the Thunderbolt-bearer and the one with matted hair, are well-united with the Saugati mantras.
When joined with all worldly mudrās as well, they bestow the fruit of the intended purpose;
these five great mudrās, when joined with mantras, bestow the fruit of the intended purpose.
Having abandoned that which is to be conceptualized as residing in mantras, it yields fruit through mudrās;
it is a great protection and a source of great merit for embodied beings merely by being bound.
483) By these great mudrās when merely remembered, great protection is attained;
how much more so by those who rely on mantras and mudrās while they are being recited!
Or rather, all those who perform the recitation will certainly attain enlightenment;
others, however, are the great mudrās arising from the trident and the spear.
Now, the Great Sūla among mudrās is said to be most terrible and fierce;
it is joined here with the principal Wrathful King, Yamāntaka.
He performs various terrible deeds that obstruct life and bestow great fear, even upon a high-souled Vipasvin.
Created for the destruction of wicked beings within the abode of the three worlds,
various mantras have been joined with them, relying upon diverse mudrās.
They were always created by the supreme Victors for the very purpose of destroying those [obstacles];
they were devised for the sake of the teaching, endowed with the meaning of mantra practice.
The mudrās, which reveal the meaning of the tantras, have been prescribed by the Lords of the World as a remedy for the poison,
sin, and diseases employed by wicked beings.
It was taught for the very purpose of destroying them, performing all aims and rites;
for the destruction of Yama’s command and for liberation from the noose of death.
This mudrā, when employed constantly in conjunction with the mantra, is known as the destroyer of messengers of Yama;
it is meritorious and remembered as the annihilator of death.
She is remembered as the restorer of life for those led by the command of Yama;
she brings about the destruction of all diseases and strikes even Yama with fear.
Likewise, this life-sustaining [practice] is beneficial when joined with the foremost sages;
for those who have faith in this teaching, protection is ordained for their welfare.
The Goddess Mahāmudrā is praised as fruitful, destructive of the wicked, delightful in sound, beneficial, and the bestower of all goals.
Regarding the great weapon, they say there is another supreme mudrā:
likewise, having placed the hands together, the two index fingers should form a noose.
484) One should always indicate the two little fingers by joining them in the form of a fist;
the two hands are always joined in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭita*), with both thumbs raised.
This mudrā is of great merit; it is employed in the Great Sūcī (Mahāśūla) and arises from various weapons produced by the Lords of the World.
Whatever weapons an incantation-practitioner might imagine for an enemy, by that very [visualization] he would cut the enemy's body; it would come to pass through the mere arising of that thought.
When mudrās and mantras are applied together, they will certainly destroy the enemy;
they shall slay all hosts of enemies, even those possessed of great supernatural power.
The hosts of Yama’s messengers, the obstacles, the planets, and likewise the Mātṛs;
Pūtanā, Skanda, Rudra, and also the pretas of great supernatural power.
Having recited [this] over the worlds of Vaivasvata, including all those of Indra,
one should employ no other mantra than this Yamāntaka-krodharāja.
One should then employ these mudrās, which are equal to a great spear;
they would instantly slay even Vaivasvata—what need is there to mention mere humans on earth?
This seal, which destroys all wicked beings and acts as a weapon against all,
was established by the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds and leaders of the world.
In the same way, having placed the hands together, one should form [the mudrā] by joining the middle fingers;
likewise, having positioned the hands here, one should form it by means of the fist-union.
The tips of the two thumbs are pressed together;
the fingers are joined with hollow spaces, and the middle fingers are raised up.
Likewise, when the two needle-tips are always resting upon the index fingers,
the best of sages call this excellent and formidable mudrā the "Trident" (śūlā).
When both index fingers are slightly bent, it is the Mahāśūla;
when they are extended, it is known as the Paṭṭiśā—the supreme and excellent Mahāmudrā.
When those same fingers have their tips contracted and are raised by three finger-breadths,
the wise declare this to be the Triśūla-mudrā (the Trident Gesture).
485) They should be known as having various weapons when both thumbs are raised;
for these are like great spears, possessing great heroism and being terrifying.
In this supreme Mañjurava Tantra, for the sake of destroying evil beings,
these Great Mudrās of wondrous activity have been tamed, for they are indeed difficult to subdue.
Fierce and life-taking, arising from a distorted form,
it is most exceedingly terrible, violent, and established in extreme cruelty.
The most formidable and excellent Jyeṣṭhā goddesses, possessing many forms, have been revealed;
everywhere, those Buddhas who recite [their mantras] are freed from old age and disease.
These perfected practitioners of recitation always wander through these worlds;
they were ordained by the Fully Awakened Ones, the preeminent sages, for the destruction of death.
One should employ these [mantras], which destroy old age and disease, for the sake of destroying death;
when joined by the practitioners of mantra, they are terrifying even to Death himself.
The glorious and supreme Lord manifested the mudrā in the excellent city of Śuddhāvāsa for the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men and the son of the most eminent sage.

The Buddhas do not speak mantras, nor do they [teach] mudrās for those who perform cruel deeds; rather, it is out of affection for the sake of sentient beings and for the purpose of fulfilling the goal of omniscience.

Whether for the purpose of sporting with supernatural powers, for the sake of gathering the equipment for enlightenment, for the sake of training beings through skillful means, or for the purpose of establishing them in the supreme Mahāyāna.
It fulfills the great saṃsāra;
by the power of their resolve, it proclaims the mantras and mudrās for sentient beings.
Even "space" is that which the Buddhas have not conceptualized through speech; for those who are endowed with the non-proliferated reality, how could it be within the scope of discursive thought?
The ultimate state is equal to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and equal to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
for those joined with mantra, the ultimate state is sealed by the mudrā.
They declare that it is always the cause for the liberation of the factors of existence;
it is called the seal of the Omniscient One, which fulfills the purpose of all-knowledge.

486) The seal and the sealing have been proclaimed by the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas, whose spheres of activity are inconceivable and beyond thought, for the purpose of honoring the meaning that is endowed with reason.
The seals (mudrās) of the All-Knowing Seer, such as the Uṣṇīṣa and others, have been manifested;
likewise, the Avalokita seal belongs to Vajrapāṇi, as do those of the worldly [deities].
For the sake of the welfare of embodied beings, they have been spoken and will be spoken by the sons of the Buddha and the supreme sages, as far as these mudrās have been proclaimed.
The mudrā that fulfills all aims is inconceivable in its power;
indeed, mantras have been taught in three ways for the sake of the conceptualization of beings.
There is but one mantra which has been spoken by the Buddhas;
for the sake of the Sugatas' purpose, indeed, this single mantra is proclaimed among all mantras.
The glorious Lord of the Uṣṇīṣa, who is always of one color,
shall eternally become a universal monarch (cakravartin) when the letter *ta* is joined with the letter *ra*.
Constantly joined with the letter *ū*, it is then proclaimed as the *yukta* [syllable];
he shall become the glorious Cakrin, the foremost among the Buddhas, born from their head.
They say that the letter *ma* is the supreme mantra of the wise Son of the Buddha;
by its power it should be known as equal to that [mantra], and it is sung as having the meaning of the final syllable.
This renowned heart-mantra of Mañjughoṣa, born from the crown of the Buddha’s head,
should be known for its extraordinary power, great merit, and vast supernatural efficacy.
The mantra fulfills all aims;
together with the five-crested mudrā, they fulfill the aims of both.
The five-crested mudrā, or even joined with the syllable *ma*, brings about the realization of the ultimate meaning; it bestows both wealth and enjoyment right here in this world.
They call this another mantra:
the letter *ja* joined with the letter *ra*, honored by the meaning of the *ava-ūṣman*.
This indeed is the supreme and foremost mantra, born from the head of Abjaketu; when joined with the excellent lotus mudrā, it brings prosperity to those who give birth to noble purposes.
487) For those who recite [mantras], it shall bring about the accomplishment of rites and the fulfillment of all aims.
Furthermore, for the Vajrin, there are the mantras consisting of the syllable *hraṃ* produced from the base of the arm and the head.
This supreme and foremost mantra is indeed proclaimed as Caṇḍa;
when applied with the Vajrālaya mudrā, it shall accomplish the desired aims for those engaged in ritual action.
This mantra is a formidable tamer of the difficult-to-subdue and a cause of destruction;
one should perform the prescribed rite as stated for the purpose of teaching and for the sake of instruction.
One should not perform evil deeds out of a zeal for the suppression of sentient beings;
nor should one ever employ the supreme mantra against gentle beings at any time.
One should not commit an offense even with a slight fault; one should release living beings by destroying their [karmic] nature.
One should not, out of delusion, treat creatures with such disregard for even minor faults.
For those with malicious intent toward the teaching, for the sake of inspiring faith in the faithless,
and for the sake of disciplining beings and subduing the flesh-eaters.
This supreme and foremost mantra has been taught for the purpose of subduing the wicked and for pleasing those of gentle nature; one should never employ it to take a life.
This supreme and excellent mantra is declared to be the foremost for all worldly mantras, for the Vajra-holder of great supernatural power, and for all worldly deities.
This other supreme mantra is indeed known as the crown of all worldly deities' mantras; therefore, Śiva is the single-syllabled one.
The Lord is the master of all worlds and the sovereign of worldly mantras;
they call him the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), and the wise know him as Svakāra.
Indeed, all mantras whatsoever that are known as worldly are sung;
they are all bound within this mantra and are honored everywhere.
These mudrās have indeed been prescribed by the best of sages and are to be employed everywhere;
they are considered most auspicious, supreme, the foremost among worldly things, and composed in concentration.
Indeed, [the goddess] Vipaśyagrahamātṛ includes within herself Īśvara and the others,
as well as the Kaṭapūtanas, Yakṣas, and other flesh-eating Rākṣasas.
488) These mudrās of Viṣṇu, whose banner is Garuḍa, and also of Brahmā, have been proclaimed; indeed, they are prescribed as beneficial for subduing those who are difficult to tame.
For these mudrās have been declared by the wise to be praiseworthy and auspicious;
they are the causes for subduing, entering, and attracting beings.
But in a secluded place, always beautifully adorned with white flowers,
well-swept, and scented with the perfumes of the Siddhas, white sandalwood, and saffron;
Having worshipped the Lord Sugata— the Lion of the Śākyas, the one of great merit, the sovereign of all mantras, and the all-pervading master— with garlands of *jātī* flowers;
Having prostrated with devotion at all times before the Tathāgata, the Omniscient One,
as well as the Lord of Mantras, Lokeśa, and Vajrin, according to one's ability.

From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvataṃsaka*, this is the forty-third chapter, being the fourth in its own series, on the detailed exposition of mudrās, sealed with the seal of the inconceivable dharmadhātu of all Tathāgatas.
512) Now follows the forty-sixth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [spoke].
He addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī!

This fifth extensive chapter on mudrās is yours; it has entered into the Dharma-treasury of all Tathāgatas, is supremely most secret, and is sealed with the mudrās of the Dharma-realm, which are incalculable and inconceivable."
I shall now speak of that which has entered into the practice of all mantras, which is the most supreme secret, the most excellent among all that transcends the world,
and the most joyful among all worldly practices; it is that which was previously spoken by the Tathāgatas.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, who has become a youth (kumārabhūta), rising once again from his seat and prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "It would be well, Blessed One, if you would teach for the sake of all sentient beings and for our own, the entry into the practice of all mantras."
And out of compassion, for the sake of fulfilling the conduct that leads to the seat of great awakening— the great accomplishment of the great vow—

And it is the boundless seal of abiding,
for the sake of fulfilling all desires, hopes, and intentions through the rites of summoning and dismissal,

"For the sake of entering all mudrās through the great samaya that satisfies all sentient beings; now is the time for this, as I deem it."

This entire earth trembled in six ways;

Born of the Śākya clan and skillful, he taught the mudrā at that very moment;
by binding which, wise men are surely destined for enlightenment.
All mantras shall be accomplished— both those of the Sugatas and those that are worldly—
