Thus concludes the forty-fourth chapter, the extensive section on the Great Mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and that great assembly circle (*parṣanmaṇḍala*), [spoke].
He entered the samādhi named "The Practice of All Mantras, the Most Secret of All Secrets, the Infinite Secret, the Manifestation of the Radiance of All Luminosities Adorned with Infinite Arrays.
As soon as the Blessed One had entered it, rays of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows, and from all sides...

Having illuminated all around in the ten directions— above, below, and across— with a great radiance, and having summoned all the mantras, they vanished once again into the Bhagavat’s *ūrṇā* hair-tuft. Immediately upon their disappearance, by means of those rays of light, four maidens together with their brothers appeared in the four directions, as well as below and above, in that very place.
In the great assembly circle, near the king of mountains, Sumeru,
he was empowered by the empowerment of the Buddha; he had gathered and sat down for the purpose of demonstrating the display of supernatural powers of the Great Bodhisattva Kumārabhūta.

For the sake of accomplishing the practice of the great mantra, and for the sake of entering into, mastering, attracting, comforting, and penetrating the playful practice of all mundane and supramundane mantra practices.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having glanced slightly at the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi— who was gathered in that very assembly— as well as the entire host of Bodhisattvas, [spoke].

Then that entire assembly, as well as this great earth surrounded by hosts of deities—the abode of the single mantra of the great elements—caused the medicinal herbs, the great luminaries, and the mountains to tremble; it shook, quaked, rattled, vibrated, was agitated, and was thoroughly convulsed; the southern quarter rose up and the northern quarter sank down.

The western direction rose up while the eastern direction sank down; the edges sank down while the center rose up, and the center sank down while the edges rose up; and there appeared in the world a great radiance.

Furthermore, countless other immeasurable, marvelous, and wondrous miracles were displayed. And those hosts of gods entered the samādhi called "the state of peace through the knowledge of the great object free from conceptual proliferation," which cannot be attained even by all the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Mahābodhisattvas.

How much more so, then, to fully enter into them? It is for the purpose of surpassing all other mundane and supramundane shrines of non-Buddhist sects, for the purpose of entering into all mantra-tantras,
for the purpose of fulfilling all dharmas of liberation, and for the sake of all sentient beings.
For the sake of attaining the state of peace,
out of compassion for all beings, he ascended and sat upon the Vajra-throne at the seat of awakening— the unthinkable *tathatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
And for the purpose of attaining that state, the Blessed One Śākyamuni remained absorbed in meditation.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas: "Speak, speak, O Son of the Jina!
Speak that which is the entry into the practice of all mantras, the essence of all worldly mantras."

This is the supreme secret for all beings and sentient beings, the entry into the samaya that fulfills all intentions and desires according to their inclinations; O Son of the Conquerors, you have been authorized by all the Blessed Buddhas.

For the sake of fulfilling the omniscience of the treasury of mantras of the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present; for the sake of displaying here, in this detailed exposition of the King of Rituals (Kalparāja), all playful sports, inconceivable wonders, and marvelous transformations;
and for the sake of manifesting the knowledge of the Omniscient One.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, O Dharmadhara! I shall [speak] the discourse on the skillful preservation of the equality of all Tathāgatas, concerning these four maidens together with their brother."

The secret ritual manual includes the rules for the procedure of the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), recitation (*jāpa*), and the timing of rites; the procedure for the image (*pratimāvidhāna*); the commitments (*samaya*) of the mandala; the invocation (*āhvānana*), dismissal (*visarjana*), and worship (*apūjana*); and the sequence of rules regarding the means and goals of practice (*sādhanasādhyopāyaniyamakrama*), including offerings of water (*argha*), lamps, perfumes, incense, garlands, ointments, powders, garments, food-offerings (*nivedana*), banners, flags, bells, necklaces, and the ritual for flower-garlands.
Peaceful rites, enriching rites, malevolent rites, invisibility, traveling through the sky, walking upon water, subjugation, possession, causing hatred, eradication, withering, stupefaction,
paralyzing, and killing.
One who performs various actions involving the making of diverse forms of sentient beings, as well as their tormenting, threatening, reviling, and the creation of many-footed or footless creatures;
one who displays paths and effects desired karmic results;
and one who is situated in places suitable for the accomplishment of all rites, mantras, and tantras, including binding, climbing, and making [actions] fruitful.
Application is the fulfillment of accomplishment; listen to that, O Son of the Victor!
Then the glorious Vajrapāṇi, having prostrated before the Sugata, the All-pervading Lord,
spoke these sweet words adorned with both sound and meaning.
It brings about what is not harmful, is pleasant to the ear, and is sweetly modulated in meaning;
it accomplishes many purposes, is desirable, serves as the foundation for all mantras, and resounds with the voice of Brahmā.
Possessing a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, clear, profound, and self-restrained,
he is one who explains the subtle reality of the meaning.
Then the Vajra-holder spoke these words concerning the sovereign of all mantras:
"Listen, all you hosts of spirits and all you assemblies of gods of great supernatural power!"

Likewise, the ritual manual (*kalpa*) to be described hereafter, which is detailed and efficacious for all rites, consists of four forms of great majesty that assemble from the four directions. (266, p. 516)
It is endowed with four classes and adorned with four syllables.
That man, endowed with the four mantras, has resorted to the fifth;
he possesses the majesty of the fourth state and the union of the four elements.
With his brothers as the fifth, he is the eldest, born from the space of the great elements;
unobstructed everywhere, supreme, and the means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras.
It performs all rites, is worthy of worship, the eldest, auspicious, and the destroyer of sins;
it has proceeded for the welfare of all beings in the form of mantra.
She is renowned as the Four Maidens, with the Youth as her fifth self;
she consists of wind, water, fire, earth, and space as her fifth element.
For those embodied beings, the ripening [of karma] occurs in the form of mantras;
the fifth is the foremost of blessings, the king of mantras in the form of a brother.
I shall proclaim their mantra; listen to me, O Aparā.
Then all those beings indeed became joyful in heart.
Seated, having realized the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), with gentle minds and composed,
everyone indeed desired to hear, their eyes steady and wide open.
Then the glorious Mañjuvara, looking up at the son of the Sugata,
[beheld] Vajrapāṇi, the great yakṣa, the abode of all lords of mantras.
In that interval, another appeared whose heart was drawn by compassion;
indeed, all the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas [were present].
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who abide on the ten stages,
as well as all those in the world who are foremost and most eminent among all beings.
Seated everywhere, they are joined to all five states of existence;
they are the foremost among living beings, supreme, and honored by others.
From the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, she pervades the infinite realms;
extending to the limit of three births as the presiding witness, she is the supreme sovereign of the ten stages.
517) For all of them, desiring to hear, sat down for that assembly;
then Vajradhara, the presiding lord, perceiving that everyone had arrived—
[He beheld] sentient beings and bodhisattvas, the abode of all lords of mantras,
the gods who are the eldest among the deities, and those who are masters of the ten stages.
Having understood all these sentient beings to be well-disposed toward the Buddha’s teaching,
the wise one, the Lord of the Mantra Sovereigns, should then recite the mantra.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded and who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms! Oṃ tura tura hulu hulu!
Do not delay; remember your pledge! Accomplish my purpose! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

This mantra is all-purposeful. It is the heart-mantra of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the root-mantra of all mundane and supramundane lords of all diseases and sovereigns; by means of this, one should perform all rites.
One should accomplish all substances; the omnipresent Lord performs every rite.
With this [mantra], one should always perform the ritual for the swift accomplishment of one's goals.
In this regard, I shall proclaim the mantra; O assembly of gods, listen to me!

*Oṃ deva svāhā*. This is the mantra of Tumburu, the caravan leader. *Oṃ jaye svāhā*, *Oṃ ajite svāhā*, *Oṃ aparājite svāhā*. These are the root mantras of the four sisters together with their brother.

These are the heart-mantras (*hṛdaya*) of those who are worshipped by the world. For them, they are: *oṃ rūpiṇi oṃ virūpiṇi viśvātmane*. These mantra-born mantras belong to Tumburu’s heart. [The following] are the near-heart-mantras (*upahṛdaya*): *oṃ deveśāya svāhā*; *oṃ vāmāni piśāci oṃ mahārākṣasi svāhā*; *oṃ vikṛtarūpiṇi*.

Svāhā! Oṃ, you whose hair is disheveled, you who have the form of Kṛtānta, svāhā! Oṃ, you who have the form of a vajra, O terrifying night of Kṛtānta, svāhā! This is the upahṛdaya (near-heart mantra) of Tumburu, the caravan leader: Oṃ, you whose body is adorned with four faces, three-eyed, pot-bellied, possessing many forms, svāhā! Oṃ dhudhu, cause all directions to blaze, svāhā! [This applies] to all of them.

This is the divine mantra for the sisters together with their brothers: Oṃ hūṃ—this is the *śikhā* (crown lock) for all. Oṃ hrīḥ jaḥ—this is the *śiras* (head) for all. Oṃ dhyāyini svāhā—this is the general mantra for all. Oṃ dṛk—this is the *netra* (eye) for all.
And this is the *samaya* (pledge) for the sisters together with their brothers, who are anointed with sandalwood and saffron.
Of those who are protected (268,
p. 518), who roam the Himalayas and the oceans, who are firm in their vows, and who are authorized by the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.

Śrīḥ | Hrīḥ | Rīm | Vrīḥ | Bhujaḥ | This is the great mantra for the bodies of all sisters together with all brothers; it is effective for all rites, renowned for all activities, and most supremely secret. Oṃ āyāhi mahādeva viśvarūpiṇe svāhā | Oṃ tumbure, this is the invocation mantra of the caravan leader Sārthavāha. Oṃ.
"Go, go, Mahādeva! To the Universal Self, svāhā!"—this is the dismissal mantra for Tumburu, the caravan leader.
"Oṃ! Come, O Goddess Kumārikā! Why do you delay? Remember your pledge! Accomplish my task, svāhā!"—this is the invocation mantra for Jayā. "Oṃ! Come, O Great Enjoyer! Accomplish my task!"
*Samayamanusmara svāhā*. *Oṃ mahāyogāndhari vistīrṇadhanapriye svāhā*. This is the invocation mantra of Ajitā.
*Oṃ śmaśānavāsini rūpaparivartini dehānucare svāhā*. This is the invocation mantra of Aparājitā.
Furthermore, one should draw all the maṇḍalas, both mundane and supramundane, and [employ them] in all rites.
One should apply [the practice]. Even by means of the ritual procedures of other *kalpas*, one shall accomplish the desired goal.

Within this very extensive *kalpa*, in the chapter on the equality of the King of Root *Kalpas*, this mantra of the four maidens together with the youth is declared first; it is the son of the Buddha, by which one may achieve whatever one desires.
The sons of the Buddha, possessed of great supernatural power, declare him to be effective for all rites;
he is the foremost of families, the chief of mantras, the sovereign lord of all mantras, and the all-pervading one.
It performs various and diverse actions that are well-described by the virtuous;
it even forcibly captivates the minds of living beings born of the three realms.
Driven by the power of its destiny and the cause of its subjection, the being, having emerged from its place of birth, forcibly performs actions arising from the afflictions of its offspring.
They are renowned as the Four Sisters,
who always dwell together with their brothers in the great ocean.
Embarked upon a ship were they, five in number including their brother;
their helmsman was one known by the name Tumburu.
Intent on bestowing favor upon sentient beings, they wander over the entire earth,
assuming various forms and adorned with diverse ornaments.
They wander over the entire earth, including its mountains and oceans, experiencing diverse fruits of their actions honored with various requisites.
519) Among them, the mantra of Mahājyeṣṭhā is held to be that named Tumburu;
and the mantra of Sārthavāha belongs indeed to Tryambaka, O lord of men.
The four-syllable combination ending in *oṃ* is the foremost of all mantras; one should perform its worship with special offerings of perfumes, incense, lamps, garlands, and oblations.
Having presented the ritual bali offering, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) in a secluded place with clear and orderly syllables.

Having taken up one of these excellent mantras, one should recite it eight thousand times at the three periods of the day. Having offered the *argha* (water of respect) to her as she arrives, one should perform all rites. And here is the *argha* mantra: *oṃ pravigṛhṇatu bhaginyaḥ sabhrātṛsahitā argham | samayam adhitiṣṭhantu svāhā*. This is the *argha* mantra.

For all [the deities] together with their brothers, there are mantras for all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*). Oṃ jvala jvala mahāhutāśārci mahādyutīnāṃ svāhā! These are the lamp mantras for all. Oṃ dhūṃ dhūṃ!
O you who dwell in the enemy’s abode, crest of incense, charming with fragrant scent, may the goddesses together with their brothers accept [this offering].

*Dhyāyantāṃ svāhā*. This is the incense mantra for all. *Oṃ kusumavāsini kusumāḍhye surabhimāle sugandhimanohare vane kusumā jātāḥ sukumārāḥ sugandhinaḥ | tāṃ nivedito bhaktyā pratigṛhṇadhvaṃ manojavā svāhā*. This is the flower mantra. With this, one performs the worship.

One should perform [the ritual]. *Oṃ gandhagandhādhivāse svāhā*. This is the mantra for incense (*gandha*). *Oṃ balite balini svāhā*. This is the mantra for the food offering (*bali*). *Oṃ lālāvati svāhā*. This is the mantra for the food offering (*nivedya*). *Oṃ sū*. This is the mantra for the garment (*vastra*). *Oṃ phaṭ*. This is the mantra for the bell (*ghaṇṭā*). *Oṃ svaravyañjanamantrā*. This is the mantra for the vowels and consonants. *Oṃ chādaya*. This is the mantra for the parasol (*chatra*). *Oṃ dodhūyate*.

*Dhūyate svāhā*. This is the mantra for the chowrie (*camara*). *Oṃ keli-mahokali-hṛdayaṅgame svāhā*. This is the mantra for all substances, implements, collyrium, *rocanā*, mirrors, and ornaments. *Oṃ samastavyāpini svāhā*.
This is the mantra for the vajra-fence that binds all directions. *Oṃ maṇḍaline svāhā*. Thus [for] above and below.

This is the binding mantra. It effects a complete and universal binding on all sides without exception. Oṃ, homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ hūṃ haḥ! This great king of vidyās is named Śāsana; it brings all activities under control and subjugates all spirits and the four young maidens.

The one who afflicts, withers, obstructs, and binds those together with their brothers; the subjugator who delights in restraint and favor; whose command is unimpeded in all rites, O Mother of the Grahas of all beings—he causes whatever is desired to be done by the four sisters together with their brothers when he is recited in a secret place or a secluded chamber.
When she is being asked for whatever boon pleases him, he should quickly ask for that boon; she will then grant the boon. Thus...

They perform such acts as binding, beating, threatening, killing, and so forth. When tormented by this very King of Vidyās and recited together with him, they accomplish all activities. Their mantras are as follows;
they perform tasks such as dismissal and supplication: *Oṃ rūpiṇi gaccha gaccha*.

*Samayamanusmara svāhā*. This is the dismissal mantra (*visarjanamantra*) for Jayā: *Oṃ vāmane piśāci prakīrṇakeśi viśvarūpiṇi gaccha gaccha mama kāryaṃ sādhaya svāhā*. This is the dismissal mantra for Vijayā:
*Oṃ lahu lahu rūpiṇi gaccha gaccha samayamanusmara mama kāryaṃ samādāya svāhā*.

The dismissal mantras for Ajitā: *Oṃ viśvarūpiṇi vikṛte vikṛtānane sarvaduṣṭanivāraṇi gaccha gaccha mamārthaṃ sādhaya svāhā*. These are the dismissal and supplication mantras for Aparājitā. Having filled one's joined palms (*añjali*) with various flowers, [one should offer them] for whatever task is desired.
Having made supplications and having propitiated them, [the offerings] should be cast before the goddesses together with their brothers;

then they become liberated. Together with their brothers, they grant their presence and bestow boons as desired; they move about according to their pleasure. This should be spoken daily with one's voice.

When their duties are thus obstructed, they do not abandon their presence because of the need for liberation; otherwise, if their constant activity were obstructed, they would no longer persist in what must be done.

Then those sisters, together with their brother, trembling and oppressed, overcome by a shudder and seized with fear through the power of the Bodhisattva, approached from the four directions and uttered these words: "Save us, Blessed One Vajrapāṇi! Save us! We are being tormented."
“Blessed One, we are greatly oppressed; no other refuge is found. You alone, Blessed One, are our refuge; you alone are our protection.”

In the meantime, by the Great King of Vidyās, all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans within the teaching were well-governed; and all sentient beings, including those comprised within all states of existence, were well-disciplined and well-instructed by the Great King of Vidyās.
Through the power of the Lord of Vajras, those sisters, together with their brother, stood there terrified, well-disciplined, and crying out in piteous tones.
Then Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, addressed that goddess together with her sisters: "Do not fear, sisters; do not be afraid! Go for refuge to the Buddha!"
521) Go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost among the two-footed; go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost among those free from passion; [go for refuge to] the foremost among assemblies.

Then those sisters, with their brother as the fifth, went for refuge to the Buddha; they went for refuge to the Saṅgha in this way. Thereupon, they became possessed of happiness and gladness, endowed with the highest happiness and gladness, and perceived themselves as being released from tight bonds.
Endowed with the bliss of joy, their hair standing on end from the supreme rapture born of having attained serene confidence, they uttered this inspired utterance:
Oh, what a marvel has been attained at the source of the Three Jewels!
Having gained this for a moment, we are made happy and freed from all miserable rebirths.
May heaven and liberation in a happy destiny always be established in your mind;
therefore, with a contented heart, gaze upon Mañjughoṣa.
Having prostrated with my head at your feet, I utter these words:
"O Protector, you are the savior from all sufferings; O One of Great Splendor, you are our refuge."
O Protector, you who teach the profound, syllable-less state of all phenomena— you who have become our kinsman, homage be to you!
"Command me, O Great Hero, Lord of Mantras, Son of the Conquerors! What have we been brought here by the Lord for? What command shall I carry out?"
Thus addressed, the heroic and all-pervading Lord, the son of all Buddhas,
being urged by the deities, spoke these sweet words.
Go once more for refuge to Vajrapāṇi, the Son of the Victors;
indeed, the irreversible Saṅgha arises from the foremost of Bodhisattvas.

Placing the Three Jewels at the forefront, you who are born of the lineage of the sons of the Supreme Victors, arouse the mind of awakening; be full of loving-kindness and be eager for liberation from existence.
Then, having acted thus in every way, they struck him down, the abode of well-being;
thereafter, all those deities prostrated before the Son of the Conqueror.
522) Having fulfilled every command, they all then turned toward him; having paid homage to that Vajrapāṇi of great splendor, they quickly [approached].
Having offered praise, all those born from his mouth then stood there,
gazing upon the maiden who was accompanied by her four brothers as the fifth.
Gazing upon Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas, they stood there;
these goddesses became the eternal refuge, adorned with the meaning of impermanence.
I utter sweet words, beautiful with the meaning of my own mantras:
"Homage to you, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power!"
O one of great splendor, we shall explain the Pratyekabuddha-saṅgha, the assembly of non-existent yogins, and the extensive meaning of the mantras of the Self.
For the sake of people’s realization of reality as it truly is upon the surface of the earth,
[I shall explain] the secret mantras together with their esoteric keys, which have issued forth from your own mouth.
"For the purpose of protecting the mantras, and for the sake of their foundation, meaning, and ornament.
When this was said, the Lord of Mantras, Vajrapāṇi of great splendor, [replied].
With a face lit by a gentle smile, looking upon her with a blossoming countenance,
he honored that maiden along with her brothers and her circle of friends.
"I have granted you permission; you shall be free from doubt, having been instructed in the extensive ritual manual together with its secrets and its maṇḍala."
"Always honored by living beings, you shall grant boons at all times;
you are honored by sages, as well as by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras."
By the Garuḍas, the gods, and the Gandharvas, as well as by the Asuras of great supernatural power,
by the Kūṣmāṇḍas and all the Mātṛs, and by the Moon and the Sun;
It was as if this earth were being presided over by the world-protectors, the lords of wealth, and the Vasus as they descended,
along with those lords of the gods, the Piśācas, the Uragas, and human beings.
By the presiding spirits of the elements, the lords of the night, the flesh-eating *vyantara* demons,
and the chief leaders of the *rākṣasa*s— those of fierce mind who cause harassment.
523) Together with hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, Yamas, and pretas of great supernatural power,
as well as with humans and non-humans, and even with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
"You shall be honored by the foremost of the gods, the great elders, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Pūtanas, as well as by yogins and the sons of the Victors."
There is no doubt regarding the powers and the excellent sequence;
they say that the mantra of Jayā is [found] in the extensive expansion of the ritual manual.
There are ninety million mantras, along with their extensive tantras and ritual manuals;
furthermore, sixty victorious mantras are proclaimed to have been obtained.
For Ajitā, however, there would be sixteen hundred thousand;
for the maiden Aparājitā, four crores are proclaimed.
When the caravan leader Tumburu sings for nine koṭis [of years],
there shall be kalpas of that same duration, honored by men, gods, and asuras.
All this is known as Śaiva by all the inhabitants of the earth;
it was previously expounded by me in detail in this very Kalpa.
Afterwards, other people spoke of the individual kalpa-mantras:
those of Tumburu for the caravan leader, and those of the wise Tryambaka.
Infinite are the expanses of eons for this Śarva, the one with matted hair,
by whose power the mantras shall attain accomplishment upon the earth.
"Then you are indeed authorized; therefore, in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), always speak forth the mantras and tantras, together with their secrets and in full detail."
"Containing secrets and most secret, bringing about the arising of happiness for all sentient beings"—
having spoken thus, the glorious Vajradhṛk playfully took hold of the vajra.
Then he remained silent upon that raised jeweled lotus;
thereafter, those maidens, together with their brothers as the fifth, quickly [departed].
Having prostrated before the Lord of Mantras, the Sovereign of Yakṣas, the Son of the Supreme Victor,
Vajrapāṇi, the Great Hero, the All-pervading Lord and Master of the Lords of Mantras.
524) He spoke these sweet words one by one in due order:
"I shall describe the mandala briefly, as it arises from the two arms."
They call it the "Jyeṣṭha-maṇḍala"; Jayā sang the Jyeṣṭha in a secluded, private place, when the great crowd had departed.
In a secluded spot on a riverbank crowded with reeds, upon a mountain peak,
in a solitary and delightful forest, or in a dwelling once inhabited by a Buddha;
In an empty temple, or in purified empty dwellings,
under a single auspicious and beautiful tree, or by the shore of the great ocean.
In the Ekaliṅga cremation ground, free from smoke and dust,
at the most meritorious Vajrāsana and the exceedingly beautiful Dharmacakra.
Where the Buddha attained peace, and where the Great Sage was born—
these places are preeminent and auspicious for the drawing of mandalas.
Then, along the entire bank of the Gaṅgā, including its islands and sandy shores,
there are the foremost rivers, the best of streams, which are celebrated and renowned throughout the world.
On all those shores, one should constantly draw a mandala everywhere,
extending all around to the ends of all waters, submerged within the great ocean.
Having set out from the Himavat and Vindhya mountains toward the ocean at their watery ends,
one should draw the mandala on the banks of the most excellent rivers.
Or else, in a secluded spot on the earth, or in a beautifully adorned mountain cave, or in delightful temples of the gods, or even at a very lofty stūpa.
Likewise, in the relic-chambers, in shrines, and also by ponds, wells, and pathways;
everywhere on those banks and in their centers, they were beautifully adorned.
In a cow-pen, by a lotus pond, or anywhere near a body of water, or in other excellent locations always adorned with pleasure-gardens and groves.
On the earth frequented by sages, there is satisfaction for one whose mind acts as it pleases,
[finding delight] in mountain peaks, planets, and caves marked with ridges.
525) With divine dwellings that were peaceful and devoid of living beings, and with planets, [the place was] excellent,
conducive to meditation, and frequented by the foremost of sages.
Or rather, one should draw the mandala wherever there is satisfaction of the mind;
for in these places, when properly honored according to the instructions, [the practice] is always effective.
The deities quickly descended and established their presence;
at that place, the ritual procedure for the sequence of recitation and fire-offerings was then made perpetual.
Those mantras to be accomplished, whether they be the foremost, inferior, or middling—
all such mantras indeed attain success here in the fields of accomplishment that have been proclaimed.
All mantras—whether superior, middling, or inferior—are indeed accomplished;
for accomplishment in this world is manifold, and the ritual procedure is likewise threefold.
Mantras are of three types according to the threefold division of time;
at the three junctions of the day, all mantras are oriented toward the results of their respective actions in these three ways.
The rite of pacification (śāntika) is prescribed in the auspicious mandala called Jaya;
that for the sake of nourishment (pauṣṭika) is in the one called Vijaya; and the rite of sorcery (abhicāruka) is in the one called Ajita.
Likewise, for minor rites, that which is designated as "Aparājita" is always prescribed;
however, for all rites, the knower of mantras should draw the one called "Tumburu."
Five mandalas are to be known for those dwelling in the ocean;
one should dig into the earth a square shape on all sides, merely according to the instruction.
Having cleared an area of four or eight cubits with his hand, he should again remove gravel,
charcoal, husks, hair, and refuse.
Then, having personally cleared away the impurities of skulls, bones, and excrement from that place with his hand,
he should cause others to recite the mantra over all the refuse there.
The practitioner, having diligently cleansed [the area] infested with worms and insects,
should fill it with pure and fragrant clay from the forest.

[One should fashion it] from pure materials grown on a riverbank, or from those found at the top of an anthill, or from substances produced in the middle of a cow-pen or on the ground, or from other earth-born materials.
526) Having covered it on all sides with sand, or else with earth mixed with cow dung, one whose mind is serene [should do so] on every side.
One should quickly smear [the image] all over with various unctuous substances mixed with saffron and blended with fragrances, combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having carefully smeared the ground all around with clay, the knower of mantras and the knower of the mantra-tantras should indeed prepare the maṇḍala on every side.
One should draw the divine mandala, measuring four cubits on all sides, using various powders of five ingredients that have been perfumed with incense.
A mandala measuring eight cubits is called the largest;
four cubits is the smallest, while that which is in between is proclaimed as the medium.
Then there was the renowned Pañcahasta, and then the six-handed Muktavān;
these were for all the goddesses, together with their brothers.
Having stated the measurement of the mandala, it is described as being square on all sides,
with four doors, four corners, and adorned with four archways.
One should draw a divine mandala, praiseworthy and beautiful in form;
having depicted the Youth in the center, adorned with the ornaments of childhood.
Then, in the middle of the left [hand], there is a blue lotus situated,
possessing a luster like the color of saffron and adorned by a hand placed upon it from all sides.
The great lord Mañjughoṣa, the deity who bestows boons, holds in his right hand a long, auspicious *śrīmāla* fruit.
With eyes slightly opened, one should indeed draw the deity of the slight glance all around with the right hand, [surrounded] by the great ocean.
Standing there, one should draw the Goddess seated upon a boat with her brother as the fifth,
well-attired and of beautiful form, together with the Mantras and Vidyās.
Adorned with various ornaments and brandishing diverse weapons,
she possessed the form and gestures of a maiden, yet exhibited the prowess of a young prince accompanied by his brothers.
Tumburu [is the leader] of the caravan of women embarked upon a ship, five in number including her brothers,
accompanied by a helmsman.
The great ocean stands on all sides within the mandala;
it is filled with creatures such as fish and others, and is adorned with water-bubbles.
The wise one should draw the maṇḍala in a secret and secluded place on all sides,
exactly as prescribed by the ritual rules and as the reality itself has been proclaimed.
One should perform all of that quickly and apply it specifically to worldly matters;
whatever [is taught] in this Śaiva Tantra and also in the Gāruḍa Tantra.
By Brahmā and the other foremost sages— Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Kāśyapa—
as well as by the excellent sages Mārkaṇḍeya, Pulastya, and Agasti;
By the Vasus, the Śakra-gods, Rudra, Indra, and the Sun;
by various eminent beings, and by Yama and others who possess great supernatural power as lords of the departed spirits (pretas).
Together with the planetary mothers and kūṣmāṇḍas, who are worshipped by yakṣas and rākṣasas,
they are the masters of the mind in the world of humans and non-humans, possessing great supernatural powers.
Worshipped by Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra throughout the expanse of the kalpas,
they have proclaimed the greatness of the kalpas in their entirety upon the earth.
When applied within that mandala, they are accomplished here without a doubt—
by means of various primary wombs and various forms of conduct.
They have spoken and will speak at length on the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of the goddesses;
at that time, they are to be appointed in the mandala called Jaya as "the earth" (*bhūmi*).

Thus concludes the first section of the most secret samaya for entering the maṇḍala of the four sisters, from the forty-fifth chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
528) Now follows the forty-eighth chapter.
Then, indeed, the goddess named Vijayā, having assembled and taken her seat right there in that very assembly, [spoke] her own...
He spoke the ritual procedure for the means of accomplishment (sādhana) regarding the service of the mandala.

First of all, in a secluded place, hidden and private, one should draw a mandala using five-colored powders— white, black, yellow, red, and green— on either the fifth day of the auspicious bright or dark fortnight, or on the fourth day. It should measure four cubits in extent, being square and having four corners on all sides.

One should draw a great ocean in the center of the mandala, adorned on all sides with four archways and embellished with four mudrās. In the center is the Sārthavāha, having the form of a mudrā-maṇḍala and shining with the color of the moon.
In the northeast corner is the mudrā of Jayā, white and shaped like a half-moon; in the southeast corner is the mudrā of Vijayā.

In the southwest corner, the mudrā of Ajitā is triangular in shape and yellow in luster; in the northwest corner, the mudrā of Aparājitā is in the form of a bond (bandha) and red in appearance; and the mudrā of [Gaurī] is in the form of a vajra and black in luster. Furthermore, all the mudrās should be depicted with garlands of flames.
Having first become pure in conduct, one should place four full jars at the four corners,
their mouths covered with mango sprouts and their interiors filled with all kinds of grains and jewels;
in the center, however, is the fifth jar for the caravan leader Tumburu.

In the same manner, their faces should be covered with mango sprouts and wrapped in fresh cloth. Furthermore, the offerings of oblations, flowers, and so forth, as well as the mudrās, should be prepared exactly as described. The colors of the flowers, incense, perfumes, and all else should correspond to those [deities], and everything must be performed accordingly. An oblation should also be cast in the four directions.

At midnight and at midday, one should employ [the rites] for malevolent magic (abhicāruka); at dawn, for nourishment (pauṣṭika); and in the afternoon or when the sun has set, for pacification (śāntika).

Furthermore, these three types of rites should be applied according to the prescribed times during the construction of the maṇḍala, the fire sacrifice (homa), the recitation (japa), and the ritual accomplishment (sādhana).

Pure men and women of skillful character, who are free from distress, should be admitted; likewise, female attendants who maintain the secret mantras should be admitted first. Having seated them facing the east, one should consecrate water with the root mantra of Vijayā, reciting it seven times, and sprinkle it over everyone.

Having fasted for one day and night and being clothed in clean garments, he should cause eight or more [disciples] to enter through the western door facing eastward; having covered their freshly washed faces, having each bound the seal of Vijayā and joined their palms, and having offered yellow flowers, he should cause them to cast [the flowers].
Having recited the mantra of Vijayā and cleansed the face, one should cause [the disciple] to behold the maṇḍala.
One should also cause him to perform a circumambulation to the right. One should show all the mudrās. Then, in due order, all—
They should be introduced until there are eight.
First, one should invoke the deities together with their brothers using the invocation mantra and the root mantra,
offering appropriate flowers. Having first and then offered incense and performed the appropriate salutation,
the disciple— whether a woman, a man, a boy, or a girl— should enter that maṇḍala wherever he or she has the inclination.

He should be consecrated outside with all the requisite implements like a king, or with whatever is desired; he should be consecrated by means of that which would please the Maṇḍala-ācārya or by that through which he himself would be satisfied. Having been consecrated, one or three should be consecrated by the Noble Consecration (āryābhiṣeka). And this one thing must be said: "Listen, O son of good family, or daughter of good family!"

"You, having received initiation and being authorized by all the deities together with your brothers within your own mantra-tantras, should draw the mandala as you wish and bestow the extensive ritual manuals for the conduct, rules, and procedures of your own mantras"—thus it should be said. Others should be consecrated with the *vidyā*-initiation; this applies to two or three persons, while the rest...
Having instructed them in the practice of their own mantras, they should be dismissed.

Then, the mandala master, having sprinkled [the deity] with sandalwood water and offered the *argha*, should dismiss the deity with his own mantra using incense, flowers, and so forth. All the ritual implements should be taken by himself;
having taken them, he should give his own portion—the third part—to all those who are destitute, and the remainder [should be cast] into the water.

That area of ground should be sprinkled with water; having made it well-smeared, beautifully adorned, and free from dust, one may proceed as desired. Just as in their own mantra-practices, so should they be instructed. All the disciples should be made to bind the mudrās of their respective deities in a secluded, private place, away from the movement of people.
By means of those very mantras previously specified, all mantras especially attain accomplishment.
Especially regarding the mantras for rites of swift accomplishment,
it has been stated in the Jayākhyamaṇḍala by means of the previously specified reasons.
Prescribed by the ritual rules for that rite, in the auspicious mandala named Vijaya,
they say this is the second mandala as taught by the mantra-practitioners who know the true meaning of reality.
530) Vijayā should be known by her measure; she accomplishes the purpose of all rites.
The knower of mantras shall accomplish all desired objects through her among all mantras.
When a mantra has been previously recited by a human being for all rites,
protection by that very deity is proclaimed as leading to victory.
There is the overcoming of obstacles and the commencement of undertakings facing fruition in the second mandala, known as Vijaya, which accomplishes all aims.
From touching [the image], the knower of mantras releases all sins of men through long [practice];
and from recitation and yoga, purification from evil arises.
And there shall be the defeat of other mantras on the surface of the earth,
as well as the faults of those who have fallen into opposing factions, whether born of a wicked or non-wicked womb.
The mantra-practitioner destroys [the enemy] in that very instant when surrounded by the mandala called Vijaya;
they say it is effective for all rites, bringing about subjugation, attraction, and prosperity.
In this world, that which is born of ritual action is fruitful, accomplishing nourishment, pacification, and all goals;
for this [deity], who arises from the ocean of the mandala, is indeed the accomplisher of all aims.
In the place called Vijaya, he is highly esteemed, meritorious, praiseworthy, and honored by Soma;
he is eternally eternal, pure, auspicious, and the destroyer of misfortune.
One becomes handsome, possessed of beauty, fortunate, and an achiever of all goals;
by writing [this], practitioners quickly attain upward movement and the accomplishment of their aims. Thus it is said.
Thus they spoke, being filled with faith in the Buddha’s teaching: "The three maṇḍalas are indeed one, as proclaimed by Ajita, and are honored by the world."
This was previously taught by the foremost sages, distinguished throughout the world;
now I shall proclaim the mandala known as Ajita.
Or rather, one should apply it exactly as it is;
however, the superior color is red, using red powders as well.
In the same manner, with offerings of food, flowers, and so forth, and with perfumes, incense, and other rituals in due order,
the exterior is entirely composed of red substances, beautiful with its limbs drenched in blood.
In the same way, one should everywhere separate the *mudrā* from Bhīmā;
the application of the rites of *bali* and *homa* should also be performed with red substances.
One should likewise cause water-pots of a reddish hue to be given, along with red garments;
and similarly, a cloth for veiling the face or a red parasol.
One should likewise employ a seat, a bed, a vehicle, and even red unguents; for these are the means for achieving the purposes of both men and women through the use of red mantras.
Mantras for the sake of passion are appropriate only for one who possesses passion;
the knower of mantras should not direct his mind toward other mantras that are like mere grass.
The wise one, ever-yoked and knowing the mantra, should utter the mantra for the sake of desire,
to attain prosperity, and as a cause for subjugation and attraction.
One shall obtain all wondrous perfections within the mandala named Ajita;
this mandala is manifested upon the earth for the purpose of bringing all beings under one's control.
The ministers have constantly declared that, for the sake of preventing distraction of the mind,
one should draw forth the activity of the great light— the physical behavior of the elements— and bring it under control.
A mortal whose mind is distracted indeed becomes possessed by her who gazes with unblinking eyes;
he arrives as a slave, accepting all that she knows.
Seeing such a human being who has come under their control, rendered helpless and subject to the power of the servants, one should release him once again.
Whether it be a woman, a man, a boy, or even a girl,
one should liberate them once again by means of the very root mantra of Ajita.
And with the previously described rites performed according to the rules upon the surface of the earth,
the wise one should draw the maṇḍala and employ it at all times.
Action accompanied by mantra is declared to be fruitful in the performance of mantric rites;
one should accomplish this supreme procedure through the preliminary applications of other methods.
For all the hosts of Maheśvara, when being accomplished, are indeed perfected through the knowledge of the ritual procedure,
as well as form, mudrā, mantra, purpose, and tantra.
532) However, the measurement for the ritual yoga is being described with excessive detail;
understand that this [mandala] should be known according to these measurements within this mandala.
Whether measuring seven cubits, or six, five, or four,
or even two cubits or just one cubit in length, when surrounded [by the proper materials], it shall arise as a mandala.
Eight cubits is the largest, while seven, six, and five are the middling sizes;
four cubits, two cubits, or even a single cubit is the smallest.
One should perform rites for pacification (śāntika) in the superior [maṇḍala], and likewise rites for enrichment (pauṣṭika) in the middling;
one should perform rites of sorcery (ābhicāruka) within the mantras in the inferior maṇḍala.
For the sake of subjugating all beings, and for constant paralyzing and deluding,
the practitioner who delights in mantra should always perform all rites while engaged in recitation.
The mandala named Ajita has been taught, which grants liberation from all seizing spirits;
therein reside the bhūtas, piśācas, grahas, mātṛs, and pūtanās.
As soon as they are seen, they constantly come under one's control, deluded by yawning;
by merely seeing them in the maṇḍala, they always quickly go into a state of subjugation.
Then the goddess Aparājitā, having prostrated before the Son of the Best of Jinas,
[prostrated] before Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, and Mañjughoṣa, who is beautifully adorned.
He should address these words to all the sons of the Buddha, those of great majesty, and to this goddess together with her five brothers.
"I too shall perform such a task for the sake of the mandala," he said, giving rise to a logical argument;
and he chose auspicious singing, for this is the conjunction of words with logical meaning.
He is considered to possess great majesty and great power, the subduer of the unsubdued;
he is accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, has the luster of a dark complexion, and a radiance equal to the Night of Doom.
Resembling the color of those known as the messengers of Yama,
he was the manifest Vivasvat himself— terrible, a taker of others' lives, and a source of fear.
Just as it was previously specified for the mandala of the goddesses,
one should perform all of that in exactly the same way, with the exception of the colors.
533) One should always draw [the deity] in a cemetery, always to the south of the city,
in a place filled with smoke, enveloped in garlands of flames, and surrounded by skeletons of bones.
On a level piece of ground situated in a neutral location,
one should draw [the diagram] upon the black-colored surface of the earth using cremation-ground ashes.
Just as the sequence of the ritual procedure for worship has been previously described by means of the mantras,
the mantra-practitioner should quickly apply all of that in its entirety.
One's own mantra, the Lord of Mantras, Tumburu the caravan leader,
and [the land] surrounded by the great ocean...
In the Ajitā [mandala], Vijayā is swiftly designated as holding a sword in her hand;
one should always designate that goddess Jayā as holding a bow in her hand.
For these [goddesses] possess diverse weapons, are adorned with diverse ornaments,
are known for their diverse movements and beings, and have diverse appearances and gestures.
Having drawn this mandala here upon the ground in black color,
one should know that this mandala practiced on earth is indeed a destroyer of the life-force of others.
Mantras have various ritual functions, and various rites arise from them;
having performed all of that as previously described, one should subsequently commence the rite.
Mantras are exhausted by recitation and fire-offerings, and likewise, the mandalas are seen;
for entry into this mandala occurs through the rites arising from that which precedes it.
Thus, this mandala of the foremost goddess in her minor form has been described briefly, though it could be told at great length.
It is to be known by the name Aparājita, a mandala renowned on earth;
it was previously unconquered from all sides by the lords of the rākṣasas and the kinnaras.
[He was surrounded] by Bhūtas, the chief Daityas, Yamas, Mātṛs, and Sagrahas,
as well as by Kūṣmāṇḍas, Vyantaras, Piśitāśas, and Pūtanās.
But in the Tantra, [it is taught] that from all sides there are mantras consisting of flesh-eaters accompanied by impurities,
the most terrible lords of the asuras, and the great manifestations of all bhūtas.
534) Then Tumburu, the caravan leader, spoke to the entire assembly:
"O mortals, let that one called Tumburu, who holds the vajra on the left, protect us."
Having bowed their heads to the wielder of the thunderbolt, they spoke these words once more on the surface of the earth, saying, "It has been previously described."
The entire previously described mandala has four risings;
the first concludes all ritual actions, while the second is now being explained here.
Likewise, the fourfold mandala, which is mixed according to the proper method and has come down through successive tradition, is the accomplisher of all beings.
Always in an empty house, or likewise constantly in an empty temple;
in a secluded, private place, in confidence, whether in one's own home or even in a small hut.
With various ornaments and dress, with various beautiful full vessels,
and with powders of five colors or various substances derived from fruits.
With various bright powders made from ground śāli rice,
combined with white pigments and perfumed with the incense of sandalwood and agallochum.
With blended powders of sandalwood joined with saffron and aloe-wood,
sprinkled with camphor and musk, along with *priyaṅgu*, *kesara*, and other such ingredients.
One should constantly draw the mandala with various fragrant powders mixed with spṛkkā and sīra, and well-perfumed with black agallochum.
One who bathes three times a day, performs recitation and fire-offerings, changes his garments three times,
and likewise practices mantra on the mixed lunar fortnight clearly distinguished as white and black;
On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, one should always draw the mandala according to the prescribed ritual,
measuring four cubits in size.
The wise one should carefully inscribe all that with his mind— the mantra—
within a square enclosure having four gates and provided with four archways.
One should always draw Śāriputra in the center of this mandala,
seated upon a lotus in the middle, turning the Wheel of Dharma.
The minister should depict the Buddha Śākyasiṃha, the Great Hero;
the remainder [of the assembly] should quickly be depicted with the best mudrās, together with his five brothers.
The mantra-practitioner should draw [the mandala] on all sides, with four corners on every side;
the Elder stood upon the excellent lotus below the ocean of the Buddha.
One should draw the seal of Tumburu, who is white in color in every respect;
all [the deities] possess a white radiance, with the luster of the kunda flower, the moon, and the moonlight.
Resembling the appearance of a white water lily and perfectly white in all its parts,
the knower of the ritual procedure for the goddesses should act according to the previously described yoga.
The mantra-practitioner should perform all of that for the sake of accomplishing every ritual action;
just as one would employ the entire mandala upon a cloth painting, so should one apply it here.
The threefold cloth has been prescribed for this mandala according to the rule;
the remainder may be performed as desired, whether on a cloth mandala or on the ground.
In this system of mantra-tantra, as prescribed in the doctrine,
there is a painting on a wooden board or a cloth, produced from whatever wood is appropriate.
All the deities should be painted together with their brothers as the fifth;
just as everything is arranged in the maṇḍala, all of that should be painted upon the cloth.
Or it is prescribed in the sky, according to the appropriate source;
thus it is taught by those who know the mantras of the cloth-painting, while for images, it is proclaimed as follows.
Those who know the mantras should always employ sandalwood from the Malaya mountains, saffron along with its filaments, and *punnāga* in the images.
One should find *piyāla*, *padmaka*, and *rodhra* wood upon the earth,
as well as *sarala*, *devadāru*, and *kāśmīra* together with the *ghaṇṭaka*.
A cloth made from the wood of *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, *jambu*, *priyaṅgu*, and *uḍumbara*,
or especially from red sandalwood, is prescribed.
Wood from the Plakṣa and Udumbara trees, and especially from the Sahakāra; as well as the Puṇḍarīka, Sarja, Sinduvāra, and the wood arising from the Siddhas.
(286, p. 536) The *vakula*, the *tilaka*, the *kāṣṭha*, and likewise the *saptacchada*—
these various species of trees are [classified as] male, female, and neuter.
The collection of all [parts] is from the wood; the root and the rhizome are taken from there upwards;
from the branches, [the parts] are to be gathered from all sides, as are those of the *madhuka* and bitter woods.
Likewise, one should use *picumanda* wood, as well as *ariṣṭa*, *bhūtataru*,
and *putrañjīvaka* wood, for rites of constant malevolent magic (*abhicāruka*).
One should know that the rite for pacification (śāntika) is performed with aśvattha wood or even with wood from the surface of the earth;
for the purpose of nourishment (pauṣṭika), it is said that aśoka wood or the head [of a tree] is used.
One should employ all rites at all times and with all types of wood; however, for the consecration of an image under its natal asterism, one should use wood from its root.
Then, one should join a piece of wood made for a pillar with the constellation Jyeṣṭhā;
thereafter, one should join a piece of wood made for a beam with all the constellations.
Thereafter, one should have it performed under the asterism Revatī on a Monday;
indeed, the pillar is observed under Mūla on a Sunday, with Venus and other [planets] being auspicious.
Accompanied by all the chief attendants and all the hosts of planets,
he would go to the root of the netherworld (rasātala) and enter the body of Āsuri.
Then, by means of wood produced from the *tamba* tree and also from the *gāṇḍa* tree,
[one achieves] the subjugation and attraction of spirits, as well as the paralyzing, immobilizing, and deluding of enemies.
One should indeed perform the rite of sorcery; the image shall enter into them, and thereafter it shall ascend to the vault of heaven by means of upward-pointing wooden sticks.
O Goddess, one should place the image upon a divine vehicle;
then, moving everywhere along the branches, one attains the arising of bliss through invisibility.
The mantra practitioner may commence the rite in any direction as desired; indeed, all directions have been specified, and the characteristics of the image are now required.
And they were mounted upon a boat, beautifully adorned with the form of goddesses;
yet they bore the marks of the form of maidens, with hair in five braids.
537) In that very same way, we have indeed been awakened within this mandala with our hands placed [in the gesture].
Tumburu is truly the caravan leader, the helmsman of great splendor.
Then, with a sword placed in the left hand,
the mantras are recited transversely, arising from intervals of three or two finger-breadths.
One should have a boat well-constructed, either one *vitasti* in length or even longer;
it should be beautifully finished, white in appearance, and resembling the whiteness of a conch shell or the moon.
The wise one should especially have Jayā fashioned, as well as Tumburu;
likewise Vijayā, who shines with a yellow luster, and Ajitā, who is deep red.
One should designate Aparājitā as being black in color, and Śuklā as being white; one should likewise point out Prasannā in the form of Tumburu and Jayā.
Vijayā and Aparājitā, with slightly furrowed brows, and Ajitā, who has a gentle appearance— these should be depicted on all sides of the Goddess.
Whether the size of a thumb-joint or the measure of the little finger,
all these dimensions designated as "attire" have been taught by all the mantra-practitioners.
The *dantī* is known as the *bhogagadā*, produced from gold or earth; one who desires sovereignty over the earth should fashion this very beautiful [mace].
An image made of silver or even of copper is said to bring subjugation;
indeed, on this earth, one made of bell-metal is declared to be for the summoning of spirits.
Indeed, for the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*), an image is prescribed to be made of tin, lead, or iron;
likewise, it may be fashioned from various precious gems or from coral and crystal.
Those desiring swift success should fashion a gentle image;
however, rites arising from impurity should be performed with images made of skulls and bones.
Just as those who have attained their goals succeed through various principal peaks and so forth,
so indeed do all mantras and even minor mantras on this earth achieve success.
"Acquisitions occur according to possibility; when the attainment of the goal is possible, they are accomplished from every source, having been joined with the images. Thus it is said.
538) Then Tumburu, the caravan leader, explained the general procedure for the accomplishment of all [deities]:
having fashioned an image of the goddesses made of ivory, the size of the little finger, in a very secret place...
Having summoned [the deity] with the root mantras and offered incense with the left hand, one should recite the root mantra of Jayā.
Having performed the recitation eight thousand or eight hundred times, she reveals in a dream everything that is desired.
The recitation should be performed at the three junctions of the day for seven days; she accomplishes all that is wished for.

They perform all minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*), such as subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and liberation from planetary afflictions (*grahavimokṣaṇa*). Or, for the purpose of bringing beings under one's control as desired, they demonstrate the signs for rites such as the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*).
One should strike the images of the goddesses with *jātī* flowers; the king will become submissive. [One should strike] the goddesses with *jātī* buds...
One should strike the image eight hundred times with five *kalikā* flowers at the three junctions of the day for seven days.

Whatever princess one desires—one endowed with great wealth and possessing an excellent form—one obtains her. With five *jātī* flowers, each image should be struck one by one eight hundred times at the three junctions of the day for seven days.

Whichever excellent woman he desires, he obtains her. Taking that very image and holding it upon his head, having covered it with his hair, she becomes his wife and remains as his servant. If he places it between his thighs, he attains supreme good fortune. If he takes it and travels on a journey, he is not robbed by thieves. [He conquers] the enemy force.

Having seen [the enemy], he paralyzes them; he may enter into battle and is not struck by weapons; he bewilders the foe and paralyzes the opposing army as it moves about with elephants, horses, and chariots. Having consecrated collyrium, one should recite the mantra over one’s eyes;
whoever one looks upon becomes his servant. Having consecrated *gorocanā*, one should apply a tilaka mark on one’s own face.
Having prepared it, whoever he looks upon becomes subject to him. As long as the *tilaka* remains, for that long he remains continuously engaged in sexual union.

In this manner, having consecrated seven times special garments, incense, perfumes, garlands, flowers, and various requisites— including the sacrificial thread, staff, water-pot, wooden items, sandals, beds, vehicles, seats, food, and all other such special implements— one should perform the rite oneself or cause it to be performed by others.

All sentient beings become submissive and obedient like servants. Having consecrated a *māṣa*-bean and a *jambulikā* fruit seven times with mantras, one should offer eight thousand oblations into the fire before the goddesses in a secluded place during the three junctions of the day for seven days;
then all widows, all *ḍākinīs*, all spirits and planetary grahas, and all afflictions (*kaśmalas*) will be brought under control.

They become followers of the servants, capable of traveling to and fro for hundreds of *yojanas*. Having ground [the ingredients] with cow urine, one should take *piṇḍārakabandaka* and *āmrabandaka* in the forenoon, prepare them in the amount of a thousand, and smear it on the foot.

It should be employed in all rites with divine water or *jyeṣṭha* water, and in all honored rituals even according to the supreme mantra procedures. However, this is the distinction: in whichever maṇḍala there is the Caravan Leader Tumburu, the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, the Buddha, the foremost of all beings.

Śākyamuni is depicted in that maṇḍala; for one who has seen the samaya, the rites should be performed. All rites are swiftly accomplished. Ten thousand recitations of the preliminary service (pūrvasevā) should be performed.

Then Jayā speaks her own ritual manual: having fashioned an image of the four sisters, the goddesses, together with their brother, mounted upon a boat— made of emerald, sapphire, ruby, crystal, and so forth, or of special gems such as coral sprouts, agate, lapis lazuli, gold, or silver— at the very least...

Having fashioned an image as before, [one should place it] in a pure location sprinkled with water of sandalwood, saffron, and camphor; having constructed a mandala with those same [substances], in a very secret place during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the full moon of Kārttika, or during another bright fortnight, [one should worship] the goddesses according to their specific ornaments and weapons.
On the arrival of the *prātihāraka* flowers, or on another auspicious bright day, on a favorable lunar date, under the weekday of the Moon or Venus,

and during the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Revatī, Anurādhā, or Jyeṣṭhā, one should first recite one hundred thousand syllables of the *Jayā* mantra while subsisting on alms-food, or water and barley-meal, or by consuming sacrificial oblations, fruits, bananas, mangoes, and coconuts.

Having recited the mantra and completed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), Tumburu— having beheld the maṇḍala of the arising image of the Tathāgata, having performed the protection ritual, wearing white garments, adorned with garlands, and with his head bound with *mālatī* flowers— should remain fasting for a day and night and then enter the practice of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Having offered the water of honor (*argha*) as before, he should offer a profusion of *jātī* flowers.

Having performed a great worship with *mahākṛpāpiṇḍī*, *tagara*, *nāgakeśara*, or *puṇṇāga*— or with any one of these, or with fresh flowers— one should take five *mālatī* blossoms at a time and strike the goddesses,
along with their brothers, three hundred thousand times. Within six months, one becomes a *vidyādhara* in an instant.

He goes even to the Brahma-world; possessing a divine form, moving according to his will, he lives for an intermediate kalpa. Furthermore, by means of the ritual procedures of other kalpas, he achieves success through all worldly mantras.

Ajitā speaks her own ritual manual, as does Vijayā, the female practitioner (mantriṇī). Both of these great goddesses perform all rites as before, being born from the source of their respective mantras. However, this is the distinction between them:
for Vijayā, it is with yellow flowers; for Ajitā, it is with red flowers, and with various implements of those same colors.

One should accomplish all rites. Vijayā also says this: an image should be made yellowish-red. Having constructed the Tathāgata maṇḍala as before, [one should worship] Tumburu, the caravan leader (sārthavāha).

The image of Ajitā should be made of copper or red sandalwood; however, in my own ritual manual (*kalpa*), it should be made of silver or gold, shining yellow, and smeared with *gorocanā* and saffron. Everything else is exactly as previously described. Thus both goddesses, Vijayā and Ajitā, spoke to one another regarding whatever is desired by the mind and sought after.
"Accomplish all activities."

Aparājitā spoke thus: "I too shall speak a ritual procedure (*kalpa*). Whatever has been stated by me regarding this mandala must all be performed exactly so with one’s own mantra. Having drawn an image of the goddesses using charcoal from a cremation ground or cremation ash, and having worshipped it with black flowers, one should recite [the mantra] in secret while grasping the name of the enemy."

In a region or in a cremation ground, [the victim] dies instantly, or becomes insane, or is seized by epilepsy, or causes the destruction of his lineage. According to the will of the practitioner, one should offer human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*) right there in that cremation ground; this destroys, paralyzes, and withers enemies by means of a great *rākṣasa*.

He causes [the victim] to be seized, or he brings about the destruction of the lineage at the will of the practitioner. He causes the entire realm and its inhabitants to be seized by a great epidemic and affliction, and then restores them to health. Thus are all the cruel rites that take the lives of others and cause immediate harm, performed during the dark fortnight.

Rites should be performed on the fourteenth, ninth, eighth, sixth, fourth, and other such lunar days. All actions achieve success on the days of the sun, Mars, and Saturn. Without any effort, one should take charcoal from a cremation ground and write the name—or the image—of a woman in a skull belonging to a *caṇḍāla*.

Or one may draw a man; at that very moment they become enamored. Having placed a finger upon the vulva of the reflection situated in a skull-cup, a woman who is being consumed by passion arrives instantly even from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*. Taking the skull-cup and reciting the mantra, one becomes invisible. Taking the soot and applying it as collyrium to the eyes, a woman is consumed by the fire of passion.
He comes; all ritual actions are to be performed.
Thus addressed, the goddesses entreated the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lord of Dharma,
speak his own mantra and the practice of his own mantra for our sake out of compassion, and for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings."

Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the son of the Sovereign of the Śākyas, having gazed slightly upon that maiden together with her brothers, uttered these words: "O maidens, you five including your brother,
are not [fit] to hear the greatness of the qualities of the Tathāgata, the power of the practice of mantras, or the conduct."

Who else in this world, including the gods, among the community of ascetics and brahmins, would be able to hear or practice such a course of conduct, except for those who have already generated the mind of awakening?

Who else is capable of hearing or understanding this teaching— the crown of which is not distinct from the illusory wisdom of all Tathāgatas, and which involves the entry into and accomplishment of all mantra practices by the lords of Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages?
In order to explain the entry into the practice of mantra and to reveal it to all sentient beings— with the exception of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas,
and those beings who have entered that path and generated the thought of awakening— you maidens are not capable [of doing so]. Therefore, indeed...
"Generate the mind of awakening! Toward all sentient beings, be possessed of a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit."
Having spoken thus, those maidens, having taken up the three refuges and generated the mind of enlightenment, sat down in silence to listen to the Dharma.

From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, this is the second chapter on the ritual procedure for entering the maṇḍala as part of the second means of accomplishment, extracted from the forty-sixth section. It is titled "The Chapter on the Four Maidens."
It is concluded.
542) Now begins the forty-ninth chapter-section.

Then those deities, having circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni, all the bodhisattvas, and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas three times, bowed their heads in prostration and stood gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One, as they gazed.

And they spoke the extensive ritual manuals of their respective tantras; they spoke of their own mudrās and medicinal herbs as they desired. Having been authorized by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha for the benefit of sentient beings, each spoke their own detailed collection of all mudrās and mantras.
They spoke the chapter on mudrās and the ritual manual for medicinal herbs.

Tumburu, the caravan leader, spoke thus: "First of all, having rubbed one's hands with perfume—either sandalwood mixed [with other substances] or with other types of fragrant scents—one should stand before the goddesses facing either east or north.
Then, grasping the thumb of the right hand with the left hand using a fist-like grip, one should rotate it counter-clockwise."

One should place it at the region of the navel; or, by means of the fist-gesture (*muṣṭiyoga*), one should place it at the location of the head. "O Blessed One! This is my Samaya-mudrā of Tumburu, the Caravan Leader. Those same hands which accomplish the purpose of the ritual—having inserted the thumb of the left hand inside and firmly grasped it with the fist-gesture—at the region of the navel."

One should place [the hand]. O Blessed One! This is my Jaya-mudrā, which performs all rites. Having opened that same fist with the index finger, one should threaten; thus all obstacles in the southern direction are destroyed. This is the second great mudrā.
Having raised the second finger, one should turn it toward the western direction. This is the second great mudrā.

It paralyzes all malevolent *nāgas* and should be employed for the purpose of neutralizing poison. Raising the third finger and directing it toward the northern quarter, all *yakṣas*, *yakṣīs*, *kinnaras*, *mahoragas*, and *kūṣmāṇḍas* become submissive; this is the rite of summoning.
The third is the Mahāmudrā, which fulfills all hopes; all activities become manifest.

Having spread out the fourth finger and contracted the thumb situated within, one should direct [the hand] toward the eastern direction from the palm; all gods will become submissive. Facing eastward in front of the gods—
Having manifested it, one should display it. All spirits become submissive, and one becomes beloved by all sentient beings.

This is the fourth great mudrā, which bestows the fruit of all desires. Joining both hands together, extending all the fingers in the form of a hollowed palm (añjali), one should touch the crown of the head. One should then gaze upward and downward.
From the Brahma-world down to the pillar of the universe, and below to the netherworld (rasātala), he brings all gods and dānavas under his control.
This is the fifth great mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all activities. O Blessed One, this indeed is the fivefold...
Mahāmudrā bestows the fruit of all desires.

Vijayā spoke thus: "O Blessed One, I have five great mudrās. Having placed the left hand inside [the right] so that the nails are not visible, and having made a firm fist, one should look downward by means of the yoga of striking and wiping away. This is the first."

The great seal (mahāmudrā). A second [seal] is for looking upward; a third for looking toward the southern direction; a fourth for grasping all directions; and a fifth is placed upon the head. These very five great seals bestow the fruits of all desires.

Ajitā spoke thus: "Having joined both hands together, having placed both thumbs in the middle, having formed the shape of a hollowed *añjali*, having made the two middle fingers like needles and the two little fingers raised in the shape of a noose (*pāśa*), and likewise holding both index fingers and ring fingers [together]— this is named Ajitā."

The Mahāmudrā arises; it is the subduer of the unsubdued, meritorious, and the accomplisher of the purpose of all activities. One should direct that very mudrā toward the southern direction. The second Mahāmudrā is named Vijayā; one should direct it thus toward the western direction. The Mahāmudrā named Jayā arises; one should direct it thus toward the northern direction.
One should not summon her. She is known as the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) named Aparājitā. In this way, one should not summon her in the eastern direction;
she is the Great Seal named Mahāsārthavāha. These very five Great Seals fulfill all hopes and aspirations.

Aparājitā spoke thus: "O Blessed One, I have five great mudrās. Having washed the hands as before, they should be bound during the dark fortnight. They are to be applied according to that same procedure as in this *sādhana*. Standing facing south in front of the goddesses, one should join both hands together."

Having formed a trident (*triśūla*) with the middle, ring, and index fingers and so forth in the shape of three needles, one should place it upon the head—having inserted the little finger, the middle [of the hand], and the thumb into the center of this palm. This is the first *mahāmudrā*, named Aparājitā; in this manner, all [the others] are to be employed.
Just as in the case of Ajitā, sisters who share the same name as their brothers, together with those brothers, become the Mahāmudrās for all. That which is on the palm of the hand is this Sāgara;
that which is the thumb is the brother Tumburu; and these fingers are all the sisters known by their successive names: the index finger is Jayā.
Madhyamā is Vijayā, anāmikā is Ajitā, and the little finger (kanyasā) is Aparājitā; these should be applied to the two feet according to this sequential order. (294, p. 544)
When meditated upon and honored, they provide their presence. Whether visualized or not visualized, they become mudrās.
They perform all activities and fulfill all hopes; these great mudrās should be visualized when one is in a state of distress, for then no fear shall arise.

Tumburu, the caravan leader, spoke thus: "Now, there is a general designation for these remedies. And the power of our medicinal herbs is such that by it all spirits (*bhūta*) become submissive. What is it?
Having taken the shoots of the *aśvattha* and *nyagrodha* trees, one should grind them with milk, stir them with cow's milk, [and administer this] during the bright fortnight."

Under the Aśvinī nakṣatra, on a Monday, on the seventh lunar day (tithi), in the forenoon, one should recite the Sārthavāha mantra seven times over a woman who is in her fertile period but not subject to miscarriage; likewise, having formed the mudrā, one should cause her to drink [the water] while making her face the east. Thus, the woman will conceive a fetus and give birth to a son.

One should sleep with a long-lived husband. Taking the roots of those very plants, one should have them ground into fine powder on a Sunday when the moon is in the constellation Mūla and the sun has moved toward the northern direction;
he to whom this is given becomes submissive in matters of food, drink, and sustenance.

One should employ perfumes, garlands, betel, and so forth; it should be done in such a way that [the essence] enters the bodies. Or, if it touches with speech, one approaches with the quality of being (sattva). In that very manner, by that same procedure, as with a woman, so too with oneself should one drink.
Even if one approaches a hundred women, his semen remains uninterrupted; likewise even with a woman.

It brings about the state of having large genitals. A *gorjaruka* or a centipede, as well as the testicles of a man—this powder should likewise be drunk with milk by one who has a hundred women in his house. In this manner, having first prepared one's own seal (*mudrā*) along with the mantra, one should employ everything, including poisons and secondary poisons (*viṣa* and *aviṣa*).
And in all rites, these are to be accomplished as the supreme means for the subjugation of all beings.

Jayā said: "Taking the root of the *jayantī* plant, one should perform it in such a way that it accomplishes all the rites of Tumburu. Now, if one should desire to travel through the sky: having wrapped the root of the *jayantī* with the three metals, [one should do so] under the conjunction of Puṣya, on a Monday, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, or on the full moon."

On the fourteenth or the eighth day [of the lunar fortnight], having fasted for three nights and being pure, one should mix [the powder] with saffron and place it in the mouth. When the moon is released from an eclipse, one becomes invisible. Having recited one hundred thousand times one's own mantra and placed the pill [in the mouth], when the moon is released from an eclipse, one becomes a Vidyādhara, able to assume any form at will and moving wherever he desires.
He lives for twenty thousand years; when he has vomited it up, he is seen again, and in the human world he performs all his activities in this very manner.

545) Vijayā spoke thus: "However, there is this distinction: having taken agasti-vandāka, having ground it with *jyeṣṭha*-water or divine water, and having consecrated it with one's own mantra, one should smear it on the feet; [then] one will travel a hundred *yojanas*."

He performs going and coming; without weariness, he does not abandon it until [the goal is reached]. Taking the root of Vijayā, one should act in exactly the same way. Thus, one performs everything for the sake of Jayā.

Ajitā spoke thus: "Taking the root of Ajita, one should proceed exactly as before; it accomplishes everything. Aparājitā spoke thus: "Taking the root of Aparājitā, together with its leaves, fruit, and roots—both white and black—one should proceed exactly as the caravan leader did. However, this is the distinction: it acts swiftly and quickly."
"It is accomplished. Putrañjārī, Kṛtāñjali, Sahā, Sahadevā, and the great herb (mahoṣadhī); likewise the goddess Chatrādhicchatrā and the renowned Mahākāla.
Nākulī, gandhanākulī, and likewise saṅkucitakarṇikā.
Having taken the roots of these, one should have powders of *śūrja* prepared;
by this, living beings come under one's control as soon as they are touched.
The husks of red śāli rice, saffron, and sandalwood,
combined with musk and immersed in divine water;
The knower of mantras should fashion a pill from the three metals as prescribed;
having made it the size of a seed of the *akṣa* tree, he should then place it in his mouth.
Or during a lunar eclipse, or at night, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind;
then, at dawn, having perfected the mantra, the embodied being proceeds according to his desire.
The pill always remains in his mouth as he performs the recitation;
or, assuming the form of any animal at will, he wanders everywhere across the earth.
When it is emitted, there is the same method; the intellect of recitation becomes one's own body.
Otherwise, if it remains in the mouth, it would always be of universal form.
One who has performed the recitation is especially distinguished by performing self-protection with their own mantra;
otherwise, the pill is stolen if the reciter does not perform protection.
546) All mantras, including those of all worldly kings,
are accomplished through the worship of all ritual manuals (kalpas) as spoken by everyone.
They attain success in this world through the mantras and tantras that have been proclaimed;
they wander over the entire earth, assuming various guises.
Residing in various states of existence and wombs, they take the form of dogs and crows,
as well as cats, owls, mice, frogs, and scorpions.
Crowded with all kinds of origins, bodiless yet dwelling within bodies,
they wander the entire earth, uttering the cries of all living beings.
When all beings are submissive and the welfare of all creatures arises as something dear,
and mortals always act accordingly, then one should employ those [mantras] for them.
It is not taught to others in the world, for it is honored even by the deities;
it should be known as everything in every respect, the accomplisher of all mantras.
Whatever has been spoken, and whatever other men on earth shall speak— that entire collection of ritual manuals (kalpavisara) has been declared here by the Mothers of the World.
Thus addressed, the gods, together with the Sūtrānta as the fifth,
remained silent and stood there, having bowed to the Bull among Victors.
He sat down in that most excellent assembly to hear the Dharma,
[to behold] the empowerments of the Buddhas and all the sons of the Conquerors.
Having exhorted the Great Hero, they remained silent thereafter;
then the glorious Vajradhṛk worshipped the deities.
Out of a desire to benefit those beings, he gave them his approval, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Therefore, O maidens, remain diligently within this samaya."
From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, this is the third [section] from the forty-seventh chapter-cycle:
the mudrās for the recitation rules and all the means of accomplishment pertaining to the four maidens.
The detailed exposition of the chapter on all rites concerning medicinal herbs, tantras, and mantras is hereby completed.
May there be auspiciousness.
